topics.name: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles

questions.stem: What is the 'four-foot'?
options: The walking area beside the track, measured from the outer rail
The space between the two running rails of one track
The walking route beside the outermost track
The wide gap between two pairs of tracks
questions.rationale: The four-foot is the area between the rails of a single track, named after the nominal track gauge of 4 ft 8½ in.

questions.stem: What is the 'six-foot'?
options: The space between two adjacent tracks
The space between the rails of one track
The area beyond the outermost rail
A measured clearance from a signal post
questions.rationale: The six-foot is the space between two adjacent running lines. It is not a safe place to stand when trains are running on both lines.

questions.stem: What is the 'ten-foot'?
options: The space between rails of a single track
The cess on the outside of a curve
A wider space between two pairs of running lines
The gap between the running rail and the conductor rail on DC lines
questions.rationale: On four-track railways the wider gap separating one pair of lines from the other is called the ten-foot.

questions.stem: What is the 'cess'?
options: The ballast between the two running rails
The area beside the track beyond the outermost rail
The space between two adjacent tracks
The ballast shoulder between the sleeper ends and the running rail
questions.rationale: The cess is the strip alongside the line outside the outermost rail. It is often the walking route and may provide a position of safety.

questions.stem: In Rule Book terms, being 'on or near the line' means being on the line or within what distance of a line?
options: 1.25 metres (4 feet)
2 metres (6 feet 6 inches)
5 metres (16 feet)
3 metres (10 feet)
questions.rationale: The Rule Book defines 'on or near the line' as on the line or within 3 metres (10 feet) of a line.

questions.stem: What does the abbreviation ELR stand for?
options: Emergency Line Restriction
Engineer's Line Reference
Electrified Line Route
Extended Lookout Range
questions.rationale: The ELR is a short code identifying a route section. Together with the mileage it pinpoints a location for emergencies and reports.

questions.stem: Why is the ELR and mileage important when you report an incident?
options: It lets responders find the exact location quickly
It tells the signaller which company employs you
It proves to the COSS that you are on the right shift
It shows control which train operator uses the line
questions.rationale: Precise location information speeds up the emergency response and makes sure the right lines are protected.

questions.stem: On most routes, which direction does the 'Up' line usually run?
options: Away from London on every route
Towards London or the principal destination
Away from London on every route, whatever the gradient
Towards the nearest depot
questions.rationale: By convention the Up direction is towards London or the main centre on that route, and the Down direction is away from it. Local exceptions exist.

questions.stem: What is a bi-directional line?
options: A line signalled for trains to run in either direction
A line used only by engineering trains
A line with conductor rails on both sides
A line where trains run in one direction by day and the other by night
questions.rationale: On bi-directional lines trains may approach from either end, which is one reason you must expect a train in any direction.

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the basic rule about train movements?
options: Trains only run in the direction shown in the timetable
Trains only approach in the direction shown in the timetable for that line
Trains can approach on any line, at any time, in either direction
Trains will always sound the horn before reaching you
questions.rationale: You must never assume a line is safe because of timetables, signals or direction. Always expect a train.

questions.stem: What are switches and crossings (S&C) more commonly called?
options: Catch pits
Points
Buffer stops
Check rails
questions.rationale: Switches and crossings, often called points, let trains move from one track to another.

questions.stem: Why must you never put your feet between the switch rail and the stock rail?
options: The points can move without warning and trap your foot
The rails there carry the traction supply
It stops the track circuit working
Your boot can short the track circuit and set signals to danger
questions.rationale: Points can be operated remotely by the signaller at any time. A moving switch blade can cause serious crush injuries.

questions.stem: What is a check rail?
options: A short rail fitted to check the track gauge before trains are allowed to run
A spare length of rail kept in the cess for emergency repairs
An extra rail that guides wheels through sharp curves or crossings
A rail bonded to the conductor rail to carry traction current
questions.rationale: Check rails sit inside a running rail to guide wheelsets on sharp curves and through crossings.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a fishplate?
options: To secure the rail to the sleeper
To insulate the conductor rail
To mark the boundary of a possession
To join two lengths of rail together
questions.rationale: Fishplates are bolted across rail joints to hold the rail ends in line.

questions.stem: What does CWR stand for in track engineering?
options: Continuous welded rail
Conductor wire return
Controlled working railway
Cess walking route
questions.rationale: Continuous welded rail is rail welded into long lengths. It can buckle in very hot weather and break in very cold weather.

questions.stem: Why can continuous welded rail be a hazard in very hot weather?
options: It becomes electrically live
It stops track circuits detecting trains
It can buckle as the steel expands
It makes the ballast slippery
questions.rationale: Heat causes rail to expand. If stresses are not managed the track can buckle, so report any track distortion immediately.

questions.stem: What is the main function of ballast?
options: To insulate the conductor rail from the ground
To provide a level walking surface in the four-foot
To provide a level, soft surface for staff walking along the four-foot
To hold the sleepers in place and drain water from the track
questions.rationale: Ballast spreads the load, holds sleepers in position and lets water drain away. It is an uneven surface, so take care walking on it.

questions.stem: What does a track circuit do?
options: It supplies the traction current to electric trains
It records the speed of each passing train and sends it to the driver
It detects the presence of a train by its wheels and axles
It warms the points so they do not freeze in winter
questions.rationale: A train's wheelsets short-circuit the track circuit, showing the signaller that the section is occupied and keeping signals behind it at danger.

questions.stem: What is an axle counter used for?
options: To detect trains by counting axles into and out of a section
To weigh each axle and warn the signaller when a train is overloaded
To record how many trains pass a work site
To warn track workers of an approaching train
questions.rationale: Axle counters are a train-detection method that counts axles entering and leaving a section.

questions.stem: What is a 'running line'?
options: A siding used to stable engineering trains overnight
A line permanently closed and kept only for storage
Any line within a depot or yard where trains are prepared for service
A line used for normal train movements between stations
questions.rationale: Running lines carry normal train traffic. Sidings and depot lines are not running lines and often have local instructions.

questions.stem: What is a siding?
options: The walking route that runs beside a running line
A line for stabling or loading, not for through running
A line that is signalled for running in both directions
A short section of running line that passes through a tunnel
questions.rationale: Sidings are not running lines, but vehicles still move on them, sometimes without warning. Never assume a siding is safe.

questions.stem: Which document sets out the operating rules for the GB mainline railway?
options: The Rule Book (GE/RT8000)
The Sentinel Scheme Rules
The Working Timetable
The Highway Code
questions.rationale: The Rule Book, published by RSSB as GE/RT8000, contains the national operating rules and its handbooks.

questions.stem: Who controls the movement of trains on a running line?
options: The COSS
The train driver
The site warden
The signaller
questions.rationale: The signaller controls train movements through signals and points, and is your main contact in an emergency.

questions.stem: What is a ROC on Network Rail?
options: A Rail Operating Centre that controls signalling for a large area
A Railway Occupation Certificate for track access
A Route Overhead Conductor in electrified areas
A Route Overhead Controller who switches the power for an area of OLE
questions.rationale: Rail Operating Centres are large signalling centres that are gradually replacing many local signal boxes.

questions.stem: What does PTS stand for?
options: Protected Track Section
Possession Traffic System
Primary Track Sponsor
Personal Track Safety
questions.rationale: PTS is the basic track safety competence needed to work on or near the line on Network Rail managed infrastructure.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of PTS training?
options: To qualify you to plan possessions and arrange line blockages yourself
To authorise you to operate signals
To qualify you to drive on-track plant
To help you keep yourself safe on or near the line
questions.rationale: PTS teaches the basic rules that protect you from trains, electricity and other railway hazards.

questions.stem: What is a signal post telephone (SPT) used for?
options: To call the driver of a train standing at the signal on board
To contact your employer's office
To speak directly to the signaller from the lineside
To send an automatic warning to the site
questions.rationale: SPTs connect directly to the signaller. They are a key way to report an emergency or obstruction.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a signal identification plate?
options: To show drivers the maximum permitted speed for that line
To show which electrical section the signal is fed from
To identify the signal so you can give the signaller its number
To show drivers which electrical section the signal is fed from
questions.rationale: Each signal carries a plate with its identity, which helps the signaller locate you quickly.

questions.stem: What does an AWS magnet located before a signal do?
options: It slows the train automatically whenever track workers are nearby
It detects track workers who are standing near the line
It stops every train automatically at a red signal
It gives the driver an in-cab warning about the signal ahead
questions.rationale: The Automatic Warning System gives the driver a bell or horn in the cab, depending on the aspect of the signal ahead.

questions.stem: What does TPWS stand for?
options: Track Possession and Worksite Supervision
Train Protection and Warning System
Temporary Possession Work Site
Track Patrol Walking Schedule
questions.rationale: TPWS uses track loops to apply a train's brakes if it passes a signal at danger or approaches a speed restriction too fast.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid stepping on AWS magnets and TPWS loops?
options: They carry traction current
They can be slippery and are a trip hazard
Stepping on them sets signals to danger
They give an electric shock when trains are near
questions.rationale: Lineside and four-foot equipment is a slip and trip hazard. Never step on anything you do not need to.

questions.stem: What are location cases (lineside cabinets) used for?
options: To house signalling and electrical equipment
To shelter track workers from passing trains in limited clearance
To act as a position of safety
To shelter workers in bad weather
questions.rationale: Location cases contain signalling and power equipment. They are not refuges and must not be used to shelter from trains.

questions.stem: What is cable troughing?
options: Concrete or plastic channels carrying lineside cables
A raised concrete walkway built for track workers to use as a cess path
A walking surface built for track workers
A barrier separating open and closed lines
questions.rationale: Troughing lids can be broken, loose or slippery. Do not treat troughing as a safe walkway unless you are told to.

questions.stem: What do mileposts on the lineside show?
options: The maximum line speed that applies at that location
The distance along the route from a fixed reference point
The number of minutes until the next train is due to pass that point
The number of minutes until the next train is due
questions.rationale: Mileposts and quarter-mile posts give the mileage, which with the ELR identifies your exact location.

questions.stem: Why do lines through curves and cuttings need extra care?
options: Trains must stop and sound the horn before entering a curve or cutting
Conductor rails are always present there
Sighting of approaching trains can be very limited
Trains run more slowly and quietly there
questions.rationale: Curves, cuttings, bridges and vegetation can hide trains until they are very close.

questions.stem: Which of these can make it harder to hear an approaching train?
options: Wearing orange high-visibility clothing
Wind, nearby machinery or a train on another line
Standing in the cess facing traffic
Standing in the cess and facing the direction of oncoming trains
questions.rationale: Background noise can mask a train. Never rely only on hearing to detect trains.

questions.stem: Why are modern electric trains a particular hazard to track workers?
options: They can be very quiet when approaching
They are not fitted with horns because they run in built-up areas
They only run on bi-directional lines
They never slow down for workers
questions.rationale: Electric trains can approach with little noise, especially downwind or when coasting.

questions.stem: Roughly how long can a passenger train at high speed take to stop?
options: About the length of one carriage
About the length of a platform, if the driver brakes straight away
It can stop instantly if the driver sees you
Well over a kilometre, even under emergency braking
questions.rationale: Trains cannot stop or swerve to avoid you. You must get out of the way, not expect the train to stop.

questions.stem: What is 'low adhesion' on the railway?
options: Loose ballast in the cess that makes walking difficult
Rail fastenings that have worked loose from the sleepers
Weak GSM-R radio reception in cuttings and tunnels
Slippery rails that make trains take longer to stop
questions.rationale: Leaf fall, rain and contamination reduce grip. Braking distances increase, so trains stop even later.

questions.stem: Who manages most of the GB mainline railway infrastructure?
options: The Office of Rail and Road
RSSB
The train operating companies
Network Rail
questions.rationale: Network Rail is the main infrastructure manager. Its infrastructure is often called Network Rail managed infrastructure (NRMI).

questions.stem: What is RSSB's role in the GB railway?
options: It manages industry standards, including the Rule Book
It owns and maintains the track, signals and bridges
It owns and maintains the track, signals and bridges on the network
It issues Sentinel cards and records competences
questions.rationale: RSSB (Rail Safety and Standards Board) publishes Railway Group Standards and the Rule Book.

questions.stem: What is the Office of Rail and Road (ORR)?
options: The safety and economic regulator for the railway
The company that maintains the track
The training body that sets and marks the PTS assessment papers
The body that investigates every accident
questions.rationale: ORR regulates health and safety on the railway and can enforce the law.

questions.stem: What does RAIB do?
options: It prosecutes track workers who break the Rule Book
It assesses and records Sentinel competences
It independently investigates accidents to improve safety
It sets the timetable and allocates possessions
questions.rationale: The Rail Accident Investigation Branch investigates to find causes and make recommendations. It does not assign blame.

questions.stem: What is a junction on the railway?
options: A station with more than two platforms
A place where lines meet or divide
A section of line with no signals
A place where trains change crews
questions.rationale: Junctions are complex. Trains may be routed on many paths, so it is hard to predict where a train will come from.

questions.stem: Why are junctions particularly hazardous for track workers?
options: Trains must always travel at full line speed over junctions
Trains must always travel at full line speed over junction points
Signals are switched off at junctions during engineering work
Trains can be routed over many lines and from several directions
questions.rationale: At junctions it is hard to predict which line a train will use, so you must be clear of all lines that trains may use.

questions.stem: What is a crossover?
options: A footbridge that carries staff over the railway at a station
A level crossing for road vehicles
A cable route under the track
A pair of points connecting two parallel lines
questions.rationale: Crossovers let trains move from one line to the adjacent line, so a train may appear on a line you did not expect.

questions.stem: What is a 'possession' in railway terms?
options: The ownership of a section of line
A line closed to normal traffic for engineering work
The ownership of a section of line by a train operating company
A permit to drive a road vehicle on site
questions.rationale: In a possession, normal trains are stopped, but engineering trains and on-track plant may still move.

questions.stem: What is a 'line blockage'?
options: An obstruction on the line such as a fallen tree or rubbish
A temporary speed restriction imposed after a track defect
A broken rail that has been found during a track patrol
A line closed to trains, with protecting signals kept at danger
questions.rationale: A line blockage is arranged with the signaller to stop trains entering the section where people are working.

questions.stem: What is meant by an 'open line'?
options: A line with no overhead wires
A line with no overhead wires or conductor rail fitted
A line that is not in use
A line on which trains may run
questions.rationale: Working on or near an open line is high risk because trains can approach at any time.

questions.stem: What is the 'sectional appendix'?
options: A document giving local route details such as line speeds
A list of every track worker's competences and expiry dates
The national policy on drugs and alcohol for safety roles
A register of all positions of safety on each route
questions.rationale: The sectional appendix gives route information including running lines, maximum speeds and local instructions.

questions.stem: What does a permanent speed restriction sign show drivers?
options: The safe walking speed for track workers
The walking speed allowed for staff in the cess at that point
The maximum speed allowed on that section of line
The minimum speed trains must keep
questions.rationale: Line speed matters to you because the speed decides the position of safety distance and the warning time needed.

questions.stem: Why do you need to know the maximum line speed where you are working?
options: It decides which PPE you must wear for the task
It decides the maximum length of your shift that day
It decides how far from the line a position of safety must be
It decides which organisation will be your Primary Sponsor
questions.rationale: Up to 100 mph the position of safety is at least 1.25 m from the nearest rail. Above 100 mph and up to 125 mph it is at least 2 m.

questions.stem: What is a 'whistle board' beside the line?
options: A sign telling track workers where to stand when a train approaches
A sign telling drivers to sound the train horn
A sign showing a lookout's position
A sign marking the end of a possession
questions.rationale: Whistle boards usually come before foot crossings and similar places. You must not rely on hearing the horn.

questions.stem: What is a refuge in a railway structure?
options: A recess in a tunnel, bridge or wall where you can stand clear
A hut beside the line where workers take their breaks
A cabinet that stores emergency equipment and detonators
A loop or siding where trains wait for a clear path
questions.rationale: Refuges are provided where there is limited clearance. You must know where they are before you need them.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'limited clearance'?
options: A place where the line speed has been limited for work
A site where only one worker is allowed at a time
A place without room to stand clear when a train passes
A section where the overhead wires hang lower than usual
questions.rationale: At limited clearance locations you must not be there when trains run unless a safe system of work is in place.

questions.stem: Where do you usually find signs warning of limited clearance?
options: Only inside signal boxes and electrical control rooms
Only at level crossings, where roads and the railway meet each other
At the ends of a section where there is no position of safety
Only at level crossings where roads meet the railway
questions.rationale: Signs at the ends of limited clearance areas warn you not to enter unless the safe system of work allows it.

questions.stem: Which of these places often has limited clearance?
options: Wide cess paths that are separated by fencing
Car parks and compounds beside stations
Tunnels, bridges, viaducts and narrow cuttings
Wide cess paths that are separated from the line by fencing
questions.rationale: Structures and narrow cuttings often lack room to stand clear of trains.

questions.stem: What is a level crossing?
options: A bridge that carries the railway over a road or river
A place where a road or path crosses the railway on the level
A bridge that carries the railway over a road or a river at that point
A crossover that connects two parallel running lines
questions.rationale: Level crossings bring the public close to the railway and have their own hazards, including road traffic.

questions.stem: What is an 'access point'?
options: Any gap in the lineside fence near the work
Any gap in the lineside fence that is close to where you are working
An authorised place to enter or leave the railway
A place where trains are stabled between duties
questions.rationale: Use only authorised access points. They usually have signs showing the location and local hazards.

questions.stem: What information is usually shown on signs at an access point?
options: The names of the workers booked on site that day
The location, ELR, mileage and lines at that point
The names and phone numbers of the workers booked on site that day
The Sentinel numbers of the staff on the shift
questions.rationale: Access point information helps you confirm where you are and give accurate details in an emergency.

questions.stem: What is on-track plant (OTP)?
options: Machines that work on the track, such as road-rail vehicles
Vegetation that grows in the cess beside the track
Fixed signalling equipment installed beside the line
Spare rails and sleepers stored at the lineside
questions.rationale: On-track plant can move inside a possession. Keep clear and follow the machine controller's instructions.

questions.stem: What is a road-rail vehicle (RRV)?
options: A bus used when lines are closed
A vehicle that can travel on both road and rail
A train that carries road vehicles
A vehicle allowed to cross level crossings only
questions.rationale: RRVs are common on worksites. They can move unexpectedly and have blind spots.

questions.stem: What is an 'engineering train'?
options: A passenger train that is driven by a qualified engineer
A train that runs to check the timing of the signals
A train that carries materials or machines for engineering work
Any train that runs on the line after midnight
questions.rationale: Engineering trains can move inside possessions, so a closed line is not free of moving vehicles.

questions.stem: What is a train's 'shoe gear'?
options: The brake blocks that press on the wheel treads
Equipment that collects current from a conductor rail
The brake blocks and rigging that press on the wheel treads
The device that sounds the horn on the cab roof
questions.rationale: Shoe gear on DC electric trains is live and must be treated as dangerous.

questions.stem: What is a pantograph?
options: A hand tool used by staff to measure the track gauge
The roof arm that collects current from the overhead wires
A warning horn fitted to lineside warning equipment
A small trolley used for moving rails along the track
questions.rationale: On AC electrified lines trains collect current through a pantograph touching the contact wire.

questions.stem: What voltage is the GB mainline overhead line equipment (OLE) usually energised at?
options: 750 volts DC, the same as the third rail
25,000 volts AC
230 volts AC
1,500 volts AC
questions.rationale: Most GB mainline overhead electrification is 25 kV AC. Contact can kill, and current can jump a gap.

questions.stem: What voltage is the third-rail system in the south of England usually energised at?
options: 25,000 volts AC
110 volts AC
Up to 750 volts DC
25,000 volts AC, the same as the overhead line
questions.rationale: Conductor rail systems in southern England operate at up to 750 V DC, which is easily enough to kill.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a reason to keep off the line when you do not need to be there?
options: Being on the line gives you a better view of trains
Trains can approach on any line at any time
The surface is uneven and slippery in places
Points can move suddenly without any warning
questions.rationale: Only go on or near the line when your work needs it and a safe system of work is in place.

questions.stem: What is a buffer stop?
options: A barrier between two adjacent lines
A structure at the end of a line to stop vehicles
A signal that is always at danger at the end of a running line
A device that slows trains on curves
questions.rationale: Buffer stops are found at the end of sidings and terminal platforms.

questions.stem: What is a catch point (trap point)?
options: A place where staff collect their tools at the end of a shift
A point where workers are checked in by the COSS
Points that derail unwanted vehicles to protect a main line
A rail joint designed to catch debris falling from trains
questions.rationale: Catch and trap points stop runaway or unauthorised vehicles reaching a running line.

questions.stem: Why must you take care near point machines and point rodding?
options: They give off fumes that can make you drowsy when you are close
They can move suddenly and crush or trap you
They make trains brake suddenly
They are always electrically live at 25 kV
questions.rationale: Point equipment can operate remotely at any time. Keep hands and feet away.

questions.stem: What are point heaters used for?
options: To warm track workers' huts
To dry the ballast after rain
To warm the welfare cabins for staff working near points
To stop points freezing in cold weather
questions.rationale: Point heating equipment can be electrically live and hot. Do not touch it.

questions.stem: What is a 'cutting' on the railway?
options: A place where new rails are cut to length before fitting
A place where the line runs below the surrounding ground
A section where lineside vegetation has been cleared
A short stretch of line running between two stations
questions.rationale: Cuttings can have steep sides, limited clearance, poor sighting and risk of landslips.

questions.stem: What is an 'embankment'?
options: A wall built along the boundary to stop trespassers
A raised bank of earth carrying the railway above the ground
A refuge cut into the side of a deep cutting
A raised platform edge built so passengers can board trains more easily
questions.rationale: Embankments have steep slopes and can be slippery. Use proper access routes.

questions.stem: What is a viaduct?
options: A long bridge carrying the railway over a valley or obstacle
A tunnel that carries the railway through a hill
A long road bridge that carries traffic over the top of the railway line
A drainage culvert that runs under the track
questions.rationale: Viaducts often have limited clearance. RAIB investigated near misses where groups crossed viaducts at track level.

questions.stem: What is a 'TSR' on the railway?
options: A track safety report
A temporary speed restriction
A train stop request
A third-rail section reference
questions.rationale: Temporary speed restrictions are put in place for reasons such as track defects or work. Trains may still be fast nearby.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about trains and stopping is correct?
options: A driver will always stop if you wave
Trains slow down near any work site
A driver who sees you may be unable to stop in time
Trains always stop at red signals before reaching you
questions.rationale: Trains are heavy and need long distances to stop. Your safety depends on being in a position of safety in time.

questions.stem: What is the 'Rule Book handbook' that covers general duties and track safety for track workers?
options: Handbook 7
Handbook 16
Handbook 20
Handbook 1
questions.rationale: Handbook 1 covers general duties and track safety for track workers. Other handbooks cover COSS duties, electrified lines and more.

questions.stem: What kind of document is 'Handbook 16' in the Rule Book?
options: Rules for lookouts and site wardens working on open lines
Rules for possessions and worksites
Rules for working on or near AC electrified lines
Rules for train drivers at level crossings
questions.rationale: Handbook 16 covers AC electrified lines. Conductor rail (DC) lines are covered separately.

questions.stem: Which statement about sidings and depots is correct?
options: Trains never move in depots while staff are present
Local instructions may apply and vehicles can move without warning
Trains never move in depots or sidings while any staff are present there
You may walk anywhere in sidings because speeds are low
questions.rationale: Depots and sidings often have their own local rules. Always find out the local arrangements before you go there.

questions.stem: Which is the safest way to think about a line that looks disused or rusty?
options: Treat it as open, because trains could still use it
Treat it as closed, because trains clearly do not run
Walk along it, because it is a quiet route
Use it as a position of safety
questions.rationale: Rusty rails do not prove a line is closed. Only the safe system of work tells you a line is blocked.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'adjacent line'?
options: The line furthest from your work
A line that has been closed permanently
A line next to the one you are working on or near
A line that has been closed to all traffic for engineering work
questions.rationale: Trains on adjacent lines can be a hazard even when your own line is blocked.

questions.stem: Why is the space between adjacent lines dangerous when trains pass on both?
options: There may not be enough room to stand clear of both trains
The six-foot always carries a conductor rail on electrified routes
It is a restricted area for signallers only
It contains the main signal cables
questions.rationale: Never use the six-foot as a position of safety unless your briefing confirms it is safe.

questions.stem: What does the term 'foul of the line' mean?
options: Dropping litter or waste materials on the railway
Dropping litter or waste materials anywhere on railway property
Reporting a fault on the line to the signaller
Close enough that a train could strike you or your equipment
questions.rationale: Anything foul of the line, including tools and materials, can be struck by a train.

questions.stem: What is a 'neutral section' on OLE?
options: A short unpowered section between different electrical supplies
A safe area under the wires where workers can stand
A section of overhead line that is permanently safe for workers to touch
A part of the OLE that is never energised at any time
questions.rationale: Neutral sections separate electrical feeds. Never assume any part of OLE is dead unless you are told it is isolated and earthed.

questions.stem: What is a 'traction return' or bond cable?
options: A cable that connects signal post telephones to the signaller
A cable that holds the contact wire at the correct height
A steel cable used to lift rails onto wagons
A cable that carries return current between rails or structures
questions.rationale: Bonds and traction return cables carry current. Never disconnect or damage them.

questions.stem: Who publishes the national Rule Book that you are expected to follow?
options: The Department for Transport
The Sentinel scheme
RSSB
Your Primary Sponsor
questions.rationale: RSSB publishes the Rule Book on behalf of the industry. Network Rail standards and local instructions also apply.

questions.stem: What does NRMI stand for?
options: National Railway Maintenance Index
Network Rail managed infrastructure
Network Route Mileage Information
National Railway Maintenance and Inspection
questions.rationale: PTS and Sentinel rules apply to people working on Network Rail managed infrastructure.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign that a train may be approaching?
options: The weather suddenly becoming colder and windier
Your Sentinel card reader beeping on its own
Rails 'singing', a signal changing, or a distant horn
A level crossing barrier rising after a train
questions.rationale: Be alert to all clues, but never rely on them. A lookout or safe system must give you warning in time.

questions.stem: What is a 'train' in Rule Book terms?
options: Any movement on a line, including engineering trains and plant
Only passenger services that run to the published public timetable each day
Only vehicles with more than two carriages coupled
Only movements that are shown in the working timetable
questions.rationale: The Rule Book uses a wide definition. Any vehicle movement on the line can kill you.

questions.stem: Why might a second train be especially dangerous?
options: It can arrive on another line just after the first train passes
Second trains are always driven faster to make up lost time
Second trains never sound the horn
Second trains always run in the wrong direction
questions.rationale: After a train passes, stay in your position of safety until you are told it is safe. Another train may be hidden by the first.

questions.stem: What is the standard track gauge on the GB mainline railway?
options: 1,600 mm (5 ft 3 in), as used across the GB network
1,600 mm (5 ft 3 in)
1,435 mm (4 ft 8½ in)
1,250 mm (4 ft 1 in)
questions.rationale: Standard gauge is 1,435 mm. The 'four-foot' takes its name from this measurement.

questions.stem: What is a sleeper?
options: A rail that is only used during night-time working
A beam laid across the track that supports the rails
A worker who is booked on a regular night shift
A rail that is only used during night-time engineering work
questions.rationale: Sleepers may be concrete, timber or steel. They can be slippery, especially timber sleepers when wet.

questions.stem: Why are wooden sleepers a particular slip hazard?
options: They are always electrically live
They become very slippery when wet or icy
They move slightly under your weight when trains approach
They are treated with oil every day
questions.rationale: Never step on sleepers, rails or equipment when you can avoid it, especially in wet or icy conditions.

questions.stem: What holds bullhead rail in place on older track?
options: Fishplates bolted to the sleepers
Cast chairs and wooden or steel keys
Pandrol clips on concrete slabs
Spring clips fixed straight into concrete sleepers
questions.rationale: Bullhead rail sits in chairs held by keys. Modern flat-bottom rail usually uses spring clips.

questions.stem: What is a 'Pandrol clip'?
options: A spring fastening that holds flat-bottom rail to the sleeper
A clip used to attach a lookout's horn to a belt
A clip that short-circuits a track circuit in an emergency
A clamp that holds the overhead contact wire in place
questions.rationale: Spring clips are a common rail fastening. Do not confuse them with track circuit operating clips.

questions.stem: What is an insulated rail joint (IRJ)?
options: A joint that electrically separates track circuit sections
A joint that is used only on conductor rail systems
A joint that is welded only during hot weather
A protective cover fitted over the head of the rail
questions.rationale: Insulated joints define track circuit boundaries. Do not damage them or bridge across them with metal.

questions.stem: Why must you never lay metal objects across both running rails?
options: It will charge both rails with traction current
It will stop all trains automatically in that section
It is the approved way of marking the end of a worksite
It can operate a track circuit and affect the signals
questions.rationale: Bridging the rails can interfere with train detection and the signalling. Only trained people use track circuit operating clips.

questions.stem: What is the 'cess path' or walking route?
options: A shortcut across the tracks between two neighbouring access points
A shortcut across the tracks between two access points
A defined route beside the line for walking to and from work
A route kept clear for the exclusive use of trains
questions.rationale: Walking routes are designed to keep you clear of trains, though some still need a position of safety when a train approaches.

questions.stem: What is a 'lineside' location?
options: Any area just outside the railway boundary fence
Any area just outside the railway boundary fence, on public land
An area alongside the railway, inside the boundary fence
The edge of a platform where passengers wait
questions.rationale: Lineside means the area between the track and the boundary fence. You still need to know where trains can reach.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a boundary fence along the railway?
options: To keep the public and animals off the railway
To mark the position of safety
To support overhead line equipment
To separate open and closed lines inside a possession
questions.rationale: Damaged fences let trespassers and animals onto the line. Report fence damage.

questions.stem: What is a 'catch pit' on the railway?
options: A pit where workers wait for trains to pass
A chamber in the drainage system
A pit under the track in depots
A hole for storing detonators
questions.rationale: Catch pits, manholes and drains can be hidden by vegetation and are trip and fall hazards.

questions.stem: Why can drainage covers and manholes in the cess be dangerous?
options: They may be missing, broken or hidden by vegetation
They are always connected to the traction supply
They make approaching trains slow down automatically
They are reserved for use by signal engineers only
questions.rationale: Watch where you walk. Report missing or broken covers.

questions.stem: What is a 'station limit' area of the railway?
options: The area around a station where track safety rules do not apply
A zone where PTS rules do not apply
The area where passengers can walk on track
Parts of the line around stations, including platforms
questions.rationale: Stations have many people, platform edges and limited clearance under canopies and bridges.

questions.stem: What is the 'platform edge' hazard for track workers?
options: The platform edge is energised to stop people falling
There is often no room to stand between a platform and a train
The platform edge is energised to stop passengers falling onto the track
Trains always stop before reaching the platform end
questions.rationale: Platforms often create limited clearance on the platform side of the line.

questions.stem: What is the 'down side' of a line?
options: The side of the railway that is lower down a slope or embankment
The side with no positions of safety
The side opposite the signal box
The side of the railway next to the Down line
questions.rationale: Up side and down side describe locations in relation to the Up and Down lines.

questions.stem: What is a 'loop' line?
options: A circular line that runs right around a city centre
A short line where trains reverse at the end of a route
A line that leaves and rejoins a main line so trains can wait
A siding with a turntable for turning locomotives
questions.rationale: Trains can enter or leave loops through points, so expect movements from unexpected directions.

questions.stem: What does 'line speed' mean?
options: The maximum permitted speed for trains on that line
The average speed of trains on that line
The walking speed allowed in the cess
The average speed of all trains using that line in a day
questions.rationale: Line speed determines the position of safety distance and the warning time you need.

questions.stem: Up to what maximum line speed may a position of safety be 1.25 metres from the nearest rail?
options: 100 mph
75 mph
90 mph
125 mph
questions.rationale: Up to 100 mph, at least 1.25 m (4 ft). Above 100 mph and up to 125 mph, at least 2 m (6 ft 6 in).

questions.stem: Why do positions of safety need to be further from faster lines?
options: Faster trains create stronger air turbulence and more risk
Faster trains are built wider than slower trains
Faster lines always have conductor rails fitted
Drivers of faster trains sound their horns much later
questions.rationale: Air pressure and turbulence from fast trains can knock you off balance.

questions.stem: What is 'slipstream' (air turbulence) from a passing train?
options: Steam released from a train's brakes as it slows down
Moving air that can pull or push people and objects
Water sprayed from the train's wheels
Electrical arcing from the pantograph
questions.rationale: Slipstream can drag loose clothing and equipment towards the train. Secure items and stand firm.

questions.stem: What can a passing train's slipstream do to loose items left near the line?
options: Nothing, if they are on the ballast
Only move them if they are metal
Blow or suck them into the train's path
Nothing, as long as they are lying flat on the ballast
questions.rationale: Light items such as bags, sheets and tools can be moved by slipstream. Secure or remove them.

questions.stem: What does 'GSM-R' refer to?
options: A type of rail fastening used on high-speed lines
A satellite positioning system that tells lookouts where each train is located
A grade of high-visibility clothing for night work
The railway's dedicated radio system for drivers and signallers
questions.rationale: GSM-R lets signallers and drivers talk directly, and supports emergency calls.

questions.stem: What is an 'overbridge'?
options: A bridge that carries the railway over a road
A footbridge inside a station only
A bridge that carries something over the railway
A bridge that carries the railway over a road or river
questions.rationale: Overbridges can create limited clearance under their spans and reduce sighting.

questions.stem: What is an 'underbridge'?
options: A bridge that carries a road over the railway
A bridge that carries the railway over something
A bridge that carries a road or footpath over the railway
A cable route under the track
questions.rationale: Underbridges such as viaducts may have no cess or refuges.

questions.stem: Why can vegetation be a hazard to track workers?
options: It makes trains run more slowly through the area
It can hide trains, block walking routes and hide trip hazards
It is only a fire risk in winter, when dry leaves gather in the cess and drains
It completely blocks GSM-R radio signals to drivers
questions.rationale: Overgrown vegetation reduces sighting and can block positions of safety. Report it.

questions.stem: What does a 'yellow and black' striped sign on structures often indicate?
options: A hazard such as limited clearance or an obstruction
A safe place to stand when trains are passing
A safe place to stand when trains are passing on the nearest line
The location of the nearest first aid point
questions.rationale: Warning colours highlight hazards. Always read and follow lineside signs.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about trains on tracks next to each other is true?
options: Two trains never pass at the same place
Trains on adjacent lines always run in the same direction
A train on one line can hide a train on the next line
If one train passes, the line is then safe
questions.rationale: The first train can block your view and drown out the sound of a second train.

questions.stem: What is a 'possession limit board'?
options: A notice listing the workers in a group
A sign showing the speed limit
A board showing the position of safety
A board marking the end of a possession
questions.rationale: Possession limit boards, often with detonators, mark where the protected area ends.

questions.stem: What is a 'worksite' inside a possession?
options: The car park or compound used by the work group
A defined area of work within a possession, run by an ES
The welfare cabin and car park set up near the access point for the work group
Any part of an open line where work is planned
questions.rationale: Within a possession there may be several worksites, each with its own limits and controls.

questions.stem: What does 'line closed' on its own tell you about vehicle movements?
options: Trains may still run on it at full line speed until it reopens
Trains may still run on it at full line speed
Only freight trains may run on it until it reopens
Engineering trains and on-track plant may still move
questions.rationale: Even on a blocked line, expect authorised movements. Follow your briefing.

questions.stem: What does the term 'running rail' mean?
options: The live rail that supplies current on DC lines
The check rail through crossings
A spare rail stored in the cess
The rails that train wheels run on
questions.rationale: Running rails carry the train. Conductor rails supply power on DC lines.

questions.stem: What is a 'gradient post'?
options: A post that marks where the position of safety is
A lineside sign showing a change in the slope of the line
A post that holds the overhead contact wire
A post marking where the position of safety begins on a long walking route
questions.rationale: Gradient posts show slopes. On falling gradients trains may take longer to stop.

questions.stem: Why do falling gradients matter to track workers?
options: Trains always stop at the bottom of slopes
There are no signals on gradients
Positions of safety are not needed on gradients
Trains may take longer to stop going downhill
questions.rationale: Gradients and rail conditions affect stopping distances. Never rely on a train being able to stop.

questions.stem: What is a 'fixed' or 'permanent' structure in railway terms?
options: Infrastructure such as bridges, tunnels, walls and platforms
Any train or engineering vehicle that is parked on a siding for the night
A temporary barrier put up for engineering work
A worker who stays in one place during a shift
questions.rationale: Structures near the track often reduce the space available to stand clear of trains.

questions.stem: What is the danger of standing between a structure and a passing train?
options: You may be crushed or struck if there is not enough room
You will trigger the train's AWS equipment
You will trigger the train's AWS equipment and stop the train
You will block the signaller's view of the line
questions.rationale: Only stand in a recognised position of safety or refuge.

questions.stem: What is a 'tunnel' hazard that does not exist in open country?
options: Trains slow to walking pace in all tunnels, so you have more time
Trains slow to walking pace inside all tunnels
Tunnels are always electrically isolated for work
Echoes and darkness make trains hard to see and locate
questions.rationale: In tunnels, darkness, noise and limited clearance make train detection harder.

questions.stem: Why is a train sometimes heard from the 'wrong' direction in a cutting or tunnel?
options: Trains in cuttings are signalled to reverse a short way
Wind always blows towards the train
Sound echoes off walls and can mislead you
Signals redirect the sound
questions.rationale: Never use sound alone to judge where a train is coming from.

questions.stem: What is 'the railway boundary'?
options: The outermost running rail on a multi-track line
The furthest limit of an engineering possession
The outermost running rail on a line with more than two tracks
The edge of railway land, usually marked by a fence or wall
questions.rationale: Inside the boundary you are on railway property and railway rules apply.

questions.stem: What does 'trespass' mean on the railway?
options: Being on railway land without authority
Crossing a line at a level crossing
Walking in the cess with a COSS
Working inside a possession without a COSS briefing
questions.rationale: Trespass is dangerous and illegal. Report trespassers to the signaller or the British Transport Police.

questions.stem: Who polices the railway in Great Britain?
options: British Transport Police
Network Rail Security Service
The Office of Rail and Road
RAIB
questions.rationale: British Transport Police deal with crime, trespass and many incidents on the railway.

questions.stem: What is a 'rail head'?
options: The leading end of a train as seen by track workers
The person in charge of a site
The top part of the rail that wheels run on
The start of a possession
questions.rationale: The rail head is often polished and slippery. Avoid stepping on rails.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid stepping on the rail head?
options: It is smooth and can be very slippery
It is live with traction current
It sends an alert to the signaller
It sends a signal to the driver that someone is on the track
questions.rationale: Slips onto the line can put you in the path of a train.

questions.stem: What is the 'Hazard Directory' or similar local information used for?
options: To list the names and roles of track workers
To record train delays caused by engineering
To record known hazards at locations along the route
To list the names, roles and competences of the track workers on site
questions.rationale: Planners and COSSs use hazard information to plan safe systems of work.

questions.stem: Which statement about electrified railways is true?
options: Electrification equipment must be treated as live at all times
Equipment is only live when a train is close by
Equipment is switched off every night for work
Equipment is switched off every night so maintenance can be carried out
questions.rationale: Unless you have been told it is isolated (and earthed for OLE), treat it as live.

questions.stem: What does DCCR mean in PTS training?
options: Direct contact cable route
DC conductor rail
Dual control crossing rule
Danger cess clearance requirement
questions.rationale: PTS courses may include AC (overhead) and DCCR (third rail) modules depending on where you will work.

questions.stem: What is the 'fourth rail' system?
options: A DC system with a separate rail for the return current
A spare running rail kept for use in emergencies
A spare running rail laid beside the track for use in emergencies
A rail that carries signalling data to trains
questions.rationale: Some systems, such as London Underground, use a fourth rail. Both conductor rails can be live.

questions.stem: Which of these must be treated as able to move at any time?
options: Only trains shown in the timetable
Only trains on running lines
Only trains on running lines that appear in the timetable
Points, trains, on-track plant and hand trolleys
questions.rationale: Assume anything on the track can move. Your briefing explains the hazards on your site.

questions.stem: Why are night shifts riskier for track workers?
options: More trains run at night than during the day
Line speeds are raised at night when there are fewer trains
Line speeds are raised during the night
Visibility is lower and fatigue is more likely
questions.rationale: Darkness, fatigue and cold all add risk. Lighting and fatigue controls are important.

questions.stem: What is a 'hand trolley' on the railway?
options: A trolley used to sell food and drink on trains
A small unpowered trolley for moving materials on the rails
A device pushed along to test track circuits
A device pushed along the rails by hand to test the track circuits
questions.rationale: Trolleys can run away on gradients. They must be controlled and protected.

questions.stem: Why do you need to understand track layout before going on site?
options: So you can tell approaching drivers which route to take
So you can choose your own safe system of work on site without needing a COSS
So you can skip signing the briefing if you know the area
So you know which lines are open, which are blocked and where to go
questions.rationale: RAIB has found that poor information about track layout has led workers onto the wrong lines.

questions.stem: What is the danger of confusing line names on site?
options: You may go onto an open line thinking it is blocked
You may wear the wrong type of PPE for that line
You may report to the wrong Primary Sponsor
You may be paid at the wrong rate for the shift
questions.rationale: Always confirm which lines are blocked and which are open before going on or near the line.

questions.stem: What is an 'Engineering Supervisor' (ES)?
options: The signaller's assistant who records each train as it passes
The person who designs track
The train driver of an engineering train
The person who manages a worksite within a possession
questions.rationale: The ES controls access to the worksite and the movement of trains and plant within it.

questions.stem: What is a PICOP?
options: Person in Charge of Plant
Person in Charge of the Possession
Primary Inspector of Conductor Power
Possession Information Control Point
questions.rationale: The PICOP arranges and manages the possession with the signaller.

questions.stem: What is a COSS?
options: Chief Officer of Safety Standards
Controller of Site Safety
Coordinator of Signal Systems
Conductor rail Operations Safety Supervisor
questions.rationale: A COSS sets up and manages the safe system of work for a group working on or near the line.

questions.stem: What is the role of a site warden?
options: To watch for trains and sound a horn when one approaches
To check everyone's Sentinel card at the access gate
To warn anyone about to leave the safe area towards an open line
To watch for approaching trains and sound a horn so the group can get clear
questions.rationale: Site wardens are used in separated working to stop people straying towards open lines.

questions.stem: In railway terms, what is a 'lookout'?
options: A person who watches for trains and warns the group in time
A person who guards tools and materials against theft
A person who guards tools and materials against theft during a shift
A camera fitted to a signal to watch the line
questions.rationale: Lookout working is now heavily restricted because it depends on human detection of trains.

questions.stem: What does IWA stand for in track safety?
options: Independent Warning Arrangement
Individual Working Alone
Isolated Working Area
Initial Worker Assessment
questions.rationale: IWA is a separate competence. A PTS holder cannot work alone on or near the line unless qualified and authorised.

questions.stem: What is a 'Track Visitor Permit' for?
options: To allow a PTS holder to work on the line alone
To let someone without PTS go near the line under escort
To let members of the public walk along the line
To allow a PTS holder to work on or near the line alone
questions.rationale: Track visitors must be accompanied and supervised by a competent person.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of 'Network Rail Close Call'?
options: A system for reporting near misses and unsafe conditions
A direct phone line to the signaller in an emergency
A warning given by a lookout as a train approaches
A type of emergency hand signal shown to drivers
questions.rationale: Reporting close calls helps fix hazards before they cause harm.

questions.stem: What is CIRAS?
options: The national register of PTS holders and their cards
A confidential reporting service for safety concerns
A laboratory that carries out drugs and alcohol tests
The computer system used to plan possessions
questions.rationale: CIRAS lets people raise safety concerns confidentially if they do not feel able to report through normal routes.

questions.stem: Which document should tell you the specific hazards for your work location?
options: The national timetable for the route
The details stored on your Sentinel card
The national timetable for passenger and freight trains on the route
The safe work pack or briefing for that work
questions.rationale: Your COSS or person in charge briefs you from the planned safe system of work.

questions.stem: What does 'authorised' mean when talking about access to the line?
options: You are carrying a PTS card and wearing correct PPE
You have permission and a safe system of work for the task
You have seen other people working on that track
You are carrying a PTS card and wearing the correct PPE for the task
questions.rationale: Holding PTS alone does not give you the right to go on the line. You also need a reason, permission and a safe system.

questions.stem: What is a 'stock rail' in a set of points?
options: A spare rail kept in stock at the depot for repairs
The fixed rail that a switch blade rests against
The movable blade that guides wheels onto the new route
A short rail that carries signal cables under the track
questions.rationale: Switch blades move against the fixed stock rails to set the route.

questions.stem: What is the 'crossing nose' (frog) in a set of points?
options: The front end of a train as it approaches the points
Where two rails cross so wheels can pass
A signal mounted on a post beside the points
A drain built where two tracks meet each other
questions.rationale: The crossing allows wheel flanges to pass through where rails intersect.

questions.stem: What does 'S&C' stand for?
options: Signals and cables
Sleepers and chairs
Switches and crossings
Safety and compliance
questions.rationale: S&C is the engineering term for points and crossings.

questions.stem: What is 'plain line' track?
options: Track that has no signals of any kind
Track that is not electrified
Track without switches or crossings
Track used only by freight trains
questions.rationale: Plain line is ordinary track between areas of S&C.

questions.stem: What is a 'point machine'?
options: A machine that tamps ballast under the points
A ticket machine at a station
Equipment that moves the switch blades
A device that counts axles at a junction
questions.rationale: Point machines can operate remotely without warning.

questions.stem: What is 'cant' on a curve?
options: The outer rail is raised above the inner rail
The rails are laid closer together than normal
The sleepers are spaced further apart than normal
The track is laid on a slope up a hill
questions.rationale: Cant helps trains go round curves. It can affect footing near the track.

questions.stem: What is a 'tamper' in track engineering?
options: A device that stops tampering with signals
A tool used to cut rails to length
A worker who inspects tunnels
A machine that packs ballast under sleepers
questions.rationale: Tampers are on-track plant used in possessions.

questions.stem: What is a 'ballast regulator'?
options: A machine that shapes and spreads ballast
A person who orders ballast for depots
A sign showing the type of ballast used
A valve that controls water in drains
questions.rationale: Regulators and other machines move within worksites.

questions.stem: What does 'OTM' stand for in track engineering?
options: On-track machine
Overhead traction maintenance
Open track monitoring
Operational train manager
questions.rationale: OTMs include tampers and regulators that run on rails.

questions.stem: What is a 'worksite marker board'?
options: A board used to record work completed
A board showing the limit of a worksite
A board where workers sign in and out
A board showing the train timetable
questions.rationale: Worksites within a possession are marked so their limits are clear.

questions.stem: What is a signal box?
options: A metal cabinet beside the track holding cables
A metal box beside the track that holds spare signal lamps and fuses for repairs
A booth at a station where tickets are checked
A building from which signals and points are controlled
questions.rationale: Many signal boxes are being replaced by Rail Operating Centres.

questions.stem: What is an 'automatic' signal?
options: A signal that never shows a red aspect to drivers
A signal worked by passing trains, not a signaller
A signal operated by a lookout's button on site
A signal that switches off automatically at night
questions.rationale: Automatic signals return to danger as trains pass.

questions.stem: What is a 'controlled' signal?
options: A signal used only in emergencies
A signal operated by a signaller
A signal that controls road traffic
A signal fitted with a camera
questions.rationale: Controlled signals are set by the signaller.

questions.stem: What does a 'banner repeater' signal do?
options: Displays a message to passengers on platforms
Repeats the train horn for track workers
Gives advance information about the next signal
Shows the line speed for engineering trains
questions.rationale: Banner repeaters help drivers when a signal's view is restricted.

questions.stem: What is a 'ground position light' signal used for?
options: Lighting the ground for track workers at night
Controlling shunting moves at low speed
Marking the edge of the cess on curves
Showing drivers where to stop at a platform
questions.rationale: These signals control movements in yards and at junctions.

questions.stem: Which direction is 'Up' on a route where it is not towards London?
options: As defined for that route in the sectional appendix
Always north, whatever the route
Always towards the sea or the nearest coastline
Always the direction with more trains
questions.rationale: The direction is defined locally; check the route information.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'trap point'?
options: To catch rubbish blown onto the track
To derail runaway vehicles before they reach a running line
To collect litter and debris that blows onto the running line
To trap trespassers inside a fenced area
questions.rationale: Trap points protect running lines from unauthorised movements.

questions.stem: What is a 'run-round loop'?
options: A walking route around a depot for staff
A loop that lets a locomotive move to the other end of its train
A circular test track used for new trains
A circular walking route that staff use to reach the far platforms
questions.rationale: Movements in loops can come from unexpected directions.

questions.stem: What is a 'headshunt'?
options: The front cab of a locomotive
A hand signal shown with the head
A short siding used for shunting
A safety helmet used in depots
questions.rationale: Shunting areas have frequent, low-speed movements.

questions.stem: What is an 'Up Fast' line?
options: The faster of two Up lines on a multi-track route
Any line where trains exceed 100 mph
A line used only by express trains in the morning
A line used by trains travelling uphill
questions.rationale: Line names identify which track is which.

questions.stem: Why do multi-track routes name lines such as 'Up Slow' and 'Down Fast'?
options: So passengers know which trains are delayed
So signallers can charge different fees
So everyone can identify each line clearly
So track workers can choose the quietest line
questions.rationale: Clear line names avoid dangerous confusion.

questions.stem: What is a 'reversible' line?
options: A line that can be removed and relaid quickly
A line where trains reverse into a station
A line used only when another line is closed
A line signalled for use in either direction
questions.rationale: On reversible lines trains can come from either end.

questions.stem: What is 'single line' working?
options: Only one train allowed on the route per day
Trains in both directions using one line
Work carried out by a single person
A line with only one rail
questions.rationale: Single line working can mean trains come from an unexpected direction.

questions.stem: What are 'sleeper ends'?
options: The last sleepers before a buffer stop
The ends of the sleepers, often near the cess
The time when a night shift finishes
Broken sleepers stacked for disposal
questions.rationale: Sleeper ends are often within reach of trains.

questions.stem: What is 'track geometry'?
options: The shape and alignment of the track
The pattern of sleepers in a crossover
The study of train timetables
The layout of the welfare cabin
questions.rationale: Faults in geometry can affect train safety.

questions.stem: What is a 'speed board' or 'speed sign'?
options: A board where track workers record their walking speed
A lineside sign showing a permitted speed
A display at a station showing train arrival times
A sign telling lookouts how fast to react
questions.rationale: Line speed affects position of safety distances.

questions.stem: What is a 'warning board' for a temporary speed restriction?
options: A board warning workers to stand clear
A board marking the end of a possession
A sign telling drivers a restriction is ahead
A board telling drivers to sound the horn
questions.rationale: Temporary restrictions are often linked to track defects or work.

questions.stem: What is the 'outside rail' on a curve?
options: The rail nearest the cess on straight track
A spare rail kept outside the boundary
The rail on the outer side of the curve
The conductor rail on DC lines
questions.rationale: On curves, the outside rail is usually higher.

questions.stem: Why is the inside of a curve often worse for sighting trains?
options: Trains are lower on the inside of curves
Structures and cuttings can block the view
Trains lean away from the inside of curves
The inside rail is always electrified
questions.rationale: Sighting depends on the geography.

questions.stem: What does 'fouling point' mean at a junction?
options: Where a vehicle on one line could be hit by one on another
Where litter collects in the points
Where drivers must stop for workers
The place where rubbish and leaves collect in the switch blades
questions.rationale: Vehicles beyond the fouling point may be struck.

questions.stem: What is a 'clearance' in railway terms?
options: Permission to leave the site early
The space between trains and nearby objects or people
The removal of vegetation from the cess
The time allowed between two trains on the same line
questions.rationale: Limited clearance means not enough room to stand clear.

questions.stem: What is a 'structure gauge'?
options: A tool for measuring bridge heights
A record of bridge inspections kept by engineers
A list of all station buildings
The space kept clear of structures for trains
questions.rationale: Anything inside the gauge can be struck by trains.

questions.stem: What is 'kinematic envelope' in simple terms?
options: The size of a train when stationary
The envelope used to post rail tickets
The area where workers take breaks
The space a moving train can occupy
questions.rationale: Moving trains sway and need more room than their size.

questions.stem: Why might a train sway towards a person standing near the track?
options: Drivers steer trains towards people
Trains are drawn towards hi-vis clothing
Trains move sideways on curves and uneven track
The wind always blows trains sideways
questions.rationale: Do not stand close to passing trains.

questions.stem: What is a 'cess drain'?
options: A gap in the fence for walking through
A cable route under the four-foot
A path between two platforms
A drain beside the track carrying water away
questions.rationale: Drains and catch pits can be hidden trip hazards.

questions.stem: What is a 'culvert'?
options: A wall supporting a cutting
A retaining wall that holds back a cutting slope
A channel or pipe carrying water under the railway
A sleeper made of steel
questions.rationale: Culverts can be hazards for falls and flooding.

questions.stem: What is a 'retaining wall' beside the railway?
options: A wall that stops trains leaving the rails
A wall around a signal box
A wall built to keep trespassers in
A wall holding back earth beside the track
questions.rationale: Retaining walls can create limited clearance.

questions.stem: What is a 'parapet' on a railway bridge?
options: The deck that carries the track
The arch that supports the bridge from below
The pier standing in the river
The low wall along the edge of the bridge
questions.rationale: At Maesyfelin bridge, workers jumped onto the parapet to escape a train.

questions.stem: What is a 'portal' of a tunnel?
options: A refuge cut into the tunnel wall
A ventilation shaft above the tunnel
A door for staff inside the tunnel
The entrance or exit of the tunnel
questions.rationale: Tunnel portals often mark the start of limited clearance.

questions.stem: What is a 'ventilation shaft' in a railway tunnel?
options: A pipe that carries drainage water
A cable route for signalling
A vertical opening that lets air in and out
A refuge built into the tunnel for track workers
questions.rationale: Shafts can affect air and noise in tunnels.

questions.stem: What is a 'cutting slope' hazard after heavy rain?
options: Rails becoming electrified
Trains running faster
Sleepers floating away
Landslips onto the track
questions.rationale: Earthworks can fail in wet weather.

questions.stem: What is an 'earthwork' on the railway?
options: A cutting, embankment or similar engineered slope
Soil left over from track work
A garden next to a station
Spoil and soil left beside the track after renewals
questions.rationale: Earthworks need monitoring for movement.

questions.stem: What is a 'mile and chain' location?
options: A location where chains are used to secure trains
A distance measured with a chain that is used only on freight routes
A measurement of track gauge used on curves
A position given in miles and chains from a reference point
questions.rationale: A chain is 22 yards; 80 chains make a mile.

questions.stem: How many chains are in a mile?
questions.rationale: Railway mileages are often given in miles and chains.

questions.stem: How long is a chain in railway measurement?
options: 22 yards (about 20 metres)
100 metres
100 metres, the same as a hectometre
1 mile
questions.rationale: Chains are still used in railway location references.

questions.stem: Why are railway distances still given in miles and chains?
options: Because metric units are not allowed on the railway
Because drivers cannot read metric signs
Because chains are more accurate than metres
They match historic route records and lineside markers
questions.rationale: Use the system shown on lineside posts and documents.

questions.stem: What is a 'quarter-mile post'?
options: A post marking a quarter of a possession
A signal post with four lamps
A marker every quarter mile along the line
A post showing a quarter speed limit
questions.rationale: These posts help pinpoint location.

questions.stem: What is a 'lineside telephone' other than an SPT?
options: A phone for passengers to call taxis
A fixed phone for contacting control or the signaller
A phone used only by lookouts to warn their groups
A phone that plays recorded train times
questions.rationale: Use them for reporting and emergencies as instructed.

questions.stem: Where should you enter the railway to start work?
options: At whichever gate is closest to the work, as long as you hold PTS
At an authorised access point named in your briefing
Over a platform end ramp without permission
Wherever the walk to site is shortest
questions.rationale: Authorised access points are assessed for safety and are linked to your safe system of work.

questions.stem: Before you go on or near the line, what must you have?
options: A valid Sentinel card and a colleague who knows the area
A reason to be there, the right competence and a safe system of work
Verbal permission from any experienced PTS holder who happens to be on site
High-visibility clothing and a charged mobile phone
questions.rationale: You must be authorised, competent and protected by a safe system of work before you go on or near the line.

questions.stem: When walking to or from a work site, which route should you normally use?
options: The four-foot, because the sleepers give a level and even surface
A designated walking route or the cess, if it is safe
The six-foot, because it is between lines
The rail head, because it is clear of ballast
questions.rationale: Walk in the cess or along a designated walking route. Avoid the four-foot and six-foot unless your safe system allows it.

questions.stem: When walking in the cess, which direction should you face where possible?
options: Away from trains so you are not dazzled
Away from trains on the nearest line, so you are not dazzled by lights
Towards trains approaching on the nearest line
It does not matter which way you face
questions.rationale: Facing approaching traffic on the nearest line gives you the best chance of seeing a train early.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid walking in the four-foot?
options: It is reserved for signal engineers
It always contains a conductor rail
You would be directly in the path of any train
It is reserved for signalling staff carrying out inspections
questions.rationale: The four-foot is the train's path. Only enter it when your safe system of work allows.

questions.stem: How should you cross a line when it is necessary and authorised?
options: Diagonally, so you can watch for trains while you walk
Along the rail head, where the footing is more level
At right angles, after looking both ways, stepping over the rails
Diagonally along the rails, so that you can keep watching the oncoming traffic
questions.rationale: Cross directly at right angles, look both ways, and step over rails and equipment rather than onto them.

questions.stem: Why should you cross the track at right angles?
options: It means you do not need to look both ways first
It means the track circuit will not detect you as a train
It keeps your time in the path of trains to a minimum
It stops the track circuit from detecting you
questions.rationale: Crossing squarely reduces the time you spend foul of the line.

questions.stem: Before crossing a line, what must you check?
options: That no train is approaching in either direction on any line
That the timetable shows no trains due in the next hour
That the nearest signal is showing a green aspect
That the line you are crossing looks rusty and unused
questions.rationale: Trains can come from either direction. Look both ways on every line before you cross.

questions.stem: What should you NOT step on when crossing the line?
options: The ballast between the sleepers in the four-foot
Rails, sleepers, point equipment or conductor rails
The cess path on the side where you start
A purpose-built crossing surface provided for staff
questions.rationale: Rails and equipment can be slippery, moving or live. Step over them.

questions.stem: If there is a barrow crossing or foot crossing nearby, what should you do?
options: Use it to cross where it is safe and practical
Avoid it because members of the public use it
Use it only when working at night
Use it only if you are carrying heavy equipment
questions.rationale: Crossings give a level, safer surface. They do not remove the need to check for trains.

questions.stem: Why should you never cross the line close in front of a train that has stopped?
options: The driver will report you to the signaller for causing a delay
It is only allowed once you wave to the driver
It could move off without warning and hide other trains
Stopped trains usually reverse a short distance
questions.rationale: A stationary train can start at any time and blocks your view of other lines.

questions.stem: Is it safe to climb between or under railway vehicles to get across the line?
options: Yes, if the train is stopped at a signal
No, vehicles can move without warning
Yes, if you are quick
Yes, if the engine is switched off
questions.rationale: Never go under, between or over vehicles unless your work is protected and it is authorised.

questions.stem: What should you do if the access point signs do not match the location in your briefing?
options: Carry on, because access point signs are often out of date
Go to the nearest other access point and start from there
Work from the briefing alone and ignore the signs
Stop and check with the COSS before going any further
questions.rationale: RAIB has investigated incidents where workers accessed the wrong lines because of poor signs or wrong documents.

questions.stem: Before leaving an access point and going on or near the line, what should you confirm?
options: Which lines are open and which are blocked
How many trains ran yesterday
Which train company operates the line
The name of the signaller and the signal box they work from
questions.rationale: You must know which lines may have trains and where your positions of safety are.

questions.stem: What should you do if you need to walk on or near the line but no safe system of work has been set up?
options: Do not go on or near the line
Walk quickly and keep looking
Go if you hold PTS
Ask a colleague to watch you
questions.rationale: No safe system of work, no access. Raise it with your supervisor.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to carry long items such as scaffold poles near the line?
options: Upright on your shoulder so others can see them
Horizontally and low, keeping them clear of the line
Over your head, holding them with both hands
Dragged along behind you on the rail head
questions.rationale: Carrying long items horizontally helps you stay clear of trains and overhead lines.

questions.stem: Why must you carry long items horizontally in electrified areas?
options: So that trains can see them
Because vertical items set off alarms
To keep them well away from overhead line equipment
So that train drivers can see clearly what you are carrying
questions.rationale: You and anything you hold must stay at least 2.75 m from live OLE.

questions.stem: How should you walk on ballast?
options: Quickly, so you spend less time near the line
Quickly, looking only at the track ahead so you can see trains
Carefully, watching for uneven ground and trip hazards
On the sleeper ends for a firmer surface
questions.rationale: Ballast moves underfoot. Watch for holes, troughing, cables and debris.

questions.stem: Which of these is a common trip hazard on the lineside?
options: Orange high-visibility clothing
Cables, cable troughing lids and signal wires
Painted access point signs that are fixed to the boundary fence
Neatly stacked sleepers away from the line
questions.rationale: Lineside equipment and loose materials cause many slips and trips.

questions.stem: What should you do if a walking route is blocked by vegetation or materials?
options: Stop and get advice rather than walking on the line
Walk in the four-foot until you are past it
Climb over the obstruction as quickly as you can
