Walk in the six-foot between the two lines instead
questions.rationale: Do not improvise. Report it and wait for a safe alternative.

questions.stem: When leaving the railway at the end of work, what must you do?
options: Leave by an authorised access point and tell the COSS you are clear
Leave by the shortest route back to your vehicle once your task is done
Leave without telling anyone if your work is finished
Leave your equipment on the line for the next shift
questions.rationale: The COSS must know everyone is clear before giving up the safe system of work.

questions.stem: RAIB found that a worker was killed at Reading in 2007 while doing what?
options: Placing detonators at the limit of a possession
Climbing an overhead line structure to inspect it
Driving a road vehicle over a level crossing
Walking from site after the protection had been removed
questions.rationale: Protection must stay in place, or another safe system must apply, until everyone is clear of the line.

questions.stem: Can you use a platform end ramp to reach the track?
options: Yes, at any time as long as you hold a valid PTS
Yes, provided there are no trains in the station
Only if it is an authorised access point for your work
No, platform ramps can never be used to access the line
questions.rationale: Platform ends can be authorised access points. Follow your briefing and local signage.

questions.stem: What is the danger of using a mobile phone while walking on or near the line?
options: The phone signal may change the points
You may be distracted and miss an approaching train
The phone signal can interfere with the train's AWS equipment
It is fine if you use a headset
questions.rationale: Do not use phones while walking on or near the line unless it is an emergency and you are in a safe place.

questions.stem: May you wear personal headphones while walking along the cess?
options: Yes, as long as the volume is kept low
No, you must be able to hear warnings and trains
Yes, as long as you stay in the cess
Yes, as long as the volume is kept low enough to hear a horn
questions.rationale: Anything that stops you hearing warnings is dangerous.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a train approaching while you are walking on or near the line?
options: Get to a position of safety at once and acknowledge the driver
Keep walking but move a little nearer to the cess edge
Stop exactly where you are and stand completely still
Stop exactly where you are, stand completely still and wave both arms at the driver
questions.rationale: Get to a position of safety immediately and raise one arm above your head to acknowledge the driver's warning.

questions.stem: What must you do after a train has passed you while you were walking in the cess?
options: Continue at once, because the line is now clear
Check that no other train is approaching before moving on
Walk in the four-foot behind the train
Cross quickly behind the train while you know the line is clear
questions.rationale: Another train may be close behind or on another line.

questions.stem: Why is crossing the line behind a train that has just passed dangerous?
options: The train that has just passed may reverse back
The rails are too hot to step over straight away
The signaller may be about to move the points
A train on another line may be hidden by the first
questions.rationale: The passing train can block your view and sound of trains on other lines.

questions.stem: What does a lineside sign showing 'No position of safety' or limited clearance mean for walking?
options: Walk through the area as quickly as possible
Walk through as quickly as possible, but only during daylight hours
Do not pass unless your safe system of work allows it
Walk through in single file and keep talking
questions.rationale: If there is no position of safety, you must not be there when a train passes.

questions.stem: When walking as a group in the cess, how should you walk?
options: Side by side, so you can talk to each other
Side by side in pairs, so that you can keep an eye on each other
Spread out across the cess and the six-foot
In single file, so everyone can reach safety quickly
questions.rationale: Single file keeps the group compact and clear of the line.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid walking backwards near the line?
options: It confuses the signaller watching on CCTV
It can operate the track circuits by mistake
It is against the rules on wearing PPE
You cannot see trains or hazards behind you
questions.rationale: Always look where you are going and keep watching for trains.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are unsure whether you are on the right side of the line?
options: Stop, stay clear of the line and confirm with the COSS
Cross the line to see if the other side looks right
Follow the nearest worker and assume they know which side is right
Follow the nearest worker and assume they know
questions.rationale: RAIB has reported staff accessing the opposite side of the line from that expected.

questions.stem: Which is the safest place to stand while waiting for your briefing at an access point?
options: On the ballast shoulder close to the nearest rail
In the six-foot between the two running lines
At the edge of the platform where you can be seen
Clear of the line, ideally off the railway altogether
questions.rationale: Wait in a safe place. Do not go on or near the line until you have been briefed.

questions.stem: If your access route crosses a level crossing, what extra hazard must you consider?
options: The crossing is always electrified
Trains always stop at crossings
Level crossings are never used at night
Road vehicles and members of the public
questions.rationale: Level crossings combine road and rail risks.

questions.stem: When walking through a station area to reach the track, what should you remember?
options: Station staff will warn you of every approaching train
Follow station rules and use authorised routes to the track
Trains do not run through platforms while you are there
You may walk on the track to avoid the crowds
questions.rationale: Stations have local instructions and many people. Access the line only as authorised.

questions.stem: What is the danger of using a shortcut across the tracks to get back to your van?
options: You might lose your way and arrive back late
You may be struck by a train you are not protected from
Your shift may be recorded as longer than it was on your timesheet
Your shift may be recorded as longer than it was
questions.rationale: Shortcuts across open lines kill. Use the planned route.

questions.stem: When must you not walk through a tunnel?
options: Only during the day when the tunnel is busiest
Only when the tunnel lighting has been switched off for maintenance work
Only when it is raining and the walls are wet
When trains could approach and no safe system covers it
questions.rationale: Tunnels usually have limited clearance and poor sighting. Only enter as authorised.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find a fence or gate at an access point unlocked or damaged?
options: Ignore it, as it is not your job
Report it so it can be secured
Remove the gate to make access easier
Leave it open for the next shift
questions.rationale: Insecure access points let trespassers onto the railway.

questions.stem: When climbing up or down an embankment to the line, what should you do?
options: Slide down the slope to save time and effort
Carry heavy loads in both hands to keep balanced
Use steps or an authorised route and keep a firm grip
Jump the last part of the way onto the ballast
questions.rationale: Steep slopes cause falls. Use the proper route.

questions.stem: Why should you not walk on the sleeper ends or 'shoulder' of ballast close to the rail?
options: You would be within the area a train could strike
It damages the sleepers and loosens the ballast
That area is reserved for lookouts on duty
That area is reserved for lookouts who need a clear view of the line
questions.rationale: Being close to the rail may put you foul of the line.

questions.stem: What does 'egress' mean in railway safety?
options: Entering the railway safely
Leaving the railway safely
A type of warning signal
A rail fastening
questions.rationale: Safe access and egress cover getting to and from your work without putting yourself at risk.

questions.stem: What should you do if your access point is inside a different electrical section from the one isolated?
options: Assume all OLE in the area is isolated
Treat the equipment there as live and follow the briefing
Assume it is isolated, as access points are always in the same section
Climb the structure to read the section plate
questions.rationale: Isolation covers specific sections only. Everything else stays live.

questions.stem: Before walking through an area at night, what extra precaution helps your safety?
options: Walking faster so you spend less time on the line in the dark
Wearing dark clothing
Using suitable lighting such as a head torch
Switching off your lamp near trains
questions.rationale: Good lighting helps you see trip hazards. Do not shine lights at drivers.

questions.stem: Should you shine a torch directly at an approaching train driver?
options: Yes, it is the best way to show you are there
Yes, but only in fog or other poor weather
No, it could dazzle the driver or look like a signal
Yes, as long as you are standing in the cess
questions.rationale: Only use lights as signals when trained and when the situation requires it.

questions.stem: When you arrive on site, what should you look for in addition to the briefing?
options: Only the location of the welfare cabin and toilets
Only the location of the welfare cabin, toilets and first aid kit
Nothing, because the briefing covers everything needed
Any changes to site conditions since the work was planned
questions.rationale: Conditions change. Report anything that may affect the safe system of work.

questions.stem: What is the main reason access points are planned in advance?
options: So sponsors can charge staff for parking spaces
So that trains can be stopped to let workers cross at that point
So people can reach work without walking on open lines
So trains can be stopped to let workers cross
questions.rationale: Good access planning reduces the time people spend near open lines.

questions.stem: If you drop a tool on the line while walking in the cess, what should you do?
options: Step into the four-foot quickly and pick it up
Leave it unless your safe system allows you to recover it
Ask the driver of the next train to stop for you
Kick it towards the cess from where you are standing
questions.rationale: Do not put yourself at risk for equipment. Tell the COSS.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best practice when carrying equipment from the access point?
options: Carry as much as possible to save trips back
Leave the heavy items in the four-foot until later
Carry only what lets you still move quickly to safety
Ask the lookout to carry some of the equipment
questions.rationale: Heavy or awkward loads slow you down and can make you trip.

questions.stem: What should you do before you step off a platform or walkway onto the ballast?
options: Check it is safe and that you are authorised
Take off your helmet so you can see the ballast clearly
Shout to let the signaller know
Take off your helmet so you can see
questions.rationale: Uneven ground and trains are both hazards. Take care.

questions.stem: During your walk to site you see a group working on an open line with no lookout. What should you do?
options: Walk past, because it is not your group
Join them to help finish quickly
Take a photo of it and post it online to raise awareness
Stop and challenge it, or report it immediately
questions.rationale: Everyone has a duty to challenge unsafe work. Margam (2019) showed the cost of unsafe informal practice.

questions.stem: You arrive at the access point and the COSS is not there yet. What should you do?
options: Walk to the site and start setting up the equipment
Start work on the lineside fence while you wait
Phone the signaller and ask if you can make a start
Wait off the line until the COSS arrives and briefs you
questions.rationale: Do not go on or near the line until you have been briefed on the safe system of work.

questions.stem: Why should you tell the COSS if you need to leave the site early?
options: So they can sign your timesheet before you go
So they can update your PTS record on Sentinel before you go
So they can update your PTS record on Sentinel
So they know where everyone is and can account for you
questions.rationale: The COSS must know who is on site and that everyone is clear before ending the safe system of work.

questions.stem: What should you do if you must walk past a parked engineering train in a possession?
options: Walk under the train if it is not moving and the driver is away
Walk under the train if it is not moving
Keep clear of it and follow the route in your briefing
Walk on the adjacent open line to get past
questions.rationale: Vehicles can move without warning. Keep a safe distance.

questions.stem: Which of these access routes is usually the safest?
options: One that keeps you away from open lines all the way
The one with the shortest walking time to the site
One that crosses several lines at a level crossing
One through a tunnel that has refuges at intervals
questions.rationale: Planned routes aim to separate people from moving trains as far as possible.

questions.stem: Why might you be told to approach a site from a particular side of the railway?
options: To avoid paying for parking
To avoid crossing open lines
To keep the work secret
Because only one side has mobile signal
questions.rationale: Approaching from the correct side reduces the need to cross lines.

questions.stem: If you need to pass through a limited clearance area to reach your site, what must be in place?
options: A lookout standing within the limited clearance area
A colleague walking close behind you to watch for trains
Your hi-vis jacket fully zipped and your torch switched on
A safe system that does not rely on a position of safety there
questions.rationale: With no position of safety, you must not be there when a train passes.

questions.stem: You notice the cess path is flooded. What should you do?
options: Walk in the four-foot until past the flood
Use the conductor rail as a stepping stone
Wade through quickly so that you do not hold up the group
Stop and get advice; do not walk on the line to avoid it
questions.rationale: Do not improvise a route onto the line. Flooding can also hide hazards and conduct electricity on DC lines.

questions.stem: Which of these is an unsafe act when accessing the line?
options: Using a locked access gate with a key
Climbing over a lineside fence to save time
Checking signs at the access point
Waiting at the access point until the COSS has briefed you
questions.rationale: Only use authorised access points.

questions.stem: What should you do if a member of the public asks to follow you through a railway access gate?
options: Let them through if they look responsible
Hold the gate open for them
Refuse and secure the gate behind you
Give them your spare hi-vis
questions.rationale: Members of the public must not be allowed onto the railway.

questions.stem: After you pass through an access gate, what should you do with it?
options: Close and lock it if required
Leave it open for others
Prop it open with a sleeper
Leave it open so that the next person can get through easily
questions.rationale: Open gates can let trespassers and animals onto the railway.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to walk between two lines that are both open to traffic?
options: Trains could pass on both sides with no room for you
The ballast between the lines is softer and unstable
Signals cannot be seen from between the lines
Walking there will trigger the trains' AWS
questions.rationale: The six-foot may not give a position of safety when trains pass on both sides.

questions.stem: During your walk you hear a train but cannot see it. What should you do?
options: Move to a position of safety immediately
Wait until you can see it before moving
Stand still in the cess until you can see which line it is on
Turn around to look and keep walking
questions.rationale: Do not wait to see the train. Move to safety at once.

questions.stem: Which statement about walking on or near the line in darkness is correct?
options: Train lights make it easy to judge how far away they are
Trains are required to slow down at night
Train lights make it hard to judge speed and distance
Lookouts are not needed after dark because lights are visible
questions.rationale: Judging speed and distance of lights at night is difficult.

questions.stem: What should you check before stepping down from a road-rail vehicle near an open line?
options: That you step down on the side away from the open line
That the driver is watching you as you climb down
That the vehicle's radio has been switched off
That the driver is watching you as you climb down from the cab
questions.rationale: Step down into a safe area, not towards an open line.

questions.stem: What is the main reason not to sit or lean on lineside equipment while waiting?
options: It is uncomfortable and makes you tired
It will change the aspect of the nearby signal
It belongs to another department and may be damaged
It may be live, may move, or may put you foul of the line
questions.rationale: Do not sit or lean on rails, equipment or structures near the line.

questions.stem: Where should you take a rest break during a shift on site?
options: In a safe place away from the line
On the ballast shoulder
In the six-foot
On a stack of rails beside the line
questions.rationale: Take breaks clear of the line, ideally off the railway.

questions.stem: If you feel unwell while walking to site, what should you do?
options: Stop in a safe place and tell the COSS
Carry on and hope it passes
Lie down in the cess until you feel well enough to carry on
Leave without telling anyone
questions.rationale: Being unwell affects your ability to react to trains.

questions.stem: Your briefing says the access is from the Up side, but the gate is locked. What should you do?
options: Climb over the gate, as it is the agreed access
Cross to the Down side and use the gate there
Ask the COSS for a safe alternative; do not cross lines
Cross over to the Down side and use the gate there, as it is usually unlocked
questions.rationale: Changing your route can expose you to open lines. Get advice.

questions.stem: What is a safe way to move equipment across the line when authorised?
options: Slide it under the rails between two sleepers to the other side
Slide it under the rails between the sleepers
Throw it across to a colleague on the other side
Lift and carry it squarely across without dragging it
questions.rationale: Dragging items can damage equipment and interfere with track circuits.

questions.stem: When walking along a cess with a fence on one side and the line on the other, what should you look out for?
options: Gaps in the fence you could use as shortcuts
Gaps in the boundary fence that the group could use as shortcuts to the van
Signals you can wave at to alert the signaller
Places where the cess narrows and there is no safe position
questions.rationale: Know where positions of safety are before you need them.

questions.stem: In which situation must you not use a walking route even if it exists?
options: When your briefing says it is not safe for that shift
When it is raining lightly and the ballast is wet
When a train can be seen in the distance on the line beside it
When a train can be seen in the far distance
questions.rationale: Always follow your briefing.

questions.stem: What is an 'access point' sign most likely to warn you about?
options: The opening hours of the nearest station shop
Local hazards such as limited clearance or electrification
The maximum number of hours you are allowed to work during that particular shift
The colour of high-visibility clothing to wear
questions.rationale: Read access point signage carefully.

questions.stem: Why should you not leave a vehicle parked across an access point?
options: It will be struck by trains
It could block emergency access
It may set off the alarms on the access gate
It is not covered by insurance
questions.rationale: Access points may be needed by emergency services.

questions.stem: Which is the safest action if you realise you have entered the railway at the wrong access point?
options: Walk along the line to the right site
Leave the line and contact the COSS
Carry on working where you are
Cross the line to look for the group
questions.rationale: You are not protected at the wrong location.

questions.stem: If you are carrying a ladder near overhead line equipment, how must you carry it?
options: Upright, so that others can see it coming from a distance
Over your shoulder with the top end raised
Horizontally and low, by two people where needed
Balanced on your head to keep hands free
questions.rationale: Keep yourself and anything you carry at least 2.75 m from OLE.

questions.stem: Why might steps or stairs at an access point be dangerous?
options: They can be slippery, damaged or overgrown
They are electrified to keep trespassers off the railway
They move when trains pass
They are only for emergency services
questions.rationale: Take care on steps, especially in wet or icy weather.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a colleague walking in the four-foot of an open line?
options: Ignore it if they are experienced
Join them to keep them company
Warn them and tell them to move to a safe place
Report it next week in the safety meeting
questions.rationale: Intervene immediately when you see an unsafe act.

questions.stem: What should you do if you must pass a lookout or site warden during your walk?
options: Stop and have a chat to keep them alert
Ask them to carry some of your tools
Walk between them and the line to pass quickly
Follow their instructions and do not distract them
questions.rationale: Lookouts and site wardens must concentrate on their duties.

questions.stem: What is the danger of carrying equipment that blocks your view?
options: You may damage the equipment against a fence
You may get tired more quickly on the walk
You may damage the equipment against the fence as you walk
You may not see an approaching train or a trip hazard
questions.rationale: Carry loads so that you can still see and react.

questions.stem: When working near a level crossing, how should you leave the railway?
options: Using an authorised route, watching for road traffic
By walking along the road rails
By ducking under the barriers once the train has gone past
By running across when the lights flash
questions.rationale: Never cross when the crossing is warning of a train.

questions.stem: What does 'egress plan' usually mean in a briefing?
options: The arranged route and method for leaving the site
The route that trains will take past the site
The plan for taking rest and lunch breaks
The emergency number for train drivers to call
questions.rationale: Knowing how to leave safely is as important as getting there.

questions.stem: Why must you know the emergency egress route from your site?
options: So you can avoid signing out at the end of work
So you can get away quickly and safely in an emergency
So you can leave early without the COSS knowing
So you can find the welfare cabin more easily
questions.rationale: In fires, injuries or OLE failures you may need to leave quickly.

questions.stem: You need to walk past a stationary train in a platform road to reach your site. What is the main risk?
options: Passengers might complain about workers on the platform
The train could move off and you could be caught by it
The train's headlights might dazzle you
The train doors might open onto the track side
questions.rationale: Stationary trains can move without warning.

questions.stem: When walking on or near the line, what should you do with your hands where possible?
options: Keep them free to help balance and react
Keep them in your pockets for warmth
Carry heavy loads in both
Hold your phone so you can call for help quickly
questions.rationale: Free hands help you keep your balance on uneven ground.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find you are walking towards an area of limited clearance with a train approaching?
options: Run through the limited clearance area before the train arrives
Lie flat in the four-foot and wait for it to pass
Stop and get to the nearest position of safety before it
Climb onto the nearest structure to get above it
questions.rationale: Know where your positions of safety are along your route.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep to the walking route described in your briefing?
options: The safe system of work was planned for that route
It is the route with the best view of the line
Other routes cross private land outside the boundary
It is always the shortest route to the work
questions.rationale: A different route may not be protected.

questions.stem: If you need to enter an area under the control of a depot, what must you do first?
options: Nothing, because PTS covers you inside depots
Nothing, because your PTS covers all depots and sidings
Get permission from the person in charge of the depot
Walk in and find someone to ask once inside
questions.rationale: Depots have local rules and controls on movements.

questions.stem: Which of these can make access points dangerous in winter?
options: Longer daylight hours
Lower train speeds
Fewer trains run, so lookouts are not as alert
Ice, snow and short daylight hours
questions.rationale: Plan for weather. Take extra care on slopes and steps.

questions.stem: If a planned access point has been closed, what should happen?
options: You should find any other way in and carry on
Work should continue exactly as originally planned
The safe system should be reviewed and a new route agreed
The COSS should cut the fence to make an opening
questions.rationale: Changes to access can affect the whole safe system of work.

questions.stem: What is the safest place to put down equipment you have carried to site?
options: Clear of the line and secured against slipstream
In the four-foot so it stays close to the work
In the four-foot so that it stays close to where the work is
In the six-foot between the two open lines
questions.rationale: Equipment must not be foul of the line.

questions.stem: You have been told to leave the line because a train is due. Where should you go?
options: To the six-foot between the two running lines
To the nearest structure so you can lean on it
To the position of safety or safe area in the briefing
Wherever you happen to be, as long as you stand still
questions.rationale: Use the arranged position of safety.

questions.stem: What makes it unsafe to use a road-rail vehicle as a walking aid or shelter?
options: It can move without warning
It is too cold
It belongs to another company
It may be locked
questions.rationale: Keep clear of plant unless you are part of the operation and authorised.

questions.stem: If your access route needs you to walk on a line that is open, what must protect you?
options: The safe system of work set up by the COSS
Your PTS certificate and Sentinel card
Your helmet and high-visibility clothing
Walking quickly and keeping a lookout yourself
questions.rationale: PTS alone does not protect you. A safe system of work does.

questions.stem: In which direction should a group look when crossing a line together?
options: Each person should look both ways for themselves
Only the leader needs to look, as the group follows them across
Only towards the nearest station
Nobody needs to look if a lookout is present
questions.rationale: Take personal responsibility even when a lookout is used.

questions.stem: Why should you not run when walking on the ballast?
options: It disturbs the ballast profile around the sleepers
It disturbs the ballast profile and damages the track
It can set off the automatic warning systems
You are more likely to trip and fall towards the line
questions.rationale: Move quickly but safely.

questions.stem: Which of these should you report if found at an access point?
options: A clean, locked gate with a working padlock
Missing signs, damaged steps or an insecure gate
A well-lit car park with clear markings beside the access point
A well-lit car park beside the access point
questions.rationale: Reporting defects helps keep access safe.

questions.stem: Why do RAIB investigations often highlight signage at access points?
options: Drivers rely on access point signs to know when to slow down
Poor signage has led workers to the wrong lines
Drivers rely on access signs to slow down
Access signs are used to control train speed
questions.rationale: Clear, accurate signage helps workers identify lines correctly.

questions.stem: At South Hampstead in 2018, what contributed to a near miss with a train?
options: The overhead line had fallen across the track in high winds
Workers went onto the wrong lines, partly due to poor signs
The overhead line had fallen across the track
The train was travelling well above line speed
questions.rationale: RAIB found that missing track layout signage contributed. The workers had about two seconds' warning.

questions.stem: What is the safest attitude to 'familiar' access routes you have used many times?
options: Skip the briefing because you already know the area
Use the shortcuts you have learned over the years
Check them each time, as conditions may have changed
Use the shortcuts you have learned, as you know where it is safe
questions.rationale: Familiarity can lead to complacency. Conditions change.

questions.stem: Which of these is the most important before you cross any line?
options: Being sure the driver of any train will see you
Being sure it is daylight and visibility is good
Being sure you are authorised and no train is coming
Being sure that the driver of any train will see you in time
questions.rationale: Authority plus a clear line is essential.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to get from a road to the cess?
options: Over the nearest low section of boundary fence
Down the embankment at the point closest to the work
Through an authorised access point
Along the platform ramp from the nearest station
questions.rationale: Access points are assessed and signed.

questions.stem: Why might an access point have a padlocked gate?
options: To keep the public off the railway
To stop trains leaving the railway
To mark the end of a possession
To stop track workers leaving early
questions.rationale: Lock gates behind you where required.

questions.stem: What should you check before driving a van into a railway compound?
options: That the compound has free parking
That the van is the right colour
That nobody can see you enter the compound gate
That you have permission and know the site rules
questions.rationale: Compounds and road-rail access points have their own rules.

questions.stem: Where should vehicles never be parked at an access point?
options: Facing out towards the road
Where they block access or the emergency route
In the marked parking area
Facing out towards the road so it can leave quickly
questions.rationale: Keep access clear for emergencies.

questions.stem: Why are access points often numbered or named?
options: So people and emergency services can find them
So workers can rate them online
So they can be sold to developers
So that drivers know where to stop to pick up staff
questions.rationale: Clear identification helps in emergencies.

questions.stem: What should you do if the steps down to the line are icy?
options: Take extra care, use handrails, or find a safer route
Slide down them to save time
Slide down them carefully on your back to save time
Carry heavy tools in both hands
questions.rationale: Slips can put you near the line.

questions.stem: You must walk 800 m along an open line to reach the site. What should the plan include?
options: Protection or warning for the walk, and positions of safety
Nothing, as walking is not work
Nothing extra, because walking to site is not counted as work
Only the direction of travel
questions.rationale: Walking on or near open lines needs a safe system.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid walking with your hands in your pockets on ballast?
options: You cannot steady yourself if you slip
It looks unprofessional to the public
It stretches your clothing
It stops you carrying tools
questions.rationale: Keep hands free.

questions.stem: What is a 'walking route' sign used for?
options: To show the line speed for walkers
To show where to park
To show an approved route beside the line
To mark a position of safety
questions.rationale: Follow signed routes where provided.

questions.stem: What should you do if the walking route is narrow and a train approaches?
options: Use the briefed position of safety
Stand still on the route
Step into the six-foot
Run along the route to the next wide section
questions.rationale: Know your positions of safety along the route.

questions.stem: When leaving the site at night, why should you check that everyone is together?
options: So you can share a taxi
So nobody is left on or near the line
So the lights can be switched off
So the van can be locked
questions.rationale: Account for everyone.

questions.stem: What should you do if a gate at the access point will not lock after you?
options: Leave it open
Remove it
Tie it with tape and forget it
Report it so it can be secured
questions.rationale: Insecure gates allow trespass.

questions.stem: Why might an access point be closed at certain times?
options: Because staff are on holiday
Because the staff who hold the keys are on holiday
Because local hazards or work make it unsafe
Because drivers asked for it
questions.rationale: Check access arrangements in the plan.

questions.stem: What should you do if your planned access involves crossing a busy road?
options: Run across quickly
Stop traffic with a red flag
Use a proper crossing and take care
Walk along the road
questions.rationale: Road hazards near access points are real.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to bring a trolley onto the track?
options: Push it down the embankment and lift it onto the rails
Carry it across an open line
Only as planned, with protection and competent staff
Leave it on the rails overnight
questions.rationale: Trolleys need authorised arrangements.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to access the railway from a platform end without authority?
options: Station staff may be annoyed
You may be seen by passengers
Trains may be approaching and you are not protected
Station staff may be annoyed at people using the ramp
questions.rationale: Use authorised access only.

questions.stem: What is the best way to carry a heavy tool bag down steps to the line?
options: Throw it down first
Drag it behind you down the steps
Get help or use a lifting aid
Carry it on your head
questions.rationale: Avoid falls and strains.

questions.stem: Why should you face the steps when climbing down a steep access ladder?
options: You can see trains better
It is faster than facing outwards
It is safer and gives a better grip
It is required for photos
questions.rationale: Maintain contact with the ladder.

questions.stem: What should you do if access steps are overgrown with brambles?
options: Push through them to reach the work on time
Use the embankment instead
Cut them with your knife
Report it and use a safe alternative
questions.rationale: Report defects.

questions.stem: What does a sign saying 'No unauthorised access' at a railway gate mean?
options: Anyone with hi-vis may enter
The gate is broken
Only authorised people may enter
The line is closed
questions.rationale: Authority is required.

questions.stem: Why should you tell the COSS when you arrive at the access point?
options: So they can sign your timesheet
So they know you are there and can brief you
So they can check your van
So they can order lunch for the whole group
questions.rationale: The COSS must know who is on site.

questions.stem: What is the danger of walking along the line wearing a hood up?
options: It makes you too warm on a long walk
It covers your name badge
It is against dress code
It can block your view and hearing
questions.rationale: Keep senses clear.

questions.stem: You arrive at an access point and see a train has stopped near it. What should you do?
options: Walk round the front of it
Ask the driver to move
Wait clear until it is safe and you are briefed
Walk round the front of it so you can reach the site
questions.rationale: Stopped trains can move.

questions.stem: What should you do if your access route crosses a bridge with no refuges?
options: Run across between trains
Run across in the gaps between the passing trains
Only cross under protection agreed in the plan
Cross in single file quickly
questions.rationale: Bridges often have limited clearance.

questions.stem: Why might you need to sign a register at some access points?
options: So you can claim parking
So you can claim back the cost of parking later
So the site knows who is on the railway
So you get a free drink
questions.rationale: Registers help account for people.

questions.stem: What should you do if your access involves stepping down from a high platform edge?
options: Jump and roll as you land on the ballast
Sit and slide down
Use the platform ramp anywhere
Use steps or a proper access, not jump
questions.rationale: Jumping risks injury and falling towards the line.

questions.stem: Why should you report broken handrails at access points?
options: People could fall
They look old
They are expensive
They block the view
questions.rationale: Report defects.

questions.stem: Why might a COSS choose a longer access route?
options: To give the group more exercise
To pass a café so the group can buy food
To avoid crossing or walking near open lines
To avoid the public seeing the work
questions.rationale: Safety over convenience.

questions.stem: When walking to site in a group, who should know the route?
options: Only the COSS
Only the lookout
Only the newest person
Everyone
questions.rationale: Everyone should understand the route and positions of safety.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a stranger following your group through an access gate?
options: Stop them and report it
Let them follow
Give them a hi-vis
Ignore them
questions.rationale: The public must not enter the railway.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid walking on the cess edge near a steep embankment?
options: You could slip down the slope
It is reserved for drivers
It damages the cess
It confuses signals
questions.rationale: Stay on firm ground.

questions.stem: What should you do if you need to leave site before the end and the COSS is busy?
options: Wait until you can tell the COSS
Leave without telling anyone
Tell the lookout and go
Text the COSS and go
questions.rationale: The COSS must know you have left the line.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to leave a possession at the end of work?
options: As briefed, before the possession is given up
By any route that looks quickest once work is finished
By any route that is quickest
By walking along the open line
questions.rationale: Be clear before protection ends.

questions.stem: Why can using a mobile phone torch be risky on site at night?
options: Phone torches are banned on the railway
The phone torch can change the aspect of nearby signals and confuse drivers
Phone torches are banned on the railway by law
It can dazzle others and drain your phone for emergencies
questions.rationale: Use a proper torch.

questions.stem: What should you check about your route before a night shift?
options: The weather forecast for the following month
The timetable for tomorrow
Hazards that may be harder to see in the dark
The colour of the gate
questions.rationale: Plan for darkness.

questions.stem: Why should you not climb over a stationary wagon to cross a siding?
options: It might be dirty
It could move or you could fall
It belongs to someone else
It wastes time
questions.rationale: Never climb on or through vehicles.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find a gate at an access point has been forced open?
options: Close it and say nothing
Fix it yourself
Report it as possible trespass
Use it and leave it open
questions.rationale: There may be trespassers on the line.

questions.stem: Where should equipment be carried when walking along a narrow cess?
options: On the side nearest the line
Above your head
On the side away from the line
Dragged behind you
questions.rationale: Keep loads away from passing trains.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid stepping on cable drawpit lids?
options: They are live
They are slippery only in summer
They are private
They can break or move
questions.rationale: Lids may not be designed for walking on.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of 'safe walking route' assessments?
options: To find the fastest route
To count steps for fitness
To identify routes that keep people clear of trains
To find the fastest route for staff walking to work
questions.rationale: Planners use them to set access.

questions.stem: What is a 'position of safety'?
options: Any place inside the four-foot that is away from the points
A place beside the signal box where the signaller can see you
Any place from which you can clearly see the train coming
A place far enough from the line to be safe as a train passes
questions.rationale: A position of safety keeps you clear of passing trains and their air turbulence.

questions.stem: On a line with a maximum speed of 100 mph or less, how far from the nearest rail must a position of safety be?
options: At least 0.5 metres (1 foot 8 inches)
At least 3 metres (10 feet)
At least 1.25 metres (4 feet)
At least 2.75 metres (9 feet)
questions.rationale: Up to 100 mph the minimum is 1.25 m (4 ft) from the nearest rail on which a train may approach.

questions.stem: On a line with a maximum speed above 100 mph and up to 125 mph, how far from the nearest rail must a position of safety be?
options: At least 1.25 metres (4 feet)
At least 2 metres (6 feet 6 inches)
At least 1 metre (3 feet 3 inches)
At least 1.25 metres (4 feet), the same as slower lines
questions.rationale: Above 100 mph and up to 125 mph the minimum is 2 m (6 ft 6 in).

questions.stem: From where is the position of safety distance measured?
options: The centre line of the four-foot of the nearest track
The centre of the nearest four-foot, wherever the train is coming from
The railway boundary fence on your side of the line
The nearest rail of a line on which a train may approach
questions.rationale: Measure from the nearest rail of any line on which a train could approach.

questions.stem: How long before a train arrives must you be in your position of safety?
options: At least 10 seconds
At least 2 seconds
At least 5 seconds
Just before it passes
questions.rationale: You must reach your position of safety at least 10 seconds before the train arrives.

questions.stem: Why must you be in a position of safety at least 10 seconds before a train arrives?
options: So the driver has time to sound the horn twice
So the train can slow down before reaching you
To give a margin so you are settled and clear in time
So the driver has time to sound the horn twice before passing
questions.rationale: The margin allows for delays and makes sure you are stable and clear.

questions.stem: The line speed is 90 mph. Which of these is a valid position of safety?
options: 1.5 metres from the nearest rail with no obstructions
1 metre from the nearest rail on firm, level ground
In the four-foot of an adjacent line that is blocked
On a narrow ledge 0.9 metres from the nearest rail
questions.rationale: At 90 mph you need at least 1.25 m from the nearest rail.

questions.stem: The line speed is 110 mph. Which of these is a valid position of safety?
options: 1.5 metres from the nearest rail, which is enough at any speed
2.2 metres from the nearest rail on firm ground
1.25 metres from the nearest rail
In the six-foot between two open lines
questions.rationale: Above 100 mph you need at least 2 m from the nearest rail.

questions.stem: What should you do once you are in your position of safety and a train is passing?
options: Turn your back to the train so that dust does not get in your eyes
Step towards the train to read its number for the log
Stay there, face the train and keep clear until it passes
Start walking back towards the work to save time
questions.rationale: Stay alert and stable. Keep facing the train where possible.

questions.stem: After a train has passed your position of safety, when can you return to the line?
options: When you are told it is safe and no other train is coming
As soon as the last vehicle of the train has passed you
After counting slowly to five once the train has passed
As soon as the last vehicle of the train has passed your position
questions.rationale: Another train may be approaching on any line.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a suitable position of safety?
options: A wide cess 2 m from the rail on a 75 mph line
A narrow gap between two open lines
A refuge in a bridge wall
A designated safe area behind a barrier
questions.rationale: The six-foot between two open lines usually gives no safe clearance from trains on both sides.

questions.stem: Where is the best place to stand in your position of safety?
options: On a sloping cutting edge with a good view of the line
On firm, level ground where you cannot slip towards the line
On top of the cable troughing so you are higher up
On loose ballast at the sleeper ends near the work
questions.rationale: A position of safety must be stable as well as far enough away.

questions.stem: What should you do with tools and equipment when you move to a position of safety?
options: Leave them in the four-foot so they are ready to use
Lay them on the rail head where they are easy to see
Throw them into the six-foot away from your line
Take them with you or place them clear of the line
questions.rationale: Equipment left foul of the line can be struck and thrown.

questions.stem: Why must you know where your position of safety is before you start work?
options: So you can tell drivers where you will be standing
So you can store your tools there during the work
So you can store your tools there during work
So you can reach it quickly when a warning is given
questions.rationale: Your briefing should tell you where your positions of safety are.

questions.stem: When the train horn sounds as a warning, what should you do?
options: Wave both arms to make the train stop
Get to a position of safety and raise one arm
Carry on working until you can see the train
Shout to the driver to tell them you are there
questions.rationale: Raising one arm acknowledges the warning so the driver knows you have seen the train.

questions.stem: Why do you raise one arm above your head when a driver sounds the horn at you?
options: To ask the driver to slow down until they are past the group
To tell the driver to slow down
To signal that the line is clear
To show the driver you have seen the train
questions.rationale: Raising one arm is the acknowledgement. Both arms raised above the head is used to signal a driver to stop.

questions.stem: Which signal would tell a driver to stop in an emergency if you have no flag or light?
options: One arm raised above your head
One arm pointing at the train
Both arms raised above your head
One arm raised above your head and held still
questions.rationale: Both arms raised is the emergency stop hand signal. Only use it in an emergency.

questions.stem: What is the danger of standing on a sloping embankment edge as your position of safety?
options: It blocks the driver's view of signals
You could slip back towards the passing train
It is always outside the boundary
Nothing, as long as it is more than 1.25 m from the rail
questions.rationale: Distance is not enough. The ground must also be stable.

questions.stem: If you cannot find a position of safety at your work location, what must happen?
options: You can use the six-foot as a position of safety
The lookout can tell the driver to stop the train
Work must not go ahead there unless trains are stopped
You can lean against the structure when trains pass
questions.rationale: Where there is no position of safety, a protected safe system of work such as a line blockage is needed.

questions.stem: In a tunnel, where should you go when a train approaches?
options: Against the tunnel wall anywhere
Into the four-foot of the other line
Against the tunnel wall at whatever point you happen to be
Into a refuge identified in your briefing
questions.rationale: Tunnels often have limited clearance. Refuges are provided where needed.

questions.stem: Why must you be careful using the six-foot as a position of safety?
options: The six-foot always carries a conductor rail
The six-foot is reserved for lookouts on duty
The six-foot is always inside the possession limits
A train could pass on the adjacent line at the same time
questions.rationale: Only use it if your briefing confirms it is a position of safety for that location.

questions.stem: Which factor does NOT change the position of safety distance you need?
options: The maximum line speed
Which line a train may approach on
The colour of your hi-vis clothing
Whether there is room on firm ground
questions.rationale: Line speed and site geometry decide the distance and suitability.

questions.stem: On a four-track railway, which line do you measure your position of safety from?
options: The fastest line, wherever it is in relation to you
The line you are working on only
The line furthest from you
The nearest line on which a train may approach
questions.rationale: Measure from the nearest rail of any line on which a train could approach.

questions.stem: What should you do if a passing train's air turbulence makes you unsteady?
options: Stand further back and brace yourself for the next train
Step closer to the line, where the wind is weaker
Crouch down in the four-foot below the slipstream
Hold on to the rail so you cannot be blown over
questions.rationale: Faster trains cause more turbulence. More distance is safer.

questions.stem: Why should you keep your hi-vis jacket fastened in a position of safety?
options: It is required so the signaller can see your logo
Loose clothing can be pulled by a train's slipstream
It is only a uniform rule, with no real safety purpose behind it
It prevents the train's AWS from being triggered
questions.rationale: Secure clothing and items so they cannot be drawn towards a train.

questions.stem: What is a 'refuge' in a viaduct or bridge?
options: A recess where you can stand clear of trains
A drainage outlet built into the parapet to clear water
A drainage outlet built into the parapet
A crossing point for cables under the track
questions.rationale: Refuges may be provided where there is no other position of safety. Never block them.

questions.stem: What should you do if a refuge is blocked by rubbish or vegetation?
options: Stand in front of it instead
Use it anyway by squeezing in
Do not rely on it and report it
Ignore it because trains are slow there
questions.rationale: A blocked refuge is not a position of safety.

questions.stem: During a warning, you realise your planned position of safety is blocked by a parked vehicle. What should you do?
options: Stand in front of the parked vehicle until the train passes
Stay where you are and hope the train is on another line
Go to the nearest other position of safety straight away
Climb onto the parked vehicle to get above the train
questions.rationale: Always know more than one position of safety where possible.

questions.stem: Which of these is the safest place to wait for a train to pass?
options: On the ballast shoulder close to the nearest rail
A position of safety on firm ground, facing the train
In the middle of the six-foot between two lines
On top of a location case, so you have a better view of the line
questions.rationale: Be clear, stable and alert.

questions.stem: Why must lightweight equipment be secured when trains pass?
options: So it does not get covered in dust and dirt
Slipstream can move it into the path of the train
So it is not stolen while you are distracted
So the train driver cannot see it and report it
questions.rationale: Even light items can become dangerous projectiles.

questions.stem: If you are in a position of safety and see a colleague still on the line, what should you do?
options: Warn them immediately and loudly
Wait for the lookout to deal with it
Go and drag them off the line
Wave to the driver
questions.rationale: Everyone should look out for each other.

questions.stem: What does 'clear of the line' mean in practice?
options: Being off the rail head only
Being anywhere off the sleepers
Standing in the cess with one foot on the ballast shoulder
Being far enough away that a train cannot strike you
questions.rationale: Clear means outside the area trains or their turbulence can reach.

questions.stem: Why is crouching down in the cess not a substitute for a position of safety?
options: You may still be within reach of the train or turbulence
It is uncomfortable to hold for the length of a passing train
It is uncomfortable to hold for a long time
Crouching is against the rules on wearing PPE
questions.rationale: Use the correct distance, not posture, to stay safe.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the 10-second margin before a train passes?
options: To give the train time to slow down as it approaches
To allow for delays so you are clear before the train arrives
To give the signaller time to change the signal
To give the train driver enough time to slow down when they see the group ahead
questions.rationale: The margin protects you from unexpected delays in reaching safety.

questions.stem: If you are on a line where trains pass at up to 125 mph, what distance should you plan for?
options: At least 1.25 metres
At least 1.25 metres, as long as you face the train
At least 3 metres on one side only
At least 2 metres from the nearest rail
questions.rationale: Above 100 mph and up to 125 mph the minimum is 2 m.

questions.stem: Where a line has bi-directional running, which direction should you watch from your position of safety?
options: Only the normal direction of travel
Only towards the nearest signal
Only the direction of the wind
Both directions
questions.rationale: Trains may approach from either direction.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are uncertain whether a place is a position of safety?
options: Assume it is safe if others use it
Treat it as unsafe and ask the COSS
Measure it after the train has passed
Stand there and hold onto something
questions.rationale: If in doubt, do not rely on it.

questions.stem: What is the main danger of leaving your position of safety too early after a train passes?
options: You may miss your break while waiting
You may step into the path of a second train
The ballast will still be hot from the train
You may block the signal for the next train
questions.rationale: Wait until it is confirmed safe to return.

questions.stem: When a train approaches while you are carrying a heavy item, what should you do?
options: Keep carrying it to save time getting back to work
Keep carrying it all the way so that it is not left anywhere near the line
Put it down clear of the line if you can, then get to safety
Hold it up above your head so the driver can see it
questions.rationale: Your safety comes first. Do not leave items foul of the line if you can avoid it.

questions.stem: Which of these would make a position of safety unsuitable?
options: It is 2 m from the rail on a 75 mph line
It is behind a fixed barrier, more than 2 m from the rail
It is behind a fixed barrier
It is on top of a steep, crumbling cutting edge
questions.rationale: Unstable ground can cause you to fall towards the train.

questions.stem: In a position of safety, why should you avoid sitting on the ground?
options: The ground is always damp and will soak through PPE
It is against the dress code
Trains will stop if they see you sitting
You may not be able to react or move quickly
questions.rationale: Stay standing and alert so you can move if needed.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a COSS identifying positions of safety in the briefing?
options: So everyone knows exactly where to go when warned
So people can choose where to take their breaks
So equipment can be stored there during the work
So drivers can see where the workers will be
questions.rationale: A clear plan avoids hesitation when trains approach.

questions.stem: What is the best action if a train approaches and you are in an area of limited clearance with no refuge nearby?
options: Get clear of the train's path as quickly as you can
Lie flat in the four-foot and keep your head down
Stand perfectly still with your back against the wall
Run towards the train so the driver sees you sooner
questions.rationale: You should never be in such a position. If it happens, get clear as quickly as possible and report it.

questions.stem: Why is a 'position of safety' only one part of keeping safe?
options: It is only needed at night when trains are harder to see
It only applies to lookouts
You also need a warning in time to reach it
It is only needed on electrified lines
questions.rationale: A position of safety works only if you get enough warning to reach it.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a fixed barrier between a work area and an open line?
options: To slow down trains passing on the open line
To mark the end of a possession so that drivers can see it
To physically stop people moving towards the open line
To mark the end of a possession for drivers
questions.rationale: Fenced working uses a barrier so people cannot stray towards the open line.

questions.stem: In separated working, what is the minimum gap kept between the work area and the nearest open line?
options: 1 metre
1.25 metres
5 metres
2 metres
questions.rationale: Separated working keeps a 2 m gap from the open line, with a site warden.

questions.stem: When working near a line where trains pass at 100 mph, which of these is the safest position for a lookout?
options: In the four-foot, where the view is better
On the rail head, where drivers can see them clearly and slow down in time
In a position of safety with a clear view of trains
In the six-foot between the two open lines
questions.rationale: Lookouts must work from a position of safety.

questions.stem: You are 1.3 m from the nearest rail on a line with a maximum speed of 125 mph. Are you in a position of safety?
options: Yes, anything over 1.25 m is safe
Yes, anything over 1.25 m is safe whatever the speed
No, you need at least 2 m at that speed
Yes, if you hold on to a fence
questions.rationale: Above 100 mph you need at least 2 m.

questions.stem: You are 1.5 m from the nearest rail on a 60 mph line, on firm ground. Are you in a position of safety?
options: No, you need at least 2 m at any speed
No, you need at least 3 m from the rail
Yes, provided no other line is nearer to you
Only if a lookout is also on duty nearby
questions.rationale: Up to 100 mph, 1.25 m from the nearest line on which trains may approach is the minimum.

questions.stem: Which of these increases the time you need to reach a position of safety?
options: Heavy equipment, rough ground and a long walk
Wearing orange high-visibility clothing
Having a lookout who gives an early warning
Standing in the cess rather than the six-foot
questions.rationale: Warning time must allow for everything that slows you down.

questions.stem: What is 1.25 metres approximately in feet, as used in position of safety rules?
options: 2 feet
6 feet 6 inches
4 feet
10 feet
questions.rationale: 1.25 m is about 4 ft. It is the minimum for lines up to 100 mph.

questions.stem: What is 2 metres approximately in feet and inches, as used in position of safety rules?
options: 4 feet
6 feet 6 inches
9 feet
3 feet 3 inches
questions.rationale: 2 m is about 6 ft 6 in. It is the minimum for lines over 100 mph and up to 125 mph.

questions.stem: Your COSS has briefed a position of safety in the cess on the Down side. A train approaches on the Up line. What do you do?
options: Go to the briefed position of safety and stay clear of all lines
Move to the Up side cess, nearer the train
Move to the Up side cess, nearer the approaching train, so it sees you
Stay where you are as the train is on the other line
questions.rationale: Use the briefed position of safety. Do not cross lines in front of a train.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid crossing a line to reach a position of safety when a train is approaching?
options: It confuses the lookout
You may be struck while crossing
It is slower than walking along the line
It sets off the AWS
questions.rationale: Positions of safety should be on your side of the line wherever possible.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best description of a good position of safety?
options: Close enough to the line to watch the train's wheels pass
Right next to the work so you can carry on while trains pass
In the shade of a structure that is close to the rail
Clear of all lines where trains may come, stable and easy to reach
questions.rationale: Distance, stability and accessibility all matter.

questions.stem: When you reach a position of safety, what else should you check?
options: That your tools are on the rail where you can find them
That you are not foul of any other line
That the driver has seen your face
That the signal behind you is red
questions.rationale: A spot clear of one line may be close to another.

questions.stem: If the cess is very narrow at a location, what should the planner and COSS consider?
options: That people can stand closer to the rail
That trains will slow down there
That it may not provide a position of safety
That lookouts are no longer needed because trains slow down
questions.rationale: Narrow cesses often mean limited clearance.

questions.stem: At a location with limited clearance, what is the safest type of safe system of work?
options: One where workers stand flat against the wall
One with a single lookout watching both directions
One where the line is blocked so no trains can approach
One where workers stop now and then to listen
questions.rationale: Where there is no position of safety, blocking the line is the safe option.

questions.stem: When working on one line of a double track with the other line open, where is your position of safety likely to be?
options: In the six-foot next to the open line
In the four-foot of the open line
In the cess on the side away from the open line
In the six-foot between the line you are on and the open line
questions.rationale: Keep as far as possible from the open line.

questions.stem: Which of these most affects how quickly you can reach a position of safety?
options: The colour and condition of your helmet
The time the last train passed the site
How far away it is and what you must carry
The name and number of the line you are on
questions.rationale: Plan warning time around real movement times.

questions.stem: What should you do if, while in your position of safety, a train passes very close and you feel unsafe?
options: Ignore it, because it was within the rules
Move closer next time
Report it so the position of safety can be reviewed
Keep it to yourself, as it was still within the rules
questions.rationale: Report concerns so planning can be improved.

questions.stem: Why might a position of safety that was fine in daylight be unsuitable at night?
options: Trains are wider at night than during the day
Trains are wider at night because of their lights
Positions of safety change location at night
It may be hard to find and the ground may be unseen
questions.rationale: Lighting and visibility affect how quickly and safely you can reach a position of safety.

questions.stem: When you hear a warning from a lookout, what should you do first?
options: Look along the line for the train before deciding whether to move
Look along the line for the train before moving
Stop work and move to your position of safety at once
Ask the lookout which line the train is on
questions.rationale: Act immediately on any warning.

questions.stem: You are in a position of safety on a 100 mph line, 1.25 m from the nearest rail. A train passes on a line further away at 125 mph. Is your position still valid?
options: Yes, a line further away never affects the distance
Yes, if you are also 2 m or more from that faster line
Yes, a line further away never affects the distance you need
No, you must move to the other side of the railway
questions.rationale: Check the distance to each line where a train may approach, using that line's speed.

questions.stem: Which item must you NOT leave in the four-foot when moving to safety?
options: Only heavy tools that could derail a train
Anything at all, including tools and materials
Only items longer than about one metre, which could foul a train
Only items longer than about one metre
questions.rationale: Anything left foul of the line can be struck.

questions.stem: Why should you not stand directly behind a train-passing obstruction such as a signal post as your position of safety?
options: Signal posts carry the traction supply and can give you a shock if you touch them
The signal might fall over in the slipstream
It may not give the clearance needed and could trap you
Drivers cannot see you behind the post
questions.rationale: Only use proper positions of safety.

questions.stem: What should you do if your group has more people than the position of safety can hold?
options: Squeeze in when a train comes and hold on to each other
Let some stand in the six-foot
Let the slowest stay on the line
Raise it with the COSS before work starts
questions.rationale: Everyone needs a safe place to go.

questions.stem: Which statement about 'safe' places near platforms is correct?
options: The platform face is always a position of safety
Trains always stop before they reach a platform
You may stand under the overhang of the platform edge
There may be no position of safety on the platform side
questions.rationale: Platforms often create limited clearance.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid standing near the end of a refuge's opening?
options: You would block the drainage outlet
You would set off the alarm fitted to the refuge
You would set off the refuge alarm
You might not be fully clear of the train
questions.rationale: Get fully into the refuge.

questions.stem: If you see the train approaching but have not been warned, what should you do?
options: Move to safety and warn others
Wait for the lookout's warning
Keep working because you were not warned
Shout at the lookout first
questions.rationale: Never wait for a warning if you see a train coming.

questions.stem: Which of these is the minimum standard for the time you must be in your position of safety before the train arrives?
options: 30 seconds
10 seconds
1 minute
There is no minimum
questions.rationale: At least 10 seconds before the train arrives.

questions.stem: What makes positions of safety on curves more risky?
options: Trains are built wider for running on curves
Trains appear suddenly and you have less time
Curves are always electrified with third rail
There are never any signals on curves
questions.rationale: Curves reduce sighting distance.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to wait in a position of safety when trains pass in both directions?
options: Move back to the work after each train passes
Stay in place until it is confirmed safe to return
Move back to the work after each train has gone past
Walk along the line between the passing trains
questions.rationale: Stay put until it is confirmed safe.

questions.stem: What can happen if you stand on a cable troughing lid as your position of safety?
options: You will be electrocuted by the cables inside the trough
You will stop the signals
The lid may break or tip, causing you to fall
You will be too far from the line
questions.rationale: Troughing is not designed to be stood on.

questions.stem: Why is the space between a train and a platform or wall especially dangerous?
options: It is always wet and slippery underfoot
You can be crushed or struck with no room to escape
It is where the conductor rail is usually placed
It is where trains stop to let passengers off
questions.rationale: Never put yourself between a train and a structure.

questions.stem: You are working in the cess on a curve with poor sighting. What is the most important thing to know?
options: How many trains passed the location the previous day
How many trains passed the location on the previous day
Where your position of safety is and how long it takes to reach
The names of the drivers booked on the route and the times of their trains
questions.rationale: Poor sighting means less warning. Plan your movement in advance.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a reason to choose a position of safety on the same side as your work?
options: You will not need to cross the line
It allows you to keep working while trains pass
You avoid being trapped between two trains
You avoid being trapped between trains
questions.rationale: You must stop work and go to safety. You cannot work while trains pass if you are in a red zone.

questions.stem: What should you do if a train passes and something falls from it near you?
options: Go and collect it at once before another train comes
Kick it clear of the line from where you are standing
Throw it back towards the train to alert the driver
Stay in your position of safety and report it afterwards
questions.rationale: Do not go on the line until it is safe. Report it to the COSS or signaller.

questions.stem: What should you do if a stone or debris is thrown up by a passing train?
options: Step closer to the train
Protect your eyes and face and keep clear
Lift your visor so you can see where the debris has gone
Turn your back and crouch on the rail
questions.rationale: Debris is a hazard. Wear eye protection where required.

questions.stem: What should you do if you have to wait a long time in a position of safety?
options: Sit down on the rail to rest your legs
Go back to work in the gaps between trains
Take a short nap to recover your energy
Stay alert and do not drift back towards the line
questions.rationale: Stay alert and in place until told it is safe.

questions.stem: You are briefed that the position of safety is behind a fence. Why is this better than an open cess?
options: The fence is electrified to keep people back from the line
The fence stops you stepping or being drawn towards the train
The fence hides you from the driver so they do not brake
The fence makes passing trains slow down automatically
questions.rationale: Physical separation adds protection.

questions.stem: Why should you never stand on the rail to look for an approaching train?
options: It confuses the signaller watching the line
You would be in the train's path and could slip
It damages the rail head and fastenings
It damages the rail head and loosens the fastenings
questions.rationale: Never stand on rails.

questions.stem: During a warning, what should you do if you are carrying a long item near OLE?
options: Keep it horizontal and low as you move to safety
Raise it over your head to keep it clear of the ground
Plant it upright in the ballast
Throw it towards the cess
questions.rationale: Keep long items at least 2.75 m from OLE at all times.

questions.stem: If a position of safety is on an embankment above the line, what should you check?
options: That it has a good view of the station
That there is a safe path to it and firm footing
That it is shaded and has a good view of the station
That it is out of mobile range
questions.rationale: A good position of safety must be safely reachable.

questions.stem: What is the best reason for having a planned position of safety for each part of the work?
options: So you can take rests in different places
So drivers can find you more easily
So you can photograph the work from each spot
The work may move and the safe place changes with it
questions.rationale: As the work moves, positions of safety must be checked again.

questions.stem: Can a stationary vehicle on an adjacent line be used as protection instead of a position of safety?
options: Yes, if it is a heavy freight train
Yes, if the driver is not on board
Yes, if it is a heavy freight train with no driver on board
No, it may move and offers no proper clearance
questions.rationale: Vehicles can move. Use a proper position of safety.

questions.stem: What should you do if a train stops next to your position of safety?
options: Walk round the front of it to carry on
Climb into the cab to speak to the driver
Return to work immediately as it has stopped
Stay where you are and wait for instructions
questions.rationale: A stopped train can move again. Follow instructions from the COSS.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of positions of safety in RAIB's view of track worker protection?
options: A way of removing the need to plan the work
A last line of defence when lines are open to trains
A way to let people keep working while trains pass
A reason why lines never need to be blocked
questions.rationale: RAIB emphasises that separating people from trains is the most effective control.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about positions of safety and line speed is correct?
options: All line speeds need exactly the same distance
Slower lines need a greater distance than faster ones
Higher line speeds need greater distance from the line
Slower lines need more distance because trains linger longer
questions.rationale: Up to 100 mph: 1.25 m. Over 100 mph up to 125 mph: 2 m.

questions.stem: Where should a lookout stand in relation to the group they protect?
options: In the four-foot facing the group so everyone can see them
Behind the group with their back to approaching trains
Behind the group with their back to trains so they can watch the work
In a position of safety where they can see trains and be heard
questions.rationale: Lookouts must be safe themselves and able to warn the group effectively.

questions.stem: Which two things must a position of safety give you?
options: A view of the signal box and shelter from rain
A place to sit down and store your tools
Enough distance and stable footing
A view of the train's number and its driver
questions.rationale: Distance from the line and safe ground are both needed.

questions.stem: Why should a position of safety be on the same side as your work where possible?
options: So the lookout can see your face
So you do not have to cross the line
So you can keep working as trains pass
So it is closer to the welfare cabin
questions.rationale: Crossing in front of a train is dangerous.

questions.stem: A line has a maximum speed of 40 mph. What is the minimum position of safety distance?
options: 0.5 metres, because the line is slow
2 metres, the same as for all lines
3 metres, as for being near the line
1.25 metres from the nearest rail
questions.rationale: Up to 100 mph the minimum is 1.25 m.

questions.stem: A line has a maximum speed of 125 mph. What is the minimum position of safety distance?
options: 1.25 metres, the standard distance
2.75 metres, as for OLE
5 metres, because of the high speed
2 metres from the nearest rail
questions.rationale: Above 100 mph and up to 125 mph the minimum is 2 m.

questions.stem: Where should you be standing at least 10 seconds before a train arrives?
options: In your position of safety
Walking towards your position of safety
Picking up your last tool
Halfway across the line
questions.rationale: Be settled and clear with time to spare.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to wait until you see the train before moving to safety?
options: You may not be able to read its number
The driver may not see you waving
You may not have enough time to get clear
You will miss the horn
questions.rationale: Move on the warning.

questions.stem: What should you do if your position of safety is on loose, sloping ballast?
options: Dig your heels into the ballast
Hold on to the rail so you cannot slide down
Find firmer ground or raise it with the COSS
Kneel down to stay low
questions.rationale: Positions of safety must be stable.

questions.stem: What should you do if a passing train throws up loose ballast?
options: Stay back and protect your face
Lean forward to watch it
Turn your back and step closer
Pick up the stones
questions.rationale: Wear eye protection where required.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a refuge?
options: A gap between two parked trains
A recess in a tunnel wall
The area under a platform overhang
The space behind a signal post
questions.rationale: Refuges are purpose-built recesses.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find a refuge full of rubbish?
options: Stand in front of it instead
Squeeze in when a train comes
Report it so it can be cleared
Throw the rubbish onto the track
questions.rationale: Blocked refuges are not safe.

questions.stem: Why are positions of safety checked again when work moves along the line?
options: To keep people busy between trains
Conditions change from place to place
To give the lookout a rest
To count the trains
questions.rationale: Each location may differ.

questions.stem: What is the danger of standing between a passing train and a stack of rails?
options: The rails might rust
The driver cannot see the rails
There is no danger
You could be trapped or struck
questions.rationale: Avoid narrow gaps next to trains.

questions.stem: How should you stand when a train passes your position of safety?
options: With your back to the train
Crouching close to the rail
Facing the train, balanced and alert
Sitting on the ballast to keep low
questions.rationale: Be ready to react.

questions.stem: Why should you not shelter behind a lineside cabinet as a position of safety?
options: It is always electrically live
It may not give enough clearance
It is reserved for lookouts
It blocks the drainage
questions.rationale: Use proper positions of safety only.

questions.stem: What should you do if two trains pass your position of safety at the same time on adjacent lines?
options: Move towards the slower train
Stay put until both have passed and it is safe
Move towards the slower train, which is less dangerous
Step back towards the work
questions.rationale: Wait for confirmation.

questions.stem: At a site where the cess is only 1 m wide on a 90 mph line, what does this suggest?
options: The cess may not be a position of safety
The cess is ideal for working
Trains will slow down because of the narrow cess
You can stand sideways in it
questions.rationale: 1.25 m is the minimum at that speed.

questions.stem: What is the best way to know where your positions of safety are on a long site?
options: Ask the driver of the first train where to stand
Follow the lookout
Have them identified in the briefing and on site
Ask the train driver
questions.rationale: Know them in advance.

questions.stem: Why is the position of safety distance measured from the nearest rail rather than the centre of the track?
options: The centre is hard to find
The rail is closest to the train's side
The centre moves with the train
It is much easier to measure from a rail than from anywhere else
questions.rationale: Trains overhang the rails.

questions.stem: What should you do if a position of safety is 'just about' far enough?
