options: Choose somewhere with a comfortable margin
Use it, as it meets the rule
Lean back when trains pass
Hold on to the fence firmly when trains go past
questions.rationale: Extra margin is safer.

questions.stem: Which of these would NOT stop a place being a position of safety?
options: It is 1 m from a 75 mph line
It is shaded from the sun
It is on a crumbling slope
It is between two open lines
questions.rationale: Shade does not affect safety.

questions.stem: Why should you keep your arms by your sides when a train passes?
options: So the driver cannot see you
So that the driver can see you are not waving at them
So you look professional
So nothing extends towards the train
questions.rationale: Keep everything clear.

questions.stem: What should you do with a loose hi-vis jacket flapping in the wind as a train approaches?
options: Take it off and hold it up
Let it flap so the driver sees it
Fasten it or hold it secure
Throw it clear of the line
questions.rationale: Loose clothing can be drawn towards trains.

questions.stem: Why is a position of safety behind a fence better than in an open cess?
options: The fence slows trains down
The fence hides you from drivers
The fence stops you moving towards the line
The fence is electrified to keep people back
questions.rationale: Physical barriers add protection.

questions.stem: What is the main hazard of standing in the cess on the outside of a curve?
options: The cess is always narrower there
Trains go slower on curves
Trains may lean and appear suddenly
Signals are harder to read
questions.rationale: Curves affect sighting and clearance.

questions.stem: Why should you not stand on a platform edge as a position of safety?
options: Passengers on the platform might complain about workers being there
It is reserved for station staff
There is no clearance from a passing train
It is too high to stand on safely
questions.rationale: Platform edges are close to trains.

questions.stem: What should a COSS do if a position of safety becomes unusable during work?
options: Carry on and tell people to improvise
Ask everyone to stand closer together
Stop and arrange a new one
Use the six-foot instead
questions.rationale: Every person must have a usable position of safety.

questions.stem: Why should your position of safety not require you to climb?
options: Climbing is against dress code
Drivers cannot see climbers
Climbing takes time and risks a fall
It wastes energy
questions.rationale: Reaching safety should be quick and simple.

questions.stem: If a train is passing and you start to slip, what should you do?
options: Lower your centre of gravity away from the train
Grab the train for support
Grab hold of the passing train to steady yourself
Jump towards the train
questions.rationale: Move away from the train, not towards it.

questions.stem: Why do faster lines need positions of safety further away?
options: Faster trains are longer than slower ones
Faster trains create stronger air pressure
Faster trains have bigger wheels
Faster lines have wider tracks
questions.rationale: Air turbulence increases with speed.

questions.stem: What should you do after a train passes if you are not sure another is coming?
options: Go back to work quickly while the line is clear
Cross to look down the line
Shout to ask the driver
Stay in safety until it is confirmed clear
questions.rationale: Wait for confirmation.

questions.stem: What is a 'cess position of safety'?
options: A safe place in the cess clear of the nearest line
Any part of the ballast shoulder
Any part of the ballast shoulder next to the sleepers
The space next to a signal
questions.rationale: It must meet the distance and stability requirements.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of limited clearance signs at structures?
options: To warn there is no position of safety
To show the train speed
To show staff where they are allowed to park
To mark refuges for drivers
questions.rationale: Do not be there when trains pass unless protected.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are caught in a limited clearance area and hear a train?
options: Lie flat in the four-foot
Stand still against the wall
Get to the nearest refuge or clear area at once
Stand still with your back pressed against the wall
questions.rationale: You should never be there unprotected; get clear immediately.

questions.stem: Who should know where every person's position of safety is?
options: Only the COSS
The COSS and each person
Only the lookout
Only the newest worker
questions.rationale: Everyone must know their own.

questions.stem: Why should you not run to your position of safety on uneven ground?
options: It wastes energy you need for the work
You could fall towards the line
It confuses the lookout
It annoys the driver
questions.rationale: Move quickly but safely.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to wait in a refuge?
options: Leaning out to see the train
Fully inside, facing the line, holding still
Half in and half out
Leaning out slightly so you can see the train coming
questions.rationale: Stay fully inside.

questions.stem: Why might a position of safety at night need extra lighting?
options: So drivers can see your face
So that drivers can see your face as they pass
So you can reach it safely and see the ground
So lookouts can sleep
questions.rationale: Lighting helps safe movement.

questions.stem: What should you do if your group is too big for the refuges available?
options: Share refuges by squeezing in
Let some stand in the cess
Reduce the group or use a safer system of work
Share the refuges by squeezing two people into each one
questions.rationale: Everyone needs a safe place.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign your position of safety is too close?
options: You can see the driver
You can clearly hear the train's horn before it comes into view
Passing trains make you stagger
You can see the signals
questions.rationale: Report it so it can be reviewed.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the position of safety rules?
options: To keep you in sight of the lookout
To keep you clear of trains and their air turbulence
To keep you in sight of the lookout at all times
To stop drivers sounding horns
questions.rationale: Distance protects you.

questions.stem: What is the main duty of a lookout?
options: To carry the group's tools to site and guard them there
To carry the group's tools to site and guard them while the work goes on
To operate the signals so trains stop for the group
To watch for trains and warn the group in time to get clear
questions.rationale: The lookout's warning must give everyone time to reach a position of safety at least 10 seconds before the train arrives.

questions.stem: Who appoints and briefs a lookout?
options: The signaller who controls trains through the site
The driver of the first train through the area
The signaller who controls train movements through the work site
The COSS or person in charge of the safe system of work
questions.rationale: The COSS (or person in charge) appoints competent lookouts and briefs them.

questions.stem: Where must a lookout stand while on duty?
options: In the four-foot, facing the group they protect
Next to the group in the six-foot between lines
In a position of safety with a clear view of trains
Next to the group in the six-foot between lines, so they can be heard
questions.rationale: A lookout must not put themselves at risk. RAIB has investigated lookouts killed while on duty.

questions.stem: May a lookout do other work while acting as lookout?
options: Yes, provided the COSS has agreed to it during the briefing
Yes, during quiet periods between trains
Yes, provided the COSS has agreed to it
No, a lookout must only carry out lookout duties
questions.rationale: Any distraction can mean a missed train.

questions.stem: May a lookout use a mobile phone while on duty?
options: Yes, to call the signaller about delays
Yes, if using a hands-free headset
Yes, if it is used only to call the signaller about delays
No, it would distract them from watching for trains
questions.rationale: A lookout must give their full attention to approaching trains.

questions.stem: What must a lookout do if their view of approaching trains becomes reduced, for example by fog?
options: Carry on and rely on listening harder for trains
Move into the four-foot to see further along the line
Tell the group to work faster to finish before it worsens
Warn the group to stop and move clear, then tell the COSS
questions.rationale: If sighting is reduced, the required warning time cannot be given.

questions.stem: Why is 'sighting distance' important for a lookout?
options: It decides how much warning the lookout can give
It decides how far the group can walk
It decides the colour of the warning flag
It decides how far the group can walk from the access point
questions.rationale: The lookout must be able to see trains far enough away to give the minimum warning time.

questions.stem: What is the 'minimum warning time'?
options: The interval between trains shown in the working timetable
The time a driver needs to bring a train to a stand
Time to stop work, clear the line and be safe 10 s before a train
The time the COSS needs to complete the briefing forms
questions.rationale: Minimum warning time is calculated for the specific work, group and site.

questions.stem: Which of these should be included when working out minimum warning time?
options: Only the braking distance of the fastest train that uses the line
Only the braking distance of the fastest train on the line
Time to stop, clear equipment and walk to safety, plus 10 s
Only the 10-second margin, as the rest varies too much
questions.rationale: All the steps needed to get clear must be included.

questions.stem: Approximately how many metres per second is 100 mph?
options: About 27 m/s
About 45 m/s
About 62 m/s
About 100 m/s
questions.rationale: 1 mph is about 0.447 m/s, so 100 mph is about 44.7 m/s.

questions.stem: Roughly what is 50 mph when converted to metres per second?
options: About 13 m/s
About 31 m/s
About 50 m/s
About 22 m/s
questions.rationale: 50 x 0.447 is about 22.4 m/s.

questions.stem: A lookout needs the line speed in metres per second. For a 75 mph line, which figure is closest?
options: About 20 m/s
About 45 m/s
About 34 m/s
About 60 m/s
questions.rationale: 75 x 0.447 is about 33.5 m/s.

questions.stem: At 125 mph, about how many metres does a train cover every second?
options: About 45 m/s
About 70 m/s
About 56 m/s
About 35 m/s
questions.rationale: 125 x 0.447 is about 55.9 m/s.

questions.stem: At 60 mph, how much line does a train cover during a 30-second warning time?
options: About 536 metres
About 1,073 metres
About 400 metres
About 805 metres
questions.rationale: 60 mph is about 26.8 m/s. 26.8 x 30 is about 805 m.

questions.stem: A train at 100 mph travels roughly how far in 30 seconds?
options: About 1,341 metres
About 894 metres
About 1,800 metres
About 670 metres
questions.rationale: 100 mph is about 44.7 m/s. 44.7 x 30 is about 1,341 m.

questions.stem: For 20 seconds of warning on a 125 mph line, roughly what sighting distance is needed?
options: About 894 metres
About 1,400 metres
About 560 metres
About 1,118 metres
questions.rationale: 125 mph is about 55.9 m/s. 55.9 x 20 is about 1,118 m.

questions.stem: A COSS needs 20 seconds of warning on a 75 mph line. About how far must the lookout be able to see?
options: About 671 metres
About 447 metres
About 894 metres
About 1,000 metres
questions.rationale: 75 mph is about 33.5 m/s. 33.5 x 20 is about 671 m.

questions.stem: On a 40 mph freight line with a 25-second warning time, roughly what sighting distance is needed?
options: About 358 metres
About 600 metres
About 447 metres
About 250 metres
questions.rationale: 40 mph is about 17.9 m/s. 17.9 x 25 is about 447 m.

questions.stem: Trains run at 90 mph and the group needs 25 seconds of warning. Which sighting distance is closest to the minimum?
options: About 805 metres
About 1,006 metres
About 1,250 metres
About 600 metres
questions.rationale: 90 mph is about 40.2 m/s. 40.2 x 25 is about 1,006 m.

questions.stem: How far does a 50 mph train move during a 30-second warning?
options: About 671 metres
About 447 metres
About 894 metres
About 1,341 metres
questions.rationale: 50 mph is about 22.4 m/s. 22.4 x 30 is about 671 m.

questions.stem: A train at 80 mph is 15 seconds away from the site. Roughly how far away is it?
options: About 358 metres
About 715 metres
About 1,200 metres
About 536 metres
questions.rationale: 80 mph is about 35.8 m/s. 35.8 x 15 is about 536 m.

questions.stem: If a 110 mph train is 20 seconds from the site, about how far away is it?
options: About 805 metres
About 983 metres
About 1,229 metres
About 600 metres
questions.rationale: 110 mph is about 49.2 m/s. 49.2 x 20 is about 983 m.

questions.stem: On a 30 mph line, what distance does a train cover in 20 seconds?
options: About 268 metres
About 179 metres
About 402 metres
About 600 metres
questions.rationale: 30 mph is about 13.4 m/s. 13.4 x 20 is about 268 m.

questions.stem: A group needs 5 seconds to stop work, 5 seconds to clear equipment and 10 seconds to walk to safety. What is the minimum warning time?
options: 20 seconds
25 seconds
15 seconds
30 seconds
questions.rationale: 5 + 5 + 10 = 20 seconds, plus the 10-second margin gives 30 seconds.

questions.stem: A group needs 8 seconds to stop work and clear the line, and 7 seconds to reach safety. What is the minimum warning time?
options: 25 seconds
15 seconds
20 seconds
35 seconds
questions.rationale: 8 + 7 = 15 seconds, plus 10 seconds gives 25 seconds.

questions.stem: A group needs 12 seconds to clear the line and 8 seconds to walk to safety. What is the minimum warning time?
options: 20 seconds
22 seconds
30 seconds
40 seconds
questions.rationale: 12 + 8 = 20 seconds, plus 10 seconds gives 30 seconds.

questions.stem: Trains run at 100 mph and the minimum warning time is 25 seconds. Roughly what sighting distance is needed?
options: About 894 metres
About 1,118 metres
About 1,341 metres
About 671 metres
questions.rationale: 44.7 m/s x 25 s is about 1,118 m.

questions.stem: A lookout can see 600 metres along the line. Trains run at 60 mph. Roughly how much warning can the lookout give?
options: About 22 seconds
About 10 seconds
About 35 seconds
About 60 seconds
questions.rationale: 600 m / 26.8 m/s is about 22 seconds.

questions.stem: A lookout can see 1,000 metres. Trains run at 100 mph. Roughly how much warning can the lookout give?
options: About 10 seconds
About 45 seconds
About 22 seconds
About 100 seconds
questions.rationale: 1,000 m / 44.7 m/s is about 22 seconds.

questions.stem: A lookout can only see 500 metres on a 125 mph line. Roughly how much warning can they give?
options: Less than 10 seconds, which is not enough
About 30 seconds, which is more than the minimum needed
About 30 seconds, which is enough
About 50 seconds, which is plenty
questions.rationale: 500 m / 55.9 m/s is about 9 seconds, which is less than the 10-second margin alone.

questions.stem: Roughly how long does a train at 100 mph take to travel one mile?
options: About 60 seconds
About 36 seconds
About 10 seconds
About 100 seconds
questions.rationale: A mile is about 1,609 m. 1,609 / 44.7 is about 36 seconds.

questions.stem: Roughly how long does a train at 60 mph take to travel one mile?
options: About 30 seconds
About 2 minutes
About 1 minute
About 10 seconds
questions.rationale: At 60 mph a train covers one mile per minute.

questions.stem: If the line speed doubles but the warning time stays the same, what happens to the sighting distance needed?
options: It halves
It stays the same
It increases by 10 metres
It doubles
questions.rationale: Distance = speed x time, so double the speed needs double the distance.

questions.stem: If the minimum warning time increases from 20 seconds to 30 seconds at the same line speed, what happens to the sighting distance needed?
options: It doubles
It increases by half
It stays the same
It reduces by a third
questions.rationale: 30 is 1.5 times 20, so the distance needed is 1.5 times as much.

questions.stem: Which method of warning is generally considered the least safe?
options: Automatic Track Warning System (ATWS)
Unassisted lookout warning
A line blockage
A fenced safe area
questions.rationale: RAIB found unassisted lookout working was linked to many accidents. Network Rail has heavily restricted it.

questions.stem: What does ATWS stand for?
options: Automatic Track Warning System
Assisted Track Worker Supervision
Advanced Train Warning Signal
Approved Track Walking System
questions.rationale: ATWS detects approaching trains and gives warnings automatically.

questions.stem: How does an ATWS give warnings?
options: A lookout presses a button whenever they see a train coming
The signaller phones each member of the group in turn
Approaching drivers sound a special two-tone horn at the site
It detects trains automatically and gives sound and light warnings
questions.rationale: ATWS removes reliance on a human lookout to detect trains.

questions.stem: What does LOWS stand for?
options: Limited Overhead Wire Supervision
Lookout Operated Warning System
Limited Overhead Wire System
Local Operator Warning Station
questions.rationale: In LOWS a lookout triggers the warning, which is then given by equipment at the site.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of a LOWS over a lookout with a horn?
options: It needs no lookout at all once it has been set up
It applies the brakes of approaching trains automatically
It needs no lookout at all once the equipment has been set up at the site
Site equipment gives the warning, so the lookout can stand further away
questions.rationale: LOWS transmits the lookout's warning to sirens or beacons at the site.

questions.stem: What does TOWS stand for?
options: Track Overhead Wire System
Train Operated Warning System
Traffic Observation Warning Station
Timed Operator Warning Signal
questions.rationale: TOWS is a fixed installation where approaching trains trigger warnings at the lineside.

questions.stem: Where are train operated warning systems (TOWS) typically installed?
options: Inside signal boxes and rail operating centres, not on the lineside
Inside signal boxes and rail operating centres only
At fixed locations such as busy junctions where work is frequent
On the COSS's armband so it moves with the group
questions.rationale: TOWS is permanent lineside equipment triggered by trains approaching.

questions.stem: Why are hand-held radios not to be used to give warnings of approaching trains?
options: Radios need a separate licence for every lookout using them
Radios interfere with signals
Messages can fail, be missed or arrive late
Radios are only for drivers
questions.rationale: At Maesyfelin bridge in 2016, a radioed warning was not received and workers had to jump onto the parapet.

questions.stem: What should the group do when a lookout gives a warning?
options: Finish the task first so the line is left safe
Stop work immediately and move to the position of safety
Look for the train before deciding whether to move
Look for the train first, so you know which line to move away from
questions.rationale: Respond at once. Do not wait to see the train.

questions.stem: What should a lookout do if a member of the group does not respond to the warning?
options: Wave to the train driver to slow down instead of warning again
Give a further warning, including by touch if needed
Wave to the train driver to slow down instead
Leave the site and report it to the COSS later
questions.rationale: The lookout must make sure everyone has responded.

questions.stem: Which of these must a lookout be told in their briefing?
options: Which lines and directions to watch, and the warning time
The cost of the work and the deadline for finishing the job
The cost of the work and the deadline for finishing
The weather forecast for the rest of the week
questions.rationale: A lookout needs clear instructions to do the job.

questions.stem: What should a lookout do if they feel unwell or tired while on duty?
options: Carry on until the end of the shift
Sit down where they are and carry on watching as best they can
Ask a colleague to take over without telling anyone
Warn the group to stop work and move to safety, then tell the COSS
questions.rationale: An unfit lookout cannot protect the group.

questions.stem: What is a 'touch warning'?
options: A warning caused by a train's wheels touching the rail
A button on an ATWS that silences the alarm
Touching someone to warn them when they may not hear
A tap on the signal post telephone to call the signaller
questions.rationale: In noisy conditions, a touch warning makes sure the person knows to move.

questions.stem: Why can noisy equipment be dangerous when relying on audible warnings?
options: Noise from tools sets the signals to danger automatically
Workers may not hear the warning or the train
Noise from tools sets the signals to danger
Noise from tools stops ATWS from working
questions.rationale: At Margam in 2019 noise was a factor. Noisy work needs suitable warning arrangements.

questions.stem: Which of these conditions should cause a lookout to stop the work?
options: A train passes on a line further from the work
Their view is blocked or they cannot give enough warning
The group is working well and ahead of schedule
The sun comes out after a long period of rain and the group speeds up
questions.rationale: If the lookout cannot give enough warning, the group must not be on the line.

questions.stem: Can a lookout protect a group working at a location where sighting gives less than the minimum warning time?
options: Yes, as long as they stand closer to the approaching trains
No, a different safe system of work is needed
Yes, if they stand nearer the train
Yes, if the group works faster
questions.rationale: Insufficient sighting means lookout protection is not suitable.

questions.stem: What must a lookout do before handing over to another lookout?
options: Make sure the new lookout is briefed and in place first
Leave as soon as their booked time on duty ends
Tell the group to carry on without a lookout briefly
Hand over by radio while walking back to the van
questions.rationale: There must be no gap in protection.

questions.stem: What equipment does a lookout typically use to give a warning?
options: A hand-held radio linked to each worker
A mobile phone set to call the COSS
A horn or whistle that the whole group can hear
A hand-held radio linked to the earpiece of each member of the group
questions.rationale: Audible equipment gives a warning everyone can hear at once. Radios are not used for train warnings.

questions.stem: Why must a lookout be clearly identified?
options: So drivers know which person to report after the shift
So members of the public can find them if needed
So drivers know which person to report to after the shift
So the group knows who gives warnings and leaves them alone
questions.rationale: A lookout is identified, for example by an armband, so everyone knows their role.

questions.stem: Must a lookout hold a lookout competence?
options: Yes, they must be trained and assessed as competent
No, any PTS holder can act as lookout
No, if the COSS is present
No, any PTS holder can act as lookout for a short time
questions.rationale: Lookout duties need specific training and competence.

questions.stem: What is a site warden's main job in separated working?
options: To warn anyone about to leave the safe area towards the open line
To watch for trains and sound a horn when one approaches
To arrange line blockages with the signaller for the group
To check that everyone's PPE is correct at the access gate
questions.rationale: Site wardens keep people within the safe area. They do not warn of trains.

questions.stem: Which statement about lookouts and site wardens is correct?
options: Site wardens warn of trains, while lookouts guard the group's tools
Site wardens warn of trains; lookouts guard the group's tools
Lookouts warn of trains; site wardens keep people in the safe area
Both roles may also do light work when trains are not due
questions.rationale: Know the difference: lookouts detect trains, site wardens control the boundary.

questions.stem: From December 2025, what change did Network Rail make to lookout working?
options: It made a lookout mandatory on every work site
It allowed lookouts to give warnings by radio
It restricted lookout working to cases with no safer option
It allowed lookouts to give warnings by hand-held radio
questions.rationale: Lookout warning is now a last resort, with tight limits on where and when it can be used.

questions.stem: Roughly what proportion of Network Rail work activities used unassisted lookout working in 2023, according to RAIB?
options: About 25%
About 50%
About 75%
About 1%
questions.rationale: RAIB reported unassisted lookout working had fallen to about 1% of activities by 2023.

questions.stem: Which conditions make lookout warning unsuitable?
options: Bright daylight on long straight sections of track
Darkness, poor visibility, tunnels and complex junctions
Low line speeds with very long sighting distances
Light work in a wide cess on a quiet branch line
questions.rationale: Lookouts depend on seeing trains early. Conditions that reduce sighting make it unsafe.

questions.stem: What is the role of a distant lookout under older lookout arrangements?
options: To watch further along the line and relay warnings back
To stop approaching trains by showing a red flag
To stop approaching trains by showing them a red flag
To phone the signaller each time a train passes
questions.rationale: Distant and intermediate lookouts were used to extend sighting. They are now banned on Network Rail infrastructure.

questions.stem: In the Network Rail hierarchy, why is ATWS preferred to lookout warning?
options: It lets the work carry on while trains are passing the site
It detects trains automatically instead of relying on people
It does not need any planning before it is used
It lets the work continue while trains pass by
questions.rationale: Automatic detection reduces human error.

questions.stem: What should happen to the work when ATWS develops a fault?
options: Work continues and the group listens for trains instead
Work stops and everyone moves to safety until it is fixed
The COSS acts as lookout without changing the plan
The group works faster to finish before trains come
questions.rationale: Without the planned warning, the safe system of work is not in place.

questions.stem: If you can no longer hear a warning device because of your work noise, what should you do?
options: Carry on and look up often
Turn your ear defenders off
Ask the lookout to shout louder and carry on working
Stop and tell the COSS before carrying on
questions.rationale: You must be able to receive warnings at all times.

questions.stem: Why is 'looking up from time to time' not a safe system of work?
options: It is too tiring to do for a whole shift
A train could arrive while you are looking down
It is too tiring to keep up for the whole of a shift
It is only permitted during the night
questions.rationale: Informal practices like this have led to deaths, including at Margam in 2019.

questions.stem: When a lookout gives a warning, what should you do with your tools?
options: Leave them running in the four-foot so you can carry on
Finish the cut you are making before you put them down
Leave them running in the four-foot so you can carry on afterwards
Stop using them and clear them from the line if there is time
questions.rationale: Clear the line quickly if you can do so within the warning time.

questions.stem: Should a lookout give warnings for trains on a line that is blocked?
options: Never, because blocked lines have no movements
Only if the train driver sounds the horn first
Only if the approaching train is a passenger train
They must follow their briefing on which lines to watch
questions.rationale: Briefings explain exactly which lines and movements the lookout watches.

questions.stem: What is the danger of a lookout standing with the group in the work area?
options: The lookout will block the group's light at night
The lookout will block the group's light when working at night
The lookout could be struck and distracted by the work
There is no danger if the lookout is experienced
questions.rationale: At Newark North Gate (2014), a lookout moved into the path of a train and was killed.

questions.stem: What should a lookout do if they see a train approaching on a line they were not told to watch?
options: Ignore it as it is not their line
Wait to see which line it uses
Warn the group anyway and move them to safety
Ignore it, because it is not on a line they were told to watch
questions.rationale: If in doubt, warn.

questions.stem: What is the safest response if a lookout's warning seems to be a false alarm?
options: Ignore it if you cannot see a train
Ask the lookout to check again before anyone moves
Keep working until you hear the train
Move to safety anyway; never ignore a warning
questions.rationale: Always respond to every warning.

questions.stem: Why is it important that the lookout can see the whole group?
options: To check that everyone in the group is working hard
To check that everyone in the group is working hard enough
To make sure everyone has reached safety after a warning
To take photographs of the work for the client
questions.rationale: The lookout confirms that the group has responded.

questions.stem: What should happen if a lookout is needed but none is competent and available?
options: Anyone can act as lookout
The work must not go ahead on that basis
The COSS can work and look out at the same time
The group can listen for trains
questions.rationale: Never start work without the planned protection.

questions.stem: At Egmanton in 2017, what happened to a group of track workers?
options: They had to jump clear with under two seconds' warning
They were struck by overhead wires that had fallen
They were struck by overhead wires that had fallen in a storm
They were injured by a road vehicle at a crossing
questions.rationale: RAIB found confusion about the lookout's role and reluctance to challenge unsafe arrangements.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes 'red zone' working?
options: Working in an area with red signage
Working in areas marked with red signs or barriers
Working on or near a line that is open to trains
Working on a closed line
questions.rationale: Red zone working depends on warnings. Network Rail now aims to plan work on closed lines wherever possible.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes 'green zone' working?
options: Working only in grassy areas well away from structures, platforms and bridges
Working with a lookout who has a long sighting distance
Working where trains cannot reach you, or you are kept away from them
Working on any line during the night when trains are fewer
questions.rationale: Green zone arrangements include line blockages, possessions, and fenced or separated areas.

questions.stem: Why is green zone working preferred over red zone working?
options: It is always quicker to set up than red zone working
It does not need a briefing before the work starts
It is always quicker to set up and does not need a COSS or any briefing
It separates people from trains rather than relying on warnings
questions.rationale: Separation is the most effective control.

questions.stem: In the safe system of work hierarchy, which comes higher (safer)?
options: A fenced safe area
ATWS warning
Lookout warning
Unassisted lookout
questions.rationale: Safeguarded, fenced and separated systems sit above warning systems.

questions.stem: In the safe system of work hierarchy, which comes lowest (least safe)?
options: Safeguarded (line blocked)
Separated working
Lookout warning
ATWS warning
questions.rationale: Lookout warning relies entirely on a person seeing the train in time.

questions.stem: Which statement about warning systems is correct?
options: Warning systems stop trains automatically
A warning system does not stop trains; it only tells you to get clear
A warning system means you no longer need a position of safety
Warning systems remove the need for a position of safety
questions.rationale: You still need a position of safety and time to reach it.

questions.stem: What must you do if you are working with ATWS and the warning sounds?
options: Check your phone for a message
Wait for a second warning
Stop work and go to your position of safety
Look along the line for the train before deciding to move
questions.rationale: Treat every warning as real.

questions.stem: Why might a warning system be set up to warn for trains on adjacent lines too?
options: To test the equipment every time a train passes
Because the timetable requires it on all running lines
Trains on adjacent lines may pass close to the work
Because the timetable requires it on all lines
questions.rationale: Protection must cover all lines that put the group at risk.

questions.stem: What is the danger of a group spreading out along the line while using a single lookout?
options: Some people may be out of sight or hearing of the lookout
The work will take longer to complete overall
Train drivers will be confused by the spread
Train drivers will be confused by people spread along the line
questions.rationale: Stay within the area the lookout can protect.

questions.stem: What should the COSS check about the lookout before work starts?
options: That they are competent, fit, briefed and in the right place
That they know the passenger timetable by heart and can predict each train
That they own a car to get to the distant position
That they are the most senior person in the group
questions.rationale: Lookout arrangements must be checked before anyone goes on the line.

questions.stem: Which statement about lookouts and fatigue is correct?
options: Lookout duties are fine for tired people as they are not physical
Fatigued people must not be used as lookouts
Fatigue only affects drivers
Fatigue improves concentration
questions.rationale: Lookout duties need full concentration. Network Rail's fatigue standard restricts lookout duties when fatigue triggers are met.

questions.stem: What should a lookout do if a train approaches while the group is still not clear after the warning?
options: Stop warning and move further away from the line
Keep warning and, if needed, signal the driver to stop
Stop warning and move further away from the line themselves
Do nothing more, as the warning has been given
questions.rationale: Lookouts must keep trying to get the group clear.

questions.stem: Who should a lookout tell if they cannot continue lookout duties?
options: Their Primary Sponsor, before telling anyone on site
The COSS, after getting the group to stop and move clear
The driver of the next train to pass the site
Nobody, as long as the group can still see the line
questions.rationale: Make the group safe first, then tell the COSS.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the lookout's position being agreed in the briefing?
options: So they have a safe place with enough sighting for the warning
So the lookout has somewhere to rest during quiet spells
So the lookout can see the signal box and the signaller
So drivers know exactly where to stop their trains
questions.rationale: Position affects both the lookout's safety and sighting.

questions.stem: If the work moves along the line, what must happen to the lookout arrangements?
options: Nothing changes, because the original briefing still applies
The lookout follows the group along the four-foot
They must be reviewed so sighting and positions are still right
The lookout can stop, because the group knows the area
questions.rationale: Arrangements must suit the current location.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'warning' compared with 'protection'?
options: They mean exactly the same thing in the Rule Book
A warning tells you a train is coming; protection keeps it away
Protection is given by a horn, while a warning is given by showing a red flag
A warning stops trains; protection tells you to move
questions.rationale: Protection such as a line blockage is safer than relying on warnings.

questions.stem: Why did RAIB find that relying on human lookouts is risky?
options: Lookouts are not given any formal training
Lookouts cost too much to provide on every site
People can be distracted, misjudge trains or warn too late
Lookouts are not given any formal training or assessment
questions.rationale: Human error is a major factor in many track worker accidents.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a lookout's attitude to 'quiet' periods with no trains?
options: Relax until the next train in the timetable is due
Relax until the next train in the timetable is due to pass
Stay fully alert, because trains can come at any time
Check messages on a phone while the line is quiet
questions.rationale: Trains do not always follow timetables.

questions.stem: What should the group do after a warning once the train has passed?
options: Return immediately after the last vehicle passes
Return as soon as the last vehicle has gone past the site
Return once they can no longer hear the train
Wait until the lookout or COSS confirms it is safe to return
questions.rationale: There may be another train.

questions.stem: What is 'sighting' in track safety?
options: How far the signal box is from the site
How clearly the COSS can be seen by the group
How far along the line a train can be seen
How far the access point is from the work
questions.rationale: Sighting determines whether warning methods are suitable.

questions.stem: Which of these reduces sighting distance?
options: Short grass and low fencing in the cess on either side
Short grass and low fencing in the cess
Curves, structures, vegetation, fog and darkness
Wide open farmland on either side of the line
questions.rationale: Any of these can hide trains until they are close.

questions.stem: If a lookout is distracted by a conversation and misses a train, what does this show?
options: Lookout duties need total concentration and no distractions
Conversation helps lookouts stay awake on long shifts
Lookouts may chat during quiet times without risk
Trains should be told to slow down near lookouts
questions.rationale: Do not distract lookouts, and lookouts must not allow themselves to be distracted.

questions.stem: What is the danger of a COSS also acting as lookout while supervising the work?
options: They may be distracted and fail to see a train
They would be paid twice for the same shift
It is the safest arrangement on most sites
They would be paid twice for the same hours on the shift
questions.rationale: RAIB has highlighted risks when the same person leads the work and provides the lookout.

questions.stem: At Surbiton in 2021, a track worker was struck during an inspection. What system of work was in use?
options: A full line blockage
A line blockage with ATWS
An engineering possession
Unassisted lookout working
questions.rationale: RAIB noted this was the least safe system in the hierarchy. The accident sped up efforts to remove lookout working.

questions.stem: What is the safest assumption when you cannot hear a train because of wind?
options: Any train will be heard before it is close enough to matter
A train could still be approaching
Trains will sound louder later
The lookout will hear it for you
questions.rationale: Never rely on hearing trains.

questions.stem: What does SATWS stand for?
options: Site Assisted Train Watching Service
Semi-Automatic Track Warning System
Single Area Track Worker Safety
Standard Approved Train Warning Signal
questions.rationale: SATWS is activated automatically but reset manually.

questions.stem: How does SATWS differ from ATWS?
options: It is operated entirely by a lookout pressing a button
It is fixed permanently in the signal box, not on site
It uses train drivers' radios to send warnings to the group
It activates automatically but is reset manually
questions.rationale: Different warning systems sit at different levels of the hierarchy.

questions.stem: Which warning system relies entirely on a person seeing the train?
options: Train Operated Warning System
TOWS
SATWS
Lookout warning
questions.rationale: Lookout warning depends on human detection.

questions.stem: What is the role of the lookout in a LOWS arrangement?
options: To trigger the warning when a train is seen
To switch off the overhead line when a train comes
To phone the signaller to stop each train
To stand in the four-foot as a visual warning to drivers
questions.rationale: The equipment then gives the warning at the site.

questions.stem: Who decides the minimum warning time for a job?
options: Each worker decides how long they need to get clear
It is set in the planning and confirmed by the COSS
The train driver decides, based on line speed
The lookout decides on the day by watching trains
questions.rationale: Warning time is calculated for the specific site, group and task.

questions.stem: Why should warning time be checked again if the group changes size?
options: A bigger group makes trains run more slowly
Smaller groups do not need any warning at all
A bigger group may need longer to get clear
The lookout must be replaced when the group changes
questions.rationale: More people and equipment take longer to clear.

questions.stem: What is a 'site lookout'?
options: A camera that records the site for the client
A lookout who checks the site for trespassers
A lookout positioned with the group to warn them
A person who guards the van at the access point
questions.rationale: Older arrangements also used distant and intermediate lookouts.

questions.stem: What is an 'intermediate lookout' under older arrangements?
options: A lookout who works only half a shift
A trainee lookout supervised by another
A trainee lookout who is still being supervised by a qualified one
A lookout relaying warnings between distant and site lookouts
questions.rationale: Relay arrangements are now banned on Network Rail.

questions.stem: Why are relay lookout arrangements considered risky?
options: They cost too much for small jobs
They need too many radios and lots of spare batteries
They confuse train drivers
Each link adds a chance of delay or error
questions.rationale: Chains of warnings can fail. They are now prohibited on Network Rail.

questions.stem: A lookout cannot see trains on the approach because of a bridge. What is the right decision?
options: Stand on the bridge to get a better view
Rely on hearing trains as they cross the bridge
Ask drivers to slow down near the bridge
Use a different safe system of work
questions.rationale: If sighting is inadequate, lookout warning cannot be used.

questions.stem: Which of these is the lookout's responsibility after giving a warning?
options: Check that everyone has reached safety
Record the train's number for the paperwork
Tell the signaller that the group has moved
Wave to the driver to show the group is clear
questions.rationale: The lookout makes sure the group has responded.

questions.stem: What should the group do if they are not sure whether the lookout is watching?
options: Carry on and listen harder for trains
Look up more often while working
Stop work and check
Ask the newest member to keep watch
questions.rationale: Never work without confirmed protection.

questions.stem: Why must the lookout know the line speed?
options: To judge whether trains will reach the site within the warning time
To report speeding trains to the driver's manager
To report any trains that are speeding to the driver's manager
To decide the colour of the flag to use
questions.rationale: Speed affects how far away a train can be seen in time.

questions.stem: What should a lookout do if a train approaches faster than expected?
options: Wait until it is closer to be sure
Warn straight away
Check the timetable first
Phone the signaller to ask
questions.rationale: Warn as soon as a train is seen.

questions.stem: What should happen if the lookout's horn fails?
options: The lookout shouts warnings instead
Stop work until a working device is available
The lookout uses a phone alarm or shouts warnings instead
The group carries on and watches out
questions.rationale: The planned warning equipment must be working.

questions.stem: Why should a lookout stand where the group can see them?
options: So drivers can see who is in charge
So the lookout can supervise the work
So the group can see a warning even if they miss the sound
So that drivers can see who is in charge of the group
questions.rationale: Visual contact supports the audible warning.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between ATWS and TOWS?
options: ATWS is used only at night, while TOWS is used only during daylight hours
ATWS is temporary at a site; TOWS is fixed at a location
ATWS needs a lookout; TOWS needs a signaller
ATWS stops trains; TOWS only warns workers
questions.rationale: Both are automatic warnings, deployed differently.

questions.stem: What should you do if a warning system gives frequent false alarms?
options: Ignore it after the first false alarm
Turn it off to stop disruption
Only respond if you can see a train
Respond every time and report the fault
questions.rationale: Never assume a warning is false.

questions.stem: Why is 'warning fatigue' dangerous?
options: Warnings use too much battery
People may start to ignore real warnings
Warnings make trains slow down
Warnings stop the work for too long
questions.rationale: Every warning must be treated as real.

questions.stem: Who should brief the group on what the warning sounds like?
options: The train driver
The signaller
The client
The COSS
questions.rationale: Everyone must recognise the warning signal.

questions.stem: During lookout working, what should you do if you want to move to a different part of the site?
options: Tell the COSS and check you remain protected
Move quickly while no trains are coming
Ask the lookout to follow you
Move and let the lookout notice
questions.rationale: Protection covers a defined area.

questions.stem: What does 'unassisted lookout' mean?
options: A lookout warning without any automatic equipment
A lookout working with no COSS on site
A lookout who has not been trained or assessed
A lookout working only at weekends
questions.rationale: Unassisted lookout is the lowest level in the hierarchy.

questions.stem: Why might a lookout be given a different position after a train passes?
options: To give them a rest from standing in one spot
So drivers recognise them
To move them out of the sun
To keep the best sighting as conditions change
questions.rationale: Positions are chosen for sighting and safety.

questions.stem: What should the lookout do if the group moves out of their view?
options: Warn the group to stop and move back
Follow the group along the four-foot
Assume the group is safe
Phone the COSS
questions.rationale: The group must stay within protection.

questions.stem: Which of these is a lookout's essential piece of knowledge?
options: Where each person's position of safety is
The names of the train drivers
The cost of the work and who is paying for it
The location of the nearest shop
questions.rationale: Lookouts need to know the site and its safe places.

questions.stem: A lookout realises they gave a warning too late for one person. What should happen?
options: Stop and review the arrangements
Carry on, as nobody was hurt
Ask that person to work faster
Keep it quiet
questions.rationale: Near misses mean the protection is not adequate.

questions.stem: Why are lookouts not to stand in the six-foot between open lines?
options: They could be struck by trains on either line
The six-foot blocks their view of the group
The six-foot is reserved for signalling equipment
Standing there confuses drivers
questions.rationale: Lookouts must be in a position of safety.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign that warning time is too short?
options: People reach safety with time to spare
Trains pass well after people are clear
People are only just reaching safety as trains pass
The lookout waits a long time between trains
questions.rationale: Being clear only just in time means the system needs review.

questions.stem: What is the 10-second margin for in warning time calculations?
options: The time a train takes to brake
The time the lookout takes to blow the horn
The time drivers need to see workers
A safety buffer after reaching safety
questions.rationale: You must be in safety at least 10 seconds before the train arrives.

questions.stem: Which statement about ATWS is correct?
options: It stops trains automatically before the site
It isolates the overhead line when a train comes
It removes the need for positions of safety
It warns you; it does not stop trains
questions.rationale: You still need a position of safety and time to reach it.

questions.stem: Why is it important to test a warning system before work starts?
options: To warn the public that work is starting
To let the signaller know you have arrived
To make sure everyone can see and hear it
To use up old batteries
questions.rationale: A warning that cannot be received is useless.

questions.stem: During ATWS use, a train passes without the warning sounding. What should happen?
options: Carry on, as the train has passed
Stop work immediately and report the failure
Reset the system and carry on with the work
Ask the lookout to watch instead
questions.rationale: A failed warning is a serious incident.

questions.stem: Which is more reliable for detecting trains: a person or a properly working automatic system?
options: A properly working automatic system
A person, because they can think
Both are exactly the same
Neither can detect trains
questions.rationale: Automatic systems remove human error in detection.

questions.stem: What should you do if you cannot hear the warning because of wind?
options: Keep working
Tell the COSS
Ask for the horn to be blown more
Look up more often
questions.rationale: The arrangements must be changed if warnings cannot be heard.

questions.stem: Why might lookouts be given flags as well as horns?
options: To mark where the group's tools and materials are stored
So they can signal visually and, if needed, to drivers
To mark where tools are stored
To show which lookout is in charge
questions.rationale: Lookouts may need to give visual warnings.

questions.stem: What is the effect of a long walk to the position of safety on warning time?
options: It reduces the warning time needed
It has no effect
It removes the need for a lookout
It increases the warning time needed
questions.rationale: Every second of movement adds to warning time.

questions.stem: What should the COSS do if the lookout reports the train timetable has changed?
options: Nothing different: trains are always expected
Reduce the warning time
Let the group work through quiet spells
Stand the lookout down
questions.rationale: Timetables do not form part of protection.

questions.stem: Why are lookouts identified with armbands or similar?
options: So that they can claim the extra lookout payment
So everyone knows their role and does not distract them
So drivers know who to blame
So the public can find them
questions.rationale: Clear identification supports safety.

questions.stem: Who should a group member tell if they think the lookout has made a mistake?
options: The COSS
Nobody
The train driver
Their family
questions.rationale: Raise concerns straight away.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to deal with a lookout who keeps chatting to the group?
options: Join in the chat during quiet times
Stop work and get the COSS to sort it out
Ignore it
Ask them to whisper
questions.rationale: Lookouts must not be distracted.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'safe system of work' (SSOW) in track safety?
options: The planned arrangements that protect people from trains
The list of tools, materials and plant needed for a particular job
The induction course that new starters must attend
The timetable of trains that will pass during the shift
questions.rationale: A safe system of work sets out how people will be kept safe from trains and other hazards.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which is the safest type of safe system of work?
options: Lookout warning, with an experienced lookout on long straight track
Automatic track warning, with sirens fitted at both ends of the site
Safeguarded, where lines are blocked so no train can approach
Separated working, with a site warden watching the boundary
questions.rationale: Safeguarded working sits at the top of the hierarchy.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'fenced' working mean?
options: The railway boundary fence is in good condition
A physical barrier stops people from reaching the open line
The work area has a fence around the welfare cabin
A lookout stands next to the boundary fence to watch the line
questions.rationale: Fenced working uses a barrier between the work and any open line.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'separated' working mean?
options: The group splits into two teams that work at different ends
The work is done at a separate time from train movements
A 2 m gap is kept from the open line, controlled by a site warden
The lookout stands well away from the group to see further
questions.rationale: Separated working keeps everyone at least 2 m from any open line.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who is responsible for setting up the safe system of work on site for a group?
options: The COSS or person in charge of the safe system
The driver of the first train through the site, who checks it is clear
The driver of the first train through the site
The client's project manager in the office
questions.rationale: The COSS sets up, briefs and manages the safe system of work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What must the COSS do before the group goes on or near the line?
options: Phone each worker's next of kin to confirm details
Brief everyone on the safe system and check they understand
Collect everyone's Sentinel cards and keep them safe until the end
Collect everyone's Sentinel cards and keep them safe
questions.rationale: You must not go on the line until you have been briefed and understand the arrangements.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if you do not understand the COSS briefing?
options: Sign it anyway and ask a colleague later
Refuse to work without saying why
Ask questions until you understand before signing
Copy what the others do, as they have probably done it before
questions.rationale: Never sign a briefing you do not understand.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why are you asked to sign the briefing form?
options: To book any overtime you work on that shift with your sponsor afterwards
To confirm that your Sentinel card is still valid
To agree that you may work without some PPE
To confirm you were briefed and understand the arrangements
questions.rationale: Signing confirms your understanding. Only sign if you do understand.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these is usually covered in a COSS briefing?
options: The names of the drivers booked to work through the site
The names of the drivers booked to work trains through the site
Which lines are open, the warning method and positions of safety
The history of the line and when it was first built
questions.rationale: The briefing covers the hazards and the protection in place.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Must the COSS stay with the group while it is on or near the line?
options: No, the COSS can leave once work starts
Only during the first hour
No, once everyone is briefed the COSS can work elsewhere on site
Yes, the COSS must stay with and supervise the group
questions.rationale: RAIB has found that absent or ineffective leaders contribute to accidents.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does a COSS wear to identify themselves on many sites?
options: A blue armband marked COSS
A red helmet
A yellow vest
A green armband marked LOOKOUT
questions.rationale: The COSS is traditionally identified by a blue armlet or badge marked COSS.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if you think the safe system of work is not safe?
options: Start the work and report your concerns afterwards
Do the work anyway to avoid an argument on site
Leave the site without telling anyone why
Stop, challenge it and do not start until it is resolved
questions.rationale: You have the right and duty to challenge unsafe work. Network Rail calls this Worksafe.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the Worksafe procedure?
options: A form used for claiming travel and meal expenses
A shift pattern used for weekend engineering work
A form used for claiming travel and meal expenses after a shift
A process that lets you refuse work you believe is unsafe
questions.rationale: Worksafe lets anyone stop and challenge unsafe work without fear of being punished.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: At Maesyfelin bridge in 2016, what did the COSS do that RAIB said was dangerous?
options: Used unauthorised radio warnings instead of the planned system
Arranged a line blockage that had not been planned
Appointed more lookouts than the plan required, which confused the group
Refused to start work until the plan was changed
questions.rationale: Implementing unauthorised systems of work is dangerous and can lead to fatal accidents.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who arranges a line blockage with the signaller?
options: The driver of the train due through the site, using the cab radio
A competent person such as the COSS or person in charge
The driver of the train due through the site
The station manager at the nearest station
questions.rationale: Line blockages are arranged by competent people following the Rule Book.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: During a line blockage, how does the signaller protect the work?
options: By telling drivers to slow down to 20 mph through the site
By telling drivers to slow down to 20 mph through the work site
By keeping protecting signals at danger and letting no trains in
By switching off the track circuits for the section
questions.rationale: The signaller must not let trains into the blocked section.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'possession' used for?
options: To run extra passenger trains on the line for special events
To test new trains before they enter service
To close lines for larger engineering work, often for hours
To run extra passenger trains for special events
questions.rationale: Possessions allow major work. Engineering trains may still move within them.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who is in charge of a possession?
options: The signaller controlling the area (signaller)
The Person in Charge of the Possession (PICOP)
The lookout at the possession limit (PLO)
The Engineering Supervisor of each worksite (ES)
questions.rationale: The PICOP arranges and manages the possession.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who manages a worksite within a possession?
options: The Person in Charge of the Possession
The lookout at the worksite marker board
The Engineering Supervisor (ES)
The guard of the engineering train
questions.rationale: Each worksite has an ES who controls access and movements within it.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Before entering a worksite in a possession, what must the COSS do?
options: Tell the driver of the engineering train that the group is going in
Get permission from the Engineering Supervisor
Ask the signaller to open the line
Nothing, the possession protects everyone
questions.rationale: The ES controls who enters the worksite.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Within a worksite, what hazard still exists?
options: No hazards, because the line is closed
Only passenger trains that were not told about the possession
Only hazards from road traffic
Engineering trains and on-track plant can move
questions.rationale: Movements within the worksite are controlled but still dangerous.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: How are the ends of a possession usually marked?
options: With orange cones in the cess
With chalk marks on the rail
With possession limit boards and detonators
With a lookout at each end watching for approaching trains
questions.rationale: Boards and detonators warn drivers and mark the protected area.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is placing and removing possession protection equipment a risky task?
options: The equipment is very heavy and must be carried a long way
It must be done in daylight
Staff may be near open lines when doing it
It must be done by the driver
questions.rationale: RAIB has investigated deaths during placement or removal of protection, including at Stoats Nest Junction.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'safe work pack'?
options: A first aid kit kept in the COSS's vehicle
A bag of spare PPE for visitors on site
The planned documents for the work and its safe system
A first aid kit kept in the COSS's vehicle for emergencies
questions.rationale: The safe work pack sets out the plan the COSS follows on site.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should the COSS do if site conditions differ from the safe work pack?
options: Stop and get the plan changed before work goes ahead
Make up a new plan on the spot without telling anyone
Carry on as planned
Leave the site and report next week
questions.rationale: Changes must be properly managed, not improvised.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: At Morton Junction in 2024, what problem did RAIB find with the safe work pack?
options: The pack had been printed in the wrong language
The COSS was unknowingly using a pack for another location
The pack had not been signed by the planner before it was issued to site
The pack listed more lookouts than were available
questions.rationale: Check that documents match the location and the work every time, even for familiar tasks.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why did RAIB find the planning system at Margam in 2019 was unsafe?
options: It always required more lookouts than were available to the team
It did not include any line blockages for maintenance work at all
It let a COSS fall back to a less safe method if a blockage was refused
It required all maintenance to be done at night in darkness
questions.rationale: Parallel safe work packs let groups default to lookout working. Network Rail changed its planning to remove this.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a Safe Work Leader (SWL)?
options: The person who leads safe work on site under Network Rail planning
A signaller who takes charge of a possession from the control room
A train driver who leads engineering trains into a worksite
The national manager responsible for running the Sentinel scheme
questions.rationale: Network Rail introduced Safe Work Leaders to lead work safely, including the safe system of work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the role of the Person in Charge (PIC) on site?
options: To take charge of the work and the safety of those doing it
To act as the lookout for the group at all times
To issue Sentinel cards to new members of the group
To act as the lookout for the group at all times during the work
questions.rationale: The person in charge must personally observe and advise the people under their control.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does RAIB say is the most effective way of reducing risk to track workers?
options: Using more lookouts
Separating people from trains
Training drivers to stop faster
Working faster to spend less time on track
questions.rationale: By the end of 2023, over 99% of Network Rail work activities were done on lines closed to traffic.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if the COSS leaves the site without appointing a replacement?
options: Stop work and move clear of the line
Carry on, as you were briefed
Carry on, as you were briefed before the COSS left the site
Ask the lookout to take charge
questions.rationale: Without the COSS, the safe system of work is not being managed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: When a new person joins a group already on site, what must happen?
options: They can copy what the others are doing until briefed
They must be briefed by the COSS before going on the line
They can copy what the others are doing until they can be briefed
They only need to show their Sentinel card to start
questions.rationale: Everyone must be briefed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why must the COSS check everyone's competence before work starts?
options: To find out who is the fastest worker in the group
To find out who is the fastest worker so they get the hardest tasks
To decide who will drive the van home afterwards
To make sure only competent people go on or near the line
questions.rationale: The COSS checks Sentinel cards and competencies.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should happen if the planned line blockage is refused by the signaller?
options: The group should switch to lookout warning to keep to time
The group should work faster to reduce time on the line
The COSS should place detonators to block the line themselves
The work should not go ahead under a less safe improvised method
questions.rationale: The lesson from Margam is not to fall back to unsafe methods.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is meant by 'informal' or 'local' unsafe practices?
options: Unofficial methods that become routine but skip the plan
Approved local instructions published for a depot
Approved local instructions published for a particular depot or yard
Practices agreed in advance with the signaller
questions.rationale: RAIB found informal unsafe practices at Margam had been in use for a long time.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is 'peer pressure' a safety risk on track?
options: It causes people to wear more PPE than the task really needs
People may not challenge unsafe practices to fit in
It causes people to wear more PPE than needed
It makes briefings take longer than they should
questions.rationale: RAIB highlighted peer pressure at Ruscombe Junction and elsewhere.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these is a duty of every member of a work group?
options: Choose their own safe system of work for each task
Follow the briefing and tell the COSS about any danger
Brief the signaller on the work before it starts
Choose their own safe system of work for each task they do
questions.rationale: Everyone has personal responsibility for their safety and others'.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if you see the COSS doing something unsafe?
options: Challenge them and, if not resolved, stop and report it
Do nothing, because the COSS is in charge and must know what they are doing
Copy them, because they are more experienced
Leave the site quietly without saying anything
questions.rationale: Even leaders can make mistakes. Littlehempston showed a COSS's own actions can put a group at risk.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who can stop work if it is unsafe?
options: Only the COSS
Only the signaller
Anyone
Only Network Rail managers
questions.rationale: Everyone has the right to stop unsafe work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: When must you tell the COSS you have left the line?
options: Only at the end of the shift
Only if you are injured
Only at the end of the shift when you sign out
Every time you leave the site or the group
questions.rationale: The COSS must know where everyone is.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What must the COSS confirm before giving up a line blockage?
options: That everyone and everything is clear of the line
That the signaller has finished their shift
That the timetable is back on time
That the signaller has finished their own shift
questions.rationale: Lines must not be given back until they are safe for trains.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'Hand-back' at the end of a possession?
options: To return tools to the store
To hand PPE back to the sponsor
To return tools and PPE to the stores at the end
To return the line safely to traffic
questions.rationale: Lines must be safe and clear before trains run again.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What are possession protection detonators for?
options: To blast rock in cuttings during engineering work
To light up the worksite during night shifts
To signal the end of the shift to the work groups
To give an audible warning to a driver nearing the limit
questions.rationale: Detonators explode with a loud bang when a train runs over them.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these is a 'protected' arrangement rather than a 'warning' arrangement?
options: A lookout
A line blockage
A lookout with a long sighting distance
LOWS
questions.rationale: Protection stops trains entering. Warnings tell you to get clear.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who should you tell if your Sentinel competence will expire before the end of a job?
options: Nobody, it does not matter
Your sponsor and your supervisor
Nobody, as long as it is valid when you start
The train driver
questions.rationale: Only work with valid competence.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why might more than one COSS be on a large site?
options: So that all groups can share a single briefing
Each group needs its own COSS for its safe system
So that all the groups on site can share a single briefing
So that the work can be finished more quickly
questions.rationale: Each group must be under the control of a COSS.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does it mean if a line is 'open to traffic'?
options: It is open to the public
Trains can run on it
It is closed for work
It has no signals
questions.rationale: An open line is a danger unless a safe system protects you.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the 'planning' stage of a safe system of work meant to do?
options: Decide which members of the team will get overtime
Identify hazards and choose the safest practicable system
Choose the colour and type of PPE for the job
Decide which members of the team will be offered overtime
questions.rationale: Good planning puts more work on closed lines and avoids hazards.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which statement about safe systems of work is correct?
options: A plan must suit the actual site conditions on the day
A plan that has worked before at a site will always be valid again
Plans only matter for large renewals, not small jobs
A plan that worked before will always be valid again
questions.rationale: Weather, time and site changes can make a plan unsafe.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What must you have before you can work on or near the line alone?
options: Verbal permission from an experienced colleague who knows the area
Verbal permission from an experienced colleague
The Individual Working Alone (IWA) competence and authority
A lookout watching from the far end of the site
questions.rationale: Working alone needs a separate competence because you are responsible for your own protection.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who is responsible for a track visitor's safety on site?
options: The visitor, once they have been briefed
The competent person escorting them
The driver of any train that passes
The signaller controlling the area
questions.rationale: Track visitors must be escorted and supervised at all times.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why must you not let a track visitor wander away from you?
options: They might get lost on the way back to the access point
They might miss their train home after the visit
They might see work that the client wants kept private
They do not have the training to keep themselves safe
questions.rationale: Visitors rely on their escort for protection.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'machine controller' (MC)?
options: A person who repairs machines in a depot
A signaller who controls trains
A person who repairs and services machines in a depot
A person who controls the movement of on-track plant
questions.rationale: Machine controllers guide plant movements to keep people safe.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why must you stay out of the working radius of on-track plant?
options: You could be struck by the machine or its load
It slows down the work for the machine operator
It is much too noisy to stand near the machine
It confuses the signaller watching the site
questions.rationale: Keep clear unless the machine controller says it is safe to approach.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: How should you approach on-track plant that is working?
options: Only after eye contact with the operator and the controller's agreement
From behind the machine, where it is quieter and out of the way
Quickly while it is moving, so you do not hold up the work
From behind the machine, where it is quieter and you are out of the operator's way
questions.rationale: Operators may not see you. Get clear agreement before approaching.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'blind spot' on plant?
options: An area around a machine the operator cannot see
A dark area inside a tunnel with no lighting
A signal that is hidden from the driver's view
A dark area inside a tunnel where there is no lighting
questions.rationale: Never stand in a machine's blind spot.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does the COSS need to know about every person in the group?
options: Their home address and next of kin details
Their home address and the details of their next of kin
Their shoe size for ordering safety boots
Who they are, their competence and where they are
questions.rationale: The COSS must account for everyone.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should happen if the weather worsens and reduces visibility during work with a warning system?
options: Work should continue as planned
The group should carry on but work faster to finish
The COSS should stop work and review the safe system
The lookout should move closer to the group
questions.rationale: Changes in conditions can make a safe system unsafe.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is it important to plan work at a time when lines can be closed?
options: So the work looks better
So it can be done more slowly
So people can work without trains passing
So the work can be done more slowly and carefully
questions.rationale: Planning work in closures is the most effective safety measure.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'competence' recorded on Sentinel?
options: A record of your pay and any overtime you have worked
A record of your pay and any overtime you have worked this year
The travel pass that lets you use trains for free
A qualification showing you are trained and assessed for a task
questions.rationale: Sentinel records the competences you hold and when they expire.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these should you NOT do during a COSS briefing?
options: Use your phone and not listen
Ask questions
Check which lines are open
Confirm your position of safety
questions.rationale: The briefing is critical safety information.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: When must a briefing be repeated or updated?
options: Only at the start of the shift
Only if someone asks
Only at the start of the shift, never during the work
When the arrangements change during the work
questions.rationale: Any change must be briefed to everyone affected.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should the COSS do if a member of the group appears unfit for duty?
options: Let them work if they are experienced
Give them lookout duties
Ask them to work slower
Not allow them on or near the line
questions.rationale: Unfit people must not work on the railway.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why should the COSS have a means of communication with the signaller?
options: To find out train times for lunch
To arrange protection and report emergencies
To find out the train times for planning breaks
To check the weather
questions.rationale: Reliable communication is part of a safe system of work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if you see a member of another group in danger?
options: Leave it to their COSS
Take a photograph
Warn them immediately
Report it at the end of the week
questions.rationale: Look out for everyone, not just your own group.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'line blockage' protect against?
options: Trespassers getting onto the site through the fence
Road vehicles crossing at nearby level crossings
Trespassers getting onto the site through gaps in the fence
Trains entering the section where people are working
questions.rationale: Line blockages stop trains from entering.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: When a line is blocked, what about adjacent lines?
options: They are always blocked as well during the work
Trains on them must pass at walking speed while you work
Trains on them must pass at walking speed
They may still be open, so you must stay clear of them
questions.rationale: Check exactly which lines are blocked.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'T3' or 'possession' type arrangement in older terminology?
options: A type of colour-light signal used at junctions
A class of diesel train used for engineering
A type of protective clothing that must be worn by everyone inside possessions
A possession for engineering work with protection at its limits
questions.rationale: Older terms such as T2 and T3 described types of line blockage and possession.
