questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: If you hear a train on a line you were told was blocked, what should you do?
options: Ignore it, because the line has been blocked
Ignore it, because the line has been blocked for the group
Keep working and keep an eye on the train
Get to a position of safety at once and tell the COSS
questions.rationale: Mistakes happen. Always react to an approaching train.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which document describes the possession arrangements for engineering work?
options: The information stored on each worker's Sentinel card
The Weekly Operating Notice or possession planning documents
The public timetable printed for passengers
The Highway Code for road vehicles near the line
questions.rationale: Possessions are planned and published in advance.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why might the COSS refuse to let you start work even though you are competent?
options: Because they have not worked with you before
Because the sun is too bright to see trains
Because the safe system of work is not yet in place
Because the sun is too bright for the lookout to see trains
questions.rationale: Competence alone does not make it safe.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'permission to work' from the Engineering Supervisor mean?
options: Trains may now run through the worksite again
The possession has finished and lines are open
Trains may now run through the worksite again at normal speed
The COSS's group may enter the worksite on agreed terms
questions.rationale: The ES gives permission to enter and work in the worksite.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why should you not move outside the agreed worksite limits?
options: You might get lost and miss the end of shift
It is outside the area you are paid to work in
You may enter an area that is not protected
The ES will not be able to see you there
questions.rationale: At Stoats Nest, staff were killed after moving outside the protected area.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the best description of the COSS's role?
options: To make sure the work is finished as fast as possible
To make sure the work is finished as quickly as possible
To deliver tools and materials to the group
To protect the group from trains through a safe system
questions.rationale: The COSS's focus is the group's safety from train movements.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should the COSS do when all work is finished?
options: Confirm everyone is clear, then end the safe system
Leave first to hand back the protection quickly
Leave first to hand back the protection as quickly as possible
Let people leave the site by any route they like
questions.rationale: Everyone must be clear before protection is removed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the risk of having two safe work packs for the same work and location?
options: People may choose the less safe option
It doubles the paperwork only
It slows the work
It doubles the paperwork, but there is no safety risk
questions.rationale: Network Rail no longer allows parallel packs in its RailHub planning system after Margam.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these is an example of 'component working' in planning?
options: Manufacturing track components in a factory before the work
Planning every job so that it uses lookout warning only
Working without a plan when a small job comes up
Building a plan from approved parts, not parallel safe work packs
questions.rationale: Component working in RailHub replaced multiple parallel packs.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why do managers need to monitor work on site and not just check documents?
options: Documents are always completed wrongly
Unsafe practices may only be visible on site
Managers prefer visiting sites to office work
Site visits reduce the amount of paperwork
questions.rationale: At Margam, managers relied on document checks and missed unsafe site practices.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why might zero-hours or contract workers be reluctant to challenge unsafe practices?
options: Fear of losing future work
They are less trained
They do not hold PTS
They are not allowed to speak
questions.rationale: RAIB highlighted this at Egmanton and elsewhere. A just culture makes challenge normal.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'just culture'?
options: A culture where every mistake is punished strictly and quickly
A legal process used to decide who caused an accident
A training course that all new COSSs must complete
A culture where people can report and challenge without unfair blame
questions.rationale: Just culture encourages reporting so lessons can be learned.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which statement about the COSS's authority is correct?
options: The COSS can tell you to work without protection if time is short
It does not override your right to refuse unsafe work
The COSS can tell you to work without protection
The COSS can sign the briefing form on your behalf
questions.rationale: Anyone can stop and challenge unsafe work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why should briefings be given at the place of work, where possible?
options: So that train drivers passing the site can listen to it too
So that train drivers can listen to it as well
So that the briefing takes less time overall
So people can see the hazards, lines and safe places
questions.rationale: Seeing the site helps understanding.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should happen if someone arrives on site without PPE?
options: They must not go on or near the line until correctly equipped
They can borrow a jacket from a passer-by for the shift
They can work in the cess only, away from the four-foot
They can work without it if it is daylight and dry
questions.rationale: PPE is required for everyone on or near the line.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who decides which safe system of work is used?
options: The planner, using the hierarchy, confirmed by the COSS
The fastest worker in the group on the day
The train company that runs services on the line
The fastest worker in the group, based on what they see on the day
questions.rationale: Work is planned in advance and checked on site.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the main reason for 'one COSS per group'?
options: So the client saves money on supervision
So one clear person is in charge of the group's safety
So the client saves money on supervision for the work
So fewer lookouts are needed on the site
questions.rationale: Clear leadership avoids confusion.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What happened at Severn Tunnel Junction in February 1985?
options: A train derailed inside the Severn Tunnel
Overhead wires fell onto a crowded platform
Four track workers were killed while clearing snow
A train derailed inside the Severn Tunnel during heavy rain
questions.rationale: The lack of clear leadership and lookouts led to major changes in track safety rules.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: In 1999, what was the 'Person in Charge of Work' (PICOW) role renamed to?
options: Controller of Site Safety (COSS)
Person in Charge of Possession (PICOP)
Engineering Supervisor (ES)
Safe Work Leader (SWL)
questions.rationale: The role became COSS on 7 August 1999.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to work on a line you think is open, but the COSS says it is blocked?
options: Go on the line straight away because the COSS said so
Ask the COSS to confirm the blockage before going on the line
Leave the site and go home without saying anything
Ask the lookout to watch the line while you start work
questions.rationale: It is right to check. Mistakes about which lines are blocked have caused accidents.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why must the COSS know the maximum line speed?
options: It affects positions of safety and warning times
It affects how long the briefing is expected to take
It affects how long the briefing should take
It affects which colour of PPE should be worn
questions.rationale: Speed is central to planning the safe system of work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these shows good leadership by a COSS?
options: Doing the work themselves to set a good example to the team
Watching the group, stopping unsafe acts and keeping all informed
Leaving the site to fetch materials so the work keeps going
Letting the group decide the safe system amongst themselves
questions.rationale: Good leaders observe and intervene.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: At Ruscombe Junction in 2007, what factors did RAIB identify?
options: Faulty overhead line equipment and a lightning strike
Peer pressure, poor leadership and reluctance to stop work
A train driver who was under the influence of alcohol
Defective PPE that hid the welder from the driver
questions.rationale: A welder was struck. Human factors were central.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: At Newark North Gate in 2014, what did RAIB find about the COSS?
options: The COSS stopped the work correctly when the train appeared
The COSS had not been trained or assessed for the role
The COSS failed to monitor the team, and a lookout was struck
The COSS had arranged a line blockage that failed
questions.rationale: Monitoring the group is a key COSS duty.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is 'possession protection'?
options: The PPE that must be worn by everyone inside a possession
The insurance cover arranged for the engineering work
Equipment and arrangements that stop trains entering a possession
A temporary fence put up around the welfare area and car park for the shift
questions.rationale: It includes signals, boards and detonators.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who is responsible for making sure you have been briefed?
options: Only you, as the COSS just gives out information
Only you, as the COSS just gives out information to the group
The COSS, but you must also not go on the line without it
Only the signaller who agreed the protection
questions.rationale: Both the COSS and you have responsibilities.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the danger of starting work before the line blockage is confirmed?
options: The paperwork will be wrong
The shift will be longer than planned, which affects pay
The tools may be damaged
Trains may still be running on that line
questions.rationale: Never assume a blockage is in place until confirmed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these is the correct order of the hierarchy from safest to least safe?
options: Lookout, warning systems, separated, fenced, safeguarded
Separated, safeguarded, lookout, fenced
Safeguarded, fenced, separated, warning systems, lookout
Fenced, lookout, safeguarded, separated
questions.rationale: Planners should use the highest practicable level.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why should work not continue during a gap in protection?
options: Because people are not protected from trains during the gap
Because working through it breaks union agreements
Because working through the gap breaks union agreements on breaks
Because the COSS will be paid less for that time
questions.rationale: No protection, no work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'safeguarded' mean in the safe system of work hierarchy?
options: A safety barrier has been fitted along the boundary fence
Every worker has been given a personal warning device
A lookout has been posted at each end of the site
All lines at the site are closed to trains
questions.rationale: Safeguarded working is the safest level.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: In a fenced arrangement, what must the fence do?
options: Stop trains from running on the open line
Mark the edge of the cess for drivers
Keep the public away from the welfare area
Stop people reaching the open line
questions.rationale: A rigid barrier keeps people within the safe area.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is a site warden needed in separated working?
options: Because the site warden must warn of every train
Because nothing physical stops people straying
Because the site warden arranges the line blockage
Because the site warden checks Sentinel cards
questions.rationale: Without a barrier, a person watches the boundary.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does a COSS need from the signaller to set up a line blockage?
options: A list of all the trains that ran that morning
Agreement that the line is blocked to trains
Permission to use lookouts for the shift
The names of the drivers due through the site
questions.rationale: The signaller must confirm protection is in place.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should a COSS do if the signaller cannot give a line blockage?
options: Switch to lookout working to keep to time
Start work and request the blockage again later
Not start work under that plan
Place detonators and start work anyway
questions.rationale: Never fall back to a less safe improvised method.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What must the COSS tell the signaller when giving up a line blockage?
options: How many hours the group worked
That the line is clear and safe for trains
Which tools were used during the work
The names of everyone in the group
questions.rationale: The line must be safe before it is returned.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'safe system of work plan' (SSOWP)?
options: The document describing how a group will be protected
A plan showing where the welfare cabin will go
A plan for the group's travel to and from site
A rota for the lookouts on a long shift
questions.rationale: The plan sets out the protection arrangements for the work.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who checks that the safe system of work plan suits the actual site?
options: The train driver, as they pass
The COSS, on arrival
The client, from the office
The newest member of the group
questions.rationale: Plans must be checked against real conditions.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the danger of copying a safe system of work from a previous job?
options: It takes longer than writing a new one
Site conditions or lines may be different
It uses too much paper
It is against copyright rules
questions.rationale: Each job and location needs its own assessment.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why must all members of the group be briefed together where possible?
options: So the briefing can be finished more quickly
So everyone hears the same information
So the COSS only has to sign once
So the lookout can leave early
questions.rationale: Consistent briefings avoid confusion.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should a briefing include about the lines?
options: Their history and when they were opened
The number of trains that used them last year
Which are open, which are blocked and their names
The names of the companies that run trains on them
questions.rationale: You must know which lines can have trains.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the role of the Person in Charge of the Possession (PICOP)?
options: Driving engineering trains into worksites
Acting as lookout for all groups in the possession
Checking PPE for everyone on site
Arranging and managing the possession with the signaller
questions.rationale: The PICOP manages the possession limits and protection.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who authorises movements of engineering trains within a worksite?
options: The lookout
The Engineering Supervisor
The PICOP's assistant
Any COSS
questions.rationale: The ES controls the worksite.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should a COSS do before their group leaves a worksite?
options: Tell the train driver
Tell the station manager
Tell the Engineering Supervisor
Nothing
questions.rationale: The ES must know who is in the worksite.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is 'Individual Working Alone' (IWA) used for?
options: Any task at all where a lookout or COSS is not available that day
Low-risk tasks by one person under strict conditions
Work by a person who has no COSS competence
Night shifts when fewer staff are available
questions.rationale: IWA has its own competence and rules.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who can act as a COSS?
options: Anyone with more than five years' experience
The most senior person present on site
Any PTS holder who volunteers on the day
Someone holding a valid COSS competence
questions.rationale: COSS is a separate competence.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the danger of a COSS doing practical work at the same time as supervising?
options: They may finish the work too quickly
They may stop watching the group
They may damage their own tools
They may get paid less for the shift
questions.rationale: Supervision needs attention.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should you do if two COSSs give you conflicting instructions?
options: Follow whichever instruction is quicker
Stop and get it resolved before continuing
Follow the more senior COSS without asking
Ignore both and decide for yourself
questions.rationale: Conflicting instructions are a warning sign.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why must the COSS check the site before the group goes on the line?
options: To count how many trains pass
To confirm the plan matches the conditions
To find somewhere safe to park the group's vans
To choose where to have lunch
questions.rationale: Conditions may differ from what was planned.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'competence check' at the start of work?
options: A quiz about the Rule Book
A short quiz about the Rule Book before work
Confirming people hold the right competences
A drugs and alcohol test
questions.rationale: COSS checks include Sentinel cards and competences.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the danger of a COSS giving a briefing from the van far from the work?
options: The van might be needed elsewhere
The briefing will be too short to cover everything
Drivers may hear it on the radio
People cannot see the hazards being described
questions.rationale: Briefing at the work location is better where possible.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why should the COSS keep a record of who was briefed?
options: To calculate overtime for each person in the group
To send to the train operator
To decide who drives home
To show everyone was briefed and understood
questions.rationale: Briefing records support safety and investigation.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'protection' mean in safe system of work terms?
options: Stopping trains from reaching the work
Wearing PPE on site
Locking the access gate
Wearing the correct PPE while on site
questions.rationale: Protection is different from warning.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What does 'warning' mean in safe system of work terms?
options: Stopping trains before they reach the site
Telling people a train is coming so they can get clear
Putting up warning signs at the access point so the public keep away
Telling the client about delays to the work
questions.rationale: Warnings rely on people moving in time.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is protection preferred to warning?
options: It does not rely on people reacting in time
It is always quicker to arrange
It needs fewer people on site to set up
It removes the need for a COSS
questions.rationale: Protection removes the train from the equation.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the purpose of 'planning ahead' for line blockages?
options: To reduce the number of trains running
To give train drivers a day off
To make sure protection is available when needed
To give train drivers a day off while engineering work takes place
questions.rationale: Good planning puts more work in protected time.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Which of these should make the COSS stop the work?
options: The group is ahead of schedule
A train passes on a far line
A train passes on a line further from the work
Conditions change so the plan is no longer safe
questions.rationale: Stop when the plan no longer fits.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should happen if a group member leaves and another joins mid-shift?
options: The new person copies the old one
The new person is briefed first
Nothing; the briefing still applies
The new person works as lookout
questions.rationale: Everyone must be briefed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the purpose of the 'Hazard Directory' or similar route information in planning?
options: To help planners identify known hazards
To list drivers' names
To record overtime and travel time for staff
To show where to buy food
questions.rationale: Planners use known hazard information.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should a COSS do if the group is too large to supervise properly?
options: Carry on and supervise from a distance
Split it with additional COSSs or reduce it
Appoint the oldest worker as assistant
Ask the lookout to supervise half of them
questions.rationale: Effective supervision needs a manageable group.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is it important to know the 'limits' of a line blockage?
options: Inside the limits PPE is not needed
The limits show where to park
Outside the limits trains can still run
The limits show where to take breaks
questions.rationale: Know exactly where protection starts and ends.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the danger of working 'just outside' the limits of a blockage?
options: You are not protected there
The work will be slower
You will need a different COSS
There is no danger
questions.rationale: Stay within the protected area.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who is responsible for removing possession protection at the end?
options: Any track worker leaving site
The driver of the first train
The station staff at the nearest station
Competent people as arranged by the PICOP
questions.rationale: Protection is removed under control.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why might a safe system of work be changed during a shift?
options: Because the group is bored with the job
Because the COSS wants to leave
Because conditions or tasks have changed
Because the timetable changed
questions.rationale: Changes must be planned and briefed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What must happen when the safe system of work changes during the shift?
options: Only the lookout is told
Nothing until the next shift
Everyone is re-briefed
The change is written down only
questions.rationale: Everyone must understand the new arrangements.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is a 'Close Call' report used for?
options: Booking a line blockage
Reporting hazards and near misses
Claiming overtime
Ordering PPE and replacement tools
questions.rationale: Close Calls help fix issues before harm occurs.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the role of 'Worksafe' in safe systems of work?
options: It protects your right to refuse unsafe work
It sets out which tools to use
It records hours worked by each person on site
It replaces the COSS briefing
questions.rationale: You can stop and challenge without fear.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should the COSS do when a worker uses Worksafe to challenge a task?
options: Send the worker home and carry on with the job
Carry on and review later
Stop and resolve the concern before continuing
Report the worker to the sponsor
questions.rationale: Concerns must be addressed.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Who should be told if a planned safe system of work cannot be delivered?
options: The train companies that run on the line
The planner or manager responsible
The train company
The public
questions.rationale: Planning issues must be fed back.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why do planners aim to reduce the time people spend on or near open lines?
options: It saves money on PPE
It reduces paperwork
Less exposure means less risk
It allows faster trains
questions.rationale: Exposure to open lines is the key risk.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should the COSS do if the agreed access point is unsafe on arrival?
options: Use it carefully, as it was in the plan
Not use it and get a safe alternative agreed
Use any nearby gap
Ask the group to vote
questions.rationale: Access is part of the safe system.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: Why is the COSS required to stay with the group?
options: To keep them company
To supervise and react to changes
To carry the equipment
To sign timesheets at the end of the shift
questions.rationale: The COSS's presence is essential.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a site warden's armband or identification?
options: So the group knows who controls the boundary
So drivers know who to report
So the public can ask directions
So that they can be paid at a higher rate
questions.rationale: Clear roles help everyone respond correctly.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What should the COSS check about the lookout's sighting before work starts?
options: That it gives the full warning time
That it includes the signal box
That it is in the shade
That it is near the van
questions.rationale: Sighting must support the required warning time.

questions.topic: Safe Systems of Work & Site Roles
questions.stem: What is the safest way to handle work that cannot be done with lines open?
options: Do it quickly between trains
Use two lookouts instead
Do it at night when trains are fewer
Plan it for a line blockage or possession
questions.rationale: If it cannot be done safely with trains running, protect it.

questions.stem: What does OLE stand for?
options: Open line equipment
Operational lineside electrics
Overhead lighting equipment
Overhead line equipment
questions.rationale: OLE is the system of wires and supports that supplies power to trains through the pantograph.

questions.stem: How should you treat OLE unless you are told it is isolated and earthed?
options: As dead unless a train is near
As live and dangerous at all times
As live only while a train is drawing power nearby
As safe if it is not sparking
questions.rationale: Never assume OLE is dead.

questions.stem: What is the minimum distance you and anything you carry must keep from live OLE?
options: 1.25 metres (4 feet)
2.75 metres (9 feet)
0.5 metres (1 foot 8 inches)
1 metre (3 feet 3 inches)
questions.rationale: Keep yourself and anything you hold at least 2.75 m from live OLE parts.

questions.stem: Why can you be injured by OLE even without touching it?
options: The wires give off radiation that burns nearby skin
25,000 volts can arc across a gap to you or what you hold
The wires heat the surrounding air to dangerous levels
The wires send signals that interfere with heart rhythm
questions.rationale: High voltage can jump through the air, so keeping your distance is essential.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see OLE that is damaged or hanging down?
options: Keep well away, keep others away and report it at once
Move it out of the way with a wooden pole
Touch it with a dry wooden handle to see if it is still live
Wait for it to stop sparking, then move it
questions.rationale: Damaged OLE may still be live. Report to the signaller or electrical control.

questions.stem: A wire from the OLE is lying on the ground. What should you assume?
options: It is dead, because the supply trips when it falls
It is live, and anything touching it may be live too
It is safe to move once it has stopped moving
It is dead, because the supply trips out whenever a wire falls
questions.rationale: Fallen wires can energise rails, fences and the ground nearby.

questions.stem: What are the main parts of OLE that may be live?
options: The contact wire, catenary and other wires and fittings
Only the contact wire that touches the pantograph
Only the contact wire that the pantograph actually touches
Only the parts painted with yellow warning bands
questions.rationale: Treat all OLE wires and fittings as live unless isolated and earthed.

questions.stem: Who controls the electrical supply to OLE?
options: The signaller who controls trains in the area
The driver of the train drawing the current
The Electrical Control Operator in electrical control
The signaller who controls trains through the electrified area
questions.rationale: Electrical control manages isolations and responds to OLE faults.

questions.stem: Before anyone works within 2.75 metres of OLE, what is normally needed?
options: Rubber gloves and boots for everyone working in the group
An isolation, with the OLE earthed and a permit to work
Rubber gloves and boots for everyone in the group
Permission from the driver of the next train
questions.rationale: OLE must be isolated, earthed and the work authorised.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of earthing OLE after it has been isolated?
options: So it cannot become live while people are working
So passing trains are protected from damage by the wires
So the humming noise from it is reduced
So passing trains are protected from it
questions.rationale: Earths protect against accidental re-energising and induced voltages.

questions.stem: Who is allowed to apply or remove OLE earths?
options: Anyone who holds a valid PTS with AC module
Only people trained and authorised to do so
The lookout, once the trains have stopped
The guard of the engineering train
questions.rationale: Earthing is specialist work.

questions.stem: Why must you not climb on a vehicle such as a wagon roof under OLE?
options: You could come within 2.75 m of live wires
It may damage the wagon's roof and its load
It is against the dress code
The driver might move the train
questions.rationale: Climbing on vehicles can bring you close to live OLE.

questions.stem: What should you do with a long tool such as a measuring staff near OLE?
options: Hold it upright so that drivers can see it clearly
Hold it upright so that train drivers can see it clearly
Keep it low and horizontal so it stays clear of the wires
Hold it above your head so it does not hit anyone
questions.rationale: Long items are a common cause of OLE contact.

questions.stem: Why are metal ladders particularly dangerous near OLE?
options: They are too heavy to carry safely on ballast
They are too heavy to carry safely along the ballast shoulder
They conduct electricity and bring you near the wires
They make a lot of noise when they are moved
questions.rationale: Use only approved equipment under authorised arrangements near OLE.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of an OLE hazard?
options: Blue signs with a train symbol
Blue signs with a train symbol and a speed
White signs with a speed number
Yellow warning signs with a lightning symbol
questions.rationale: Electrical danger signs warn of live equipment.

questions.stem: What is the danger of using a water hose or jet near OLE?
options: Water can conduct electricity from the wires to you
Water damages the ballast under the sleepers
Water makes passing trains slip on the rails
Water makes passing trains slip on the rails and lose grip
questions.rationale: Never direct water towards OLE.

questions.stem: What should you do if someone has been electrocuted by OLE and is still in contact with it?
options: Pull them away by their clothing as quickly as you can
Do not touch them; keep clear and get the power switched off
Use a metal bar to push them clear of the equipment
Pour water over them to cool any burns straight away
questions.rationale: You could become a second casualty. Get the power isolated first.

questions.stem: Which statement about isolated OLE is correct?
options: It is safe as soon as trains stop running on that line
It is safe once the last train has lowered its pantograph
It is safe as soon as trains stop running on that particular line
It is only safe once isolated, earthed and confirmed to you
questions.rationale: Only work on OLE when properly isolated and earthed.

questions.stem: What is a 'return conductor' on AC electrified lines?
options: A wire that guides trains back to the depot at night
A spare contact wire kept ready for emergency repairs
A cable that connects the signal post telephones
A wire that carries current back and must be treated as live
questions.rationale: Return conductors and similar wires may carry dangerous voltages.

questions.stem: What is a 'booster transformer' on OLE?
options: Equipment that helps manage return current; treat it as live
A device that boosts the speed of electric trains
A battery fitted to the train for emergency lighting
A transformer inside the signal box that powers lamps
questions.rationale: All OLE electrical equipment should be treated as live.

questions.stem: Why must you never touch an OLE mast that has a fallen wire across it?
options: The mast may be energised by the wire
The mast may be hot from the current that has passed through it
The mast is private property
The mast may be wet
questions.rationale: Anything touching a fallen wire can be live.

questions.stem: Can induced voltage be present on isolated OLE?
options: No, once isolated the equipment is completely safe
Only in wet weather when the insulators are damp
No, once isolated the overhead equipment is completely safe to touch anywhere
Yes, live lines nearby can induce voltage, so earths are used
questions.rationale: Induced voltages from adjacent live equipment can be dangerous.

questions.stem: What is the 'contact wire'?
options: The wire used for signal post telephones
The wire that carries signalling data to the train
The fence wire on the boundary
The wire that the train's pantograph touches
questions.rationale: The contact wire supplies power directly to the train.

questions.stem: What is the 'catenary' wire?
options: The supporting wire that holds up the contact wire
The wire that supplies power to the signals
The wire that supplies electricity to the lineside signals
The cable that feeds a third-rail line
questions.rationale: Catenary and contact wire are both usually live.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a pantograph tangled in the OLE?
options: Climb up and free it
Tell the driver to raise the pantograph
Keep clear and report it immediately
Ignore it if no sparks are seen
questions.rationale: Damaged OLE and train equipment may be live and unstable.

questions.stem: Why should you take care with cranes and lifting equipment near OLE?
options: They pull the overhead wires out of their correct alignment
They pull the overhead wires out of alignment
They make passing trains reduce their speed
Jibs and loads can come within 2.75 m of live wires
questions.rationale: Lifting near OLE needs special planning and controls.

questions.stem: Why should you not fly kites, drones or balloons near OLE?
options: They can touch the wires and cause shocks or damage
They need a licence before they are used near the railway
They are too noisy near residential areas
They need a licence before use near railways
questions.rationale: Objects in contact with OLE can carry current to people.

questions.stem: In 2010 at St Pancras International, what happened to the OLE?
options: A 25 kV overhead wire parted and fell to the ground
The OLE was switched off for a festival
A train lost power for an hour
The OLE was switched off for a special event at the station
questions.rationale: RAIB investigated this event, which showed risks from broken wires in stations.

questions.stem: What is a 'section insulator' or 'neutral section' for?
options: To protect birds from shocks
To make the wires stronger
To support the masts and keep the wires at the right height
To separate electrical sections of the OLE
questions.rationale: Electrical sections let parts of the OLE be isolated separately.

questions.stem: If one OLE section is isolated, what about the next section?
options: It may still be live, so treat it as live
It is isolated at the same time as yours
It is always earthed when work is nearby
It is isolated at the same time as your section
questions.rationale: Know the exact limits of an isolation.

questions.stem: What is a 'permit to work' for OLE isolation?
options: A licence that allows a person to drive a train
A record on the Sentinel card of your competences
A licence that allows a person to drive an electric train
A document confirming the OLE is isolated and earthed
questions.rationale: Permits control electrical safety on site.

questions.stem: Who normally issues the permit to work for OLE isolations?
options: Any member of the group who holds PTS AC
A Nominated Person or similar authorised person
Any member of the group who holds PTS with the AC module
The signaller's assistant in the signal box
questions.rationale: Authorised people manage isolation arrangements.

questions.stem: What is the danger of a broken insulator on OLE?
options: Trains will run faster through the section
Live parts may be exposed to structures or people
The overhead wires will make a loud noise
Trains will run faster through that section of line
questions.rationale: Report damaged OLE equipment.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are not sure whether OLE is live?
options: Touch it with a dry glove
Ask a passing driver
Assume it is dead at night
Treat it as live
questions.rationale: If in doubt, it is live.

questions.stem: Which of these is a safe action under live OLE?
options: Standing on a stack of sleepers to reach a sign
Lifting a pole upright to measure height
Lifting a pole upright to check the height of the wires
Keeping long tools low and horizontal while walking
questions.rationale: Stay low and keep everything well clear.

questions.stem: What is the main danger of 'step potential' near a fallen OLE wire?
options: You could trip over the wire in the dark
Voltage in the ground can pass through your legs
The ground under the wire could collapse
You could trip over the wire in the dark and fall
questions.rationale: Keep well back from fallen wires and anything they touch.

questions.stem: If an OLE wire falls on a road vehicle you are in, what should you generally do?
options: Stay inside unless there is fire, and warn people away
Get out quickly and walk away from the vehicle
Touch the outside of the vehicle to test it first
Pull the wire off the roof with a dry cloth
questions.rationale: Staying inside usually avoids contact with ground voltage. Follow emergency advice.

questions.stem: Which line voltage applies to most of the GB mainline OLE?
options: 25 kV AC
750 V DC
11 kV DC
400 V AC
questions.rationale: Most GB mainline electrification is 25 kV AC.

questions.stem: What makes OLE more dangerous in wet weather?
options: OLE switches off in rain
OLE is switched off whenever it rains heavily
Water helps current to travel and arc
Rain makes trains slower
questions.rationale: Wet conditions increase electrical risk.

questions.stem: What should you do if a tree has fallen across the OLE?
options: Cut it up straight away with a chainsaw
Pull it off the wires using a long rope
Keep clear and report it as an emergency
Wait for it to burn through, then remove it
questions.rationale: The tree and the ground may be live.

questions.stem: Why should you report scaffolding or structures being built near OLE without authority?
options: They block the view of the station from the road
They may come dangerously close to live equipment
They need planning permission from the council
They make too much noise for nearby residents
questions.rationale: Third-party works near OLE need control.

questions.stem: Why should you not touch a train's roof equipment under OLE?
options: It may be hot
It is fragile
It may be live from the OLE
It is fragile and easily damaged by hand
questions.rationale: Train roof equipment can be live.

questions.stem: What is the safest attitude to OLE equipment painted with warning labels?
options: Ignore labels if the equipment looks old
Only obey labels at night
Follow the warnings and keep away
Only engineers need to read them
questions.rationale: Warnings are there for everyone's safety.

questions.stem: Why are bonding cables between rails and OLE masts important?
options: They hold the masts upright in high winds
They carry signal messages between locations
They make the copper harder for thieves to steal
They give a safe path for fault and return currents
questions.rationale: Never disconnect or damage bonds.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find a bonding cable cut or stolen?
options: Reconnect the ends by twisting them together
Remove the rest of the cable to stop theft
Leave it, because bonds are not safety critical
Do not touch the ends and report it at once
questions.rationale: Cut bonds can mean dangerous voltages.

questions.stem: Which statement about OLE and pantographs is correct?
options: The pantograph and train roof equipment can be live
Only the very tip of the pantograph is ever live
Pantographs are earthed whenever the train stops
Pantographs are earthed automatically whenever the train stops
questions.rationale: Keep clear of train roof equipment under OLE.

questions.stem: Which is the key rule when working near OLE that has NOT been isolated?
options: Keep yourself and all you hold at least 2.75 m away
Wear rubber boots and you may then touch it
Wear rubber boots and you may then touch it for a moment
Only touch it with completely dry hands
questions.rationale: Distance is the protection.

questions.stem: Why must you take extra care with OLE when using a long-handled shovel or tamping bar?
options: It might scratch the rail head and cause a defect
Raising it could bring it within 2.75 m of the wires
It might break if used to lever heavy ballast
It might make the track circuit show occupied
questions.rationale: Watch the height of any tool you lift.

questions.stem: Who should you report an OLE defect to in an emergency?
options: Your family first, so they know you are safe, and then social media
Social media, so others can avoid the area
The signaller or electrical control, giving the location
The station café, so they can tell the staff
questions.rationale: Fast reporting allows power to be switched off.

questions.stem: What does the warning 'Danger: overhead live wires' tell you?
options: There is a risk of death from the overhead equipment
There are telephone cables running overhead
The overhead wires have been disconnected
There are telephone cables running overhead nearby
questions.rationale: Take the warning seriously and keep clear.

questions.stem: You are asked to fix a sign on an OLE mast. The OLE has not been isolated. What should you do?
options: Climb the mast carefully and keep away from the wires
Refuse until it is planned with proper electrical controls
Use a wooden ladder and finish the job quickly
Ask a colleague to hold your legs while you reach up
questions.rationale: Work near live OLE must be planned and authorised.

questions.stem: You see a colleague lifting a scaffold pole upright under the OLE. What should you do?
options: Let them carry on if they are careful
Help them lift it higher so it clears the people below
Shout to stop them and tell them to lower it
Wait and report it later
questions.rationale: Immediate intervention can save a life.

questions.stem: A fallen OLE wire is lying across the cess. A colleague is about to step over it. What should you do?
options: Warn them to stop and keep everyone well away
Let them step over if they wear boots
Kick the wire out of the way
Let them step over it as long as they wear safety boots
questions.rationale: Never approach fallen wires.

questions.stem: What is the safest assumption about a rail near a fallen OLE wire?
options: It is safe because rails are earthed
It is only live if a train is present
It may be live
It is safe once the wire stops moving
questions.rationale: Fallen wires can energise rails and nearby metalwork.

questions.stem: You smell burning and see sparks from the OLE. What should you do first?
options: Throw sand or ballast on the sparks to put them out before they spread
Move everyone to a safe distance and report an emergency
Move closer to find out what is causing it
Spray the wires with a fire extinguisher
questions.rationale: Do not approach. Get the power switched off.

questions.stem: Why should you not use a metal tape measure upwards near OLE?
options: It could come close to or touch live wires
It might bend and give a false reading
It might be inaccurate over long distances
It might rust if left out in the rain
questions.rationale: Use approved non-conductive measuring equipment and keep it low.

questions.stem: Which of these must stay at least 2.75 m from live OLE?
options: Only metal tools and equipment, not people
Only metal tools and equipment
Only items longer than 3 metres
You and anything you are holding or carrying
questions.rationale: The distance applies to you and anything you hold.

questions.stem: When an OLE isolation is in place, how do you know which wires are dead?
options: By looking for sparks or arcing on the wires
From the authorised person's briefing and permit limits
By listening for a humming sound from the wires
By looking for sparks or arcing along the wires above you
questions.rationale: Never decide for yourself that equipment is dead.

questions.stem: What is a 'Nominated Person' in AC electrification work?
options: A person authorised to manage OLE isolations on site
The person nominated to arrange meals for the shift
The lookout nominated to watch the overhead wires
The driver of the engineering train in the possession
questions.rationale: Nominated persons control isolations and earthing.

questions.stem: What should you do if the earths on isolated OLE are removed while you are still working?
options: Stop work and keep clear, as the OLE may become live
Put the earths back on yourself straight away and carry on
Put the earths back on yourself straight away
Ignore it as long as no train is approaching
questions.rationale: Earths are part of your protection.

questions.stem: Why must you not touch any part of an OLE structure that is damaged?
options: It belongs to another department
It is too heavy
It may be painted
It may be live or unstable
questions.rationale: Report damaged structures and keep clear.

questions.stem: Why is standing on a ballast wagon under OLE dangerous?
options: It brings you much closer to the live wires
It is uncomfortable to stand on for long
It is uncomfortable to stand on for long periods
It makes too much noise for the group
questions.rationale: Raised positions reduce clearance to OLE.

questions.stem: Which item would be the safest choice for a task near OLE, if approved?
options: A long steel bar for extra reach
A non-conductive tool used below the safe distance
A long steel bar for extra reach to the equipment
A rope that has been soaked in water
questions.rationale: Conductive items increase risk.

questions.stem: If you need to work at height near OLE, what is required?
options: Specific planning, isolation where needed and authorised controls
Just a harness and a colleague to hold the ladder
Just a harness and a colleague to hold the ladder, as long as it is daylight
Nothing extra, as long as it is done in daylight
questions.rationale: Work at height and electricity are both lifesaving rule risks.

questions.stem: A road vehicle hits an OLE mast and a wire is dangling over the road. What should you do?
options: Move the wire off the road with a broom
Keep people away and call 999 and the railway
Move the wire off the road with a broom handle
Climb the mast to see what is damaged
questions.rationale: Protect the public and get the power isolated.

questions.stem: Why can wet ground near a fallen wire be extra dangerous?
options: Water helps current spread through the ground
Water makes the wire heavier
Water makes the area slippery only
Water makes the wire heavier, so it falls further
questions.rationale: Keep well away from fallen wires in wet conditions.

questions.stem: Why might OLE wires sag lower than normal?
options: They are lowered every night for maintenance
Trains pull them down a little on purpose
Heat, damage or a fault can change their height
They are lowered every night for maintenance work
questions.rationale: Do not assume the normal clearance applies. Report sagging wires.

questions.stem: Which of these must you do before raising anything near OLE?
options: Check the height and clearance to the wires
Check the timetable for the next train due
Check the weather forecast for next week
Check the train company
questions.rationale: Always look up.

questions.stem: What is the danger of OLE in station areas?
options: Station OLE works at a much lower, safer voltage
Station OLE works at a much lower voltage
Station OLE is isolated whenever trains stop
Wires are close to platforms, canopies and the public
questions.rationale: St Pancras (2010) showed the risk from wires falling in stations.

questions.stem: Which statement about OLE masts is correct?
options: Masts are always safe to climb to look at the wires
Masts support the OLE and may become live in a fault
Masts are only there to hold up signs and lights
Masts are always safe to climb to look at the wires up close
questions.rationale: Do not climb masts unless authorised and the OLE is isolated.

questions.stem: Why are birds' nests on OLE a hazard?
options: Nesting birds may attack track workers
Nests block the view of signals for drivers
Nesting material can cause faults and fires
Nests make trains stop for inspections
questions.rationale: Report nests or debris on OLE.

questions.stem: Which of these would be unsafe near live OLE?
options: Walking in the cess with tools held low
Throwing a rope over the wires
Keeping 3 m from the wires
Reading a warning sign
questions.rationale: Anything that could touch the OLE is dangerous.

questions.stem: If you feel a tingling sensation when touching metalwork near OLE, what should you do?
options: Hold on to see whether it gets any stronger
Let go if you can, move away and report it at once
Touch it again with your other hand to confirm
Ignore it, as a slight tingle is normal near OLE
questions.rationale: This may mean stray voltage. Keep others away.

questions.stem: Why do workers apply portable earths at both sides of the work area?
options: To mark the limits of the work site for drivers
To protect against the OLE becoming live from either side
To hold the wires up while components are changed
To stop thieves stealing the copper wire while the power is switched off
questions.rationale: Earthing at both sides gives protection from both supply directions.

questions.stem: Where should you go if a train's pantograph damages the OLE above you?
options: Under the train to shelter from falling parts
Towards the nearest mast so you can hold on to it
Onto the train roof to help free the pantograph
Away to a safe distance, keeping clear of fallen wires
questions.rationale: Get clear and report.

questions.stem: What does 'isolation' mean for OLE?
options: The electrical supply to a section is switched off
The OLE is moved away from the track
Workers are separated from each other
The line is closed to all trains for the work
questions.rationale: Isolation alone is not enough; earths must also be applied before work.

questions.stem: Which of these is a correct statement about AC and DC electrified areas?
options: OLE and third rail are never found together
Some locations have both OLE and conductor rail
DC lines never carry dangerous voltages
OLE and third rail are never found at the same location
questions.rationale: Some areas have both systems. Know what is present on your site.

questions.stem: You are working near an OLE mast and need to lean a ladder. What should you do?
options: Only do it if authorised and the OLE arrangements allow
Lean it on the mast, because OLE masts are always earthed and safe to touch
Lean it against the wires for extra support
Lean it on a stationary train beside the mast
questions.rationale: Work near OLE must be authorised.

questions.stem: Why must you not use the OLE masts as a handhold while walking?
options: They are private property of the energy supplier
They may be live in a fault and put you foul of the line
They are private property of the energy company
They are reserved for train drivers to hold on to when they leave the cab
questions.rationale: Do not touch electrical structures without need.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of OLE warning signs at access points?
options: To show the times of trains passing the access point
To show drivers the line speed for that section
To show staff where they are allowed to park
To warn people that the area has live overhead equipment
questions.rationale: Check access point signs for electrical hazards.

questions.stem: Which of these would most likely come within 2.75 m of OLE?
options: A person kneeling on the ballast to inspect a sleeper
A person standing on a wagon roof
A person kneeling on the ballast
A person sitting in a van
questions.rationale: Height reduces clearance.

questions.stem: Which of these is the correct first step if you see someone receive an electric shock from OLE and they are no longer touching it?
options: Pour cold water over them straight away to cool the burns
Pick them up and carry them to your van as fast as you can
Leave them where they are and go to find your manager
Make sure the area is safe, then call for help and give first aid
questions.rationale: Only approach when safe, then call for help and give first aid if trained.

questions.stem: What makes high-voltage electrical injuries especially serious?
options: They only cause a minor tingling sensation
They only ever affect the hands and arms
They only cause a minor tingling sensation in most cases
They can cause severe burns and stop the heart
questions.rationale: Electrical injuries are often fatal.

questions.stem: Who can authorise work within 2.75 m of live OLE?
options: Only those authorised under specialist electrical arrangements
Any COSS who has checked the wires visually first
Any PTS holder who has completed the AC module and checked the wires visually
The driver of the next train due through the area
questions.rationale: Most PTS holders must never work within 2.75 m of live OLE.

questions.stem: You must walk under a low bridge where the OLE is close to the parapet. What should you do?
options: Keep items low and follow the briefing on clearances
Reach up and touch the bridge to judge the height
Carry long tools on your shoulder through the bridge
Walk along the parapet to stay away from the wires
questions.rationale: Clearances are smaller under structures.

questions.stem: Why is it unsafe to stand on a raised platform such as a trolley under OLE?
options: Trolleys are owned by contractors and are not insured
It raises you closer to the live wires
Trolleys are owned by contractors
Trolleys are made of plastic
questions.rationale: Raised positions under OLE need careful control.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a reason why OLE may become live after an isolation?
options: A switching error
Induced voltage from adjacent lines
A worker forgot their helmet
Earths being removed too early
questions.rationale: Earths and permit controls protect against re-energising.

questions.stem: Which phrase best summarises OLE safety for PTS holders?
options: Keep away, keep low, treat as live
Touch only with gloves
Touch only with dry gloves, and only in daylight
Live only when trains are near
questions.rationale: Stay at least 2.75 m away and keep items low.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid parking a road vehicle with a raised crane or tipper near OLE?
options: The raised part could come close to or touch the wires
It might block the road for other site vehicles
It might be stolen if it is left unattended
It might be scratched by the overhead wires
questions.rationale: Plan vehicle movements near OLE.

questions.stem: When should a member of the group report a damaged OLE dropper?
options: At the end of the week in the weekly report
At the end of the week in the weekly defect report
Only once the dropper has actually fallen
Immediately, through the COSS or to the signaller
questions.rationale: Report OLE defects promptly.

questions.stem: If a train is stopped under damaged OLE, what should you avoid?
options: Touching the train or the damaged equipment
Moving away to a safe distance
Moving to a safe distance away from the train
Keeping the public away
questions.rationale: The train may be live.

questions.stem: What is the safe distance from live OLE often called on PTS courses?
options: The 2.75 m rule
The 1.25 m rule
The 10-second rule
The 3 m rule
questions.rationale: Keep yourself and anything you hold at least 2.75 m from live OLE.

questions.stem: Roughly how far is 2.75 metres in feet?
options: About 4 feet
About 6 feet 6 inches
About 15 feet
About 9 feet
questions.rationale: 2.75 m is about 9 ft.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT part of the overhead line equipment?
options: The conductor rail
The contact wire
The catenary wire
The OLE structures and insulators
questions.rationale: The conductor rail belongs to DC third-rail systems.

questions.stem: Why should you not stand on top of a stack of sleepers under OLE?
options: It reduces your clearance from the wires
Sleepers are always electrically live
It blocks the driver's view of signals
The stack will be counted as a refuge
questions.rationale: Any raised position reduces clearance.

questions.stem: Who should you contact to report a sagging OLE wire near a road?
options: The local council's highways department only
The nearest police station, by email when you get home
Nobody, as wires often sag in summer
The signaller or electrical control, and keep people away
questions.rationale: Low wires near roads are dangerous to vehicles and people.

questions.stem: Why are 'height gauges' sometimes fitted at level crossings under OLE?
options: To measure the height of passing trains
To warn tall vehicles about the overhead wires
To stop cars entering the crossing
To count the number of vehicles using the crossing
questions.rationale: Tall vehicles could contact the wires.

questions.stem: What should a driver of a tall vehicle do at a level crossing with OLE?
options: Lower the tyre pressure to reduce height
Cross quickly before the wires move
Ask a track worker to lift the wires
Check the vehicle height against the signs
questions.rationale: Vehicles over the limit must not cross.

questions.stem: You are asked to cut a tree branch close to OLE. What must be in place?
options: Only a lookout to watch for trains
Only a lookout watching the line for trains while you cut
Specific arrangements, which may include an isolation
Nothing, if the branch is not touching
questions.rationale: Vegetation work near OLE needs planning.

questions.stem: Why can tree branches near OLE be dangerous even if they do not touch the wires?
options: Leaves conduct electricity from a distance
They can fall onto the wires or cause arcing when wet
Trees attract lightning onto trains
Branches slow down trains when they brush past
questions.rationale: Vegetation management protects OLE and people.

questions.stem: What should you do if an OLE wire is touching a fence along a footpath?
options: Lift it off the fence with a dry stick
Keep people away and report it as an emergency
Put a warning sign on the fence and leave
Touch the fence to see if it is live
questions.rationale: The fence may be live.

questions.stem: How should you treat a train's roof equipment in an AC depot unless told otherwise?
options: As safe once the train has stopped
As safe once the doors are open
As live only when the lights are on
As potentially live
questions.rationale: Roof equipment can be live from the OLE.

questions.stem: In an AC depot, what is the hazard of climbing a train's roof access ladder?
options: You could set off the fire alarm
You could damage the roof paint
You could block the driver's view
You could approach live OLE
questions.rationale: Access to roofs is strictly controlled under OLE.

questions.stem: What is an 'electrical section' of OLE?
options: A length of OLE that can be switched separately
A part of the line with no signals
A short stretch where trains coast
A section of track used only by electric trains
questions.rationale: Isolations are arranged section by section.

questions.stem: What does 'Danger: do not touch' on an OLE structure mean?
options: The paint is wet
The equipment may be live
It is private property
It belongs to a different company
questions.rationale: Obey electrical warning signs.

questions.stem: Why must people not climb onto signal gantries under OLE unless authorised?
options: They may damage the signal lights
They may come close to live wires
Gantries are reserved for drivers
They may be seen by passengers
questions.rationale: Access to structures near OLE is controlled.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an OLE 'feeder station'?
options: To supply power to the overhead line
To feed staff on long shifts
To store spare wires and fittings
To charge workers' phones
questions.rationale: Feeder stations connect the OLE to the power supply.

questions.stem: Why should you be careful using a metal detector or probe near buried cables on electrified lines?
options: The detector may confuse trains
Buried cables may be live
The detector may stop the signals
There is no electrical risk underground
questions.rationale: Cables under the ground can carry high voltages.

questions.stem: What is a 'section switch' on OLE?
options: A switch that changes the points
A switch that controls platform lights
A switch that turns off signals
A switch used to isolate parts of the OLE
questions.rationale: Only authorised people operate OLE switches.

questions.stem: Who may operate OLE isolating switches?
options: Only authorised and competent people
Any PTS holder in an emergency
Any COSS on site
The lookout
questions.rationale: Switching is specialist work.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see children climbing an OLE structure?
options: Shout at them until they climb down by themselves
Call for help immediately and report it as an emergency
Shout at them until they climb down
Ignore it, as they will get bored
questions.rationale: They are in grave danger.

questions.stem: Which of these is true about OLE in wet weather?
options: Arcing is more likely
The voltage is reduced
The wires are switched off
The risk disappears
questions.rationale: Wet conditions increase electrical risk.

questions.stem: What should you do if a fallen OLE wire is touching a train you are near?
options: Keep well clear of the train and the wire
Open the train doors to let people out
Touch the train to check it is safe
Pull the wire off with a rope
questions.rationale: The train may be live.

questions.stem: If an OLE wire falls in a station, what should be done with the public?
options: Let them step over it carefully
Keep them well away
Tell them to touch nothing but carry on
Ask them to help move it
questions.rationale: Clear the area and report.

questions.stem: What is the hazard of using a high-reach machine under OLE?
options: The boom could block the signals
The machine will slow down trains
The machine will make too much noise
The boom could come within the danger zone
questions.rationale: Plant near OLE needs height controls and planning.

questions.stem: What controls are often used for plant working under OLE?
options: Bright paint and flashing lights only
Height limiters and specific supervision
A lookout watching for trains only
Nothing, if the driver is careful
questions.rationale: Engineering controls reduce the risk of contact.

questions.stem: Which statement about OLE and isolation timing is correct?
options: OLE can be re-energised once the isolation ends
Once isolated, OLE stays dead for the whole night
Isolations last until the next train passes
OLE never becomes live again after work
questions.rationale: Know when your isolation ends and be clear before then.

questions.stem: Why must everyone be clear of OLE before an isolation is given up?
options: The signals will change aspect
Trains will run faster
The lights will go out
The wires will become live again
questions.rationale: Re-energising with people near is lethal.

questions.stem: Why are earthing points painted or marked on OLE structures?
options: So authorised staff can apply earths correctly
So that train drivers can see them clearly when passing at night
So passengers know where the wires are
So track workers can lean on them
questions.rationale: Earthing is done by trained people at set points.

questions.stem: Who is allowed to apply portable earths to OLE?
options: Anyone who has seen it done before
Any member of the work group who has seen it done
Authorised staff under the isolation arrangements
The driver of the engineering train
questions.rationale: Earthing is specialist work.

questions.stem: Which is true about OLE on lines where trains are not running?
options: It can still be live
It is always switched off
It is safe to touch
It is only live at night
questions.rationale: No trains does not mean no power.

questions.stem: What is a 'catenary mast'?
options: A pole used for lookout flags
A pole used to hang lookout flags beside the track
A structure that supports the overhead wires
A tall lamp post at a station
questions.rationale: Masts may become live under fault conditions.

questions.stem: Why should you report damaged OLE warning signs?
options: The signs are expensive to replace
Drivers rely on them to stop
People may not know about the danger
They count as track defects
questions.rationale: Warnings must be visible.

questions.stem: What is the main risk of metal fencing near OLE during a fault?
options: It may rust faster
It may become live
It may block the view
It may bend in the heat
questions.rationale: Faults can energise nearby metalwork.

questions.stem: How should you treat a broken OLE dropper hanging down?
options: As dead, as droppers carry no current
As safe to tie back with tape
As something to remove yourself
As live, keeping clear and reporting it
questions.rationale: Treat damaged OLE components as live.

questions.stem: Which of these is the safest attitude near OLE?
options: Respect it as always live unless proven otherwise
Assume it is dead unless it is sparking
Assume it is safe if birds are sitting on it
Assume it is only live near stations
questions.rationale: Birds sit on wires because they are not earthed; you could be.

questions.stem: Why can birds sit on live wires without harm, but people cannot touch them safely?
options: Birds are protected by their feathers
The wires are not live where birds sit
Birds do not form a path to earth; people usually do
Birds only ever sit on wires that are switched off
questions.rationale: Current needs a path. A person touching OLE and earth is that path.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of OLE 'insulators'?
options: To keep the wires warm in winter
To hold signal cables
To mark electrical sections
To stop current passing to the supports
questions.rationale: Damaged insulators can make structures live.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see an insulator that is cracked or smoking?
options: Report it and keep clear
Pour water on it
Climb up to look closer
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Faulty insulators can fail and cause danger.

questions.stem: Which item should never be thrown near OLE?
options: Only metal items
Only items made of metal, such as wire or tools
Anything, including rope, wire or tools
Only long items
questions.rationale: Anything thrown could contact the wires.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to get a load onto a wagon under OLE?
options: Throw it up by hand quickly
Climb onto the wagon and pull it up
Climb onto the wagon and pull the load up with a rope
Only under planned arrangements, often with isolation
questions.rationale: Loading under OLE needs planning.

questions.stem: What is the conductor rail (third rail)?
options: An extra rail beside the running rails that powers trains
A rail-shaped trough that carries signalling and power cables
A rail that guides train wheels through tight curves
A rail-shaped trough that carries signalling cables
questions.rationale: On DC lines, trains collect current from the conductor rail through shoe gear.

questions.stem: Up to what voltage is the GB third-rail system usually energised?
options: 25,000 volts AC
110 volts DC
1,500 volts AC
750 volts DC
questions.rationale: 750 V DC is easily enough to kill.

questions.stem: How should you treat the conductor rail at all times unless told otherwise?
options: As dead unless a train is near
As safe if it is dry
As safe at night
As live and dangerous
questions.rationale: Treat it as live unless you have been told it is isolated under proper arrangements.

questions.stem: Should you ever step on the conductor rail?
options: Yes, if wearing safety boots
Yes, if no trains are near
Yes, at the ramp ends
No, never
questions.rationale: Never touch or step on the conductor rail or its guard boards.

questions.stem: Where should you never put your feet on DC electrified lines?
options: In the cess on the side away from the conductor rail
Between the conductor rail and the nearest running rail
On a purpose-built crossing provided for staff
On the ballast shoulder on the side away from the conductor rail
questions.rationale: A slip between the conductor rail and running rail could cause contact.

questions.stem: What are guard boards on a conductor rail for?
options: To make the conductor rail safe to stand on when crossing
To make the conductor rail safe to stand on when you cross
To reduce the risk of accidental contact with the live rail
To mark the position of safety on DC electrified lines
questions.rationale: Guard boards are not safe to step on. Treat them as part of the live equipment.

questions.stem: May you step on a conductor rail guard board?
options: Yes, they are insulated
Yes, guard boards are insulated, so they are safe to stand on
No, guard boards must not be stepped on
Yes, if no trains are running
questions.rationale: Guard boards can break or slip, causing contact with the live rail.

questions.stem: How should you cross a DC electrified line where it is authorised?
options: Step over the conductor rail without touching it or its guard boards
Step on the conductor rail briefly to keep your balance
Jump from the conductor rail down onto the cess, keeping your feet together
Put one foot on the guard board while stepping across
questions.rationale: Step over carefully. Use crossing points or gaps where available.

questions.stem: Where might there be a gap in the conductor rail?
options: Only inside depots where trains move slowly
Nowhere, because the conductor rail is continuous
At level crossings, junctions and some crossing points
Nowhere, because the conductor rail runs continuously along the line
questions.rationale: Gaps exist but trains can bridge them, so the rail either side is still live.

questions.stem: Why are conductor rail ramp ends dangerous?
options: They are dead and safe to stand on
They are dead and only become live when a train touches them
They are only for drivers
They are still live and can trip you
questions.rationale: Ramp ends are part of the live conductor rail.

questions.stem: Why must you not touch a stopped train's shoe gear?
options: It is very hot from braking and will burn you
It is fragile and easily damaged by hand
It can be live even when the train is not moving
It belongs to the train company, not Network Rail
questions.rationale: Shoe gear can be live from the conductor rail or the train.

questions.stem: What is the danger of using metal tools near the conductor rail?
options: They will damage the guard boards if they touch them
They could bridge the conductor and running rails, causing a flash
They will become magnetised by the current and give false measurement readings
They will rust quickly because of the electrical field
questions.rationale: Keep tools away from the conductor rail and use insulated tools where required.

questions.stem: Why is a metal tape measure dangerous on a DC line?
options: It might snap if it catches under the rail
It gives inaccurate readings near steel rails
It could touch the conductor rail and carry current to you
It gives inaccurate readings when it is close to steel rails
questions.rationale: Use non-conductive measuring equipment.

questions.stem: What can happen if an object bridges the conductor rail and the running rail?
options: The train will speed up
A violent flash, burns and fire
Nothing, they are the same voltage
The signals will turn green
questions.rationale: Short circuits release large amounts of energy.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see someone in contact with the conductor rail?
options: Pull them off the rail with your bare hands
Use a metal bar to push them clear of the rail
Do not touch them; get the power isolated as an emergency
Use a metal bar to push them clear of the rail as quickly as possible
questions.rationale: Make sure you do not become a casualty too.

questions.stem: Who controls the electrical supply to DC conductor rails?
options: The train driver
An electrical control room
The COSS of the nearest work group
The lookout
questions.rationale: Electrical control manages isolations and emergencies.

questions.stem: What must be in place before work that could bring people into contact with the conductor rail?
options: A lookout watching for trains on the line and a rubber mat over the rail
An isolation under proper arrangements, such as a permit
A rubber mat laid over the conductor rail
Good daylight so the rail can be clearly seen
questions.rationale: Work on or near the conductor rail must be authorised and the rail isolated.

questions.stem: What are short-circuiting devices (SCDs) used for on DC lines?
options: To stop trains from entering the section of line
To measure the voltage on the conductor rail before each train comes past
To hold the conductor rail down on its insulators
To make sure an isolated conductor rail cannot become live
questions.rationale: SCDs connect the conductor rail to the running rail after isolation.

questions.stem: Why can flooding be especially dangerous on DC lines?
options: Water stops the conductor rail working, so trains lose power
Water can conduct current from the conductor rail
Water stops the conductor rail working
Water makes signals fail
questions.rationale: Take extra care in wet conditions and near floodwater.

questions.stem: Why must liquids not be poured near the conductor rail?
options: They damage the ballast
They can create a path for current
They make the rail rusty
They make the guard boards rot and fall off
questions.rationale: Keep liquids away from live equipment.

questions.stem: What should you do if a long item you are carrying could touch the conductor rail?
options: Carry it so that it cannot touch the conductor rail
Drag it along the ballast behind you
Rest it on the guard board while walking
Drag it along the ballast behind you so it stays low down
questions.rationale: Plan how to carry items in DC areas.

questions.stem: Which of these indicates a conductor rail is present?
options: An extra rail on insulators beside the running rails
A yellow line painted along the edge of the platform
A yellow line painted along the platform
A green signal aspect on the line ahead
questions.rationale: Learn to recognise conductor rail equipment.

questions.stem: Where is the conductor rail usually positioned?
options: On insulators alongside one of the running rails
Above the train, supported on masts like overhead wires
Between the sleepers below the ballast
In the six-foot only
questions.rationale: It may be on either side and can change sides.

questions.stem: Can the conductor rail change from one side of the track to the other?
options: No, it is always in the six-foot
No, it is always in the cess
Yes, so you must check where it is as you move
No, it is always on the cess side of the track
questions.rationale: The conductor rail position varies along the line.

questions.stem: What is 'fourth rail' DC electrification?
options: A spare running rail that is kept for use in emergencies
A rail that sends signalling information to passing trains
A system with a separate live rail for the return current
A rail that is laid only for heavy freight trains
questions.rationale: Both the conductor rail and the fourth rail can be live.

questions.stem: Which is the safest way to walk on a DC line where you must be near the track?
options: On the conductor rail side, where the ground is usually more level
On the guard boards, which give a firm and even surface
Away from the conductor rail side where possible, watching every step
In the four-foot, where you are further from the conductor rail
questions.rationale: Plan your route to stay clear of the conductor rail.

questions.stem: What is a 'conductor rail permit'?
options: A licence that allows you to drive a DC train
A record of competences held on your Sentinel card
A permit to cross the line at a level crossing
A document confirming the conductor rail is isolated
questions.rationale: Permits control electrical safety on DC lines.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid kneeling near the conductor rail?
options: It ruins your trousers on the ballast
It makes you harder for drivers to see
Your body could come into contact with it
It makes you harder for approaching drivers to see
