questions.rationale: Keep all parts of your body clear.

questions.stem: What is the risk of wearing metal jewellery near the conductor rail?
options: It can catch on the guard board and be lost in the ballast
It reflects light
It can conduct electricity and cause burns
It is against PPE colour rules
questions.rationale: Remove conductive items when working near live equipment.

questions.stem: Which of these is a correct statement about the conductor rail and trains?
options: Trains switch off the conductor rail when stopped
Conductor rails are only live when a train is on them
A train can make the conductor rail live even across a gap
A gap in the conductor rail always means the rail is dead there
questions.rationale: Never assume a gap means the rail is dead.

questions.stem: What is the safest action if you drop a tool near the conductor rail?
options: Pick it up quickly with your hand
Pick it up quickly with your hand before a train comes
Leave it and get help to recover it safely
Use another metal tool to hook it
questions.rationale: Do not reach near the live rail.

questions.stem: Why are insulated troughs and covers used on DC lines?
options: To protect people and equipment from live conductors
To keep the cables warm during cold weather
To keep the cables warm and dry in cold weather
To mark the edge of the cess for walking
questions.rationale: Insulation reduces the risk of contact.

questions.stem: What is the danger of using a ladder near the conductor rail?
options: It could touch the rail or slip into the live area
It is too heavy to carry along the ballast
It blocks the driver's view of the line
It blocks the driver's view of the line ahead
questions.rationale: Use non-conductive equipment and keep clear.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a conductor rail that is damaged or out of position?
options: Push it back with your boot
Push it back into place with your boot if it is only slightly out
Keep clear and report it immediately
Ignore it if no train is coming
questions.rationale: Damaged conductor rail is a serious hazard.

questions.stem: How can you tell whether a conductor rail is isolated?
options: By touching it briefly with the back of your hand
Only by being told under the proper isolation arrangements
By listening for a humming sound from the rail
By looking for sparks at the rail joints or listening for a humming sound
questions.rationale: Never test by touching.

questions.stem: Why should you take extra care on DC lines in the dark?
options: The voltage is raised at night to reduce power losses
The voltage is raised at night to save power
The conductor rail is harder to see and easier to touch
Guard boards are removed at night for checks
questions.rationale: Good lighting helps you see the conductor rail.

questions.stem: What should you do if a colleague is about to sit on the conductor rail during a break?
options: Join them
Let them if it is dry
Ignore it
Stop them immediately
questions.rationale: Sitting on the conductor rail can kill.

questions.stem: What do yellow and black warning signs near DC lines often mean?
options: Danger from live conductor rails
The line is closed to trains for engineering work
Trains are slow here
A station is ahead
questions.rationale: Electrical warning signs must be obeyed.

questions.stem: Which of these is safe on a DC line?
options: Stepping on the conductor rail where it is dry
Using a proper crossing point and stepping over the rails
Stepping on the guard boards to keep balance
Kneeling between the conductor rail and running rail
questions.rationale: Use proper crossings and keep clear of live equipment.

questions.stem: Why is the space between the conductor rail and running rail dangerous for feet?
options: It is very muddy and can trap boots
It is very muddy there and can trap your boots
A slip could cause contact with the live rail
It contains signal cables that can trip you
questions.rationale: Never step there.

questions.stem: Why should hosepipes and water jets not be pointed at the conductor rail?
options: Water can conduct electricity back to you
The water will cool the rail too quickly
The water jet will move the rail out of line
The water will make the rail rust faster
questions.rationale: Keep water away from live equipment.

questions.stem: Which equipment may be live on DC trains?
options: Only the train's headlights and tail lights
Only the equipment inside the driver's cab
Shoe gear and associated exposed equipment
Nothing at all once the train has stopped
questions.rationale: Treat train-mounted DC equipment as live.

questions.stem: Why must you know if your site has conductor rails before starting work?
options: So you know which colour of PPE you must wear
So you know whether to bring a metal ladder or a wooden one for the job
So you can call the driver before trains arrive
So you can follow the right rules and plan safe movement
questions.rationale: Your briefing should cover electrical hazards.

questions.stem: What is the safest attitude to the conductor rail?
options: Never touch it, never step on it, always treat it as live
Touch it only when you are wearing work gloves
Touch it only when wearing insulated work gloves
Treat it as live only when trains are running, and as dead between them
questions.rationale: Simple rules prevent fatal accidents.

questions.stem: What can happen if your clothing touches the conductor rail?
options: Nothing, because work clothing is fully insulated
You could get a shock or burns through damp or conductive cloth
It will only scorch the clothing, not the person
Nothing at all, because railway work clothing is fully insulated against current
questions.rationale: Keep clothing and body clear.

questions.stem: Why are conductor rail areas often protected by fencing at depots?
options: To stop trains leaving the depot without permission
To keep tools and materials inside the depot
To mark out the parking areas for staff vehicles
To stop people accidentally walking near live rails
questions.rationale: Fencing separates people from live rails.

questions.stem: If you need to recover an injured person lying near the conductor rail, what must happen first?
options: Confirm the conductor rail is isolated before touching them
Pull them clear at once before they get worse
Use a metal pole to roll them away from the rail
Pull them clear at once by their clothing before their condition gets any worse
questions.rationale: You must not become a second casualty.

questions.stem: Why should you not stand on the end of a sleeper next to the conductor rail?
options: It damages the sleeper and loosens the fastening
That area is reserved for lookouts on duty
It is slippery, but there is no other risk
You could slip into contact with the live rail
questions.rationale: Keep clear of the conductor rail side.

questions.stem: What does 'DCCR' mean in PTS course titles?
options: DC conductor rail
Direct current control room
Danger clearance cess route
Driver controlled crossing rule
questions.rationale: PTS with DCCR covers working on lines with conductor rail.

questions.stem: You are walking in the cess on a DC line and the conductor rail is on your side. What should you do?
options: Keep well clear of it and watch your footing all the time
Walk on the guard boards, where the ground is more level
Walk on the guard boards where the ground is level
Step over it into the four-foot to walk there
questions.rationale: Stay clear and concentrate on your foot placement.

questions.stem: A colleague says the conductor rail is dead because no trains are running. What do you say?
options: Test it with a screwdriver to see whether it sparks
Treat it as live unless an isolation has been confirmed
Test it with a screwdriver to see if it sparks
Ask the driver of a passing train to confirm
questions.rationale: No trains does not mean no power.

questions.stem: You see sparks where a metal object is touching the conductor rail. What should you do?
options: Keep clear and report it as an emergency
Kick the object away from the conductor rail
Pull it out by hand while wearing gloves
Pour water on it to stop the sparking
questions.rationale: Do not approach. Get the power isolated.

questions.stem: During a group walk on a DC line, which arrangement is safest?
options: Single file on the side away from the conductor rail
Two by two, with one person on each side of the track
On the conductor rail side, where the ground is firmer
Down the middle of the four-foot, away from both sides
questions.rationale: Keep distance from the live rail.

questions.stem: Which of these is the safest way to move a long rail tool on a DC line?
options: Drag it along the ballast behind you as you walk
Carry it low and clear so it cannot fall across the rail
Drag it along the ballast behind you, resting it on the guard boards each time
Carry it across the top of the conductor rail
questions.rationale: Prevent tools bridging live and running rails.

questions.stem: You need to cross a DC line but there is no crossing point nearby. What is the safest approach?
options: Cross only if authorised, stepping over the rail without touching it
Step on the conductor rail itself to get over quickly, as long as it is dry
Jump across both the conductor rail and running rail at once
Slide across on the guard board to avoid lifting your feet
questions.rationale: Careful foot placement is vital.

questions.stem: Why should a group on a DC line keep their hands free when crossing?
options: So they can wave to drivers of passing trains
So they can wave to the drivers of any passing trains
So they can hold their phones for lighting
To keep balance and avoid falling onto the live rail
questions.rationale: Falls near the conductor rail can be fatal.

questions.stem: Which surface on a DC line is the most dangerous to step on?
options: The conductor rail and its guard board
Firm ballast in the cess
A purpose-built walkway
A purpose-built crossing provided for staff at the site
questions.rationale: Never step on live equipment.

questions.stem: After a conductor rail isolation, what must still be done before work?
options: The rail must be proven dead and protected, for example with SCDs
Nothing more, because the isolation alone makes the conductor rail completely safe
The rail must be touched briefly to check it is dead
The driver of the next train must be told about the work
questions.rationale: Follow the isolation procedure fully.

questions.stem: Which document or person tells you that a conductor rail is isolated?
options: Any track worker who has seen trains stop
A passenger waiting on the nearby platform
Any track worker who has seen that trains have stopped
The authorised person under the permit arrangements
questions.rationale: Only authorised arrangements confirm isolation.

questions.stem: What is the danger of a stolen cable on a DC line?
options: There is no danger once the cable has been removed
Dangerous voltages may be present on exposed equipment
The line will be quieter for track workers
There is no danger once the cable has gone
questions.rationale: Report cable theft and keep clear.

questions.stem: Why should you be careful with shovels near the conductor rail?
options: The shovel might be damaged by the ballast
The blade could touch both the conductor and running rail
The shovel might move the sleeper out of line
The shovel might set off the train's AWS equipment as it passes over
questions.rationale: Short circuits can cause severe flashes.

questions.stem: What should you do if you feel a tingle from a running rail on a DC line?
options: Move away and report it
Touch it again to check
Ignore it
Pour water on it
questions.rationale: This may show a fault.

questions.stem: You must place equipment near a DC line. Where is safest?
options: Clear of the conductor rail and secured so it cannot fall on it
On the guard board, where it is off the wet ballast
On the guard board, where it is off the wet ballast and easy to reach again
Between the conductor rail and the running rail
questions.rationale: Prevent accidental contact.

questions.stem: Which of these combinations makes DC work especially risky?
options: Daylight, dry ground and tools stored away
Daylight, dry ground and tools stored away from the line
Darkness, wet ground and tools near the conductor rail
A confirmed isolation with SCDs fitted
questions.rationale: Several risks together increase danger.

questions.stem: Why should you not use the conductor rail to steady yourself?
options: It is wobbly
It is live and can kill
It is slippery
It is wobbly and might move when you lean on it
questions.rationale: Never touch it.

questions.stem: Why is standing on the guard board side when a train passes dangerous?
options: You may be close to live shoe gear and the train
It blocks the driver's view of the signals
It is noisier on that side of the track
It blocks the driver's view of the signals ahead
questions.rationale: Keep clear of the conductor rail side when trains pass.

questions.stem: When working on DC lines in snow, what extra hazard is there?
options: Snow makes the conductor rail safe to touch
Snow can hide the conductor rail and guard boards
Snow switches the power off automatically to protect it
Snow switches off the power automatically
questions.rationale: Take extra care when equipment is hidden.

questions.stem: Which of these may be needed on DC lines to protect people working near the conductor rail?
options: Only a lookout to watch for approaching trains
Only a safety helmet and safety boots
Only a mobile phone to call for help
Isolation, insulated tools and suitable PPE
questions.rationale: Electrical protection is in addition to protection from trains.

questions.stem: What should you do if a train stops beside you with sparks from its shoe gear?
options: Touch the shoe gear
Walk under the train
Walk under the train to look at the shoe gear
Keep clear and report it
questions.rationale: Shoe gear is live.

questions.stem: Why might a conductor rail ramp be placed at a level crossing?
options: To slow down road vehicles approaching the crossing
The rail is gapped there, and the ramp guides the shoes back on
To slow down road vehicles and warn pedestrians that a train is coming
To provide a place to store emergency detonators
questions.rationale: Ramp ends remain live.

questions.stem: Which of these should you do if your boot gets caught near the conductor rail?
options: Grab the conductor rail to pull yourself free, as it is the nearest handhold
Kick hard against the guard board until your boot comes loose
Lie down across the rails so that you can use both hands
Stay calm, free yourself carefully without touching the rail, and call for help
questions.rationale: Panic can cause contact.

questions.stem: What is the main safety message for DC lines in PTS training?
options: Touch the conductor rail only when it is completely dry
Step on the conductor rail only at level crossings
Treat the conductor rail as dead once the last train has gone
Never touch or step on the conductor rail and keep tools clear
questions.rationale: Simple, strict rules prevent deaths.

questions.stem: Can a conductor rail be live even if the train lights on a stopped train are off?
options: No, the lights show the power
Yes, the rail can still be live
Only if it is raining
No, the lights show whether the power is on or off
questions.rationale: Never judge power by train behaviour.

questions.stem: What should a COSS brief about DC lines?
options: Only the line speed and the normal direction of traffic
Only the passenger timetable for the rest of the day
Only where the group's vehicles should be parked
Where the conductor rail is and the rules for working near it
questions.rationale: Electrical hazards must be part of the briefing.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid working near conductor rail in floodwater?
options: Water can carry current to you
The rail floats
Water cools the rail and makes it contract
Water cools the rail
questions.rationale: Stop and get advice when water is present.

questions.stem: What makes conductor rail particularly dangerous compared with OLE for people on the ground?
options: It carries a much higher voltage than overhead lines
It is always hidden under the ballast and hard to see
It is at ground level, where feet and tools can easily touch it
It carries a much higher voltage than the overhead line on AC routes
questions.rationale: Its position makes accidental contact easy.

questions.stem: What should you do if you need to use a metal bar near a DC line?
options: Lean it on the conductor rail while you work
Lean it on the conductor rail while you work so it does not fall over
Throw it to a colleague across the rail
Use it only if authorised and so it cannot touch the rail
questions.rationale: Plan tool use near live rails.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a live DC hazard on a train?
options: Passenger doors
Windows
Passenger doors and their warning lights
Exposed collector shoes
questions.rationale: Collector shoes are live.

questions.stem: What does it mean if a DC line is described as 'energised'?
options: The line is busy
Signals are working
The line is busy with many trains running
The conductor rail is live
questions.rationale: Energised means live.

questions.stem: What should you do with a damaged guard board you notice?
options: Stand on it to test whether it is still firm
Stand on it to test
Keep clear and report it
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Damaged guarding increases risk.

questions.stem: Why should you never put a hand under the conductor rail?
options: It is dirty
It is the drainage channel and will be wet
You could touch live parts or be trapped
It is the drainage channel
questions.rationale: Keep body parts clear.

questions.stem: In an emergency on a DC line, who should be asked to switch off the power?
options: The signaller or electrical control room
The guard on the nearest train
The guard on the nearest train, using the train's radio system
A passenger with a mobile phone
questions.rationale: Electrical control isolates the supply.

questions.stem: Which statement about DC isolation is correct?
options: Anyone can pull a fuse to isolate the rail
Train drivers isolate the rail from the cab
Only authorised people can arrange and confirm it
Isolation happens automatically at night
questions.rationale: Authorised arrangements must be followed.

questions.stem: What is the safest place to kneel when working on a DC line under protection?
options: Only where your briefing allows, clear of any live rail
On the guard board, where it is off the wet ballast
Next to the conductor rail
In the gap between conductor and running rail
questions.rationale: Follow your briefing and isolation limits.

questions.stem: Which of these would be a sign of a conductor rail fault?
options: A train passing quietly at normal speed
Clean, freshly laid ballast
Arcing, a burning smell or smoke near the rail
Signals changing aspect as trains pass
questions.rationale: Report electrical faults immediately.

questions.stem: What should you do if a trespasser is near the conductor rail?
options: Chase them along the line to catch them
Chase them along the line until they leave
Shout at them until they run across
Warn them to keep away and report it at once
questions.rationale: Report trespass to the signaller or British Transport Police.

questions.stem: Why are conductor rail areas at stations especially risky for the public?
options: People may fall or climb down close to a live rail
The conductor rail is very tall at stations
The conductor rail is always hidden at stations
Trains go faster through stations
questions.rationale: Report anyone on the track at stations.

questions.stem: In which part of Great Britain is third-rail DC electrification most common?
options: Northern Scotland
Central Wales
Southern England
Cornwall
questions.rationale: Much of the network south of London uses 750 V DC conductor rail.

questions.stem: Which of these is the correct description of a conductor rail 'gap'?
options: A break in the rail, often at crossings or junctions
A gap left for drainage under the guard boards
The space between the conductor rail and the cess
A missing sleeper under the conductor rail
questions.rationale: Gaps do not make the rail either side safe.

questions.stem: Why can a train bridge a conductor rail gap?
options: It carries batteries for the gap
It switches to diesel at gaps
The driver lowers a special arm
It has collector shoes along its length
questions.rationale: Shoes at different points keep contact.

questions.stem: What is the danger if you stand in a conductor rail gap when a train passes?
options: The train will stop on the gap
The gap will close suddenly
The train's shoes may still be live
There is no danger at a gap
questions.rationale: Collector shoes can carry current.

questions.stem: Which of these must you never use to cross a conductor rail?
options: A purpose-built staff crossing
A level crossing deck
A footbridge
The guard board
questions.rationale: Guard boards must not be stepped on.

questions.stem: What should you do if you need to work within reach of the conductor rail?
options: Wear rubber boots and carry on
Ask a colleague to watch the rail
Work only between trains
Only do it under an authorised isolation
questions.rationale: Close work needs the rail isolated.

questions.stem: What is a 'DC electrical control room'?
options: A room at the station for drivers
The centre that controls the conductor rail power
A store for spare conductor rail
A room at the station where drivers take their breaks
questions.rationale: Electrical control isolates and restores power.

questions.stem: What happens to the conductor rail if a short circuit occurs?
options: The rail becomes safe immediately
There may be a violent flash and the supply may trip
The rail becomes safe immediately and can be touched
Signals turn green
questions.rationale: Short circuits are dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of these could cause a short circuit between conductor and running rail?
options: A wooden sleeper under the track
A plastic bag caught on the fence
A metal bar lying across both
A worker standing in the cess
questions.rationale: Conductive objects can bridge the rails.

questions.stem: How should you carry a metal ladder near a conductor rail line, if allowed?
options: Horizontally and clear of the conductor rail
Dragged along the guard boards
Upright, leaning on the conductor rail
Across both rails as a bridge
questions.rationale: Keep conductive items away from the rail.

questions.stem: Why is the conductor rail usually on the side away from platforms?
options: To make it easier for drivers to see
To save electricity
Because trains only have shoes on one side
To reduce the risk to people on platforms
questions.rationale: It is often placed away from platforms where possible.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a passenger drop something near the conductor rail?
options: Climb down quickly to retrieve it
Tell station staff; nobody should go down to get it
Use a metal hook to fish it out from the platform
Tell the passenger to get it themselves
questions.rationale: Never go near the live rail.

questions.stem: Why are conductor rail lines particularly dangerous for trespassers?
options: Trains on DC lines are faster
The rail is hidden underground
There are no signals on DC lines
The live rail is at ground level
questions.rationale: Trespassers often do not realise the rail is live.

questions.stem: What should you do if your PTS does not include the DCCR module but your job is on a third-rail line?
options: Work there, as PTS covers all lines
Work there with extra care, as PTS covers all lines
Ask a colleague to explain the rules
Do not work there until you hold the right module
questions.rationale: Your training must match the electrification.

questions.stem: What is the risk of working on a conductor rail line in heavy rain?
options: The conductor rail will rust quickly
Trains will stop running
Water can create paths for current
The rail will cool and contract
questions.rationale: Wet conditions add to electrical risk.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see water flowing over the conductor rail?
options: Walk through it carefully
Dig a channel to drain it
Keep clear and report it
Lay planks over it
questions.rationale: Flooding near live rails is dangerous.

questions.stem: Which statement about DC lines and sparks from trains is correct?
options: Sparks can occur and may cause fires
Sparks mean the power has gone off
Sparks only happen on AC lines
Sparks are harmless
questions.rationale: Report fires and keep clear.

questions.stem: Why should you not use a metal measuring wheel across a conductor rail?
options: It might give wrong readings
It might damage the ballast
It might trigger AWS
It could touch the live rail
questions.rationale: Use non-conductive equipment near the rail.

questions.stem: Which of these indicates that the conductor rail has been isolated for your work?
options: Confirmation under the conductor rail permit arrangements
No trains have passed for an hour
No trains have passed the site for at least an hour
The lights in the station are off
questions.rationale: Only formal confirmation counts.

questions.stem: Why are short-circuiting devices fitted after isolation?
options: To stop trains entering the area
To warm the rail in winter
To stop trains from entering the area of the work
To protect against the rail becoming live again
questions.rationale: SCDs connect the conductor rail to the running rail.

questions.stem: Who is allowed to fit or remove short-circuiting devices?
options: Only competent, authorised people
Any PTS holder
The lookout
The driver of the next train
questions.rationale: This is specialist work.

questions.stem: What should you do if a short-circuiting device is removed while you are working?
options: Put it back yourself
Stop work and keep clear
Carry on quickly
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Your protection may have been lost.

questions.stem: Which of these is a live conductor rail component?
options: The ballast
The ramp end
The sleeper
The cess drain
questions.rationale: Ramp ends are part of the live rail.

questions.stem: Why are conductor rail insulators important?
options: They keep the live rail separated from the ground
They hold the running rails together
They stop trains derailing on sharp curves
They mark position of safety
questions.rationale: Damaged insulators can cause faults.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a broken conductor rail insulator?
options: Report it
Replace it yourself
Kick it back into place
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Report damaged electrical equipment.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to deal with litter caught on the conductor rail?
options: Pick it off with gloves
Burn it off with a lighter so it falls away
Kick it clear
Report it; do not remove it yourself
questions.rationale: Never touch the live rail.

questions.stem: Which of these is good practice when working near a conductor rail under isolation?
options: Keep to the limits of the permit
Work anywhere along the line
Assume adjacent lines are isolated
Assume the isolation lasts all night
questions.rationale: Isolations have limits in place and time.

questions.stem: What must happen before a conductor rail isolation is given up?
options: The lookout must go home
Everyone and everything must be clear
The trains must be in the depot
The COSS must sign out
questions.rationale: Re-energising with people near is lethal.

questions.stem: Which of these increases the risk of contact with the conductor rail?
options: Good lighting
Tiredness and rushing
Clear briefings
Proper crossings
questions.rationale: Human factors matter.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid sitting on the running rail next to a conductor rail?
options: The running rail may be too hot to sit on in summer and could burn you
It damages your clothing and makes it oily
The running rail may be too hot to sit on in summer
You could touch the conductor rail and be in the train's path
questions.rationale: Never sit on rails.

questions.stem: How should a DC line be treated if you are unsure whether it is electrified?
options: As not electrified until you see a train
As electrified only at stations
As safe at night
As electrified until confirmed otherwise
questions.rationale: If in doubt, assume it is live.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a conductor rail warning sign missing at an access point?
options: Make your own sign
Ignore it
Report it
Remove the post
questions.rationale: Warnings must be in place.

questions.stem: Why are conductor rail lines a particular hazard during snow clearance?
options: The rail may be hidden and shovels could touch it
Snow makes the rail safe
Snow makes the conductor rail completely safe to touch
Snow makes trains slower
questions.rationale: Plan clearance carefully.

questions.stem: Who should you report a person injured near the conductor rail to?
options: Your sponsor first
The station café
A passing driver only
The signaller and 999
questions.rationale: Get power isolated and help sent.

questions.stem: What is the danger of rescuing someone in contact with the conductor rail without isolation?
options: You might damage the rail
You might be late back
There is no danger if you are quick
You could also be electrocuted
questions.rationale: Wait for isolation.

questions.stem: What should you do first if you see an obstruction on a line that is open to trains?
options: Try to remove it yourself straight away
Tell the signaller immediately so trains can be stopped
Try to remove it yourself straight away before a train arrives
Wait until the end of your shift to report it
questions.rationale: The quickest way to stop trains is usually through the signaller.

questions.stem: Which of these is the quickest way to contact the signaller from the lineside?
options: Sending an email
A signal post telephone, if one is nearby
Calling the train company's customer line
Writing a note on the signal
questions.rationale: Signal post telephones connect directly to the signaller.

questions.stem: When reporting an emergency, what information should you give first?
options: Your employer's name and the address of its office
Your employer's name and the address of its head office first
Your name, exact location and what the emergency is
Your shift start time and how long you have worked
questions.rationale: Location and the type of emergency let the right action happen quickly.

questions.stem: How should you describe your location to the signaller in an emergency?
options: Using the ELR, mileage, line name and nearest signal number
By describing nearby landmarks such as a big tree or a pub
By giving the name of the nearest town or village only
By describing nearby landmarks, such as a big tree or a pub
questions.rationale: Precise information avoids delays.

questions.stem: Which emergency number should you call for the police, fire or ambulance?
options: 0800 number on your PPE
questions.rationale: Call 999 or 112 for emergency services. Also tell the signaller if the line is affected.

questions.stem: When you call emergency services to a railway incident, what else must you do?
options: Tell the signaller so trains can be stopped and help arranged
Nothing else, as the emergency services will contact the railway
Tell the train company's press office so they can update passengers
Post an update online to warn other people to stay away
questions.rationale: Emergency services may need to go on the line, which must be made safe.

questions.stem: If you need to stop an approaching train in an emergency and have a red flag, what should you do?
options: Stand in the four-foot holding the flag up so the driver sees it
Stand in the four-foot holding the flag
Throw the flag on the track
Display the red flag to the driver from a safe place
questions.rationale: A red flag or red light is a danger (stop) signal.

questions.stem: If you have no flag or light, how can you signal a driver to stop in an emergency?
options: Raise one arm above your head
Wave one arm from side to side
Raise one arm above your head and hold it still
Raise both arms above your head
questions.rationale: Both arms raised above the head means stop.

questions.stem: At night, what can you use to signal a train to stop in an emergency if you have no red light?
options: A steady white light
Any light waved violently
A green light held still
Your mobile phone screen held still
questions.rationale: Any light waved violently is treated as a stop signal.

questions.stem: Where should you stand when giving an emergency hand signal to stop a train?
options: In a position of safety where the driver can see you
In the four-foot facing the train
In the four-foot facing the train so the driver cannot miss you
Behind a structure where you cannot be seen
questions.rationale: Never put yourself in the path of the train.

questions.stem: What is 'emergency protection' in the Rule Book?
options: Basic first aid given at the lineside by trained staff before an ambulance arrives
A type of protective clothing worn when working on lines that are open to traffic
The fire evacuation procedure used in depots and stations when an alarm sounds
Arrangements to stop trains when a line is obstructed and the signaller cannot be reached
questions.rationale: It involves trained people placing detonators and track circuit operating clips.

questions.stem: Who may carry out emergency protection with detonators?
options: Anyone who holds a valid PTS certificate
Only people trained and competent to do so
Any member of the public who finds an obstruction
Any lookout, as part of normal lookout duties
questions.rationale: Using detonators needs specific competence.

questions.stem: What is a detonator used for on the railway?
options: A small explosive charge used for blasting rock in cuttings
A device that cuts the power to the overhead line instantly
A device that turns all nearby signals to red when pressed
A device clipped to the rail that bangs when a train runs over it
questions.rationale: The bang warns the driver to stop.

questions.stem: In emergency protection, how many detonators are usually placed and how far apart?
options: Three detonators, 20 metres apart
Two detonators, 100 metres apart
One detonator only, at the obstruction
Five detonators, 5 metres apart
questions.rationale: Three detonators 20 m apart is the standard arrangement.

questions.stem: In emergency protection, at what distance from the obstruction are detonators normally placed?
options: About 50 metres
About 200 metres
About 2 kilometres
About 10 kilometres
questions.rationale: The 2 km distance gives an approaching train room to stop.

questions.stem: What is a track circuit operating clip (TCOC) used for?
options: To show the line as occupied so protecting signals go to danger
To hold two lengths of rail together at a broken joint
To earth the overhead line before people start work
To hold two lengths of rail together at a broken joint until it is welded
questions.rationale: A TCOC connects the two running rails, imitating a train on the track circuit.

questions.stem: Why should you not rely only on a track circuit operating clip to protect a line?
options: It is too loud and frightens people near the line
It is too loud and frightens people standing near the line
It only works where track circuits are fitted and working
It switches off the overhead line when applied
questions.rationale: Some lines use axle counters, where a TCOC does not work.

questions.stem: If a train approaches before you reach the 2 km point when providing emergency protection, what should you do?
options: Place detonators and show a hand danger signal from a safe place
Keep walking until you reach the 2 km point and then act
Lie down beside the track so the driver does not hit you
Keep walking until you reach the 2 km point and only then place the detonators
questions.rationale: Stop the train as soon as possible using available means.

questions.stem: When a detonator explodes under a train, how far should people be from it?
options: Well away, because fragments can fly out
Right beside it to check it went off
Within 1 metre to hear it
Right beside it, so you can confirm it went off
questions.rationale: Detonators can throw out fragments. Keep a safe distance and turn away.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find an injured person on the line?
options: Move them off the line immediately, whatever the risk to yourself
Make sure you are safe, call for help and protect them from trains
Leave them where they are and finish the work you were doing
Move them off the line straight away, whatever the risk to you
questions.rationale: Your safety comes first, then call the signaller and emergency services.

questions.stem: Before helping someone who has collapsed near the conductor rail, what must you consider?
options: Whether the rail is live and whether they are touching it
Whether they are carrying a valid Sentinel card
Whether it is time for the group's lunch break
Whether they are carrying a valid Sentinel card and who their sponsor is
questions.rationale: Check for electrical danger before touching them.

questions.stem: What should you do if there is a fire on or near the line?
options: Fight it with water, even if it is near live equipment
Ignore it if it looks small and is not spreading
Keep clear, warn others and report it to the signaller and 999
Fight it with water, even if it is close to live equipment
questions.rationale: Fires near the railway can affect trains and electrical equipment.

questions.stem: Why should you not use water on a fire near electrical equipment?
options: Water is too heavy
Water makes the fire bigger only
Water damages PPE and makes it less visible
Water can conduct electricity and cause shocks
questions.rationale: Use the correct extinguisher only if trained and safe.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an emergency plan or arrangements in the briefing?
options: To show which members of the group are paid the most
To decide where the group will go for meal breaks
So everyone knows what to do and who to call if things go wrong
To show which members of the group are paid the most and who is in charge
questions.rationale: Emergency arrangements should be covered before work starts.

questions.stem: Which of these should be in the briefing about emergencies?
options: How to contact the signaller and where the nearest access point is
The names of the drivers booked on trains passing the site
The annual profits of the sponsor that employs the group
The names of all the drivers booked to work trains past the site that day
questions.rationale: Know how to get help and how emergency services can reach you.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a train with something hanging from it or on fire?
options: Report it to the signaller immediately
Try to wave the train down from the four-foot
Throw ballast at it
Ignore it, the driver will know
questions.rationale: The signaller can stop the train and arrange help.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a broken rail on a line open to traffic?
options: Report it to the signaller immediately as an emergency
Report it in the weekly defect report next week
Try to fix it yourself with a spare fishplate
Mark it with chalk and leave it for the next patrol
questions.rationale: A broken rail can cause a derailment.

questions.stem: If you see damage to a bridge after a road vehicle has hit it, what should you do?
options: Report it to the signaller at once so trains can be stopped
Wait for the road vehicle's driver to report it
Report it at the end of your shift in writing
Wait for the road vehicle's driver to report it to the police
questions.rationale: Bridge strikes can make the line unsafe.

questions.stem: What is a 'Rail Emergency Call' on GSM-R?
options: A routine call to order spare parts for broken trains
An urgent radio call that alerts drivers and signallers nearby
A call made by the COSS to book a possession
A routine call made to order spare parts for trains that have broken down
questions.rationale: It is used to stop trains quickly in an emergency.

questions.stem: After an accident or near miss, what should you do once it is safe?
options: Keep quiet about it so that nobody gets into trouble
Keep quiet about it so that nobody in the group gets into trouble
Post the details on social media to warn others
Report it so the cause can be investigated and lessons learned
questions.rationale: Reporting helps prevent repeat events.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are involved in an accident on the railway?
options: Leave the site before anyone has a chance to ask questions
Go and change your clothes before the investigators arrive
Report it and be ready for post-incident drugs and alcohol testing
Leave the site before anyone has a chance to ask questions about what happened
questions.rationale: Post-incident testing is part of the drugs and alcohol policy.

questions.stem: What is the Network Rail system for reporting hazards and near misses called?
options: Near Track
Close Call
Safe Line
Rail Watch
questions.rationale: Close Call reports help fix hazards before they cause harm.

questions.stem: What should you do if a member of the public is on the line?
options: Chase them along the track until they leave
Ignore them, as it is a matter for the police
Chase them along the track until they leave the railway
Tell the signaller immediately so trains can be controlled
questions.rationale: Trespass is a serious risk. Report it.

questions.stem: If you find an unattended bag or suspicious item on the railway, what should you do?
options: Open it to check what is inside
Throw it off the railway
Do not touch it; move away and report it
Open it carefully to see whether it is dangerous
questions.rationale: Follow security procedures and report to the signaller or police.

questions.stem: What should you do if a level crossing barrier is damaged and a train is due?
options: Lift the barrier yourself
Direct traffic across
Report it immediately to the signaller
Lift the barrier yourself and direct the traffic across
questions.rationale: Level crossing failures can cause collisions.

questions.stem: What is the safest action if a train has derailed near your site?
options: Climb onto the derailed train to help the passengers out
Keep clear, warn others and report it, as other lines may be affected
Walk along the open line to see how far the damage goes
Climb onto the derailed train straight away to help the passengers get out
questions.rationale: Derailments can block other lines and damage OLE.

questions.stem: Why should you not walk in front of a derailed train to help?
options: The driver will be angry with people near the train
Walking near it will damage the track further
Other trains may still be running and the train may move
It is outside your normal working hours
questions.rationale: Make the area safe before helping.

questions.stem: What should you do if your lookout is injured during work?
options: Carry on without a lookout, but listen harder for trains
Ask the injured lookout to continue
Let one person carry on working
Stop work, move everyone to safety and get help
questions.rationale: Without a lookout the group has no warning.

questions.stem: Who should you tell first if your group cannot contact the signaller in an emergency?
options: Nobody, because only the signaller can deal with railway emergencies
Your family, so that they can phone the railway on your behalf
Use any other available means, such as 999 or another railway contact
Your sponsor's accounts team, as they hold all the contact numbers
questions.rationale: Keep trying until someone who can help is told.

questions.stem: Where is the safest place to wait for emergency services to arrive?
options: In the four-foot so that they can see you easily
Off the line in a safe place, ready to guide them in
Next to the conductor rail where there is more room
On a signal post ladder so you are higher up
questions.rationale: Guide emergency services safely to the scene.

questions.stem: Why must emergency services not go on the line until it is safe?
options: They are not allowed on railway land
They need a Sentinel card before going on the railway
Trains and electricity are still dangerous to them
Their vehicles are too heavy
questions.rationale: The railway must make the area safe, including stopping trains and isolating power.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see an animal on the line?
options: Chase it off along the line
Ignore it
Report it to the signaller
Feed it
questions.rationale: Animals on the line can cause collisions.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a fence damaged and children playing near the line?
options: Ignore it, as the children are not on the line yet
Report it immediately and warn the children to keep away
Join them to keep an eye on them until they leave
Repair the fence first and report it afterwards
questions.rationale: Children on the railway are at high risk.

questions.stem: What is the first rule of helping in any emergency on the railway?
options: Act as fast as possible whatever the risk
Wait for a manager
Take photos first
Do not put yourself in danger
questions.rationale: You cannot help if you become a casualty.

questions.stem: What does 'hand danger signal' mean?
options: A yellow flag shown to tell a driver to slow down
A red flag or red light shown to stop a train
A yellow flag to slow down
A white light to show workers are present
questions.rationale: Red means stop.

questions.stem: What does a yellow hand signal flag mean to a driver?
options: Stop immediately
Speed up
Proceed with caution
Stop immediately at the flag
questions.rationale: Yellow means caution.

questions.stem: What does a green hand signal flag mean to a driver?
options: Stop
Proceed
Danger ahead
Reverse
questions.rationale: Only give hand signals when competent and authorised.

questions.stem: Who should give hand signals to trains during normal work?
options: The lookout, at all times during the work
Anyone on site who can see the driver
Only people competent and authorised to do so
Any passenger who sees a problem on the line
questions.rationale: In an emergency, anyone may try to stop a train.

questions.stem: If you are first on the scene of a serious incident, what should you avoid?
options: Moving anything unless it is needed for safety
Calling the signaller about the incident
Keeping other people away from the danger
Keeping other people away from the danger area
questions.rationale: Evidence may be needed for investigation.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are uncertain whether something is an emergency?
options: Wait to see if it gets worse
Ask on social media
Report it anyway; it is better to be safe
Wait and see whether it gets worse before calling
questions.rationale: Signallers would rather know.

questions.stem: A colleague is struck by a train and seriously injured. Trains are still running. What is your first priority?
options: Run onto the line to reach them before anything else happens
Get trains stopped through the signaller, and keep yourself safe
Move them off the track before calling anyone for help
Wait for the COSS to decide what should be done first
questions.rationale: Stop trains first so nobody else is hurt, then call 999 and give help.

questions.stem: Where should an injured person be moved if they are on an open line and a train is approaching?
options: Only clear of the line, and only if you can do it safely in time
Into the six-foot between the two lines, out of the way
Into the six-foot between the two lines, out of the way of the approaching train
Nowhere, because injured people must never be moved
questions.rationale: Moving a casualty may be needed to save their life, but only if safe for you.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of first aid at a railway incident?
options: To replace the need for an ambulance in most railway incidents
To replace the need for an ambulance in most railway incidents and save time
To decide who caused the accident before investigators arrive
To keep a casualty alive and stop them getting worse until help arrives
questions.rationale: Only give first aid you are trained to give, and only when it is safe.

questions.stem: In an emergency, why should you tell the signaller which lines are affected?
options: So the right lines can be blocked and trains stopped
So the signaller can update the passenger timetable
So the signaller can call your Primary Sponsor
So the signaller can write the incident report
questions.rationale: Clear information means the right protection is given.

questions.stem: What should you do after the signaller tells you trains have been stopped?
options: Go onto any line you need to, as trains have stopped
Assume all lines in the area are now closed to trains
Confirm which lines are protected before going on them
Go onto any line you need to, now that trains have stopped
questions.rationale: Make sure you understand exactly what has been protected.

questions.stem: What should you do if heavy rain causes flooding over the track?
options: Ignore it, as water drains away from the track
Ignore it, as water drains away from the track quickly
Dig a channel across the track to drain it
Report it, as trains may need to stop or slow down
questions.rationale: Flooding can wash out ballast and hide hazards.

questions.stem: What should you report if you see a landslip near the line?
options: Report it at the end of the week
Clear it yourself
Take photographs and report it at the end of the shift
Report it immediately to the signaller
questions.rationale: Landslips can block or undermine the track.

questions.stem: During a thunderstorm near OLE, what is the main extra risk?
options: Lightning and electrical faults
Trains run faster
Trains run faster to get out of the storm
Ballast gets warmer
questions.rationale: Follow your briefing and stop work if it becomes unsafe.

questions.stem: Why should you report trees leaning towards the railway after high winds?
options: They spoil the view from passing trains
They spoil the view for passengers on trains
They could fall onto the line or the OLE
They attract birds that nest on signals
questions.rationale: Fallen trees cause serious incidents.

questions.stem: What should you do if you think a train has hit something on the line?
options: Report it to the signaller immediately
Ignore it if the train kept going
Walk along the line to look
Walk along the line to look for what was hit
questions.rationale: There may be damage or an obstruction.

questions.stem: What should you do if a passenger train stops and passengers start getting off onto the track?
options: Help them walk along the open line to the next station
Tell them to cross to the other side of the railway
Ignore it, as the train crew are responsible for them
Report it immediately so trains on other lines can be stopped
questions.rationale: Passengers on the track face trains and electrical dangers.

questions.stem: Why might you need to tell emergency services which railway access point to use?
options: So they can park without paying a charge
So they can avoid the busy station area
So they can meet your sponsor on arrival
So they reach the scene quickly by a safe route
questions.rationale: Access points may be hard to find without directions.

questions.stem: What information about electrification should you give in an emergency report?
options: The colour of the OLE masts nearest to the incident
The age of the conductor rail and when it was laid
Whether OLE or conductor rail is there and if it is damaged
The colour of the OLE masts and the age of the conductor rail near the incident
questions.rationale: Electrical risks affect how emergency services respond.

questions.stem: Why should you repeat back key details when reporting an emergency?
options: Because it is the polite way to end a call
To fill time while the call is connected
So the call can be recorded for training
To make sure the message is understood correctly
questions.rationale: Repeat-back reduces misunderstandings.

questions.stem: If you witness a near miss with a train, what should you do?
options: Keep quiet about it so nobody in the group gets into trouble
Tell only your friends about it after the shift has finished
Report it only if someone was actually hurt by the train
Report it through the proper channel, even if no one was hurt
questions.rationale: Near misses are warnings. Reporting them prevents accidents.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of RAIB investigating near misses as well as accidents?
options: To find and punish the workers involved
To delay trains while evidence is collected
To learn lessons before someone is killed
To close lines that have had near misses
questions.rationale: Many RAIB investigations are into near misses.

questions.stem: If a detonator is heard going off unexpectedly, what does it usually mean?
options: The overhead line has just been switched back on after work
The overhead line has just been switched back on
The work group is being called for a meal break
A train has run over a detonator, which may warn of danger
questions.rationale: Detonators are warning devices. Be alert.

questions.stem: In an emergency, which line should you warn the signaller about first?
options: Only the line on which your own group is working, as the others are not yours
Any line that is obstructed or where people are in danger
Only the line on which your own group is working
Only lines that have overhead line equipment
questions.rationale: All affected lines need protection.

questions.stem: What should you do if you have to evacuate your work site quickly?
options: Run across the tracks by the shortest route to the road
Follow the briefed emergency route and stay clear of open lines
Leave by any route that looks quickest at the time
Wait for everyone to finish their work and leave together
questions.rationale: Plan for emergencies before they happen.

questions.stem: Why should you keep a mobile phone charged on site?
options: So the lookout can text you when a train is coming
So you can play games in breaks
So the lookout can text you warnings
So you can call for help in an emergency
questions.rationale: A phone is an important emergency tool, but never a train warning device.

questions.stem: Which of these should be reported to the signaller as an emergency?
options: Smoke coming from beneath a passing train
A passenger train running exactly on time
A clean and tidy cess with no rubbish
A worker taking a rest break off the line
questions.rationale: Fires or defects on trains need quick action.

questions.stem: If you see a signal showing no light at all, what should you do?
options: Ignore it
Change the bulb yourself
Report it to the signaller
Wave the next train through
questions.rationale: A dark signal is a fault that must be reported.

questions.stem: Why should you be careful when approaching a crashed road vehicle on a level crossing?
options: The road vehicle's driver may be angry about the crash
The crashed vehicle may be blocking road traffic
Trains may still be coming, and fuel or electricity may be a hazard
The road vehicle's driver may be angry and blame you for the crash on the crossing
questions.rationale: Make sure trains are stopped first.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find someone has been hurt by an electric shock and is not breathing?
options: Wait beside them for them to wake up by themselves
Pour cold water over them to bring them round
Make sure it is safe, call 999 and start CPR if trained
Leave them and go back to work until help arrives
questions.rationale: Fast action saves lives.

questions.stem: Why should you know where the nearest defibrillator (AED) is on a large site?
options: It can help restart the heart after a cardiac arrest
It is used to test track circuits on site
It is part of the PPE required for track work
It is used to test track circuits on the site
questions.rationale: Knowing emergency equipment locations saves time.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of 'emergency contact numbers' on site signage?
options: To help you reach the right control quickly
To order replacement PPE for members of the group
To order replacement PPE for the group
To contact your bank if you lose your card
questions.rationale: Use them in emergencies only.

questions.stem: Which is the correct sequence when you see a serious hazard on an open line?
options: Remove the hazard yourself, then report it the next day
Take photographs of it, then report it to your manager
Get to safety, report to the signaller, then warn others
Ignore it unless someone asks you to deal with it
questions.rationale: Make yourself safe and report immediately.

questions.stem: Why should you report minor injuries on site?
options: So they are recorded and the cause can be fixed
So you can be given the rest of the day off
So you can make a compensation claim later
So you can be given the rest of the day off work
questions.rationale: Reporting helps prevent more serious injuries.

questions.stem: If a road vehicle has crashed through the boundary fence onto the line, what should you do?
options: Push it clear of the track with the help of colleagues
Wait for the owner to come and deal with it
Report it to the signaller immediately and keep clear
Push it clear of the track with colleagues
questions.rationale: The line is obstructed and must be protected.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a fire in lineside vegetation that is spreading towards the railway?
options: Beat it out with your jacket
Beat it out with your jacket before it spreads
Report it to 999 and the signaller
Pour diesel on it
questions.rationale: Lineside fires can damage cables and affect trains.

questions.stem: Why should you not try to stop a train by standing in front of it?
options: The driver may be too busy to notice you standing there
The train may be unable to stop and will strike you
The driver may be too busy to notice you
It may cause damage to the front of the train
questions.rationale: Always signal from a position of safety.

questions.stem: What does the signaller need to know to stop trains approaching an obstruction?
options: The name of your COSS and their phone number
Your Sentinel number and Primary Sponsor
Which line and the exact location of the obstruction
Your Sentinel number and the name of your Primary Sponsor
questions.rationale: Location and line are critical.

questions.stem: If you call the signaller and they do not answer, what should you do?
options: Give up and go home, as you have tried to report it
Wait for the signaller to call you back the next day
Try again or use another emergency route, while keeping safe
Give up and go home, as you have tried to report it and nobody answered
questions.rationale: Persist until the emergency is reported.

questions.stem: What is the safest thing to do if you hear a train approaching while you are giving first aid near the line?
options: Get to a position of safety and signal the driver to stop if you can
Lie down next to the casualty so the train passes over you both
Stand in front of the train waving both arms until it stops
Ignore the train and carry on giving first aid to the casualty
questions.rationale: You must protect yourself.

questions.stem: What should you do if a work vehicle catches fire on site?
options: Drive the vehicle onto the track away from the work area
Move everyone away, call 999 and tell the COSS and signaller
Fight the fire with water even though OLE is overhead
Leave the vehicle burning and go home for the day
questions.rationale: Keep people safe and report.

questions.stem: Why is it important to know the location of the nearest hospital before starting work?
options: To know where to buy lunch on a break
To know where to fill in timesheets
To get an injured person to help quickly
To know where to visit friends after work
questions.rationale: Emergency arrangements should include medical help.

questions.stem: Which of these must be reported as a dangerous occurrence?
options: A train passing a worker who was not in a position of safety
A worker finishing their shift a few minutes early
A site that is left clean and tidy after work
A worker finishing their shift a few minutes early without telling the COSS
questions.rationale: Such events must be reported and investigated.

questions.stem: Who investigates serious railway accidents to find the causes?
options: The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB)
The train operating company only
The train operating company whose train was involved
The train operating company involved
questions.rationale: RAIB investigates independently to improve safety.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to give a statement after an incident?
options: Say nothing at all until you are told to speak
Give an honest, accurate account of what you saw
Agree with whatever your colleagues have said
Agree with whatever your colleagues have already said
questions.rationale: Honest accounts help prevent future incidents.

questions.stem: In an emergency, what does 'block the line' mean?
options: Park a vehicle across the track as a barrier
Stop trains from entering the affected section
Put objects on the rails to stop trains
Park a vehicle across the track as a barrier to trains
questions.rationale: Only the signaller can block the line for trains.

questions.stem: If you see a broken OLE wire across a road bridge, what should you do?
options: Pull it off the bridge onto the track below
Keep people away and report it as an emergency
Cover it with a coat so nobody touches it
Drive under it quickly before it falls further
questions.rationale: The wire may be live.

questions.stem: What should you do if a train hits a vehicle at a level crossing?
options: Climb onto the train to help the driver and passengers
Walk along the line to look for damage to the track
Wave down drivers on the other lines yourself
Report it, keep clear of other lines and wait for help
questions.rationale: Other lines may still be open.

questions.stem: Why should you stay calm and speak clearly when reporting an emergency?
options: So you sound professional to the signaller
So that you are not blamed for the incident later
So you are not blamed for the incident
So the message is understood quickly and correctly
questions.rationale: Clear communication saves time.

questions.stem: You see a train pass with a door open. What should you do?
options: Report it to the signaller
Wave at the driver from the four-foot
Run after the train to close it
Ignore it, as the guard will notice
questions.rationale: Defects on trains should be reported so the train can be stopped and checked.

questions.stem: What is the best way to describe an obstruction to the signaller?
options: How big it is compared with your van
What it is, which line and exactly where
Who you think left it there
How long you think it has been there
questions.rationale: Clear details let the signaller protect the right line.

questions.stem: In an emergency, why is it important to know which lines are electrified?
options: So you can switch off the power yourself
So you can tell drivers to lower pantographs
Emergency responders need to know the electrical risks
So you can decide which train to stop and which to let through
questions.rationale: Electrical hazards affect rescue.

questions.stem: Who should isolate the overhead line in an emergency?
options: Any track worker, by using the nearest lineside switch to cut the power off
Electrical control, after a request through the signaller or control
Any track worker, by using the nearest lineside switch
The emergency services, using their own equipment on arrival
questions.rationale: Only authorised arrangements can isolate the supply.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find a person who appears to be on the railway to harm themselves?
options: Get trains stopped and call for help
Leave them alone so you do not upset them
Physically drag them off the line straight away
Wait to see whether they leave on their own
questions.rationale: Report it immediately so trains can be stopped and help sent.

questions.stem: Why should you stay with an injured person if it is safe?
options: To make sure nobody takes their belongings
To keep them from talking to anyone about what has happened
To reassure them and update the emergency services
To finish the paperwork about the incident
questions.rationale: Calm support helps the casualty.

questions.stem: What should you do if a casualty is bleeding heavily?
options: Give them a drink of water and wait
Give them a drink of water and wait beside them until help arrives
Give them a drink of water and wait for help
Apply firm pressure if trained and safe, and call 999
questions.rationale: Severe bleeding needs urgent treatment.

questions.stem: What is the recovery position used for?
options: Lifting a casualty onto a stretcher so they can be carried away
Carrying a casualty along the track
Keeping an unconscious breathing person's airway clear
Lifting a casualty onto a stretcher safely
questions.rationale: First aid training covers this.

questions.stem: What should you do if you witness a fatality on the railway?
options: Get trains stopped, call for help and do not disturb the scene
Move the body clear of the track straight away
Take photographs to send to the newspapers
Move the body clear of the track straight away so trains can run
questions.rationale: The scene may need investigation. Support is available afterwards.

questions.stem: Why might you be offered support after a traumatic incident?
options: To decide whether you caused the incident
Traumatic events can affect mental health
To check your competences are valid
To arrange your next shift
questions.rationale: Talking to support services helps recovery.

questions.stem: What should you do if an emergency happens and you do not have a phone signal?
options: Use a signal post telephone or send someone to get help
Wait until the signal improves
Walk along the four-foot until you get a signal
Wait until the phone signal improves before trying to report anything
questions.rationale: Use every safe means to raise the alarm.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of keeping an emergency contact list on site?
options: To order lunch
To call taxis
To get help quickly
To book holidays
questions.rationale: Emergency numbers should be easily available.

questions.stem: Who should you tell first about a fire on a train?
options: The signaller
The train's operator by email
Your family
Social media
questions.rationale: The signaller can stop and control trains.

questions.stem: What should you do if a level crossing is showing lights but no train comes for a long time?
options: Lift the barriers yourself
Direct cars across
Report it as a possible fault
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Crossing faults must be reported.

questions.stem: What should you do if a crossing barrier is up while a train approaches?
options: Lower the barrier with your hands
Stand on the crossing to stop cars
Report it urgently and warn road users if safe
Wave the train through as quickly as possible
questions.rationale: This is an emergency.

questions.stem: During an emergency evacuation of a work site, where should the group meet?
options: Wherever they like
At the nearest pub
On the track where everyone can be seen
At the agreed assembly point
questions.rationale: An assembly point helps account for everyone.

questions.stem: Why is a head count important after an emergency?
options: To work out pay
To record overtime
To make sure nobody is missing
To arrange transport home
questions.rationale: Missing people may need rescue.

questions.stem: What should you do if a train strikes an animal near your site?
options: Remove the animal yourself straight away
Ignore it, as it is common
Wave the next train down
Report it and keep clear of the line
questions.rationale: There may be damage or debris.

questions.stem: What is the danger of debris left after a train strike?
options: It may obstruct the line or derail the next train
It will rust the rails if it is left for long
It will attract more animals only
It will stop signals working
questions.rationale: Report debris.

questions.stem: What should you do if a stone is thrown at you from a bridge?
options: Throw it back
Move away and report it to British Transport Police
Chase the person up the embankment
Chase the person up the embankment to catch them
questions.rationale: Do not put yourself at more risk.

questions.stem: If you discover graffiti artists on the railway at night, what should you do?
options: Confront them directly
Report it and keep away from them
Chase them along the line
Ignore it, as they are not your problem
questions.rationale: Trespassers may be aggressive; report to police.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a train stopped unexpectedly in a section?
options: Climb into the cab to find out why
Walk along the train to look
Climb into the cab to ask the driver why it has stopped
Keep clear and report it if you think there is a problem
questions.rationale: Stopped trains can move without warning.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to help passengers evacuating a train?
options: Lead them along any line you think is safe so they reach the road quickly
Only under the direction of the train crew and emergency services
Tell them to cross to the nearest road by themselves
Lead them along any line you think is safe to the road
questions.rationale: Evacuation must be controlled to avoid more casualties.

questions.stem: What should you do if a train hits a buffer stop?
options: Report it and keep clear
Push the train back
Fix the buffer stop
Ignore it
questions.rationale: There may be injuries and damage.

questions.stem: What is 'emergency stop' equipment on plant for?
options: To start the machine in cold weather
To sound the machine's horn
To call the signaller
To stop the machine quickly in danger
questions.rationale: Know where the emergency stops are on plant you work near.

questions.stem: What should you do if someone is trapped by a machine?
options: Try to pull them free at once
Reverse the machine to free them
Leave them and fetch a manager
Stop the machine and call for help
questions.rationale: Stop the machine first.

questions.stem: Why should you not move a casualty with a suspected spinal injury?
options: Moving them could make the injury worse
They will be too heavy to carry far
It is against Sentinel rules
They may not want to move
questions.rationale: Only move them if there is immediate danger.

questions.stem: When is it right to move a casualty with a suspected spinal injury?
options: Whenever it is more comfortable for them
Only if they are in immediate danger, such as from a train
Whenever the COSS asks for it to be done
Whenever it would make them more comfortable to lie on
questions.rationale: Balance the risks.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a vehicle on fire on a road bridge over the railway?
options: Ignore it, as it is not on the railway
Call 999 and report it to the signaller
Climb up to help
Wait for someone else to report it
questions.rationale: Fires above can affect the railway.

questions.stem: What information should you give the signaller about an injured person?
options: Their name and address only
Their full name and home address only
Location, number injured and whether lines are affected
Their employer's name and the name of their Primary Sponsor
questions.rationale: This helps control send help and stop trains.

questions.stem: What should you do after an incident has been dealt with?
options: Only tell your friends about it
Report it fully through the correct process
Only tell your friends about what happened
Wait to see if anyone asks
questions.rationale: Reporting allows learning.

questions.stem: Why is it important not to speculate about blame after an incident?
options: Investigations need facts, not guesses
It might upset the train company
It wastes time on site
It is against the Sentinel rules
questions.rationale: Give facts only.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to speak to the media about an incident?
options: Give them full details
Refer them to the official press contacts
Give them the full details you saw
Guess what happened
questions.rationale: Communications should go through official channels.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a train run past a signal at red?
options: Report it at next week's safety meeting
Chase the train
Report it next week
Report it to the signaller at once
questions.rationale: A SPAD is serious and urgent.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of emergency drills?
options: To practise so people react correctly
To fill time on quiet shifts
To test the train timetable
To check that PPE sizes are correct
questions.rationale: Practice improves response.

questions.stem: What should you do if your group cannot reach the planned emergency access point?
options: Agree a safe alternative with the COSS
Use any route you like
Stay where you are until someone comes to find you
Walk along the open line
questions.rationale: Emergency plans must work in practice.

questions.stem: If a colleague collapses while working on the line, what should you do first?
options: Pick them up and carry them off the line
Leave them and call their family
Make sure trains are stopped or you are protected, then help
Pick them up and carry them off the line straight away
questions.rationale: Protect yourself and them from trains first.

questions.stem: Why should emergency vehicles be met at the access point?
options: So they can be guided safely to the scene
So they can be charged for parking
So they can sign the briefing
So they can be checked for PPE
questions.rationale: Guidance saves time and keeps them safe.

questions.stem: What should you do if the emergency services ask to go on the line?
options: Let them go straight onto the line to save time
Take them along the open line
Let them go straight onto the line to save time, as they are professionals
Tell them to wait until the railway confirms it is safe
questions.rationale: The railway must confirm protection and isolation first.

questions.stem: What is the first thing to check before approaching any railway emergency?
options: That you have your camera
That the train is on time
That your timesheet is signed
That it is safe for you to approach
questions.rationale: Your safety first.

questions.stem: What colour high-visibility clothing is required on the GB mainline railway?
options: Orange
Yellow
Green
Blue
questions.rationale: Railway high-visibility clothing is orange to the railway industry standard.

questions.stem: Why is yellow high-visibility clothing not used on the track?
options: It costs more than orange and wears out much faster
It costs more than orange and the dye wears out much faster
It can be confused with signals or blend into vegetation
It is reserved for police and emergency services
questions.rationale: Orange stands out against the railway environment.

questions.stem: Which railway industry standard covers high-visibility clothing for track workers?
options: GE/RT8000, the national Rule Book
NR/L2/OHS/019, the safe working standard
EN 397, the industrial helmet standard
RIS-3279-TOM (formerly GO/RT3279)
questions.rationale: RIS-3279-TOM sets the specification for railway hi-vis clothing.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of high-visibility clothing on the railway?
options: To make you easy to see for drivers and plant operators
To show clearly which employer and sponsor you work for
To show clearly which employer you work for
To protect you from electric shock near the line
questions.rationale: Being seen is part of staying safe, but it does not protect you from being struck.

questions.stem: Does wearing high-visibility clothing mean a driver can stop for you?
options: No, trains often cannot stop in time even if you are seen
Yes, drivers must stop when they see orange clothing
Yes, but only in daylight when it is clearly visible
Yes, drivers must stop whenever they see orange clothing on the line
questions.rationale: PPE is the last line of defence. You must still get clear.

questions.stem: How should you wear your high-visibility clothing?
options: Unzipped so that it is cooler when you are working
Clean, in good condition, fastened and not covered
Under a dark jacket so that it stays clean
Tied around your waist until a train approaches
questions.rationale: Dirty or covered hi-vis is much less visible.

questions.stem: What should you do if your hi-vis clothing is dirty or torn?
options: Wear it anyway until the end of the week
Replace it before going on or near the line
Turn it inside out so the dirt is hidden
Wear it anyway until the end of the week, then replace it
questions.rationale: Damaged PPE does not give proper protection.

questions.stem: What type of footwear is required for track work?
options: Trainers with good grip for walking on ballast
Wellington boots without toe caps for wet weather
Trainers with good grip for walking long distances on ballast
Safety boots with toe protection and ankle support
questions.rationale: Safety footwear protects against crushing and ankle injuries on uneven ground.

questions.stem: Why is ankle support important in track safety footwear?
options: It makes the boots look smarter and more professional
It keeps your feet dry when walking through puddles
Ballast and uneven ground can easily twist your ankle
It protects your feet from electric shock on DC lines
questions.rationale: A fall on the ballast could put you in danger.

questions.stem: When must a safety helmet be worn?
options: Never, because helmets are not used on the railway
Never, because helmets are not normally used on the railway
Whenever the site rules or risk assessment require it
Only inside tunnels where there is falling debris
questions.rationale: Helmets protect against falling and flying objects.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of eye protection on the railway?
options: To help you see trains further down the line in bright sun
To protect against flying debris, dust and chemicals
To help you see trains further down the line
To protect you against electric shock from OLE
questions.rationale: Wear eye protection when the task or site requires it.

questions.stem: Why might you need hearing protection on site?
options: To block out the sound of train horns, which is distracting
To keep your ears warm during winter night shifts
Machinery and tools can cause permanent hearing damage
To avoid distracting conversations while you work
questions.rationale: Hearing protection must not stop you hearing warnings.

questions.stem: What must be considered if you wear ear defenders on or near the line?
options: That you can still hear warnings from the lookout or system
That they are the same colour as your high-visibility clothing
That they are wireless so the cable does not catch on tools
That they can play music to help you concentrate
questions.rationale: Warning arrangements must be suitable for noisy work.

questions.stem: Which gloves should you use for a task?
options: Any gloves you own, as long as they fit comfortably
Woollen gloves, which are suitable for every task
Gloves suited to the hazard, such as cut-resistant or chemical
Any gloves you own, as long as they fit comfortably and keep your hands warm
