options: Keep working without it
Keep working and only report it if it has not turned up in a month
Report it to your sponsor straight away
Wait a month to see if it turns up
questions.rationale: Lost cards must be reported so they can be cancelled and replaced.

questions.stem: What happens if someone uses a false identity or someone else's card?
options: It is a serious breach that can lead to removal from the scheme
Nothing happens, as long as the person is competent
Nothing happens, as long as the person really is competent
They are given a verbal warning and allowed to carry on
questions.rationale: Identity checks keep unqualified people off the railway.

questions.stem: Which of these is recorded on Sentinel?
options: Your competences, medical and drugs and alcohol status
Your bank details and the account your wages go to
Your bank details and the account your wages are paid into
Your social media accounts and online profiles
questions.rationale: These records show whether you can work.

questions.stem: How long is PTS competence usually valid for?
options: Two years
Six months
Five years
For life
questions.rationale: After two years you must recertify.

questions.stem: Within how many days of PTS expiry must recertification be completed to avoid redoing initial PTS?
options: 7 days
56 days
365 days
There is no limit
questions.rationale: If you miss the window, you must take the initial course again.

questions.stem: What is the PTS recertification course?
options: A longer course that only new starters are allowed to attend
A course that qualifies you to act as a COSS on site
A course that qualifies you to drive road-rail vehicles
A shorter course to renew PTS before or soon after it expires
questions.rationale: Recertification is typically one day.

questions.stem: Which PTS modules might be added depending on where you work?
options: Driving and catering modules
AC (OLE) and DCCR (conductor rail) modules
Signalling and ticketing modules
Driving and catering modules for welfare staff
questions.rationale: Your training should match the electrification you will work near.

questions.stem: Can you work on the railway if your PTS has expired?
options: Yes, for one month
Yes, if you are experienced
No
Yes, if the COSS agrees
questions.rationale: Only work with valid competence.

questions.stem: What does it mean if your Sentinel record shows a competence as suspended?
options: You can still do it as long as someone supervises you
It is probably a typing error and can be ignored
You must not carry out that role until it is reinstated
You can still do it as long as someone competent supervises you
questions.rationale: Suspended competences cannot be used.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for providing you with suitable PPE under the scheme rules?
options: Your sponsor
The COSS
Network Rail
You alone
questions.rationale: Sponsors must provide appropriate PPE.

questions.stem: What must every Sentinel card holder report to their sponsor?
options: Anything that may affect their ability to work safely
Their holiday plans for the rest of the year
Their holiday plans for the rest of the year and any days off
Their car mileage for each journey to site
questions.rationale: This includes medication, lack of equipment or personal circumstances.

questions.stem: What should you do if a site manager asks you to do a task you are not competent for?
options: Refuse politely and explain you are not competent
Do it anyway to avoid any trouble on site
Do it anyway so that you avoid causing any trouble on site
Ask a competent colleague to sign it off for you
questions.rationale: Only do work you are trained and competent to do.

questions.stem: How do sites check that a worker is competent?
options: By asking how long they have worked
By looking at their PPE
By checking their Sentinel card and record
By asking how many years they have worked on the railway
questions.rationale: Electronic checks confirm current competences.

questions.stem: What is a 'competence' in the Sentinel scheme?
options: A type of employment contract held with a sponsor
A type of employment contract with a sponsor
A skill or role you are trained and assessed for
A pay grade linked to your years of service
questions.rationale: Examples include PTS, COSS and lookout.

questions.stem: What does it mean to be 'sponsored'?
options: Someone has paid for your holiday or travel expenses
An organisation has accepted responsibility for you under Sentinel
You are on a training scheme and not yet allowed on track
Someone has paid for your holiday or travel expenses while you were away
questions.rationale: Sponsorship is required to work on the infrastructure.

questions.stem: What must your sponsor do before you attend PTS training?
options: Buy you a full uniform including a branded jacket
Buy you a full uniform, including a branded jacket and helmet
Make sure your profile has valid medical and D&A information
Give you a company car for travelling to site
questions.rationale: Training providers check these records.

questions.stem: Which of these is a breach of Sentinel rules?
options: Reporting a lost card to your sponsor the same day
Reporting a lost card
Working while your medical has expired
Attending recertification on time
questions.rationale: Medical and D&A requirements must be current.

questions.stem: Why is the Sentinel scheme important for safety?
options: It makes sure that trains run on time across the network
It helps make sure only competent, fit people work on the railway
It saves money for sponsors by reducing training costs
It makes sure that trains run on time across the whole of the network
questions.rationale: Competence and fitness are vital on the railway.

questions.stem: What should you do if your personal details change, such as your name?
options: Do nothing, as the card still works
Write the new details on the card yourself
Do nothing, as long as the card still works in the reader
Tell your sponsor so your record can be updated
questions.rationale: Records must be accurate.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are working for a new sponsor?
options: Keep using your old sponsor's card details
Work without a sponsor until the paperwork arrives
Make sure the sponsorship is set up before working
Ask the COSS on site to act as your sponsor
questions.rationale: You need valid sponsorship.

questions.stem: Which of these can lead to your Sentinel card being cancelled?
options: Reporting a near miss
Asking a question in a briefing
Reporting a near miss through Close Call
A positive drugs or alcohol test
questions.rationale: Under Network Rail's updated policy, cards can be cancelled for five years.

questions.stem: Does holding PTS give you the right to go on the line whenever you want?
options: Yes, at any time while your PTS is in date
No, you also need a reason, authority and a safe system
Yes, as long as you are carrying your Sentinel card with you
Yes, as long as you carry your Sentinel card
questions.rationale: PTS is a basic competence, not permission.

questions.stem: Why must the COSS check Sentinel cards at the start of work?
options: To count the number of hours each person has worked
To count the number of hours each person has worked so far this week
To confirm everyone is who they say with the right competences
To issue new cards to anyone whose card has expired
questions.rationale: This is part of the COSS's checks before work.

questions.stem: What are the Sentinel Scheme Rules?
options: The operating rules followed by train drivers and signallers
The Highway Code for vehicles at access points
The operating rules followed by train drivers
The rules for individuals and sponsors under the scheme
questions.rationale: They cover duties such as carrying cards, fitness and working hours.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to work longer hours than allowed?
options: Refuse and raise it with your sponsor
Agree, so that you keep the work with that agency
Work and hide the hours
Use a colleague's card
questions.rationale: Working hours limits protect against fatigue.

questions.stem: At Stoats Nest Junction in 2018, what did RAIB find about checks on the worker's hours?
options: Hours were checked every hour by the COSS on site
The labour supplier made no checks on staff working hours
Hours were checked by the driver of the train before it reached the site
Hours were checked by the driver of the train
questions.rationale: Contingent workers' hours must be monitored to control fatigue.

questions.stem: What is a 'contingent worker'?
options: A Network Rail manager who visits sites
A Network Rail manager who visits sites to check work
A member of the public who helps in emergencies
A worker supplied by an agency or labour provider
questions.rationale: Contingent workers need the same protection and supervision.

questions.stem: Which statement about zero-hours workers and safety is correct?
options: They must not challenge their supervisor or the COSS
They do not need a PTS if they are supervised
They have the same right to challenge unsafe work as anyone
They must not challenge their supervisor or the COSS on site
questions.rationale: A just culture should support everyone in raising concerns.

questions.stem: What should you do if your Sentinel card is damaged and cannot be read?
options: Tell your sponsor and get it replaced
Keep using it until it stops working
Tape it together so it can be read
Keep using it until it stops working altogether
questions.rationale: The card must be readable for checks.

questions.stem: Why is identity checking important on site?
options: To keep track of who has ordered lunch
To check that everyone is in the right uniform
To keep track of who has ordered lunch for the group
To make sure only the right, competent people are working
questions.rationale: Imposters could endanger everyone.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are concerned about how your sponsor manages safety?
options: Ignore it, as your sponsor knows best how to manage safety
Post about it anonymously online so that others can see it
Ignore it, as your sponsor knows best how to manage safety for its workers
Raise it through proper channels or a confidential service such as CIRAS
questions.rationale: There are routes to raise safety concerns.

questions.stem: What should you do if you will be absent from work for a long time due to illness?
options: Return to work without telling anyone, as you are now better
Tell your sponsor, as your fitness may need reviewing before you return
Nothing, as long as your medical certificate is still in date when you return
Nothing, as long as your medical certificate is still in date
questions.rationale: Fitness for duty matters on return.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sponsor's responsibility?
options: Setting the timetable for trains on the route
The safety of the people they sponsor
Setting the timetable for the route
Issuing tickets to rail passengers
questions.rationale: Sponsors are responsible for their individuals' safety.

questions.stem: Why must each person have only one Primary Sponsor?
options: It is not a rule; people can have several Primary Sponsors at the same time
So that sponsors can pay a lower rate to experienced workers
It is not a rule; people can have several Primary Sponsors
So one organisation clearly manages their hours, fitness and competence
questions.rationale: Clear responsibility helps manage fatigue and competence.

questions.stem: What happens on Sentinel when you complete a course?
options: You are given a new card with a new photograph
You get a new card every time
The competence is recorded on your profile
You lose other competences
questions.rationale: Your record shows current competences.

questions.stem: Who decides whether you can work on Network Rail infrastructure?
options: Your sponsor, based on competence, fitness and Sentinel rules
Any COSS who is in charge of a site that day
Any train driver who sees you working on the line
Any train driver who sees you working on the line during the shift
questions.rationale: Sponsors manage your eligibility.

questions.stem: What should you do if a site card reader shows your card is invalid?
options: Go on the line anyway, as the reader may be faulty
Try a colleague's card in the reader instead
Go on the line anyway, as the reader may simply be faulty
Stop and contact your sponsor; do not go on the line
questions.rationale: Invalid cards mean you cannot work.

questions.stem: Which of these must be current for you to keep working under PTS?
options: Your car insurance and full driving licence
Your gym membership and fitness record
Your PTS competence, medical and D&A status
Your car insurance and driving licence
questions.rationale: All are checked on Sentinel.

questions.stem: Why must you never sign in for a colleague?
options: It is a waste of time at the start of the shift
It costs the sponsor money each time it happens
It hides who is actually on site and breaks the rules
It is a waste of time at the start of each shift
questions.rationale: Accurate records protect everyone.

questions.stem: Which organisation's infrastructure does the Sentinel scheme mainly cover?
options: All public roads in the UK
Airports and their runways
Network Rail managed infrastructure
London Underground and all tram networks
questions.rationale: Sentinel is the competence system for NRMI.

questions.stem: Why should you keep a copy of your training records?
options: There is no need to keep any copy at all
To show your friends and family
To check your competences and expiry dates
There is no need to keep any copy
questions.rationale: Know when your competences expire.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of PTS recertification?
options: To increase your pay rate for the next two years
To give you the chance to change your sponsor
To refresh knowledge and confirm you remain competent
To increase your pay rate for the next two years of work
questions.rationale: Rules and lessons change over time.

questions.stem: You arrive on site and realise you left your Sentinel card at home. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS; you may not be allowed on the line without it
Work anyway and bring the card with you tomorrow
Work anyway and bring the card with you tomorrow, as the COSS knows you
Show the COSS a photo of the card on your phone
questions.rationale: You must carry your card on the infrastructure.

questions.stem: A colleague offers you their card so you can do a COSS role you are not qualified for. What should you do?
options: Accept for one shift
Accept if no one checks
Accept if they stay with you
Refuse and report it
questions.rationale: Working beyond your competence is dangerous and a serious breach.

questions.stem: Your PTS expires next week and the recertification course is booked for the week after. What does that mean?
options: You can keep working until the course takes place
You get an automatic extension of up to a month
You cannot work under PTS from expiry until you recertify
You can keep working as normal until the course takes place
questions.rationale: Never work with expired competence.

questions.stem: Your agency asks you to start a night shift at a different site straight after a day shift elsewhere. What should you do?
options: Accept and drink energy drinks to stay awake
Refuse, as you would not have the required rest
Accept, and drink energy drinks to stay awake
Accept and work more slowly to stay safe
questions.rationale: Sentinel rules restrict working within 12 hours of a previous shift without a risk assessment.

questions.stem: A new worker on site does not know their sponsor's name. What does this suggest?
options: Nothing, as sponsors' names are not important on site
Their sponsorship may not be set up properly and should be checked
They are very experienced and have had many sponsors
Nothing, as sponsors' names are not important once someone is on site
questions.rationale: Everyone must have a valid Primary Sponsor.

questions.stem: Why might a site use a card reader or app to check Sentinel cards?
options: To record when people take their lunch breaks
To record when each person takes their lunch break
To confirm competences are current at the time of work
To print timesheets for the sponsor's payroll
questions.rationale: Electronic checks catch expired or suspended competences.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of 'Sentinel Scheme Rules - Individual Requirements'?
options: To list train times
To set out how much each COSS should be paid
To explain level crossings
To set out what each card holder must do
questions.rationale: It covers carrying cards, fitness, reporting and working hours.

questions.stem: Which of these is a responsibility of a Sentinel card holder?
options: Being fit for work and not fatigued by excessive work or travel
Setting up line blockages with the signaller before work
Paying for their own Sentinel card each year
Choosing which competences they want to hold
questions.rationale: Fitness is a personal responsibility.

questions.stem: How should a card holder treat their competence limits?
options: Only carry out roles they hold valid competence for
Do any job they are asked to do on site
Do roles they have watched others do many times
Do higher roles at night when fewer people are around
questions.rationale: Competence protects you and others.

questions.stem: Why are drugs and alcohol test records stored on Sentinel?
options: So the results can be used for marketing campaigns
So sponsors and sites can confirm you meet the requirements
So insurers can check the results before paying any claims
So insurers can see the results before paying claims
questions.rationale: Records are stored securely in line with data protection law.

questions.stem: Which statement about a Sentinel card and PPE is correct?
options: A valid card means some PPE can be left off
PPE means the card is optional
Neither is needed in a possession
Both are needed; one does not replace the other
questions.rationale: Carry your card and wear correct PPE.

questions.stem: If a site manager asks you to work outside your sponsor's arrangements, what should you do?
options: Agree straight away
Use a different card
Check with your sponsor first
Work without telling your sponsor
questions.rationale: Your sponsor is responsible for you.

questions.stem: Why should you keep your sponsor informed about other jobs you do?
options: It is not needed, because other jobs are your private business
So they can match the pay from the other job
So they can manage your total working hours and fatigue
It is not needed, as other jobs are private
questions.rationale: Hours across jobs add up.

questions.stem: What does a valid medical on Sentinel show?
options: That you are guaranteed not to become ill before the next check
That you met the medical standard for your role at the last check
That you are medically fit to drive passenger trains
That you no longer need drugs and alcohol testing
questions.rationale: Medicals must be kept in date.

questions.stem: Who should you contact if you think your Sentinel record is wrong?
options: The train company
Your sponsor
The signaller
The police
questions.rationale: Sponsors maintain your record.

questions.stem: Which is a valid reason for a COSS to refuse to let you work?
options: Your Sentinel check shows your PTS has expired
You asked several questions in the briefing
You arrived wearing brand new hi-vis clothing
You reported a hazard on the walk to site
questions.rationale: Expired competence means you cannot work.

questions.stem: Why are 'sub-contractor' workers also covered by Sentinel?
options: Sub-contractors pay extra so that they can be included
They are not covered; only direct employees are
Joining is optional for sub-contractor companies
Everyone on the infrastructure must meet the same standards
questions.rationale: Standards apply regardless of employer.

questions.stem: What is the danger of a culture where people work on others' cards?
options: It saves time at the start of each shift
It saves time at the start of each shift on site
Untrained people may end up in safety-critical roles
It improves teamwork in the group
questions.rationale: This undermines the whole scheme.

questions.stem: Which of these could your sponsor be required to do after a safety breach?
options: Give you a bonus for reporting the breach yourself
Review your competence and arrange retraining or suspension
Ignore it if nobody was hurt as a result
Give you a bonus for reporting the breach yourself before anyone else did
questions.rationale: Sponsors manage competence after incidents.

questions.stem: Why should you be honest about your experience when starting on a new site?
options: So that you can skip the full site briefing
So the COSS can supervise and brief you properly
So that you can skip the full briefing
So that you can be allowed to work alone
questions.rationale: Newer workers may need more support.

questions.stem: If you are sponsored but have not been briefed for a site, can you start work?
options: Yes, sponsorship is enough
No, you must be briefed first
Yes, if you have been there before
Yes, if your card is valid
questions.rationale: Briefing is always needed.

questions.stem: Who should be told if you are injured at work on Network Rail infrastructure?
options: Nobody, if the injury is only minor
Only your family when you get home
Your COSS or supervisor and your sponsor
Only the driver of the next train
questions.rationale: Injuries must be reported.

questions.stem: What does 'competence assessment' involve?
options: Checking that you are being paid the correct rate
Checking that your car is safe to drive to site
Checking that you can apply your training safely in practice
Checking that you are paid the correct rate for the role
questions.rationale: Assessment confirms knowledge and skill.

questions.stem: Why might you need refresher training before recertification?
options: To fill the time before the course starts
It is never needed before a recertification course
Rules and practices change and skills fade
It is never needed for recertification
questions.rationale: Keep up to date with changes.

questions.stem: Which document should you follow if Sentinel rules and site instructions seem to conflict?
options: Follow neither of them and use your own judgement based on your experience
Follow neither of them and use your own judgement instead
Stop and get clarification from your sponsor or the person in charge
Follow whatever your more experienced colleagues are doing
questions.rationale: Clarify before acting.

questions.stem: Why is honest reporting of hours important under Sentinel?
options: Fatigue limits rely on accurate hours
It affects tax only
It affects holidays only
It only matters for calculating holiday entitlement
questions.rationale: False records hide fatigue risk.

questions.stem: What is likely to happen if you are found working with a card that is not yours?
options: A friendly reminder from the COSS on site
Nothing, if they had the right competence
Nothing, as long as they actually hold the right competence
Serious action, including removal from the scheme
questions.rationale: Identity fraud is treated very seriously.

questions.stem: Who must check that track visitors are accompanied?
options: The visitor, once they have been briefed
The driver of any train passing the site
The person responsible for the visit and the COSS
The visitor, once they have been briefed on site
questions.rationale: Visitors rely on supervision.

questions.stem: Which of these should you do if your sponsor does not give you the right PPE?
options: Buy any hi-vis from a shop and claim it back
Work without it until the right PPE arrives
Buy any hi-vis from a shop and claim it back later
Raise it with your sponsor and do not work without it
questions.rationale: Sponsors must provide suitable PPE.

questions.stem: Why are sponsors responsible for checking working hours of the people they supply?
options: To reduce the costs of the labour they supply
To reduce the cost of the labour they supply to clients
To stop fatigued people working on the railway
To decide when people can book holidays
questions.rationale: Stoats Nest showed the risk when hours are not checked.

questions.stem: What is the most important thing your Sentinel card proves?
options: Your identity and the competences recorded for you
Your home address and contact details
Your salary and the rate you are paid
Your home address and emergency contact details
questions.rationale: It links you to your record.

questions.stem: What should a new starter do if unsure about Sentinel rules?
options: Guess what the rules probably say
Ask their sponsor or supervisor
Ignore them until someone complains
Ask a passenger at the station
questions.rationale: Asking is always better than guessing.

questions.stem: What is the Sentinel card often described as?
options: Your free travel pass for trains across the network
Your passport to work on the railway
Your bank card for receiving wages from your sponsor
Your parking permit for railway car parks and compounds
questions.rationale: It links your identity to your competences.

questions.stem: Which organisation runs the Sentinel scheme on behalf of the industry?
options: The Office of Rail and Road, as the safety regulator
RSSB, as the body that writes the Rule Book
British Transport Police, as the railway police
Network Rail
questions.rationale: Sentinel is Network Rail's scheme for its managed infrastructure.

questions.stem: What happens to your competences if your Primary Sponsor ends your sponsorship?
options: They are deleted permanently and you must retrain from scratch
You cannot work on NRMI until a new sponsor takes you on
They transfer automatically to the next company you work for
Nothing changes and you can keep working as an individual
questions.rationale: You need an active sponsor to work.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'sub-sponsor' arrangement?
options: To let another organisation use a worker under agreed controls
To let a worker hold two Primary Sponsors at the same time
To let a worker avoid medical and drugs and alcohol checks
To let a worker pay for their own Sentinel card each year
questions.rationale: Arrangements must keep clear responsibility for safety and hours.

questions.stem: Which of these must your sponsor check before you work?
options: Your credit score and your home address history
Your competence, medical and D&A status
Your social media accounts and your friends
Your car's MOT and your insurance documents
questions.rationale: These are core Sentinel requirements.

questions.stem: Can a site manager add a competence to your Sentinel record?
options: Yes, if they have seen you do the task safely before
Yes, if the COSS signs a note on the day
No; competences come from approved training and assessment
Yes, if you have worked for the company for a year
questions.rationale: Competences must be gained properly.

questions.stem: What should you do if a training provider gives you a certificate but Sentinel does not show the competence?
options: Use the competence anyway, as you have the certificate
Ask a colleague to vouch for you on site
Update the record yourself on the app
Tell your sponsor before using the competence
questions.rationale: Sentinel must reflect valid competences.

questions.stem: Why is identity fraud such a serious breach of Sentinel rules?
options: It costs the sponsor money to replace the card
It could put an untrained person in danger and others at risk
It makes the site paperwork harder to complete
It confuses the payroll system at the end of the month
questions.rationale: Identity checks protect everyone.

questions.stem: What should you do if you suspect a colleague is using someone else's card?
options: Ignore it, because it is their own business
Keep quiet in case they are a friend of the COSS
Ask them for a share of their pay
Report it
questions.rationale: Fraud endangers lives.

questions.stem: What does it mean if your card is 'blocked' on Sentinel?
options: You can still work but only on the lineside
You must not work until it is resolved
You can still work as long as you carry a paper copy
You can work if you are escorted by a COSS
questions.rationale: Blocked cards stop you working.

questions.stem: Why might a card be blocked?
options: For example, after a positive D&A test or misconduct
Because the photograph is more than a year old
Because you changed your mobile phone number
Because you have taken annual leave
questions.rationale: Blocks follow serious issues.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Sentinel helpline or website for card holders?
options: To get information about the scheme and your record
To book train tickets at a discount
To report trains running late
To book train tickets at a discount for railway staff
questions.rationale: Your sponsor is the first point of contact for changes.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to work on a different infrastructure manager's railway?
options: Assume your Sentinel card covers every railway
Assume no rules apply away from Network Rail
Check you meet that railway's own requirements
Ask the driver of the first train
questions.rationale: Other railways, such as London Underground, have their own rules.

questions.stem: Why do sponsors keep records of hours worked?
options: To manage fatigue limits and rest
To set holiday dates for staff
To decide who gets new PPE
To choose who works at weekends
questions.rationale: Hours records help prevent fatigue.

questions.stem: What is a sponsor's responsibility if a worker has an accident on site?
options: Remove them from the scheme straight away without review
Support them and make sure it is reported and investigated
Ignore it if the worker was employed by an agency
Ask the worker to keep the accident quiet
questions.rationale: Sponsors manage their workers' safety.

questions.stem: Which of these is a card holder's duty under the scheme rules?
options: Choose which rules apply to their own work
Arrange their own medical tests privately
Pay their sponsor for each shift worked
Report anything that affects safe working
questions.rationale: Individuals must report issues to their sponsor.

questions.stem: Why is accurate recording of training important?
options: So people can show off their certificates
So only competent people do safety-critical tasks
So sponsors can charge clients more
So that people can show off their certificates to friends
questions.rationale: Records support safe allocation of work.

questions.stem: If your PTS recertification is missed by more than 56 days, what happens?
options: You get a free extension of one month
You can recertify online with no assessment
You must take the initial PTS course again
Nothing, as long as your medical is valid
questions.rationale: The recertification window is limited.

questions.stem: What should you do if your medical is due to expire next week?
options: Tell your sponsor so it can be renewed in time
Keep working and renew it when convenient
Ask a colleague to lend you their certificate
Assume it will be extended automatically
questions.rationale: Keep requirements in date.

questions.stem: Why do sponsors need to know about your other employers?
options: To take a share of your earnings
To manage your total hours and fitness
To check your references every year
To decide your holiday dates
questions.rationale: Fatigue depends on all work done.

questions.stem: Who can see your Sentinel competences when your card is checked?
options: Authorised people checking your eligibility
Any member of the public
Social media companies
Train passengers waiting on the nearest platform
questions.rationale: Data is managed in line with data protection law.

questions.stem: Why does Sentinel record drug and alcohol testing?
options: To show you meet the requirements to work
To decide your pay rate
To share with employers in other industries
To produce league tables
questions.rationale: D&A status is a requirement for working.

questions.stem: What is the main safety aim of the Sentinel scheme?
options: Fewer forms for sponsors and their clients to complete
Faster recruitment of new staff for engineering work
Fewer forms for sponsors and their clients to complete each week
Only competent, fit and authorised people on the infrastructure
questions.rationale: That is its core purpose.

questions.stem: Which statement about Sentinel and visitors is correct?
options: Visitors without PTS need an approved visitor arrangement
Visitors can use a staff member's card for the day
Visitors need no arrangement if they wear hi-vis
Visitors can go anywhere if accompanied by a driver
questions.rationale: Track Visitor Permits allow supervised visits.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see your Sentinel record shows a competence you never trained for?
options: Use it, as it must have been added for a reason
Report it to your sponsor and do not use it
Keep quiet in case it is removed
Use it only on night shifts
questions.rationale: Only use competences you genuinely hold.

questions.stem: What is a 'safety-critical communication'?
options: Any message sent by email between railway managers
Any message sent by email between railway managers and staff
A message arranging meal breaks during the shift
Any message that could affect the safety of people or trains
questions.rationale: Safety-critical messages must be clear, accurate and confirmed.

questions.stem: At the start of a safety-critical phone call, what should you do?
options: Start with the problem straight away
Say who you are, your role and your exact location
Ask how their shift is going so that the call starts politely
Give your Sentinel number only
questions.rationale: Clear identification avoids confusion.

questions.stem: Why should you repeat back important information in a safety-critical call?
options: To make the call last long enough to record
To confirm it has been understood correctly
Because it is the polite way to end a call
So the signaller can log the call time
questions.rationale: Repeat-back catches mistakes before they cause harm.

questions.stem: Why is the phonetic alphabet used in railway communications?
options: To make calls sound professional
To make radio calls sound more professional to the public
To keep messages secret
To avoid confusing letters that sound similar
questions.rationale: For example, 'B' and 'D' can be confused on a poor line.

questions.stem: In the phonetic alphabet, what word is used for the letter A?
options: Alpha
Apple
Able
Arrow
questions.rationale: A is Alpha.

questions.stem: A signaller asks you to spell a signal prefix that starts with B. Which word do you use?
options: Baker
Bravo-one
Bravo
Bertie
questions.rationale: B is Bravo.

questions.stem: Which phonetic word avoids confusing the letter D with B or T on a poor line?
options: David
Dog
Delta
Danger
questions.rationale: D is Delta.

questions.stem: When reading the letter M from a signal plate over the phone, which word should you say?
options: Mother
Mike
Mary
Metro
questions.rationale: M is Mike.

questions.stem: You need to say the letter S over the radio. Which word is correct?
options: Sierra
Sugar
Sam
Signal
questions.rationale: S is Sierra.

questions.stem: Which word represents V in the phonetic alphabet used on the railway?
options: Violet
Victory
Vehicle
Victor
questions.rationale: V is Victor.

questions.stem: Which of these is the correct phonetic word for F?
options: Freddie
Fox
Foxtrot
Flag
questions.rationale: F is Foxtrot.

questions.stem: Which phonetic word stands for Z?
options: Zebra
Zero
Zulu
Zone
questions.rationale: Z is Zulu.

questions.stem: How would you spell the signal number 'DM42' using the phonetic alphabet?
options: David Mary forty-two
Dog Mother four two
Delta Mike four two
Delta Metro forty-two
questions.rationale: Use phonetic words for letters and say each number clearly.

questions.stem: How would you spell 'KX' using the phonetic alphabet?
options: King Xavier
Kevin Xylophone
Key X
Kilo X-ray
questions.rationale: K is Kilo, X is X-ray.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid saying 'OK' alone to confirm a safety-critical instruction?
options: It sounds rude and unprofessional to a signaller
It sounds rude and unprofessional when speaking to a signaller
It does not confirm exactly what you have understood
It is not a word used in standard English
questions.rationale: Repeat back the details instead.

questions.stem: What should you do if you do not understand a safety-critical message?
options: Guess the meaning
Act on what you think was said
Ask for it to be repeated or explained
Act on what you think was most likely said
questions.rationale: Never act on a message you are unsure about.

questions.stem: What should you do if a radio or phone message breaks up?
options: Fill in the missing words yourself
Fill in the missing words yourself from the context
Ask for it to be repeated until you are sure
Pass on what you heard
questions.rationale: Incomplete messages are dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of these is good practice for safety-critical calls?
options: Use abbreviations only you know
Use the abbreviations your own team uses every day
Talk while walking on the line
Use clear, simple words and avoid slang
questions.rationale: Clear language prevents misunderstandings.

questions.stem: Who should lead a safety-critical conversation?
options: The most senior person on the call, and nobody else
The most senior person on the call, whatever their role or location is
The person who made the call, with both checking understanding
Nobody leads; each person says what they need to
questions.rationale: Both people share responsibility for clear communication.

questions.stem: What does a red signal mean to a driver?
options: Proceed with caution
Proceed at line speed
Prepare to stop at the next signal
Danger, stop
questions.rationale: A red aspect means stop.

questions.stem: What does a single yellow signal aspect mean to a driver?
options: Stop immediately at this signal and wait
Line speed is allowed as far as the next signal
Caution: be prepared to stop at the next signal
Track workers are on the line just ahead
questions.rationale: A single yellow warns that the next signal may be red.

questions.stem: What does a double yellow signal aspect mean to a driver?
options: Stop at this signal and wait for the signaller
Preliminary caution: the next signal shows a single yellow
Stop at this signal and wait for the signaller to give permission
The line ahead is blocked for engineering work
questions.rationale: Double yellow gives an earlier warning on faster lines.

questions.stem: What does a green signal aspect mean to a driver?
options: Track workers ahead are clear of the line
Proceed: the next signal is not at danger
Stop and wait for permission to continue
Reduce speed for a junction ahead
questions.rationale: Green allows the train to proceed.

questions.stem: Does a red signal mean that no train can approach you?
options: Yes, provided the red signal is close to where you are standing
No, trains can come on other lines or from the other direction
Yes, during daylight when drivers can see it clearly
Yes, as long as the red signal is close to where you are
questions.rationale: Never rely on signals for your own protection unless the line is blocked for you.

questions.stem: What is a 'position light' signal?
options: A signal that controls road traffic at level crossings
A light fitted to a worker's helmet for night shifts
A signal with white or red lights for shunting and slow moves
A signal that controls road traffic at a level crossing
questions.rationale: Position light signals control low-speed movements.

questions.stem: What is the AWS sound when a driver approaches a green signal?
options: A continuous horn
A bell or chime
No sound
A siren
questions.rationale: AWS gives a bell for clear and a horn for caution or danger.

questions.stem: What does the train driver have to do when AWS sounds a horn?
options: Acknowledge it, or the brakes will apply automatically
Sound the train horn twice to warn any track workers ahead
Sound the train horn twice to warn track workers
Nothing, because the horn is for information only
questions.rationale: AWS warns drivers of restrictive aspects.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the train horn when approaching track workers?
options: To greet them
To ask them to stop work for a chat
To tell the signaller
To warn them to move clear
questions.rationale: Respond by moving to safety and raising one arm.

questions.stem: How do you acknowledge a train driver's horn warning?
options: Shout to the driver and wave as the train goes past
Shout to the driver as the train passes
Raise one arm above your head once you are clear
Flash your torch towards the cab
questions.rationale: This tells the driver you have seen the train.

questions.stem: What might a driver do if they see track workers who do not acknowledge the horn?
options: Ignore them, as they are not in the driver's way
Speed up to pass them as quickly as possible
Flash the headlights to greet them as normal
Sound the horn again, apply the brakes and report it
questions.rationale: Drivers report unacknowledged warnings as safety incidents.

questions.stem: What is a signal post telephone plate used for?
options: To identify the signal and show how to use the phone
To show the times of trains due at that signal
To show the line speed past that signal
To show the times of trains that are due at that signal
questions.rationale: Plates help the signaller locate you.

questions.stem: Why must you tell the signaller the signal number when using an SPT?
options: So they can change the signal
So they can record your shift
So they know exactly where you are
So they can ring you back on your mobile phone later
questions.rationale: Location is essential.

questions.stem: Why should you never press a signal post telephone button unless needed?
options: Each call costs the railway a lot of money
Each call costs the railway a lot of money and is recorded
It takes the signaller away from controlling trains
Pressing it stops all trains in the area
questions.rationale: Use it only for proper purposes.

questions.stem: When talking to a signaller, how should you describe a line?
options: As 'the busy one nearest the station building'
As 'the busy one'
As 'the one nearest the café'
Using its proper name, such as the Up Fast
questions.rationale: Use proper line names to avoid confusion.

questions.stem: What is the danger of describing lines as 'left' and 'right'?
options: It depends on which way you face and is easily confused
It is not permitted on railways in Scotland and Wales
It is not permitted on railways in Scotland
It confuses the timetable used by signallers
questions.rationale: Use Up/Down and line names.

questions.stem: How should numbers be spoken in safety-critical messages?
options: As fast as possible to keep the line free
As fast as possible, to keep the radio channel free
Rounded to the nearest ten to keep it simple
Clearly, digit by digit where there could be confusion
questions.rationale: Say 'one five' rather than 'fifteen' if it avoids confusion with 'fifty'.

questions.stem: Why can 'fifteen' and 'fifty' be dangerous in a radio message?
options: They are the same number
They are not used on the railway
Radio rules say numbers must always be written down
They sound similar and could be confused
questions.rationale: Use digit-by-digit or repeat-back to confirm.

questions.stem: Which of these messages is clearest?
options: 'John Smith, COSS, at signal DM42 on the Up Main'
'It's me again, near that signal we talked about'
'John here, by the bridge, you know where I mean'
'COSS here, at the usual place, same as yesterday'
questions.rationale: Name, role and exact location.

questions.stem: The ELR you are reporting begins with C. How should you say that letter?
options: Charles
Cat
Charlie
Crossing
questions.rationale: C is Charlie.

questions.stem: Which phonetic word should be used for the letter O, so it is not confused with zero?
options: Orange
Oscar
Oliver
Over
questions.rationale: O is Oscar.

questions.stem: Which letter does 'Hotel Sierra' spell?
options: HC
AS
HT
HS
questions.rationale: Hotel is H, Sierra is S.

questions.stem: Which letters does 'Echo Charlie Mike' spell?
options: ECN
ACM
ECM
EKM
questions.rationale: Echo is E, Charlie is C, Mike is M. ECM is used in some ELR codes.

questions.stem: What does a yellow hand signal flag held steady mean?
options: Stop
Go at full speed
Danger behind
Caution
questions.rationale: Yellow means caution. Hand signals are only given by competent people.

questions.stem: What is a 'hand danger signal'?
options: A yellow flag shown to slow a train
A green light shown to start a train
A red flag or light shown to stop a train
A horn sounded twice by a lookout to warn the group
questions.rationale: Red means stop.

questions.stem: What is the emergency 'stop' hand signal when you have no flag or light?
options: One arm raised above your head and held still
Both arms raised above your head
Arms crossed in front of chest
One arm waved sideways
questions.rationale: Use it from a position of safety.

questions.stem: What does it mean if a driver sounds the horn repeatedly as they approach?
options: They are running late and want people to know
They are saying hello to the track workers
They are giving an urgent warning to people near the line
They are running late and want everyone along the line to know it
questions.rationale: Get clear immediately.

questions.stem: What is GSM-R used for?
options: Radio communication between drivers and signallers
Mobile phone calls made by passengers on trains
Mobile phone calls made by passengers on board trains
Switching the overhead line power on and off
questions.rationale: GSM-R includes emergency call functions.

questions.stem: What is a 'Railway Emergency Call' (REC) on GSM-R?
options: A call made to book a line blockage for planned work
A call made to report lost property that has been left on trains
A call that alerts all trains and signallers in an area to stop
A call made to report lost property left on trains
questions.rationale: It is used when there is immediate danger.

questions.stem: Why must hand-held radios not be used to warn track workers of trains?
options: They are too quiet to be heard over machinery
They need a separate licence for each user
They are too quiet to be heard over noisy machinery and tools
They can fail, or the message may not be heard in time
questions.rationale: Maesyfelin bridge (2016) showed how radio warnings can fail.

questions.stem: When should you NOT make a phone call on the line?
options: When you are reporting an emergency from a position of safety
While walking on or near the line or when you should be watching for trains
When you are in a safe place well away from the line, such as the welfare cabin
When the COSS asks you to call the signaller from a safe place
questions.rationale: Phones distract you.

questions.stem: Which of these is the safest place to make a call to the signaller?
options: In the four-foot, facing the traffic
A position of safety, or off the line
In the four-foot, facing the traffic, where signal is best
Standing on the rail head for signal
questions.rationale: Make yourself safe first.

questions.stem: Why should a COSS repeat the line blockage details back to the signaller?
options: To fill in time while the signaller finds the paperwork
Because the signaller asks for small talk
To test the phone
To confirm exactly which lines and limits are blocked
questions.rationale: Mistakes about blocked lines are dangerous.

questions.stem: What should a message about a line blockage include?
options: The lines, the limits and the time it is given
Only the time that the blockage is given
Only the names of the workers in the group
Only the names of the workers in the group on site
questions.rationale: Exact details avoid mistakes.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid using jargon with someone new to the railway?
options: They may not understand and could act wrongly
Jargon sounds unprofessional on site
Jargon takes longer to say than plain words
Jargon is banned in all briefings
questions.rationale: Make sure the message is understood.

questions.stem: What is a 'signal identification plate' and why is it useful in an emergency?
options: A plate showing the speed limits for the line
A plate showing the name of the train driver
A plate showing the speed limits that apply to the line
A plate with the signal's number that helps locate you
questions.rationale: Give the signal number when reporting.

questions.stem: What does a flashing yellow signal sequence on some routes warn a driver about?
options: A diverging route through junction points ahead
Track workers on the line in the next section
A signal that has failed and is flashing
Track workers on the line in the next section ahead
questions.rationale: Flashing yellows prepare drivers for a diverging route.

questions.stem: Why should track workers not rely on signal aspects to decide if it is safe?
options: Signals are often wrong and cannot be trusted
Signals control trains, not your protection, and can change
Signals are often wrong and cannot be trusted by anyone on site
Signals only work properly during the night
questions.rationale: Only your safe system of work protects you.

questions.stem: What does TPWS do if a train passes a red signal?
options: It switches off the overhead power supply
It sounds the lookout's horn at the site
It applies the train's brakes automatically
It switches off the overhead line power supply
questions.rationale: TPWS reduces the consequences of SPADs.

questions.stem: What is a 'SPAD'?
options: A signal passed at danger
A safety pad for kneeling
A type of spade
A speed restriction
questions.rationale: SPADs are serious incidents.

questions.stem: Why should you report a signal that seems to show the wrong aspect?
options: It looks untidy and wastes electricity overnight
It wastes power
It confuses passengers
It could lead to a train collision
questions.rationale: Report signalling faults immediately.

questions.stem: What should you do if a driver shouts to you from a stopped train asking for help?
options: Walk along the open line to reach the cab door and help
Walk along the open line to reach the cab door
Ignore them, as drivers must sort out their own trains
Stay safe and help them contact the signaller if appropriate
questions.rationale: Do not put yourself in danger.

questions.stem: Why are written forms used for some safety-critical arrangements?
options: To slow the work down so people are careful
To fill time while waiting for the signaller
To slow the work down so people are more careful
To give a clear record that both parties agree
questions.rationale: Written records reduce misunderstandings.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of poor safety-critical communication?
options: 'Confirm the Up Main is blocked between signals DM40 and DM44'
'Yeah, should be fine, carry on'
'Repeat back: line blocked, time 10:42'
'This is the COSS at signal DM42'
questions.rationale: Vague replies can lead to accidents.

questions.stem: What should you say to end a safety-critical call properly?
options: Just hang up once you have said your part
Just hang up once you have said what you needed to say
Confirm the agreed actions and that both understand
Say nothing and wait for the other person
questions.rationale: Close the loop.

questions.stem: Why should briefings use the same line names as the signaller?
options: Official names sound more professional
So everyone is talking about the same line
It is a legal requirement for every briefing
It is a legal requirement for briefings
questions.rationale: Consistent names avoid confusion.

questions.stem: Which of these should a lookout use to warn the group?
options: A text message sent to each member
A hand-held radio linked to the group
A hand-held radio linked to each member of the group
An approved horn, whistle or warning system
questions.rationale: Warnings must be immediate and audible to all.

questions.stem: Why is it important to say the time when agreeing a line blockage?
options: So people can set alarms on their phones for the end
It gives a clear record of when protection started
So people can set alarms on their phones
It is not important if the line is blocked
questions.rationale: Times help confirm arrangements.

questions.stem: What should you do if a message from the signaller does not match your briefing?
options: Stop and get clarification before acting
Follow the briefing and ignore the signaller
Follow whichever is easier
Guess
questions.rationale: Resolve conflicts before going on the line.

questions.stem: Why should you speak slowly when giving a location over the phone?
options: To save the battery on your mobile phone
So the listener can write it down accurately
To sound calm, whatever the situation
It is not needed if you speak clearly
questions.rationale: Clear delivery prevents errors.

questions.stem: What is the danger of passing a safety message through several people?
options: It takes too long, but is otherwise fine
It costs more in phone calls and radio time
It is too formal for a work site
Details can be changed or lost on the way
questions.rationale: Pass critical messages directly where possible.

questions.stem: Which piece of information is most useful to give the signaller if you have no signal number nearby?
options: The name of a nearby pub
The ELR and mileage from a milepost
The colour of a building
The name of a nearby pub or shop that they might know
questions.rationale: Mileage identifies your location precisely.

questions.stem: What should you do if your phone has poor reception during an emergency call?
options: Move somewhere safe with better signal, or use an SPT
Give up, as you have done your best to report it
Walk along the line until you find a better signal
Keep shouting louder until the signaller hears you
questions.rationale: Stay safe while finding a way to call.

questions.stem: Why might a signaller ask you to confirm you are clear of the line?
options: Before allowing trains to run again
To check your timesheet
To ask about weather
To test that your phone is working properly
questions.rationale: Only confirm when everyone is genuinely clear.

questions.stem: What does it mean to 'close the loop' in communication?
options: Confirm the message was received and understood
End the call as quickly as possible
Close and lock the access gate behind you
Close and lock the access gate
questions.rationale: Feedback confirms understanding.

questions.stem: What does a train's headlight being on during the day mean?
options: The driver has seen workers on the line ahead
It is normal; trains show lights to be seen
The train is about to stop at the site
The driver has seen workers on the line
questions.rationale: Do not read meaning into lights; always get clear.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a driver's hand signal to you from a passing train?
options: Run after the train to find out what the driver meant
Step onto the line to wave back so the driver knows
Ignore all trains from then on, as the driver has seen you
Stay in your position of safety and report anything unusual later
questions.rationale: Your priority is staying clear.

questions.stem: Why do drivers sound the horn at whistle boards?
options: To test that the horn is working properly
To greet staff at the next station
To test that the horn is still working properly
To warn people who may be on or near the line ahead
questions.rationale: Never rely on hearing it.

questions.stem: Which phrase is best when you want the signaller to confirm a line is blocked?
options: 'Is everything OK on the line now, do you think?'
'Are we good to get on with the job now?'
'Confirm the Up Fast is blocked between the stated signals'
'Is everything OK on the line now, do you think, can we start?'
questions.rationale: Be specific.

questions.stem: When you start a call to the signaller, what should you say first?
options: Your name, role and location
The reason you are calling, before anything else
The time you started your shift today
The name of your sponsor and its phone number
questions.rationale: Identify yourself clearly so the signaller knows who and where you are.

questions.stem: What should the signaller do after you give them important details?
options: Write them on a piece of paper and hang up
Pass them straight to the train driver unchecked
Repeat them back to check
Agree with you and move on to the next call
questions.rationale: Repeat-back works both ways.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid saying 'yeah' or 'right' to confirm an instruction?
options: They are rude to say to a signaller on the phone
They take too long to say in an emergency
They do not show what you have understood
They are not allowed under data protection rules
questions.rationale: Repeat the actual details back.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best way to say the number 15 in a safety message?
options: Fifteen-ish
About fifteen
One five
Fifty
questions.rationale: Saying digits separately avoids confusion with 50.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best way to give a time on the railway?
options: As 'half two', which everyone understands
As 'after lunch', to keep it simple
In the 24-hour clock, such as 14:30
As 'soon', when you are not sure
questions.rationale: 24-hour times avoid am/pm mistakes.

questions.stem: Why are clear location references vital in emergency calls?
options: Help can be sent to exactly the right place
They make the call sound more professional
They make the call shorter for the signaller
They are needed for the timesheet afterwards
questions.rationale: Wrong locations waste time.

questions.stem: What should you do if you start a call and realise you are standing in the four-foot?
options: Carry on, as the call will be short
Move to a safe place before continuing
Ask the signaller to stop trains for you
Face the traffic and keep talking
questions.rationale: Make yourself safe first.

questions.stem: Why is it unsafe to pass safety messages by text message?
options: Texts cost too much to send from site
Texts cannot include numbers or letters
Texts are always deleted after one hour
They may be delayed, missed or misunderstood
questions.rationale: Safety-critical messages need clear two-way confirmation.

questions.stem: What does a red light on a signal mean for a train driver?
options: Stop
Slow down
Sound the horn
Go on with caution
questions.rationale: Red is the danger aspect.

questions.stem: Which signal aspect sequence warns drivers of a signal at danger ahead?
options: Green
Single yellow
Flashing green
No light
questions.rationale: Single yellow means be prepared to stop at the next signal.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a train approaching a red signal at speed?
options: Stand on the line and wave
Ignore it, TPWS will deal with it
Throw something on the rail
Get clear and report it
questions.rationale: Your safety first, then report.

questions.stem: What is a 'subsidiary' signal?
options: A signal that has failed and is not used
A signal that controls road traffic nearby
A signal fixed to a lookout's helmet
A smaller signal allowing limited movements
questions.rationale: Subsidiary signals authorise restricted moves.

questions.stem: What is a 'distant' signal on semaphore lines?
options: A signal placed a long way from any station
A signal that can only be seen from far away
A signal used only by freight trains
A caution signal giving warning of the next signal
questions.rationale: Older routes still have semaphore signalling.

questions.stem: What does a semaphore signal arm raised or lowered show?
options: Which line the train must use at the junction ahead
Whether the signal is clear or at danger
The speed the train must keep
Whether workers are on the line
questions.rationale: Semaphore signals use arms rather than lights.

questions.stem: Why should track workers know what the signals near their site look like?
options: To change the signals when needed
To tell drivers which aspect to show
To decide when it is safe to work
To give accurate locations and spot faults
questions.rationale: Signals help with location and reporting.

questions.stem: When must you NOT rely on a signal aspect for your safety?
options: Always
Only at night
Only in fog
Only at junctions
questions.rationale: Signals are for trains. Your safety depends on your safe system of work.

questions.stem: What should you do if a signaller gives you an instruction you think is unsafe?
options: Follow it without question
Question it before acting
Ignore it and do your own thing
Hang up the phone
questions.rationale: Clarify any doubt.

questions.stem: What is 'GSM-R' coverage used for by track workers in emergencies?
options: Contacting signallers through railway radios where provided
Listening to music while waiting
Listening to music while waiting for the next train to pass
Listening to music while waiting for the next train
questions.rationale: Some staff carry GSM-R handsets.

questions.stem: What does 'over' mean at the end of a radio message?
options: The call is completely finished
The work is over for the day
I have finished; please reply
The train has gone past
questions.rationale: Standard radio terms help clarity.

questions.stem: What does 'out' mean at the end of a radio message?
options: Please reply now
The train is out of sight
The conversation is finished
Get out of the four-foot
questions.rationale: 'Out' ends the exchange.

questions.stem: Why should only one person speak at a time on a radio channel?
options: Messages can block each other
It saves battery power
It is a legal requirement
It makes the radio louder
questions.rationale: Radio discipline avoids missed messages.

questions.stem: What should you do if your radio message gets no reply?
options: Assume it was received
Give up and carry on
Shout the message instead
Repeat it or use another method
questions.rationale: Never assume a message got through.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest way to give your location on a long straight line without signals nearby?
options: The colour of the nearest house
The number of trains that passed
The ELR and nearest milepost
The direction of the sun
questions.rationale: Mileposts give precise location.

questions.stem: Why should briefings avoid local nicknames for places?
options: Nicknames are always rude
Nicknames are too long to say
Others may not know what they mean
Nicknames are copyrighted
questions.rationale: Use official names.

questions.stem: What should you do if someone repeats back your message wrongly?
options: Correct them and ask them to repeat it again
Let it go, as it is nearly right
End the call quickly and try someone else
Repeat your message louder only
questions.rationale: Keep going until it is right.

questions.stem: What is a 'sighting board' behind a signal for?
options: To protect the signal from vandals
To display the signal's number
To mark a position of safety
To make the signal easier to see
questions.rationale: Sighting boards improve visibility for drivers.

questions.stem: Why should you report a signal obscured by vegetation?
options: It looks untidy to passengers
It uses more power
Drivers may not see it in time
It confuses passengers
questions.rationale: Signal sighting is safety-critical.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'limit of shunt' board?
options: To mark the end of a possession
To mark the edge of the cess
To mark the line speed for shunting moves
To mark how far a shunting movement may go
questions.rationale: Shunting moves have defined limits.

questions.stem: What is a 'stop board'?
options: A sign telling drivers to stop at that point
A board for workers to rest on
A board at a station listing the stops for each train
A board marking the end of the shift
questions.rationale: Stop boards may mark the limit of a section or possession.

questions.stem: Why must hand signals be given only by competent people?
options: They are copyrighted by the railway
Incorrect signals could cause collisions
Drivers ignore untrained people
They need a special glove
questions.rationale: Hand signalling is a safety-critical task.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are unsure what a driver's hand signal means?
options: Copy the signal back to them
Step closer to ask
Stay clear and ask afterwards
Ignore all trains
questions.rationale: Stay safe; clarify later.

questions.stem: What is the benefit of using a standard briefing format?
options: Nothing important is missed
It is quicker to read aloud
It is more interesting
It saves paper
questions.rationale: Structure helps completeness.

questions.stem: What should you say if you are asked to confirm something you did not hear?
options: Say yes to keep things moving
Guess what was said
Stay silent
Say you did not hear and ask again
questions.rationale: Never confirm what you did not hear.

questions.stem: When a COSS asks 'Does everyone understand?', what should you do if you do not?
options: Nod and work it out later
Say so and ask questions
Stay quiet to avoid embarrassment
Ask a colleague after work
questions.rationale: Speak up.

questions.stem: Why are signal numbers useful in emergency calls?
options: They tell the signaller the line speed
They show the time of the next train
Each signal number is unique to a location
They show which company you work for
questions.rationale: They pinpoint where you are.

questions.stem: What should you do if you call the signaller and they say they are busy with an emergency?
options: Keep it brief, or call back if yours is not urgent
Insist they deal with you first
Insist that they deal with your call first, whatever it is about
Insist that they deal with your call first
questions.rationale: Respect priorities, but report emergencies.

questions.stem: Which of these is a safety-critical message?
options: 'Lunch will be at 13:00 today'
'The Up Main is now clear of all staff'
'Lunch will be at 13:00 today in the cabin'
'Your timesheet is due Friday'
questions.rationale: Messages that affect train or worker safety are safety-critical.

questions.stem: What does it mean to 'acknowledge' a message?
options: Forward it to someone else
Forward it to everyone else in the group
Delete it from your phone
Confirm you have received and understood it
questions.rationale: Acknowledgement closes the loop.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid using phrases such as 'all clear' loosely on site?
options: It is too formal for site use
It is reserved for lookouts only
Others might think it means trains can run
It uses too many words in a short call
questions.rationale: Use precise language about what is clear.

questions.stem: What should you do if you receive two conflicting messages?
options: Follow the last one you received
Stop and get them clarified
Follow the first one only
Follow whichever is easier
questions.rationale: Resolve conflicts before acting.

questions.stem: What is a 'COSS-to-signaller' call mainly about?
options: Ordering materials for the work
Booking accommodation for staff
Arranging or confirming protection
Reporting staff hours worked
questions.rationale: These calls are safety-critical.

questions.stem: Why should mobile phones be kept charged on site?
options: So you can watch videos at break
They may be needed to call for help
So lookouts can text warnings
So the van radio works
questions.rationale: Phones are useful for emergencies, not warnings.

questions.stem: What is the danger of using slang when giving directions on site?
options: It can be misunderstood
It is never allowed in writing
It makes calls longer
It confuses trains
questions.rationale: Plain language prevents errors.

questions.stem: Which phrase is clearest when telling a colleague to move to safety?
options: 'Watch out, mate'
'Train coming, move to your position of safety now'
'Watch out, mate, I think something is coming'
'Oi, careful'
questions.rationale: Clear, specific instructions save time.

questions.stem: You are working in the cess on a curve. A lookout warns of a train on the far line. What should you do?
options: Keep working because it is on the far line
Stop work and go to your position of safety at once
Look to check which line it is on first
Keep working, because the warning is for a train on the far line
questions.rationale: Act on every warning immediately. Trains can be routed on unexpected lines.

questions.stem: A train passes on the Down line. You are about to step back onto the Up line when you hear another horn. What is the most likely danger?
options: The first train reversing back towards you
The first train reversing back towards you on the Down line
The signaller trying to get your attention
A second train, possibly hidden by the first
questions.rationale: Stay in your position of safety until it is confirmed safe.

questions.stem: It starts to rain heavily and the lookout says visibility is reducing. What should happen?
options: Work continues at a faster pace to finish before it gets worse
The lookout moves into the four-foot to see further along the line
Everyone carries on but stops every few minutes to listen
Work stops and the group moves clear until the plan is reviewed
questions.rationale: Reduced sighting means the warning time may no longer be achievable.

questions.stem: You are using a noisy petrol-driven tool. How will you know a train is approaching?
options: Only if a suitable warning method has been arranged for noisy work
You will hear the train over the tool as long as you stay alert
You will feel the ground vibrate well before the train arrives
The driver will see your hi-vis and stop the train for you
questions.rationale: Noise hides trains and warnings. At Margam, noise was a factor in two deaths.

questions.stem: Fog rolls in during a night shift. The safe system relies on a lookout. What should the COSS do?
options: Carry on, because fog does not affect hearing trains
Carry on, because fog does not affect hearing approaching trains
Move the group closer to the lookout and carry on
Stop work, move everyone to safety and review the plan
questions.rationale: Fog and darkness drastically reduce sighting.

questions.stem: You see a colleague kneeling in the four-foot with headphones on. No warning has been given yet. What should you do?
options: Leave them, as the lookout will deal with it when needed
Leave them, as the lookout will deal with it when a train comes
Wait until the break to mention it to them quietly
Tell them to remove the headphones and report the unsafe act
questions.rationale: Personal headphones stop people hearing warnings.

questions.stem: A road-rail vehicle starts reversing towards you inside a possession. What should you do?
options: Stand still and wave both arms above your head until the operator sees you
Walk behind it so that you stay out of the operator's view
Move out of its path and make sure the controller knows where you are
Climb onto it so you are above the area it is reversing into
questions.rationale: Plant has blind spots and can move unexpectedly.

questions.stem: Your COSS tells you the line is blocked. You then see a train approaching on that line. What should you do?
options: Stay where you are, because the line has been blocked
Wave the train down from the four-foot so it stops
Stay where you are, because the COSS has said the line is blocked
Get to a position of safety immediately and tell the COSS
questions.rationale: Always react to a train, whatever you have been told.

questions.stem: You must cross the line to reach your position of safety, but a train is approaching. What should you do?
options: Cross diagonally to save time while keeping an eye on the train
Cross diagonally to save time and keep watching it
Do not cross; go to the nearest safe position on your side
Stand still between the rails so the driver sees you
questions.rationale: Crossing in front of a train is very dangerous.

questions.stem: A heavy freight train passes and kicks up dust and grit. What should you do?
options: Step closer to see the wagons
Stay in your position of safety and protect your eyes
Turn your back and crouch on the ballast edge
Walk alongside it so you can see the wagons clearly
questions.rationale: Wear eye protection where needed and stay clear.

questions.stem: You arrive at site and the cess path is overgrown, hiding the position of safety. What should you do?
options: Use the six-foot as your position of safety instead
Tell the COSS before work starts so the plan can be reviewed
Use the six-foot as your position of safety for the shift instead
Start work now and look for it later if a train comes
questions.rationale: Every person needs a known, accessible position of safety.

questions.stem: A lookout gives a warning, but you are halfway through tightening a bolt. What should you do?
options: Finish tightening the bolt first so the track is left safe
Ask how far away the train is
Wait for a second warning
Stop at once and move to safety
questions.rationale: Never finish a task after a warning.

questions.stem: It is a hot day and you notice the rail has a slight kink. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as rails often look kinked in the heat
Try to straighten it with a bar while the rail is still hot
Try to straighten it with a bar while it is hot
Report it to the signaller at once as a possible buckle
questions.rationale: Track buckles can derail trains.

questions.stem: During work in a tunnel, the lighting fails. What should you do?
options: Stop work, go to a safe place and tell the COSS
Carry on working using the light from your phone
Move into the four-foot to find the exit
Wait in the dark next to the rail
questions.rationale: Tunnels without light are extremely dangerous.

questions.stem: You are walking to site and notice the access point sign shows a different ELR from your briefing. What should you do?
options: Carry on, because access signs are often wrong
Carry on, because access point signs are often out of date
Go home, as the job must have been cancelled
Stop and check with the COSS before going further
questions.rationale: Wrong location means wrong protection.

questions.stem: A colleague says, 'We always do it this way, no need for a lookout here.' What should you do?
options: Go along with it, as they have worked here for years
Refuse to work without the planned protection and tell the COSS
Watch for trains yourself while you get on with the work
Work quickly so that you spend less time on the line
questions.rationale: Informal unsafe practices have caused deaths.

questions.stem: Your group is behind schedule. The COSS suggests skipping the warning arrangements for 10 minutes. What should you do?
options: Work with one eye on the line for the ten minutes
Agree to help, as it is only for ten minutes
Challenge it and refuse to work without protection
Ask the lookout to watch both lines for a while
questions.rationale: Time pressure is never a reason to drop safety.

questions.stem: You are working near a junction. The lookout says trains could come from three directions. Why is this significant?
options: It means that trains will be travelling more slowly
It means that trains will stop before reaching the site
It means trains will be travelling more slowly, so the lookout can relax
Trains are harder to detect in time, so a safer system may be needed
questions.rationale: Junctions complicate train detection.

questions.stem: A train sounds its horn at your group. You are already in your position of safety. What should you do?
options: Raise one arm above your head to acknowledge
Wave both arms so the driver knows you are there
Ignore it, as you are already in a safe place
Step forward so the driver can see you clearly
questions.rationale: Acknowledging tells the driver you are aware.

questions.stem: A lightweight sheet of plastic is lying in the cess near your work. Trains are passing at speed. What should you do?
options: Secure or remove it so slipstream cannot blow it onto the line
Leave it, as it is too light to cause any harm to a train
Move it into the four-foot where it is out of the way
Leave it, as it is far too light to cause any harm to a train
questions.rationale: Loose items can be drawn into trains.

questions.stem: You feel very tired halfway through a night shift and nearly trip on the ballast. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS and move to a safe place
Drink an energy drink and carry on
Drink an energy drink and carry on until the break
Keep quiet to avoid trouble
questions.rationale: Fatigue affects reactions and balance.

questions.stem: Your position of safety is on a narrow ledge above a drop. What should you do?
options: Use it carefully, holding on when trains pass
Use the six-foot instead, as it is wider
Raise it with the COSS; it may not be a suitable place
Use it, but hold on to the fence when a train passes
questions.rationale: Positions of safety must be stable.

questions.stem: During a briefing, the COSS cannot tell you where the position of safety is. What should you do?
options: Find one yourself when a train comes
Use the six-foot
Stand behind the lookout
Do not start until it is identified
questions.rationale: Know where to go before going on the line.

questions.stem: You see children on a bridge throwing stones at trains. What should you do?
options: Throw stones back to scare them away from the bridge
Ignore it, as it is not a track safety matter
Chase them along the line until they run off
Report it to the signaller or British Transport Police
questions.rationale: Vandalism endangers trains and people.

questions.stem: A train has stopped at a red signal next to your work area. Can you cross in front of it?
options: Yes, because it is stopped at a red signal
Yes, because it is stopped at a red signal and cannot move
No, it could move off at any time and hide other trains
Yes, as long as you wave to the driver first
questions.rationale: Never cross in front of a stopped train.

questions.stem: You hear a train but cannot tell which line it is on. What should you do?
options: Get to your position of safety, clear of all lines
Wait until you can see the train before moving
Stay exactly where you are until it passes
Wait until you can see the train before deciding where to go
questions.rationale: Assume it could be on any line.

questions.stem: The sun is low and shining straight into your eyes along the line. What is the main risk?
options: Your PPE will fade
Signals will be hard to read for drivers only
You or the lookout may not see an approaching train
The rails will expand in the sun and may buckle
questions.rationale: Glare reduces sighting. Review the warning arrangements.

questions.stem: Snow is covering the cess and hiding cables and troughing. What should you do?
options: Walk in the four-foot, where the snow is usually clearer
Run to get to the site faster before the snow gets deeper
Take extra care, use a known route and report hidden hazards
Walk in the four-foot, where the snow is usually much clearer
questions.rationale: Snow hides trip hazards and conductor rails.

questions.stem: Strong winds are blowing towards you from an approaching train's direction. What is the risk?
options: The train will slow down in strong wind
You may hear the train later than usual
The overhead line will switch off
The signals will fail in the wind
