questions.rationale: Wind affects how sound travels.

questions.stem: A member of your group wanders off to look at something further down the line. What should you do?
options: Call them on their mobile while you walk after them
Ignore it, as they are an adult and responsible
Ignore it, as they are an adult and responsible for their own safety
Tell the COSS at once; they may be outside the protected area
questions.rationale: Leaving the protected area is dangerous.

questions.stem: You drop your phone into the four-foot of an open line. What should you do?
options: Leave it and tell the COSS
Step in quickly to grab it
Ask the lookout to watch while you get it
Use a tool to hook it while standing on the rail
questions.rationale: No item is worth your life.

questions.stem: You notice a fence panel missing next to a school. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as the school will report it
Report it so it can be repaired quickly
Mention it to someone next month
Remove the next panel to make it tidy
questions.rationale: Children may get onto the line.

questions.stem: A bird strikes the OLE and you hear a loud bang and see a flash. What should you do?
options: Go and look closer
Touch the mast to check
Ignore it, as birds often hit the wires
Keep clear of the OLE and report it
questions.rationale: There may be damage to the OLE.

questions.stem: Water is pooling around the conductor rail after a storm. You need to pass. What should you do?
options: Walk through quickly
Step on the conductor rail to avoid water
Stop and get advice before passing
Use a metal bar to test it
questions.rationale: Water and DC electricity are a deadly mix.

questions.stem: Your group is spread out and the lookout cannot see the person at the far end. What should happen?
options: The group should close up so everyone is within the lookout's protection
The person at the far end should listen harder for the horn
The lookout should shout louder so the far person can hear
The person at the far end should listen harder for the lookout's horn
questions.rationale: Everyone must be protected.

questions.stem: You hear a train horn but the lookout has not warned you. What should you do?
options: Wait for the lookout
Ask the lookout what is happening
Move to your position of safety immediately
Keep working until the lookout gives a warning
questions.rationale: Never wait for permission to get clear.

questions.stem: During work, the ATWS warning sounds briefly and stops. What should you do?
options: Switch the system off so that it stops distracting people
Keep working but listen for a second warning
Switch the system off so it stops distracting people
Treat it as a warning, move to safety and let the COSS check
questions.rationale: Treat all warnings as real.

questions.stem: You are asked to carry a 4-metre pole along a line with OLE. How should you carry it?
options: Upright on your shoulder
Upright on your shoulder so others can see it
Dragged behind you vertically
Horizontally and low, with help if needed
questions.rationale: Keep items at least 2.75 m from OLE.

questions.stem: Your COSS's briefing mentions limited clearance under a bridge 100 metres away. What does this mean for you?
options: You can shelter under the bridge when trains are passing
You must not be under the bridge as a train passes unless protected
You can shelter under the bridge when trains are passing, as it is sheltered
The bridge abutment is a recognised position of safety
questions.rationale: Limited clearance means no safe place to stand.

questions.stem: A passenger on a platform drops a bag onto the track and asks you to get it. What should you do?
options: Jump down quickly to get it before a train comes
Reach for it with a broom from the platform edge
Jump down quickly to get it before a train comes into the platform
Do not go on the track; tell station staff or the signaller
questions.rationale: Only access the track with authority and protection.

questions.stem: You notice a colleague's hi-vis is covered by a dark backpack. Why should you mention it?
options: It looks untidy in front of the public
They may not be seen by drivers and machine operators
They may be mistaken for a member of the public
It is uncomfortable to wear all shift
questions.rationale: Visibility is important.

questions.stem: The lookout seems distracted by their phone. What should you do?
options: Keep working and keep watching for trains yourself
Stop work, move to safety and tell the COSS
Take the phone off them and carry on
Ignore it, as they are probably checking the time
questions.rationale: A distracted lookout cannot protect you.

questions.stem: You are walking with a group and someone suggests a shortcut through a tunnel. What should you do?
options: Go through quickly in single file and keep talking
Refuse and use the planned route
Go through if it is short
Go through in single file
questions.rationale: Tunnels often have limited clearance.

questions.stem: A heavy machine is working next to an open line. You need to pass between the machine and the line. What should you do?
options: Do not pass; find a safe alternative route
Squeeze through quickly
Squeeze through quickly while the machine is still
Ask the operator to stop for a second
questions.rationale: You could be trapped between the machine and a train.

questions.stem: Your safe work pack says 'line blocked', but the signaller tells the COSS the blockage has been refused. What should happen?
options: Use a lookout instead to keep to time
The work must not go ahead under that plan
Use a lookout instead so the work can stay on time
Work quickly while watching for trains
questions.rationale: Never improvise a less safe system.

questions.stem: You arrive late and the group is already working on the line. What should you do?
options: Join them and get briefed later
Join them and ask a colleague what to do
Wait off the line until the COSS briefs you
Start on another task nearby
questions.rationale: Never go on the line without a briefing.

questions.stem: A train passes and you feel a strong pull of air. Your position of safety is 1.3 m from the rail on a 100 mph line. What should you do?
options: Stay put, and report it so the position can be reviewed
Move closer to the line next time to get out of the draught
Ignore it, as you were more than 1.25 m away
Hold on to the rail next time a train passes
questions.rationale: Positions of safety should be comfortable, not just legal.

questions.stem: You are told to 'just keep an eye out' while working on an open line. What should you do?
options: Refuse; this is not a safe system of work
Agree and look up from the work often
Ask a colleague to listen out for trains
Agree, and look up from the work often
questions.rationale: Informal lookouts are not protection.

questions.stem: A colleague says the OLE is 'off' because no trains have passed for an hour. What should you do?
options: Agree, and work near it while there are no trains
Test it by touching it lightly with a wooden stick
Agree, and work near it while there are no trains running on the line
Treat the OLE as live unless an isolation has been confirmed
questions.rationale: Never assume OLE is dead.

questions.stem: You notice someone you do not recognise working near your site without hi-vis. What should you do?
options: Ignore them
Give them your spare jacket and let them work
Ask them to join your group
Tell the COSS or report it immediately
questions.rationale: They may be a trespasser or unauthorised.

questions.stem: You are clearing vegetation in the cess on a 90 mph line. Your strimmer is loud and you are wearing ear defenders. What must be in place?
options: A rule that you look up every thirty seconds
A colleague standing next to you who taps your shoulder now and then
A warning method that you will notice despite the noise
Nothing extra, because the cess is a position of safety on that line
questions.rationale: Noisy work needs a warning you will actually receive, or the line must be blocked.

questions.stem: During a drainage job, the group is working in a deep cutting where trains are hard to hear. The COSS planned lookout warning. What is the main concern?
options: Cuttings make trains run faster because of the downhill approach
Cuttings can limit both sighting and sound, so warning may be too late
Drainage work is always done under a possession
Lookouts are not allowed in cuttings during daylight
questions.rationale: Check that sighting gives the full warning time. If not, a safer system is needed.

questions.stem: You are on a fencing job at the boundary, 4 metres from the nearest rail. Do you need a safe system of work for trains?
options: Yes, you always need a lookout within 10 metres of any rail
No, fencing contractors are never covered by railway safety rules
Not for trains if you stay outside 3 m, but check your briefing
Yes, the line must always be blocked for fencing work
questions.rationale: Being 'on or near the line' means within 3 m. Work further away may not need protection from trains, but other hazards still apply.

questions.stem: Your fencing job means leaning a post towards the line while you fix it. What should you think about?
options: Only whether the post is the correct height for the fence
Whether the post is painted to match the existing fence
Whether the post or you could come within 3 m of the line, or foul it
Only whether the post is the correct height and colour for the new fence
questions.rationale: Work can bring you or materials closer to the line than you expect.

questions.stem: You are doing a track patrol on foot as part of a planned safe system. You see a broken fishplate. What should you do?
options: Remove the broken parts and carry on with the rest of the patrol
Report it as required and follow your instructions for defects
Ignore it, because fishplates often break in cold weather
Mark it with paint and mention it at the next weekly meeting
questions.rationale: Defects that affect safety must be reported promptly so trains can be controlled if needed.

questions.stem: During a patrol you find a large tree branch lying across the four-foot of an open line. What do you do first?
options: Drag it clear yourself before a train arrives
Photograph it and send it to your manager later
Leave it, as the next train will push it aside without harm
Get clear and report it to the signaller as an obstruction
questions.rationale: Obstructions must be reported at once so trains can be stopped.

questions.stem: You are waiting in your position of safety when a train passes very slowly and stops just beyond your site. What should you assume?
options: It has stopped for the group and the line is now safe
It may move again at any time, so stay where you are
It will not move until the driver speaks to the COSS
It has broken down and will be there for hours
questions.rationale: Stopped trains can restart without warning.

questions.stem: The ballast where you are standing is wet and sloping towards the line. A train is due. What should you do?
options: Move to firmer, flatter ground in a position of safety
Stay where you are and hold on to the fence behind you
Kneel down to lower your centre of gravity
Stand closer to the rail, where the ballast is flatter
questions.rationale: A position of safety must be stable.

questions.stem: You are working at night with lighting towers. A train approaches from behind the lights. What is the risk?
options: The lights may dazzle you and hide the train's approach
The lights will make the train stop automatically
The lights will make the driver slow the train down as it passes
There is no risk, as trains are easier to see at night
questions.rationale: Site lighting can affect what you and drivers can see. Plan lighting so it does not dazzle.

questions.stem: Your group is about to cross a viaduct with no refuges. What must be confirmed first?
options: That the line is protected so no train can come while you cross
That everyone can walk fast enough to cross between trains
That a lookout is standing at the far end of the viaduct
That it is daytime and the weather is dry and clear
questions.rationale: RAIB investigated a near miss at Dutton Viaduct when a group crossed at track level without adequate protection.

questions.stem: You are walking with a group on a lineside path when your COSS takes a phone call and stops watching. What should the group do?
options: Carry on walking, as everyone knows the route
Stop in a safe place until the COSS is ready to supervise again
Walk faster to reach the site before the call ends
Split up so that each person can look for trains in a different direction
questions.rationale: The COSS must supervise. If they are distracted, stop in safety.

questions.stem: During your break, you notice that your position of safety is now occupied by a stack of new sleepers. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS so a new position of safety can be agreed
Move the sleepers into the four-foot to clear the space
Use the top of the sleeper stack as your new position
Say nothing and stand between the sleepers and the rail
questions.rationale: Every position of safety must remain usable.

questions.stem: You are working in a possession and a tamping machine is approaching on your line. What should you do?
options: Carry on, because the possession protects you from all movements
Stand in the four-foot and signal it to stop with your arms
Climb onto the machine to ride to the next worksite
Move clear of its path and follow the controller's instructions
questions.rationale: On-track plant and engineering trains can move inside a possession.

questions.stem: Your group is working on the Down line under a line blockage. A train approaches on the Up line. What should you do?
options: Nothing, because the blockage on the Down line protects the whole site
Make sure you are clear of the Up line and stay clear
Wave the train down, as it is too close to the work
Cross to the Up line cess so you can see it better
questions.rationale: Adjacent open lines are still a hazard.

questions.stem: You hear a whistle from your lookout but it sounds unusual. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a warning and move to safety
Ask the lookout what it meant before moving
Ignore it until you hear the normal sound
Look for a train first and move if you see one
questions.rationale: Never ignore a possible warning.

questions.stem: You are in a group using LOWS and one of the site beacons stops flashing. What should happen?
options: Carry on, as the sirens are still working
Move closer to the beacons that are still working properly
Ask the lookout to shout instead
Stop and get clear until the system is checked
questions.rationale: If part of a warning system fails, the protection may not work.

questions.stem: A colleague jokes that they can 'beat any train' to the position of safety. What should you do?
options: Laugh it off, as experienced people know their limits
Race them to show that you are just as quick to get clear
Challenge the attitude and tell the COSS if it continues
Ignore it, because it does not affect your safety
questions.rationale: Overconfidence is a common factor in accidents.

questions.stem: You are working on a curve and the train drivers cannot see you until they are close. Why does this matter to you?
options: Drivers will always stop before the curve when workers are present
Drivers have to report every curve where they cannot see workers
Drivers may not be able to warn you or slow down in time
It does not matter because drivers always sound the horn
questions.rationale: Never rely on the driver's warning.

questions.stem: After heavy snow, the lookout's view is good but the snow muffles sound. What should the group consider?
options: Train noise and warnings may be harder to hear
Snow makes trains much louder, so warnings are easier
Snow stops trains running, so no warning is needed
Snow means positions of safety can be closer to the line
questions.rationale: Weather affects both sighting and hearing.

questions.stem: You must carry heavy equipment to site and the walking route crosses an open line. What is the safest plan?
options: Make many quick trips so you never carry too much at once
Cross only as briefed, with the line protected or clear
Leave the equipment in the four-foot and carry it later
Throw lighter items across first so that you have less to carry over
questions.rationale: Each crossing is a risk. Plan the route and loads.

questions.stem: Your COSS asks you to act as site warden, but you do not hold that competence. What should you do?
options: Agree, because it is a simple job
Agree, but only for a short time while the warden is away
Explain that you are not competent and decline
Ask another worker to sign for you
questions.rationale: Only carry out roles you are competent for.

questions.stem: You are in a fenced safe area beside an open line. A colleague leans over the fence to pick up a dropped tool. What should you do?
options: Stop them; leaning over takes them towards the open line
Help them by holding on to their belt while they reach over
Let them, because the fence keeps them safe
Tell them to be quick before a train comes
questions.rationale: The fence only protects you if you stay behind it.

questions.stem: You are working in separated working and the site warden is called away. What should happen?
options: Work stops until the site warden returns or is replaced
The group carries on but stays further from the line
The COSS takes over the warden's role by watching from the van
The group carries on because it is a green zone
questions.rationale: Separated working relies on the site warden.

questions.stem: A road-rail vehicle is placing materials. Its load swings towards the open line. What should you do?
options: Get clear and alert the controller at once
Grab the load with both hands to stop it swinging
Stand between the load and the line
Wave to the next train to slow down
questions.rationale: Loads can foul open lines or strike people.

questions.stem: You are told the line speed is 75 mph, but you see a sign showing 100 mph at your location. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS, as positions of safety and warning time may be wrong
Ignore the sign, as the briefing is always correct
Assume trains will slow to 75 mph near the work because of the group
Take the average of the two speeds for your plans
questions.rationale: Line speed affects positions of safety and warning time. Check discrepancies.

questions.stem: You are working near a level crossing. A car driver ignores the warning lights. What is the most important thing for you to do?
options: Run onto the crossing and stand in front of the car to stop it
Lift the barrier to let the car through quickly
Stay clear and report it, as you may need to warn the signaller
Stand in front of the train to slow it down
questions.rationale: Never put yourself in danger. Report crossing misuse.

questions.stem: In fog, you hear a horn but cannot see anything. What should you do?
options: Wait until you can see the train
Stay perfectly still so that you do not trip on the ballast
Shout to ask which line it is on
Move to your position of safety straight away
questions.rationale: Act on the sound, do not wait to see.

questions.stem: You are using a hand trolley under a possession on a falling gradient. What is the main risk?
options: The trolley may set off the AWS magnets in the four-foot
The trolley could run away down the slope
The trolley could charge the rails
The trolley may block the radio signal
questions.rationale: Trolleys need brakes and control, especially on gradients.

questions.stem: You arrive at a site where the COSS's briefing does not mention the conductor rail you can see. What should you do?
options: Assume it has been isolated, as it was not mentioned
Assume it is not part of your work
Ask the COSS about it before work starts
Step over it carefully and say nothing
questions.rationale: Briefings must cover electrical hazards.

questions.stem: You are working in a depot and a shunting move starts nearby without warning. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as depot moves are always slow
Step onto the line to signal the driver
Get clear of the line it is using and stay clear
Climb onto the moving vehicle to ride clear of the area
questions.rationale: Depot movements can be sudden.

questions.stem: The group is told to take a 'short cut' along the six-foot between two open lines. What should you do?
options: Agree, as long as the lookout watches both lines
Agree, if you walk quickly in single file
Refuse and use the briefed route
Agree, because the six-foot is the widest space
questions.rationale: The six-foot is dangerous when both lines are open.

questions.stem: You notice your colleague is not wearing their glasses, which they normally need. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as they can probably see well enough
Lend them your sunglasses so that they can see better
Raise it, as their sight may not meet the safety standard
Ask them to stand at the back of the group
questions.rationale: Eyesight is part of fitness for track work.

questions.stem: A strong gust of wind blows your helmet towards the four-foot of an open line. What should you do?
options: Leave it and tell the COSS; do not go after it
Run after it quickly before a train comes
Reach in with a shovel and pull it back towards you quickly
Wait for the next train to blow it clear
questions.rationale: No equipment is worth entering an open line.

questions.stem: You are working under OLE and lightning is seen nearby. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as OLE protects you from lightning
Follow the briefing, which may require stopping work
Shelter under the OLE masts, as they act as lightning conductors
Hold a metal pole to act as a lightning rod
questions.rationale: Storms create electrical risks. Follow the agreed arrangements.

questions.stem: Your COSS cancels a planned line blockage and asks the group to wait. A colleague starts work anyway. What should you do?
options: Join them so the work is done faster
Keep quiet and let the COSS notice
Tell them to stop and alert the COSS
Act as their lookout without being appointed
questions.rationale: Without protection, nobody should be on the line.

questions.stem: You see a worker from another company walking on the line without a hi-vis jacket. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as they are not in your group
Tell your COSS or report it immediately
Lend them your jacket and walk on
Shout at them to hurry off the track
questions.rationale: Anyone at risk should be reported.

questions.stem: You are measuring track with a long staff. A train is due in 5 minutes. When should you start moving to safety?
options: Only once you can actually see the train on the approach
Only after the measurement is finished
When the warning is given, or earlier if instructed
When the train sounds its horn at you
questions.rationale: Follow the warning arrangements. Do not delay.

questions.stem: Your lookout is standing in the sun and keeps shading their eyes. What concern should you raise?
options: They may get sunburnt and need to take a break
Glare may stop them seeing trains in time
They are not wearing their armband
They will get tired of standing
questions.rationale: Anything reducing sighting is a safety issue.

questions.stem: You are working at a junction and see the points move. What does this tell you?
options: The points are faulty
The line is now blocked
A train may be about to use that route
The signaller is testing the points for you
questions.rationale: Points moving can mean a train is coming.

questions.stem: You are under a line blockage and see a signal protecting your section clear to green. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as the signal is not for you
Get clear of the line and tell the COSS immediately
Wait to see whether a train actually comes before moving
Stand in front of the signal so drivers see you
questions.rationale: A protecting signal clearing may mean the blockage is not in place.

questions.stem: You are asked to walk alone to fetch equipment from the van, along the cess of an open line. What should you do?
options: Go quickly and keep looking over your shoulder
Only go if the safe system covers it; otherwise wait
Go, as walking in the cess is always safe
Go, but run so you are on the line for less time
questions.rationale: Walking alone on or near the line needs proper arrangements.

questions.stem: Your safe work pack gives a position of safety in the cess, but the cess is now a deep trench for cable work. What should you do?
options: Stop and tell the COSS before going on the line
Stand at the edge of the trench
Use the six-foot instead, as it is now the widest space left
Jump into the trench when a train comes
questions.rationale: Site changes must be reflected in the plan.

questions.stem: You notice the lookout is also using a strimmer between trains. What should you do?
options: Leave it, because they stop when trains come
Offer to take the strimmer when trains approach
Raise it with the COSS; a lookout must not do other work
Ask them to strim more quietly so that they can hear trains
questions.rationale: Lookouts must give full attention to their duty.

questions.stem: A train passes and you see something dragging underneath it. What should you do?
options: Wave at the driver from the cess to get the train to stop
Run after the train to look
Report it to the signaller immediately
Write it down for the end of shift
questions.rationale: Dragging equipment can cause derailment or damage.

questions.stem: You are working with a group of visitors on a site tour. One visitor steps towards the rail to take a photo. What should you do?
options: Stop them at once and keep them in the agreed area
Let them, as long as you watch for trains
Take the photo for them from the four-foot
Ask them to be quick and take the photo before a train comes
questions.rationale: Visitors rely on their escort to keep them safe.

questions.stem: During a possession, you need to cross an adjacent line that is still open. What should you do?
options: Only cross as briefed, never assuming it is closed
Cross anywhere, as you are in a possession
Cross quickly while the possession is in place
Cross only at night, when fewer trains use the open line
questions.rationale: A possession on one line does not close adjacent lines.

questions.stem: You are wearing a hood under your helmet in cold weather and it reduces your hearing. What should you do?
options: Keep the hood on and watch more carefully
Ask the lookout to shout louder whenever a train is coming
Ignore it, as warnings are loud
Adjust your clothing so you can hear warnings properly
questions.rationale: You must be able to hear warnings.

questions.stem: You are told 'the next train is not for 20 minutes' by a colleague. How should you treat this?
options: Use it to plan exactly when you need to stop work
Ask the colleague for the exact time
Relax until 15 minutes have passed
Disregard it; trains can come at any time
questions.rationale: Timetables are not protection.

questions.stem: You are working near a station and a train departs from the platform towards you. What should you do?
options: Stay where you are, as departing trains are slow
Move to your position of safety as you would for any train
Wave to the driver to stop until you have finished
Stay where you are, as trains leaving a platform are always very slow
questions.rationale: Every train is a hazard.

questions.stem: Your group has a lookout and is working on a curve. The lookout moves to a better viewpoint but can no longer be heard by the group. What should happen?
options: Work stops until warnings can be heard by everyone
The group should watch the lookout instead
The lookout should text warnings
The group can carry on as the lookout can see better
questions.rationale: A warning that cannot be heard is not a warning.

questions.stem: Your group is replacing a rail clip on the Up line. The Down line is open. A train approaches on the Down line. Where should you go?
options: The briefed position of safety, away from the Down line
Into the Up line four-foot, since that line is blocked for you
Into the six-foot so that you are between the two lines
Onto the Down line cess so the driver can see you clearly
questions.rationale: Stay clear of the open line.

questions.stem: You are told a train is 'clear' of your site. A minute later you hear another horn. What does this suggest?
options: The first train is sounding its horn again as it leaves the area
Another train is approaching
The signaller is testing the warning equipment at your site
The lookout has made a mistake and you can carry on working
questions.rationale: Assume any horn means a train.

questions.stem: You are halfway across a line when the warning is given. What should you do?
options: Stop in the middle of the line and wait for the train to pass
Turn back to fetch the equipment you left behind first
Lie down in the four-foot so the train passes over you
Continue to the nearest safe side quickly
questions.rationale: Get clear by the quickest safe route.

questions.stem: You arrive at a site where the lookout's view is blocked by a parked engineering train. What should happen?
options: Work should not start until sighting is restored
The lookout should stand on the engineering train for a better view
The group should work faster to finish before trains arrive
The group should rely on listening for trains instead
questions.rationale: The lookout must be able to see far enough.

questions.stem: Your COSS says 'trains are only running on the Up line today'. What should you assume about the Down line?
options: No trains will run on it all day, so it is safe to walk
Trains could still run on it unless protected
Only engineering trains will use it, and only very slowly
It can be used as a position of safety for the group
questions.rationale: Only a confirmed blockage protects a line.

questions.stem: A train has just passed and the lookout gives the 'all clear'. You see another train in the distance. What should you do?
options: Go back to work, as the lookout has given the all clear
Ignore it, as it is probably on another line
Start crossing quickly before it gets closer
Stay clear and alert the lookout
questions.rationale: Your own observations matter too.

questions.stem: Your group is behind schedule and someone suggests working through a train passing 'because it is on the far line'. What should you do?
options: Keep working, as far line trains do not affect the group
Keep working but face the far line to watch it
Ask the lookout whether you can keep working
Stop and move clear as briefed
questions.rationale: Always follow the warning arrangements.

questions.stem: You are in a cutting and the only position of safety is a narrow ledge with a steep drop. A train is due. What should you do?
options: Report it before work so a safer plan is made
Use the ledge and hold on to the vegetation behind you
Stand in the six-foot instead, as it is flatter
Lie flat at the foot of the cutting slope
questions.rationale: Unsuitable positions of safety must be dealt with in planning.

questions.stem: You are walking through a station area at night and see someone sitting on the platform edge with legs over the track. What should you do?
options: Ignore them, as they are not on the track itself
Pull them back from the edge by their arm
Shout at them until they move away
Tell station staff or the signaller
questions.rationale: Report people at risk.

questions.stem: A lookout tells you they 'nearly missed' the last train because the sun was in their eyes. What should happen next?
options: Stop and review the lookout arrangements
Carry on, as they saw it in the end
Give the lookout sunglasses and continue
Ask the lookout to try harder
questions.rationale: Near misses must lead to action.

questions.stem: You are using ATWS and hear the warning, but the train seems to be on a line not covered by your work. What should you do?
options: Keep working, as ATWS sometimes warns for any line
Move to safety as briefed
Check which line it is on before moving
Switch the ATWS off to stop false alarms
questions.rationale: Respond to every warning.

questions.stem: During work, you realise you have left your position of safety's route blocked with tools. What should you do?
options: Leave it, as you know where the tools are
Use a different route when the train comes
Clear the route straight away
Ask the lookout to give earlier warnings
questions.rationale: Keep escape routes clear.

questions.stem: You are working at night and your torch fails. What should you do?
options: Carry on using the light from the next person
Use your phone screen as a torch
Work by moonlight until the end of the shift
Stop and get a working light before carrying on
questions.rationale: You need to see hazards and your route.

questions.stem: Your COSS tells you to stand in the six-foot as a position of safety between two open lines at 100 mph. What should you do?
options: Do it, as the COSS has checked the distance
Do it, but lie down when trains pass
Challenge it; this is unlikely to be safe
Do it, but face both directions at once
questions.rationale: Positions of safety must be clear of all lines where trains may approach.

questions.stem: You see a colleague step off a platform onto the track without telling anyone. What should you do?
options: Follow them to see what they are doing
Warn them and alert the COSS
Ignore it if they have PTS
Ask the next train to slow down
questions.rationale: Nobody should go on the line without authority.

questions.stem: Your group is working on a line next to a freight yard. Wagons are being shunted. What extra hazard is there?
options: Wagons give off dangerous gases
Wagons may move without warning
Shunting makes the overhead line live
Freight trains never use horns
questions.rationale: Shunting movements can be unexpected.

questions.stem: You are waiting in a refuge in a tunnel and a train passes. The air pressure pushes you. What should you do next time?
options: Lean out to see the train coming
Stand in the cess instead of the refuge
Hold on to the train's handrail
Brace and keep fully inside the refuge
questions.rationale: Pressure changes in tunnels are strong.

questions.stem: A colleague says their phone app shows train positions, so the lookout is not needed. What should you say?
options: Agree, as apps are more accurate than lookouts
Agree, if the phone has a good signal
Apps are not a safe system of work
Agree, but only during daylight
questions.rationale: Only approved protection and warning systems may be used.

questions.stem: You are surveying with a tripod near an open line. Where should the tripod be placed?
options: In the four-foot, where the ground is level and firm
On the rail head, so it is steady on the steel
Leaning against the nearest OLE mast for support
Clear of the line and secured
questions.rationale: Equipment must not foul the line.

questions.stem: You hear a train horn sound a long continuous blast. What does this most likely mean?
options: The driver is greeting the group
The train is about to stop
An urgent warning
The horn has a fault
questions.rationale: Get to safety immediately.

questions.stem: A lookout gives a warning but you cannot see your position of safety because of fog. What should you do?
options: Stay where you are until the fog clears
Move to the nearest safe area clear of the line
Walk along the four-foot to find it
Wait for the lookout to guide you by hand
questions.rationale: Get clear by the safest available route.

questions.stem: Your COSS's briefing is rushed and does not mention the warning method. What should you do?
options: Sign it and ask a colleague later on site
Assume the usual method is being used
Ask before signing
Refuse to work without saying why
questions.rationale: You must understand the safe system before signing.

questions.stem: You are under a line blockage and need to fetch materials from a point outside the blockage limits. What should you do?
options: Ask the COSS for a safe way to do it
Walk there quickly and come straight back
Ask a colleague to watch for trains while you go
Wait until a train has passed and then go
questions.rationale: Outside the limits you are not protected.

questions.stem: A train driver sounds the horn and waves as they pass your group. How should you respond?
options: Wave both arms back to the driver
Step towards the train to wave back
Acknowledge with one raised arm, staying clear
Ignore it and carry on working as normal
questions.rationale: Raising one arm acknowledges the warning.

questions.stem: You notice the cess path is undermined by a washout. What should you do?
options: Fill it with ballast yourself
Report it and avoid using it
Jump over it carefully
Walk in the four-foot past it
questions.rationale: Washouts can also affect the track.

questions.stem: You are told to take a short break in the cess, 1.5 m from a 75 mph line. Is that acceptable?
options: Yes, because it is a position of safety
Yes, if you face the oncoming trains
Yes, if you keep your hi-vis fastened
Breaks should be taken clear of the line
questions.rationale: Rest away from the line, not just in a position of safety.

questions.stem: You are working at a level crossing and a long queue of cars builds up. A car stops on the crossing. What should you do?
options: Report it to the signaller at once
Tell the car driver to reverse later
Wait to see if it moves
Lift the barrier to let it out
questions.rationale: A vehicle on the crossing is an emergency.

questions.stem: A new worker in your group freezes when the warning is given. What should you do?
options: Leave them, as they must learn for themselves
Shout at them from your position of safety
Guide them firmly to the position of safety
Wave the train down from the four-foot
questions.rationale: Help colleagues if you can do so safely.

questions.stem: You see the lookout walk away from their position without warning anyone. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as they will be back soon
Watch for trains yourself and keep working
Stop work and move clear
Ask the next person to take over as lookout
questions.rationale: No lookout means no warning.

questions.stem: Your group finishes early and someone suggests walking along the line to the next access point instead of the planned one. What should you do?
options: Use the planned route
Agree, as the next access point is closer
Agree, if the lookout comes with you
Agree, if you walk in the six-foot
questions.rationale: Unplanned routes may not be protected.

questions.stem: You are working in a possession and see a train approaching from beyond the possession limit on your line. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as the possession protects you
Wave it down from the four-foot
Assume it is an engineering train and carry on
Get clear and tell the COSS immediately
questions.rationale: React to any unexpected movement.

questions.stem: You smell smoke and see a lineside cable trough burning. What should you do?
options: Open the trough to see what is burning
Keep clear and report it
Pour water into the trough
Stamp on it to put it out
questions.rationale: Cable fires can affect signalling and give off toxic fumes.

questions.stem: You are walking in the cess and step on a loose troughing lid that tips. What should you do afterwards?
options: Report it so it can be fixed
Throw the lid into the six-foot
Ignore it, as you did not fall
Stand on it again to check it
questions.rationale: Report trip hazards.

questions.stem: Your COSS asks you to act as lookout. You are competent but very tired. What should you do?
options: Agree, as lookout duty is not physical
Agree, but drink coffee first
Agree, and ask someone to wake you
Say you are not fit for the role
questions.rationale: Fatigued people must not act as lookouts.

questions.stem: A train approaches and you are carrying a 20 kg tool. Your position of safety is 15 metres away. What should you do?
options: Carry the tool all the way so it is not left behind
Put the tool in the four-foot and run
Hold the tool above your head so the driver sees you
Put the tool down clear if possible and get to safety
questions.rationale: Your safety comes first.

questions.stem: You are working in the cess and a strong crosswind is blowing towards the line. What should you be careful about?
options: Trains being blown off the rails
The wind making trains go faster
Loose items blowing onto the line
Signals being turned by the wind
questions.rationale: Secure light materials in windy weather.

questions.stem: Your group is working near a busy footpath crossing. A dog runs onto the line. What should you do?
options: Report it; do not chase it onto the line
Chase it along the line to catch it
Call it over to you in the four-foot
Throw food to lure it off the track
questions.rationale: Do not put yourself at risk.

questions.stem: During a briefing, you notice the COSS has the wrong date on the paperwork. What should you do?
options: Ignore it as it does not matter
Correct it yourself without saying anything
Point it out
Refuse to work without explaining why
questions.rationale: Errors in documents may mean other details are wrong too.

questions.stem: You are walking with a COSS who suddenly stops and looks worried. What should you do?
options: Stop and ask if it is safe
Walk past and keep going
Start running towards the site
Cross the line to look around
questions.rationale: Communicate when something seems wrong.

questions.stem: Your group is about to start work but a lookout's horn is missing. What should happen?
options: The lookout shouts warnings instead
The lookout uses a phone alarm instead of the horn
Work waits until the right equipment is available
The group starts and keeps an eye out
questions.rationale: The planned warning equipment must be in place.

questions.stem: You are told to wear ear defenders while a colleague uses a disc cutter nearby. How will you hear warnings?
options: You will hear trains through the ear defenders
You will feel the train through the ground
The safe system must cover warnings for noisy work
The colleague with the cutter will warn you
questions.rationale: Plan warnings for people wearing hearing protection.

questions.stem: You see a group working on an adjacent line without any obvious protection. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as they are a different company
Walk over to them across the line
Tell your COSS straight away
Wait until the end of your shift to report it
questions.rationale: Raise concerns about any unsafe work.

questions.stem: Your COSS says the position of safety is 'anywhere in the cess'. The cess varies in width along the site. What should you do?
options: Ask for specific, checked positions
Accept it, as the cess is always safe
Measure it yourself as trains pass
Stand at the widest point and hope
questions.rationale: Positions of safety must be specific and suitable.

questions.stem: You are waiting for a train to pass on a curve and cannot see it yet, but you can hear it. When should you leave your position of safety?
options: Only when told it is safe
When you can no longer hear the train
When the lookout looks away
As soon as the train comes into view
questions.rationale: Wait for confirmation.

questions.stem: You find a gap in the boundary fence with a worn path through it to the track. What should you do?
options: Use it as a shortcut to the site
Block it with lineside materials
Report it as a trespass risk
Ignore it, as it is not your job
questions.rationale: Worn paths suggest regular trespass.

questions.stem: You are working under OLE and a colleague raises a long-handled tool above their head to stretch. What should you do?
options: Let them, as it is only a moment
Warn them to lower it
Measure the gap to the wires
Ask them to do it more quickly
questions.rationale: Long items must stay well clear of OLE.

questions.stem: A heavy rainstorm starts during work in a cutting. Water starts running down the slopes. What should you consider?
options: The rain will cool the rails
The rain will make trains slow
Possible landslip or flooding
The rain will clean the ballast
questions.rationale: Watch for earthworks movement.

questions.stem: Your group is asked to work 'just ten more minutes' after the line blockage was due to end. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as ten minutes is not long
Stop unless the protection is extended
Carry on, but work faster
Carry on, but put a lookout out
questions.rationale: Work must not continue without protection.

questions.stem: You notice your colleague limping after twisting an ankle on ballast. What should you do?
options: Let them carry on, they know their limits
Give them painkillers and carry on
Let them carry on, as they know their own limits best
Tell the COSS; they may not get clear quickly
questions.rationale: Injury can affect reaching a position of safety.

questions.stem: Your group is replacing a sleeper under a line blockage. A train appears on your line. What do you do?
options: Carry on, because the line blockage means it must stop before you
Stand in the four-foot waving both arms so the driver stops
Lift the sleeper clear first so the train is not derailed
Get clear at once and tell the COSS
questions.rationale: Always react to a train, even under a blockage.

questions.stem: You are on a night shift and the lookout's torch goes out. The lookout is still watching. What should happen?
options: Carry on, as the lookout only needs to listen at night
Stop and check the lookout can still see and be seen
Ask the lookout to use their phone screen instead
Move the group closer to the lookout and keep working
questions.rationale: Lighting is part of the warning arrangements at night.

questions.stem: A train passes and you notice a colleague is missing from the position of safety. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS immediately
Assume they went back to the van for something
Wait until the next train has passed before saying anything
Walk along the four-foot to look for them
questions.rationale: Everyone must be accounted for.

questions.stem: You are working near a station and a passenger shouts at you to get off the track. What should you do?
options: Climb onto the platform to explain what you are doing
Stay calm and follow your safe system
Leave the site so the passenger is not upset
Argue with the passenger until they leave
questions.rationale: Do not get distracted.

questions.stem: You are told the next train is a slow freight. How should this change your response to warnings?
options: You can wait longer before moving to safety
You can keep working in the cess as it passes
You only need to step out of the four-foot
It should not; respond the same way
questions.rationale: All trains are dangerous.

questions.stem: During a briefing, you notice rain is forecast to turn to heavy snow. What should you ask?
options: Whether the shift can finish early for everyone
Whether the COSS has spare gloves for the group
Whether trains will stop running in the snow
How the safe system will change if conditions worsen
questions.rationale: Plans must cover changing conditions.

questions.stem: You see a worker from another group sitting on the rail eating lunch. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as they are on a break
Join them so you are not alone
Warn them and report it
Ask them to sit on the conductor rail instead
questions.rationale: Never sit on rails.

questions.stem: You are working near an AWS magnet and need to kneel. What should you avoid?
options: Kneeling on a mat on the ballast shoulder
Kneeling facing the direction of traffic
Kneeling with your hi-vis fastened
Kneeling on the magnet or other track equipment
questions.rationale: Equipment can be slippery and damaged.

questions.stem: A strong headwind blows dust into your eyes and you cannot see properly. A train is due. What should you do?
options: Stay where you are until your eyes clear
Walk along the line with your eyes closed
Get to your position of safety and clear your eyes there
Stay exactly where you are until your eyes have cleared
questions.rationale: Get to safety first.

questions.stem: You are using a hand-held radio for work talk. The lookout uses a horn for warnings. A colleague says to just radio warnings instead. What should you say?
options: Agree, as radios are quicker than horns
Radios must not be used for train warnings
Agree, if everyone has a working radio
Agree, but only at night
questions.rationale: Maesyfelin bridge showed how radio warnings can fail.

questions.stem: The COSS asks you to keep watch while they go to the van. You are not the appointed lookout. What should you do?
options: Refuse and stop work until proper protection is in place
Agree, and keep working yourself while you also keep watch
Agree, and keep working while you watch
Agree, if the group stays close to you
questions.rationale: Informal lookouts are not protection.

questions.stem: You arrive and find the work is on a line you were told was blocked, but there are no possession boards. What should you do?
options: Start work, as boards are often removed by vandals
Stop and check with the COSS before going on the line
Put up some boards yourself and start work
Assume the boards are further along the line
questions.rationale: Confirm protection is really in place.

questions.stem: A colleague drops their glasses near the conductor rail. What should you do?
options: Reach in quickly with a metal grabber
Kick them away from the rail
Leave them and tell the COSS
Let your colleague pick them up carefully
questions.rationale: Never reach near the live rail.

questions.stem: Your group's work site moves 200 metres along the line. What should happen?
options: Nothing, the original briefing still covers everything
The lookout stays in the same place as before
The group decides its own positions of safety
The COSS checks protection, positions of safety and re-briefs
questions.rationale: New locations need checking.

questions.stem: You see that a colleague has taken off their helmet to cool down near the line. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as it is hot
Take yours off too
Report them for discipline at once
Remind them to wear it as required
questions.rationale: Look out for each other.

questions.stem: A train passes and sucks a plastic sheet off a stack towards the line. What should you do next?
options: Run onto the line to grab the sheet
Report it and secure loose materials
Ignore it, as it is only plastic
Wait for the next train to blow it away
questions.rationale: Loose materials can strike or foul trains.

questions.stem: Your COSS's phone rings during a briefing and they answer it. What should you do?
options: Wait for the briefing to be completed properly
Start work while they are on the phone
Leave, as the briefing is finished
Start work while they are on the phone to save time
questions.rationale: The briefing must be complete.

questions.stem: You are working on a bridge with low parapets. What extra hazard is there?
options: Trains always slow down on bridges
Bridges are always electrified
Falling from the bridge
There are more signals on bridges
questions.rationale: Consider falls as well as trains.

questions.stem: A lookout gives a warning but the train turns out to be on a line far away. Was the warning wrong?
options: Yes; lookouts should only warn for the nearest line
No; responding to every warning is correct
Yes; the group should have ignored it
Yes; the lookout should be replaced
questions.rationale: When in doubt, warn.

questions.stem: You are asked to walk to the next access point because your van has moved. The route is not in the briefing. What should you do?
options: Ask the COSS to confirm a safe route first
Walk along the cess as quickly as possible
Follow the line until you see the van
Cross the line to the road side
questions.rationale: Unplanned walks need a safe system.

questions.stem: A road-rail vehicle operator waves you to walk past their machine. You are not sure they have seen the open line. What should you do?
options: Walk past quickly while they are waving
Wait and confirm with the machine controller
Walk on the open line side to give the machine room
Climb over the machine's arm
questions.rationale: Do not rely on informal signals.

questions.stem: You are measuring a long section of track and lose sight of the lookout. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as you will still hear the horn from further away
Stop and move back within the lookout's protection
Keep measuring and look up more often
Ask a colleague to stand in the four-foot
questions.rationale: Stay within the protected area.

questions.stem: You are working on an embankment above the line. A train passes below. Do you still need to think about the train?
options: No; embankments are always outside the danger area
Yes; you or your tools could fall onto the line
No; trains cannot reach the top of an embankment
No; only people in the cess need to think about trains
questions.rationale: Falls and dropped items can reach the line.

questions.stem: During a possession, an engineering train stops beside you and the driver leans out to talk. What should you do?
options: Stay clear of the train and keep the conversation short
Climb into the cab to talk properly
Stand between the train and the next line
Lean on the train while you talk so you can hear
questions.rationale: The train can move.

questions.stem: You are in a group walking in the cess. One person stops to tie a shoelace in the four-foot. What should you do?
options: Walk on and let them catch up when they have finished
Walk on and let them catch up
Stand next to them in the four-foot
Tell them to move out of the four-foot first
questions.rationale: Never stop in the four-foot.

questions.stem: You notice the COSS has written the wrong line speed on the briefing form. What should you do?
options: Point it out, as it affects warning time and positions of safety
Correct it yourself on the form without telling anyone at all
Correct it yourself without telling anyone
Wait until the end of the shift to mention it
questions.rationale: Line speed matters.

questions.stem: A worker says they feel fine to carry on after a fall on the ballast, but they are limping. What should you do?
options: Let them carry on, they know best
Give them painkillers and let them carry on
Tell the COSS so their fitness can be checked
Ask them to be lookout
questions.rationale: Injuries can slow their response.

questions.stem: Your group finishes and the COSS is about to give up the line blockage. You realise a tool is still on the track. What should you do?
options: Say nothing and collect it after the next train
Run back to get it without telling anyone
Leave it, as it is small
Tell the COSS immediately
questions.rationale: The line must be clear before it is given back.

questions.stem: You hear a loud bang under a passing train. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as trains often make noises
Chase the train to see
Report it to the signaller
Wait to see if it happens again
questions.rationale: It could be a defect or obstruction.

questions.stem: You notice a level crossing user has left a gate open at a user-worked crossing. What should you do?
options: Report it
Close it and walk across the line to check the other gate
Ignore it, as it is the user's job
Remove the gate
questions.rationale: Report crossing issues.

questions.stem: A strong smell of diesel comes from your generator near the line. What should you do?
options: Keep it running and light a cigarette
Stop it safely and check for a leak
Pour water on it
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Fuel leaks are a fire risk.

questions.stem: Your COSS asks for volunteers to remove possession boards. You are not trained to do so. What should you do?
options: Volunteer, as it is a simple job
Decline and explain you are not competent
Volunteer and ask someone to show you
Volunteer but only for the nearest board
questions.rationale: Placing protection is a competence.

questions.stem: During work, a train passes much faster than you expected. What should you do afterwards?
options: Raise it with the COSS so warning times can be checked
Nothing, as it passed safely
Complain to the driver
Complain to the driver at the next station stop
questions.rationale: Assumptions about speed may be wrong.

questions.stem: You see a group working beside an open line with no site warden, though their briefing said separated working. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as they are a different company
Act as their site warden yourself
Report it to your COSS straight away
Wave to them to stop
questions.rationale: Raise concerns.

questions.stem: Your lookout is standing in the cess on the inside of a sharp curve. What concern might you have?
options: They may be too far from the van
They may be too warm
Their sighting may be poor
They may be too visible
questions.rationale: Curves limit sighting.

questions.stem: You are under a possession and see a member of the public walking on the line. What should you do?
options: Report it; they could stray onto open lines
Ignore them, as the possession protects them
Ask them to help with the work
Chase them off the line
questions.rationale: Report trespass.

questions.stem: Your group is about to cross a line using a crossing point. A colleague is wearing ear defenders. What should you do?
options: Let them cross with the ear defenders on
Shout at them as you cross
Make sure they can hear warnings before crossing
Let them cross with the ear defenders on, as it is quick
questions.rationale: Everyone must be able to receive warnings.

questions.stem: A train passes and its horn sounds very close. Your colleague is still in the four-foot behind you. What should you do?
options: Run into the four-foot to pull them clear
Shout a warning and, if safe, signal the driver to stop
Look away and hope that they move by themselves
Run into the four-foot to pull them clear before the train arrives
questions.rationale: Warn without putting yourself at risk.

questions.stem: You are told to wear a mask because of dust. It makes it hard to hear. What should you do?
options: Take the mask off when trains come
Keep working and look up more
Tell the COSS so warnings can be adjusted
Remove the mask for the whole shift
questions.rationale: PPE must not stop you hearing warnings.

questions.stem: Your COSS asks the group to work on both sides of the line at once with one lookout. What should you consider?
options: Whether it will finish the job faster
Whether the van is closer to one side than the other
Whether drivers will see both groups
Whether everyone can be warned and reach safety
questions.rationale: Split groups are harder to protect.

questions.stem: You are at a junction and the lookout warns of a train. You do not know which route it will take. Where do you go?
options: A position of safety clear of every line it could use
The cess beside the line it normally uses at that time of day
The six-foot between the two most likely routes
Wherever you are standing, as you cannot predict the route
questions.rationale: At junctions, trains can take several routes.

questions.stem: Your COSS has planned work using ATWS. On arrival, the equipment has not been delivered. What should happen?
options: Work does not start under that plan
The COSS switches to lookout warning without telling the planner
The group starts and listens carefully for trains
The group works only in the cess until it arrives
questions.rationale: No planned protection, no work.

questions.stem: You are working in a station at night when a light engine moves through without stopping. What does this tell you?
options: The station is now closed to all trains
Only passenger trains need to be watched for
Light engines never come through at night
Unexpected movements can happen at any time
questions.rationale: Never assume a quiet period is safe.

questions.stem: You are told to step into a refuge as a train passes through a tunnel. The refuge is wet and slippery. What should you do?
options: Stand in the cess instead, as it is drier
Use it carefully and report the condition
Lie down in the four-foot
Lean against the tunnel wall outside the refuge
questions.rationale: Report defects, but use the refuge rather than an unsafe spot.

questions.stem: Your group is working on a line with a 25 mph speed restriction, but the line speed is normally 100 mph. Which speed should you plan for?
options: The line speed, unless the plan says otherwise
25 mph, because drivers must obey the restriction
An average of the two speeds
Whichever is quicker to plan for
questions.rationale: Trains may not be slowed as expected.

questions.stem: You see a train approaching with its headlights flashing. What should you do?
options: Wave back to the driver
Keep working as it is a greeting
Step into the four-foot to see better
Get to safety; it may be a warning
questions.rationale: Treat any unusual signal from a train as a warning.

questions.stem: You are using a measuring wheel along the cess. It drifts towards the rail. What should you do?
options: Follow it towards the rail to keep measuring
Stop and reposition so you stay clear
Push harder to keep going
Let it run into the four-foot
questions.rationale: Keep yourself and equipment clear.

questions.stem: You find a signal post telephone that does not work. What should you do?
options: Report it and use another means if needed
Ignore it, as phones are not important
Try to repair it yourself
Remove the handset
questions.rationale: SPTs are emergency equipment.

questions.stem: Your group is about to work under OLE with an isolation, but the authorised person has not arrived. What should you do?
options: Start, as the isolation was booked
Start, but avoid touching the wires
Ask a colleague to act as authorised person
Wait; do not work within 2.75 m of the OLE
questions.rationale: No confirmed isolation, no close work.

questions.stem: A strong gust blows a road sign from a nearby bridge onto the cess. What should you do?
options: Throw it back onto the road
Check it is clear of the line and report it
Leave it in the four-foot
Throw it back up onto the road where it came from
questions.rationale: Objects near the line can foul trains.

questions.stem: You are working at night in a busy station and the platform lights go off. What should you do?
options: Carry on using your torch
Carry on using your torch, as you know the site well
Stop and get to a safe place until lighting is restored
Work faster before trains come
questions.rationale: Lighting failures increase risk.

questions.stem: Your group is spread along 300 m of track and there is one lookout. What is the risk?
options: The work will be finished too quickly
Some people may not get the warning in time
Drivers will be confused
There is no risk
questions.rationale: Keep the group within protection.

questions.stem: You arrive at site and see the planned lookout position is now behind a new noise barrier. What should happen?
options: The lookout stands on top of the barrier
The lookout arrangements must be reviewed
The lookout listens through the barrier
The group works without a lookout
questions.rationale: Site changes affect sighting.

questions.stem: A colleague asks you to hold their phone while they film the train passing. What should you do?
options: Agree, as it is only a few seconds
Film it yourself instead
Refuse; stay focused on getting clear
Hold it from the four-foot
questions.rationale: Distractions near trains are dangerous.

questions.stem: You hear a train horn but the lookout says it is on a different route. Your position of safety is 3 m away. What should you do?
options: Stay where you are as the lookout said
Move to it anyway
Wait until you see the train
Ask the lookout to check again
questions.rationale: If in doubt, get clear.

questions.stem: Your work involves carrying a ladder under a bridge on an electrified line. What should you check?
options: The colour of the bridge
The age of the bridge
The age of the bridge and when it was last painted
The clearance to the OLE under the bridge
questions.rationale: Clearances are reduced under bridges.

questions.stem: You are in a fenced safe area and the fence is damaged in one place. What should you do?
options: Carry on, but avoid that spot
Tell the COSS before carrying on
Repair it with tape
Climb through it
questions.rationale: A broken fence no longer protects you.

questions.stem: A train stops at a signal next to your group. The driver opens the cab window and asks what you are doing. What should you do?
options: Walk to the cab for a proper chat
Stay clear of the train and answer briefly
Climb onto the step to speak
Stand in front of the train so the driver can hear you
questions.rationale: The train can move at any time.

questions.stem: You are working near a level crossing and the barriers come down. What should you do?
options: Lift the barrier to cross quickly
Ignore it, as you are not on the road
Walk along the line to see the train
Expect a train and make sure you are clear
questions.rationale: Barriers lowering mean a train is likely due.

questions.stem: Your COSS says a train has been 'held at the signal' so you can cross. What should you do?
options: Cross in front of the held train
Only cross if the plan and confirmation support it
Cross behind the held train without checking
Ask the driver to wait
questions.rationale: Do not rely on informal assurances.

questions.stem: Your colleague is about to step over the rail onto a wet steel cover plate. What should you warn them about?
options: It may be live
It may be slippery
It may be hot
It may be loose only in summer
questions.rationale: Steel plates can be very slippery when wet.

questions.stem: You are told the group will 'lift and shift' equipment between trains. What should you ask?
options: How much the job pays
How much the job pays and when you will finish
Who will drive home
What warning time and positions of safety apply
questions.rationale: Know the protection for each move.

questions.stem: During work, a lookout falls ill and sits down. What should the group do?
options: Carry on and keep an eye out
Stop and move to safety
Ask the lookout to keep watching
Ask a visitor to take over
questions.rationale: No effective lookout means no warning.

questions.stem: You notice the cess has a new cable trough laid since the briefing. It narrows the position of safety. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS
Stand on the trough
Ignore it
Move the trough
questions.rationale: Changes affect positions of safety.

questions.stem: Your group is working at the end of a platform. Passengers are watching. One shouts that a train is coming. What should you do?
options: Move to safety straight away
Ignore it as a joke
Wait for the lookout to confirm
Ask the passenger which line
questions.rationale: Act on any warning.

questions.stem: You see a colleague's hi-vis has the reflective tape peeling off. What should you do?
options: Ignore it
Peel the rest off
Tape over it with black tape
Suggest they replace it
questions.rationale: Reflective bands matter at night.

questions.stem: You are walking back from site and your head torch dazzles a driver. What should you do?
options: Turn it up brighter so the driver can see you clearly
Point it down and away from approaching trains
Wave it at the driver
Shine it at the signals
questions.rationale: Do not dazzle drivers.

questions.stem: A heavy storm floods the cess. Your position of safety is under water. What should happen?
options: Stand in the water
Stand in the water, as it is still the planned place
Carry on and hope
Stop and agree a new position or a safer system
questions.rationale: Positions must stay usable.

questions.stem: Your group is working beside a line that is 'out of use'. Trains appear to be absent. What should you assume?
options: Treat it as open unless confirmed otherwise
Treat it as a safe walkway
Use it as a position of safety
Store tools on it, as no trains will come
questions.rationale: Lines can be brought back into use.

questions.stem: You are asked to help a colleague who is stuck in the four-foot with a twisted ankle. A train is due. What should you do?
options: Run in without telling anyone
Wait until the train passes
Leave them and go to safety without telling anyone
Raise the alarm and help only if you can do it safely
questions.rationale: Get help, stop trains if possible, and do not become a casualty.

questions.stem: You are walking to site in the cess when you realise your walking route passes under an overbridge with no cess. What should you do?
options: Walk through quickly while no trains can be heard
Walk through in the four-foot where there is more room
Wait until a train passes, then go through behind it
Stop and check with the COSS how to pass safely
questions.rationale: Overbridges can create limited clearance.

questions.stem: A lookout warns, and you move clear. A second warning sounds before the first train has passed. What does this mean?
options: The lookout has pressed the horn by mistake
The first train has stopped and the line is now safe
The group should return to work straight away
Another train is approaching; stay clear
questions.rationale: Multiple trains can come in quick succession.

questions.stem: You are working near a depot exit and a train leaves the depot without warning. What should you have known?
options: That depot trains always sound their horn twice
That depot movements were possible from that direction
That depot trains are not allowed onto running lines
That depot trains move only during the daytime
questions.rationale: Briefings should cover all movement directions.

questions.stem: Your group is moving a long rail by hand under a line blockage. The adjacent line is open. What is the key danger?
options: The rail becoming electrically live from the ballast
The rail being too heavy to finish the job on time
The rail setting off the AWS magnets
The rail swinging towards the open line
questions.rationale: Long loads can foul adjacent lines.

questions.stem: You are told the line is blocked 'up to signal 123'. Your work is 50 m beyond that signal. What does this mean?
options: The blockage covers 50 m beyond the signal anyway
You are protected as long as you can see the signal
You only need a lookout for that last 50 m
Your work is outside the protected area
questions.rationale: Know the exact limits.

questions.stem: You see your COSS standing in the four-foot talking on the phone. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as COSSs know the risks
Stand beside them to listen
Warn them to move to a safe place
Wait until they finish the call
questions.rationale: Anyone can intervene.

questions.stem: You are working near a quarry siding where wagons are loaded. A wagon starts rolling slowly. What should you do?
options: Push against it to stop it rolling
Get clear of its path and raise the alarm
Put a stone under its wheel
Climb aboard to apply the brake
questions.rationale: Never try to stop moving vehicles by hand.

questions.stem: You are briefed that ATWS will protect you. During work you notice one of the sensors has been knocked over. What should you do?
options: Stand it back up and carry on working
Carry on, as the other sensors will still work
Ignore it until the next train passes
Stop work and tell the COSS
questions.rationale: Damaged equipment may not warn you.

questions.stem: Fog is so thick that you cannot see the next OLE mast. Your safe system relies on a lookout. What should happen?
options: The lookout should move closer to the group
Work should stop or change to a protected system
The group should rely on hearing trains instead
The group should carry on but stay in the cess
questions.rationale: Sighting is too limited.

questions.stem: Your group is working beside a busy freight route at night. Freight trains are long. Why does this matter?
options: Freight trains are always slower than passenger trains
Freight trains never use bi-directional lines
Freight trains do not need warnings
You may need to stay clear for longer
questions.rationale: Long trains take longer to pass, and others may follow.

questions.stem: During a possession, you see a red light moving towards you on your line. What should you assume?
options: It is a signal that has moved in the wind
A vehicle may be approaching; get clear
It is a lookout's torch and can be ignored
It is the end of the possession marker
questions.rationale: Movements occur within possessions.

questions.stem: A train has derailed on an adjacent line during your shift. Your line is blocked. What should you do?
options: Carry on working as normal, as your own line is still blocked
Keep clear of the derailment and follow instructions
Carry on working as your line is blocked
Take photos for the investigation team
questions.rationale: Derailments can affect other lines and OLE.

questions.stem: You arrive on site and the COSS is someone you have never met. They do not check your card. What should you do?
options: Offer your card and ask for a full briefing
Start work without saying anything
Leave, as they are unprofessional
Start work without saying anything, as you know the job
questions.rationale: Checks and briefings protect everyone.

questions.stem: You notice a train's headlight is out as it approaches at night. What extra risk is there?
options: The train will stop before your site
The train is not allowed to move
There is no extra risk
It may be harder to see the train coming
questions.rationale: Never rely on seeing lights.

questions.stem: A colleague says the 'rails are humming', so a train is coming. The lookout has not warned. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as the lookout knows best
Put your ear to the rail to check
Get clear and alert the lookout
Wait for the lookout's warning
questions.rationale: Act on any sign of a train.

questions.stem: You are working on a line where trains are being diverted because of other engineering work. What should you be aware of?
options: Diverted trains always run slower
Diverted trains do not use horns
Diverted trains run only at night
Trains may be running on unusual routes
questions.rationale: Diversions change normal patterns.

questions.stem: You are asked to cross the line carrying a gas bottle. What is the main extra hazard?
options: The gas bottle will set off the AWS
Gas bottles attract lightning
Gas bottles make trains slow down
Dropping it or tripping while carrying it
questions.rationale: Heavy or awkward loads slow you down.

questions.stem: Your position of safety is next to a lineside telephone box. A train passes very close. What should you do?
options: Lean into the telephone box next time
Ignore it, as it is a recognised spot
Hold the phone handset for balance next time
Report it so the position of safety can be checked
questions.rationale: Positions must give safe clearance.

questions.stem: You are briefed about a 'second train' risk at your site. What does it mean?
options: Two trains are coupled together
The second train is always an engineering train
The second train will stop at the site
Another train may follow or pass on another line
questions.rationale: Wait until it is confirmed clear.

questions.stem: A train passes at speed and the air blast knocks your colleague's helmet off. What does this tell you?
options: Helmets should not be worn near trains
The train was speeding illegally
Your position may be too close for that speed
Your colleague's helmet was too small
questions.rationale: Review positions of safety.

questions.stem: You are working on a platform-side line and the platform staff ask you to move so passengers can board. What should you do?
options: Climb onto the platform without telling anyone
Move into the six-foot
Carry on working
Follow the safe system and agree with the COSS
questions.rationale: Coordinate with station staff via your COSS.

questions.stem: You notice your lookout is wearing a hood that covers their ears. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as lookouts use their eyes
Tell the COSS; it may affect their duties
Lend them your ear defenders
Shout warnings for them
questions.rationale: Lookouts must be fully alert.

questions.stem: You are working at night and hear a horn but no lights are visible. What should you do?
options: Wait until you see the train's lights before moving
Shine your torch along the line
Keep working until warned
Move to your position of safety straight away
questions.rationale: Trust the sound.

questions.stem: Your group works on a line with conductor rail. Someone drops a metal spanner that lands near the conductor rail. What should you do?
options: Pick it up quickly
Kick it away
Leave it and tell the COSS
Use another spanner to hook it out
questions.rationale: Do not reach near the live rail.

questions.stem: You are told the safe system is 'separated' with a site warden. The work needs you to reach into the area within 2 m of the open line. What should you do?
options: Reach in quickly while the warden watches
Ask the warden to stand closer
Carry on, as it is only your arm
Stop; the work does not fit the safe system
questions.rationale: Separated working keeps everyone at least 2 m away.

questions.stem: During a briefing the COSS says 'the usual positions of safety'. You are new. What should you do?
options: Follow others when a train comes
Pick your own place
Stand next to the lookout
Ask exactly where they are
questions.rationale: Never assume.

questions.stem: A train passes and you feel heat and smell burning from its brakes. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as brakes always smell
Wave the next train to stop
Throw water on the rails
Report it to the signaller
questions.rationale: It could be a fault or fire risk.

questions.stem: Your group needs to cross a four-track railway with two lines open. What is the safest approach?
options: Cross all four lines in one go quickly
Use a footbridge or cross only under planned protection
Cross the open lines while watching
Cross in the gap between trains, watching both directions
questions.rationale: Crossing multiple open lines is high risk.

questions.stem: You feel unwell after lunch and dizzy. You are due to act as lookout. What should you do?
options: Tell the COSS you are not fit
Act as lookout sitting down
Drink water and carry on
Swap duties without telling anyone
questions.rationale: Lookouts must be fully fit.

questions.stem: A colleague tells you a short cut 'everyone uses' through a gap in the fence. What should you do?
options: Use the short cut as others do
Use it only in daylight
Use it if you are quick
Use the authorised access point
questions.rationale: Informal access is unsafe.

questions.stem: During a line blockage you see the signaller's protecting signal show a proceed aspect. What does it mean?
options: Protection may have been lost; get clear and tell the COSS
The signaller is testing the signal for you
A train may pass but will stop at your site
Nothing, because signals only ever affect train drivers
questions.rationale: Act immediately.

questions.stem: You are measuring a gap between rails at night and the measuring tape's reflective end catches a train's lights far away. What should you do?
options: Carry on until the train is closer
Wave the tape to signal the driver
Respond to the warning arrangements, not guesswork
Ignore it, as the train is still a long way off
questions.rationale: Follow the planned warnings.
