questions.stem: You notice the COSS has not appointed a site warden for separated working. What should you do?
options: Raise it before work starts
Act as warden yourself while working
Ignore it, the group is careful
Work closer to the fence
questions.rationale: Separated working needs a warden.

questions.stem: Your group is working by a river bridge and someone drops a tool into the water. What should you do?
options: Climb down the bridge pier to get it
Jump in to retrieve it
Lean over the parapet to reach it
Leave it and report it
questions.rationale: Do not risk a fall or drowning.

questions.stem: You are told the train timetable has been suspended for the night. What should you still do?
options: Work under the planned safe system
Work anywhere without protection
Use the line as a walkway
Stop wearing PPE
questions.rationale: Movements can still happen.

questions.stem: A lookout is standing on top of a stack of sleepers for a better view. What should you do?
options: Ignore it, as they can see further
Join them on the stack
Move the group closer to them
Raise it; they could fall or be unstable
questions.rationale: Lookouts must be in a stable position of safety.

questions.stem: You are working in the cess on a gradient and a hand trolley starts rolling towards the group. What should you do?
options: Try to stop it with your foot
Shout a warning and get clear
Jump onto it to brake it
Put a tool on the rail in front of it
questions.rationale: Runaway trolleys can seriously injure.

questions.stem: A new worker is about to step onto the conductor rail to cross. You are 5 m away. What should you do?
options: Shout to stop them immediately
Run and push them clear
Wait to see what happens
Tell the COSS later
questions.rationale: A quick warning can save a life.

questions.stem: Your group is working under bright lights at night. A train approaches from the dark side. Why is this dangerous?
options: Your eyes may not adjust to see it
The lights will make the train stop
The driver cannot see the lights
Trains slow down in the dark
questions.rationale: Lighting contrast affects vision.

questions.stem: You arrive late and the COSS briefs you quickly on the walk. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes, any briefing is better than none
Yes, if the walk is long enough
Only if it is complete and you understand it
No, briefings must always be in an office
questions.rationale: The quality of the briefing matters.

questions.stem: On 3 July 2019 at Margam East Junction, what happened?
options: A passenger train derailed after striking a fallen tree on the line
Two track workers were struck and killed by a train
A lookout was injured by a road-rail vehicle reversing inside a possession
Overhead wires fell onto a group working on a bridge during a storm
questions.rationale: Two workers died and a third narrowly escaped. RAIB investigated.

questions.stem: What was RAIB's key finding about lookouts at Margam in 2019?
options: No lookouts had been formally appointed
The lookouts had been given radios that failed during the work
Three lookouts were present but stood in the wrong positions on site
The lookouts had warned the group but the warning was ignored by all
questions.rationale: The group was working on a line open to traffic without formally appointed lookouts.

questions.stem: Which planning weakness did RAIB identify at Margam?
options: The plan required every job to be done under a full weekend possession
The plan had been written for a completely different route and region
A less safe fallback was allowed if a blockage was refused
The plan had not been signed by the client before the work began
questions.rationale: Parallel safe work packs let groups fall back to lookout working. Network Rail later removed this from its planning.

questions.stem: What did RAIB say about how long unsafe practices had gone on before Margam?
options: They had started that same morning because the group was short of staff
They had been reported many times and managers had approved them in writing
They had continued for a long time without being noticed
They had only happened once before, on a single night shift the week before
questions.rationale: Managers relied on paperwork and rarely saw what happened on site.

questions.stem: After Margam, which bodies were set up to drive change in track worker safety?
options: A new railway police force and a separate track worker trade union
A national lookout academy and a private track safety regulator
A Safety Task Force and a Track Worker Expert Group
A drivers' committee and a new passenger safety ombudsman
questions.rationale: Network Rail set up a Safety Task Force and independent experts reviewed track worker safety.

questions.stem: At Surbiton on 9 February 2021, what happened?
options: A COSS was struck while placing possession limit boards at night
A visitor fell from a platform while being escorted along the track
A lookout was electrocuted by the conductor rail during a patrol
A track worker was struck during a track inspection
questions.rationale: RAIB found the work used unassisted lookout working, the least safe system.

questions.stem: What effect did the Surbiton accident have on lookout working?
options: It sped up efforts to remove lookout working
It led to lookouts being given radios as standard equipment
It led to more lookouts being appointed on every work site
It had no effect because the cause was found to be a train fault
questions.rationale: It accelerated Network Rail's moves away from lookout protection.

questions.stem: At Stoats Nest Junction in 2018, when was the worker struck?
options: Shortly after placing protection, outside the protected area
While driving a road-rail vehicle along an open line at night
While crossing a platform to reach the welfare cabin
While acting as lookout for a group working on points
questions.rationale: Staff placing or removing protection are at risk if they move outside the protected area.

questions.stem: What employment issue did RAIB highlight at Stoats Nest Junction?
options: The worker had been dismissed the day before the accident
The worker had no Sentinel card and was working illegally
The worker was a manager who had not done PTS for years
A contingent worker's hours were not checked
questions.rationale: The labour supplier made no checks on the worker's hours, a fatigue risk.

questions.stem: At Newark North Gate in 2014, who was killed?
options: A lookout who moved into the path of a train
A COSS who was walking back from a signal post telephone
A train driver who left the cab to inspect a fault
A welder who was working under a possession
questions.rationale: The COSS had not monitored the team effectively.

questions.stem: What lesson does the Newark North Gate accident teach about lookouts?
options: Lookouts are themselves at risk and must stay in safety
Lookouts should stand in the four-foot to see further
Lookouts are protected by their armband and need no position of safety
Lookouts should also help with the work during quiet spells
questions.rationale: A lookout must work from a position of safety.

questions.stem: At Ruscombe Junction in 2007, who was struck by a train?
options: A lookout on a bridge
A welder
A signaller walking to a box
A COSS crossing a junction
questions.rationale: RAIB found peer pressure and a reluctance to interrupt work were factors.

questions.stem: What human factor did RAIB highlight at Ruscombe Junction?
options: A train driver falling asleep at the controls
A signaller misreading the track diagram
Reluctance to interrupt work
A broken rail that had been missed by patrols
questions.rationale: People did not want to stop the work, which led to unsafe decisions.

questions.stem: At Reading in 2007, a worker was killed while doing what?
options: Placing detonators at the start of a possession
Repairing overhead wires under an isolation
Acting as lookout for a large group of workers
Walking from site after protection was removed
questions.rationale: Protection must remain, or another safe system must apply, until everyone is clear.

questions.stem: At Maesyfelin bridge near Pontyclun in April 2016, how fast was the train?
options: About 20 mph
About 125 mph
About 45 mph
About 75 mph
questions.rationale: Six workers nearly collided with a 75 mph passenger train on the bridge.

questions.stem: How did some workers at Maesyfelin bridge escape the train?
options: They lay down flat in the four-foot
They ran back to the nearest access point
They jumped onto the bridge parapet
They sheltered in a refuge built into the bridge
questions.rationale: There was no position of safety on the bridge.

questions.stem: Why was the system used at Maesyfelin bridge unsafe?
options: It used too many lookouts for the size of group
It had been planned by the signaller rather than a COSS
It used ATWS, which failed in the rain
It was unauthorised and relied on radios
questions.rationale: The COSS used an unauthorised system with hand-held radio warnings. A radioed warning was not received.

questions.stem: What physical feature at Maesyfelin bridge made lookout working unsuitable?
options: A level crossing at each end of the bridge
No position of safety and limited sighting
A conductor rail running across the bridge deck
A station platform directly over the river
questions.rationale: Track curvature limited sighting and there was nowhere to stand clear.

questions.stem: At Dutton Viaduct in 2017, what did a structures examination team do?
options: Climbed the piers without any harnesses
Crossed the viaduct at track level
Worked under the viaduct during a flood
Used a drone close to the overhead wires
questions.rationale: They narrowly avoided a 125 mph passenger train. RAIB found planning deficiencies.

questions.stem: At South Hampstead in 2018, roughly how much warning did workers have?
options: About thirty seconds
About two seconds
About one minute
About ten seconds
questions.rationale: They had gone onto the wrong lines, partly due to poor signage.

questions.stem: At Egmanton in 2017, what did RAIB find about the contract staff?
options: They had been working without any PTS at all
They had refused to follow the COSS's instructions
They were all from the same family and ignored rules
They feared losing work if they challenged
questions.rationale: Peer pressure and job insecurity made them reluctant to challenge unsafe arrangements.

questions.stem: At Peterborough in 2018, workers narrowly avoided a train at what speed?
options: 25 mph
50 mph
125 mph
75 mph
questions.rationale: RAIB investigated this near miss.

questions.stem: At Morton Junction in 2024, what had changed without the COSS knowing?
options: The line speed and direction of trains
The safe work pack they were using
The members of the group and the lookout
The time of the possession and the access point
questions.rationale: The COSS used a pack for a different location and had not fully read the documentation.

questions.stem: What is the main lesson from Morton Junction for every worker?
options: Familiar jobs can safely skip a full briefing every time
The COSS should rely on memory rather than paperwork
Check that documents match the site
Documents only matter for large engineering projects
questions.rationale: Always check that the plan matches the actual location and task.

questions.stem: At Acton West in 2008, what went wrong at the access point?
options: The gate was locked and staff climbed over the fence
The access point was flooded and staff waded through
The access point had been moved to another town
Signs lacked track layout details
questions.rationale: Equipment was placed on open lines instead of the possessed lines.

questions.stem: At Severn Tunnel Junction in February 1985, what were the workers doing?
options: Replacing a rail
Clearing snow
Painting a bridge
Inspecting signals
questions.rationale: Four were killed. The lack of clear leadership and lookouts led to major rule changes.

questions.stem: What was a key failing at Severn Tunnel Junction in 1985?
options: The workers were not wearing high-visibility clothing
The train was travelling well above the line speed
No clearly defined leadership or lookouts
The signaller had given the group the wrong line
questions.rationale: This led to a clearer role for the person in charge of safety.

questions.stem: Since 2005, roughly how many RAIB investigations have involved track workers and moving trains (to May 2026)?
options: About 7
About 670
About 67
About 17
questions.rationale: Of these, 10 led to deaths and 13 to injuries.

questions.stem: By the end of 2023, roughly what share of Network Rail work was done on closed lines?
options: About 50%
About 75%
Over 99%
About 10%
questions.rationale: Planning more work on closed lines is the most effective control.

questions.stem: In how many of RAIB's track worker investigations was lookout warning the intended method?
options: None at all
Only 2
About 25
Over 60
questions.rationale: Lookout warning features heavily in incidents.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up RAIB's main lesson on track worker safety?
options: Train more lookouts so every site has two of them
Make PPE brighter so drivers can see workers sooner
Separate people from trains
Lower line speeds wherever track work is planned
questions.rationale: Separation is more effective than warnings.

questions.stem: RAIB has highlighted that the COSS or person in charge must do what?
options: Stay in the van to keep in contact with control
Act as the lookout as well as leading the work
Personally observe and advise the group
Leave the site once the briefing has been signed
questions.rationale: Active, on-site leadership prevents unsafe acts.

questions.stem: Why did RAIB say managers must visit sites rather than rely on paperwork?
options: Paperwork is always completed incorrectly by staff
Site visits count towards managers' training hours
Unsafe practice may only show on site
Visits replace the need for COSS briefings
questions.rationale: At Margam, document checks missed long-running unsafe practices.

questions.stem: What risk did RAIB find with zero-hours or contingent workers?
options: They always hold fewer competences than employees
They are not allowed to report near misses
They are banned from working at night
They may not challenge unsafe work
questions.rationale: Fear of losing work can stop people speaking up.

questions.stem: Which kind of incident is particularly linked to placing or removing possession protection?
options: Staff electrocuted by the possession limit boards
Staff injured by falling detonators from trains
Staff struck near open lines
Staff hit by road vehicles at level crossings
questions.rationale: Stoats Nest and Reading are examples of this risk.

questions.stem: What did RAIB find about the unassisted lookout method in 2023 on Network Rail?
options: It was used in about half of all activities
It had been completely banned since 2005
It was used in about 1% of activities
It was used for every task at junctions
questions.rationale: Network Rail has greatly reduced lookout working.

questions.stem: Which statement about near misses is supported by RAIB's work?
options: They are not worth reporting if nobody was hurt
They are always caused by train drivers, not workers
They only happen on lines with conductor rails
They show where the next accident could happen
questions.rationale: Near misses like Egmanton and South Hampstead had only seconds of warning.

questions.stem: What was found at Roade in 2020?
options: A train hit a road vehicle on a level crossing
A COSS used radios to give warnings
OLE fell onto a group of workers
A worker returned to the track unnecessarily
questions.rationale: The worker was struck. The system of work was inadequate.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Elstree/Borehamwood event of 2026 is correct?
options: A train derailed after a rail broke
A track worker was fatally injured
A lookout was injured by a falling tree
A bridge was struck by a lorry
questions.rationale: RAIB is investigating. It followed five years without a track worker fatality, though near misses continued.

questions.stem: At Whitehall West Junction in 2009, what method of protection was in use?
options: A full possession
A fenced safe area
ATWS
Unassisted lookout
questions.rationale: The accident was fatal.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of RAIB recommendations?
options: To decide who should be prosecuted after an accident
To set the fines that companies must pay after accidents
To decide compensation for the families of victims
To prevent similar accidents
questions.rationale: RAIB does not apportion blame or liability.

questions.stem: Which organisation tracks how RAIB recommendations are acted on?
options: The Sentinel scheme
The Office of Rail and Road (ORR)
British Transport Police
The train operating companies
questions.rationale: ORR reports on the actions taken.

questions.stem: Why do RAIB investigations matter to someone taking a PTS assessment?
options: They decide which questions appear in the assessment
They replace the need to learn the Rule Book
They show how the rules prevent deaths
They are only relevant to managers and planners
questions.rationale: Understanding real incidents helps you see why the rules exist.

questions.stem: What common factor links Margam, Surbiton and Whitehall West Junction?
options: Work on conductor rail lines in the south
Work at night under engineering possessions
Reliance on lookout warning
Work by staff without any PTS competence
questions.rationale: Each involved lookout-based protection on open lines.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes RAIB's view of 'informal' local working practices?
options: They are usually safer than the official plan
They are approved once used for a year
They only matter on high-speed lines
They can miss hazards nobody considered
questions.rationale: Following the planned safe system is fundamental.

questions.stem: What did RAIB find about information given to workers in several incidents?
options: It was too detailed and took too long to read
It was unclear, inaccurate or missing
It was given only in writing and never verbally
It was perfect, but workers ignored it
questions.rationale: Workers need concise, accurate and relevant information, including signs.

questions.stem: At Sundon and Llandegai Tunnel, what went wrong?
options: Staff worked without any hi-vis clothing
Staff were hit by falling rocks in a cutting
Staff were trapped by a fire in a tunnel
Staff accessed the wrong side of the line
questions.rationale: Poor information about access and layout contributed.

questions.stem: What did the near miss at Littlehempston show?
options: A COSS's own actions can endanger the group
Lookouts are always more reliable than ATWS
Visitors cannot be taken on the track at all
Drivers must sound the horn at every site
questions.rationale: Leaders must follow the rules too.

questions.stem: In which year was the role of PICOW renamed COSS?
questions.rationale: The role became Controller of Site Safety on 7 August 1999.

questions.stem: From April 1992, what change was made to the person in charge of work (PICOW) role?
options: Appointment became mandatory with a formal course
The role was abolished and replaced by lookouts
The role was given only to train drivers
The role was limited to work at night
questions.rationale: Fatalities in 1990–1991 led to the role being formalised.

questions.stem: How many Lifesaving Rules does Network Rail have?
options: Three
Twenty-five
Ten
Fifty
questions.rationale: Network Rail's ten Lifesaving Rules cover the main causes of death and life-changing injury.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of Network Rail's Lifesaving Rules?
options: To speed up engineering work so trains run on time
To decide which contractors can bid for railway work
To get everyone home safe every day
To replace the Rule Book for experienced track workers
questions.rationale: The rules target the activities most likely to kill or seriously injure.

questions.stem: Which of these is one of Network Rail's main high-risk areas covered by the Lifesaving Rules?
options: Working in offices and meeting rooms
Answering customer complaints by phone
Working with electricity
Ordering stationery for depots
questions.rationale: Risk areas include contact with trains, electricity, work at height, moving equipment and driving.

questions.stem: Which electrical Lifesaving Rule message is correct?
options: Assume equipment is dead once trains have stopped running
Touch equipment briefly to check whether it is live
Never assume it is isolated; test before touch
Electrical equipment is only live during daylight hours
questions.rationale: Always prove equipment is dead before touching it, through authorised arrangements.

questions.stem: Which of these is a Network Rail driving Lifesaving Rule?
options: Always drive at the speed limit to save time
Always wear a seat belt
Always use a hands-free phone while driving
Always drive the shortest route even when tired
questions.rationale: Driving rules include seat belts, no speeding, no phones and no drink or drugs.

questions.stem: Under Network Rail's driving Lifesaving Rules, may you use a hands-free phone while driving?
options: Yes, if it is mounted in a proper cradle
No, never use a phone while driving
Yes, for calls to the COSS or signaller
Yes, on motorways but not on minor roads
questions.rationale: The rule is never to use a mobile phone, even hands-free.

questions.stem: What does Network Rail's 'Fair Culture' aim to do?
options: Understand why rules were broken and respond fairly
Punish every rule break with immediate dismissal
Ignore rule breaks as long as nobody was hurt
Let each team decide which rules it will follow
questions.rationale: Consequences should be fair and proportionate, and lessons learned.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of 'work at height' on the railway?
options: Walking along the cess on level ground
Working on a bridge or a ladder
Kneeling on the ballast to check a clip
Sitting in a van at the access point
questions.rationale: Falls from height cause serious injuries. Use proper access and fall protection.

questions.stem: What should you do before working on a bridge parapet or high structure?
options: Make sure fall protection is planned and in place
Check the weather forecast for the following week
Ask a colleague to hold on to your jacket
Remove your helmet so it does not fall off
questions.rationale: Work at height needs specific planning and controls.

questions.stem: What is the main hazard of 'moving equipment' on site?
options: Being dazzled by the machine's paint
Losing your Sentinel card in the cab
Being struck or crushed
Getting lost following the machine
questions.rationale: Keep clear of moving plant and follow the controller's instructions.

questions.stem: What is 'manual handling'?
options: Operating signals by hand from a box
Writing records by hand on site forms
Handling the controls of a road vehicle
Moving loads by hand or bodily force
questions.rationale: Poor manual handling causes many back and muscle injuries.

questions.stem: Before lifting, what is the first thing to consider?
options: How quickly you can carry it to the van
Whether the load is a nice shape to carry
Whether you can avoid lifting it by hand
Whether anyone is watching you lift it
questions.rationale: Avoid manual handling where possible; use mechanical aids.

questions.stem: What is noise-induced hearing loss?
options: Temporary deafness that always recovers overnight
Hearing loss caused only by ear infections
A condition that affects only train drivers
Permanent damage caused by loud noise
questions.rationale: Use hearing protection and limit exposure.

questions.stem: Why can silica dust be harmful?
options: It makes the ballast slippery underfoot
It can cause serious lung disease
It damages the paint on rail vehicles
It blocks GSM-R radio signals near the line
questions.rationale: Cutting concrete or stone creates silica dust. Use controls and respiratory protection.

questions.stem: What should you do with a substance you do not recognise on site?
options: Keep clear and report it
Smell it to work out what it is
Wash it away with water into the drains
Pick it up and take it to the van
questions.rationale: Unknown substances may be hazardous.

questions.stem: Where should you find the hazards and controls for a chemical you use?
options: In the train timetable
On your Sentinel card
In the Highway Code
In its COSHH assessment
questions.rationale: COSHH assessments explain risks and the PPE needed.

questions.stem: What is the main danger of working near water such as rivers under bridges?
options: Electric shock from fish
Sunburn from reflections
Losing your Sentinel card
Drowning
questions.rationale: Plan for water hazards with suitable controls and rescue arrangements.

questions.stem: What is a hazard when working near a lineside fire or burning vegetation?
options: Smoke can hide trains and harm breathing
Fire makes approaching trains travel faster
Smoke improves sighting of distant trains
Fire switches off the overhead line automatically
questions.rationale: Keep clear and report fires.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find drug-taking equipment such as needles on site?
options: Pick it up and put it in your pocket
Kick it into the ballast to hide it
Throw it over the boundary fence
Do not touch it; report it for safe removal
questions.rationale: Needlestick injuries can transmit disease.

questions.stem: Why should you report trespass and vandalism you see?
options: So the vandals can be offered a job
So the area can be closed permanently
So drivers can sound the horn louder
It can endanger people and trains
questions.rationale: Report to the signaller or British Transport Police.

questions.stem: What is the best response to aggressive members of the public near a site?
options: Argue with them until they leave
Avoid confrontation and get help
Chase them off along the track
Invite them onto the site to talk
questions.rationale: Your safety comes first; call the police if needed.

questions.stem: Why should vehicles at access points be parked facing out where possible?
options: So the headlights can light the track
So drivers can see the train timetable
So nobody can see inside the van
So they can leave quickly in an emergency
questions.rationale: Planning for quick exit helps in emergencies.

questions.stem: What should you do before driving a work vehicle after a night shift?
options: Make sure you are rested enough to drive
Drink an energy drink and set off at once
Open the window and turn the radio up loud
Drive faster to get home before you get tired
questions.rationale: Fatigue is a major cause of road deaths.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign you are too tired to drive?
options: Drifting lanes or heavy eyelids
Wanting to listen to the radio
Feeling hungry after a shift
Being keen to get home quickly
questions.rationale: Stop somewhere safe and rest.

questions.stem: Why is good housekeeping important on a work site?
options: It prevents trips and items fouling the line
It makes the site look better in photographs
It reduces the number of briefings needed
It allows the group to work without PPE
questions.rationale: Keep sites tidy and clear.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a colleague using a damaged power lead?
options: Wrap the damaged part with insulating tape
Ignore it if the tool still works
Stop them and take it out of use
Use it yourself to finish the job
questions.rationale: Damaged leads can cause shocks and fires.

questions.stem: Why should you not work under a raised load?
options: It blocks the sunlight from the work
It confuses the lookout's view
It makes the work go more slowly
It could fall and crush you
questions.rationale: Never stand under suspended loads.

questions.stem: What is an 'exclusion zone' around plant?
options: An area where only managers are allowed to stand
An area where PPE does not need to be worn
An area people must not enter while it works
An area set aside for taking breaks
questions.rationale: Exclusion zones keep people out of reach of moving parts and loads.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a near miss involving plant?
options: Report it
Keep quiet so nobody is disciplined
Tell the operator off and leave it
Take a video and post it online
questions.rationale: Close calls help prevent accidents.

questions.stem: Why is it important to know where the first aider is on site?
options: So they can sign your timesheet
So help can be given quickly
So you can avoid them during breaks
So they can act as lookout
questions.rationale: Quick first aid can save lives.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to use a tool you have not been trained on?
options: Refuse until you are trained
Watch a colleague use it, then try it yourself
Use it slowly and carefully the first time
Read the box and start using it
questions.rationale: Only use equipment you are trained and competent to use.

questions.stem: Which of these is a heat illness warning sign?
options: Feeling slightly warm after a walk
Wanting a cold drink at break time
Feeling slightly warm after a long walk to the site
Confusion, dizziness or no longer sweating
questions.rationale: Heat stroke is a medical emergency.

questions.stem: What is the first thing to do if someone shows signs of heat stroke?
options: Tell them to carry on and drink later
Get them somewhere cool and call for help
Give them an energy drink and leave them
Wrap them in warm clothing
questions.rationale: Cool them and get medical help.

questions.stem: Why are long sleeves useful even in hot weather on track?
options: They protect against sun, cuts and give visibility
They make you sweat more and stay cool
They hide tattoos from members of the public
They are only needed for photographs
questions.rationale: Network Rail requires orange clothing covering arms and legs for most work.

questions.stem: What is hypothermia?
options: A dangerous drop in body temperature
A type of electrical injury from OLE
A fever caused by hot weather
A reaction to drinking cold water
questions.rationale: Cold, wet and windy conditions increase the risk.

questions.stem: Which is the best way to prevent cold stress on winter nights?
options: Work faster to keep warm
Drink alcohol to warm up
Wear layers and take warm breaks
Wear dark coats over hi-vis
questions.rationale: Plan clothing and rest breaks.

questions.stem: Why should you not wear earphones to listen to music while driving a site vehicle?
options: Music makes the vehicle use more fuel
You could miss warnings and hazards
Earphones interfere with the engine
The battery would drain the vehicle
questions.rationale: Stay alert when driving.

questions.stem: What should you do if a site task feels unsafe but you are not sure why?
options: Carry on and hope it is fine
Wait until the task is finished to mention it
Stop and ask
Ask someone from another site
questions.rationale: Trust your instincts; stop and get advice.

questions.stem: What is a 'dynamic risk assessment' on site?
options: A written plan made months before the work
A test of how fast you can run to safety
A medical check carried out by a doctor
Checking for new hazards as conditions change
questions.rationale: Keep looking for changes during the work.

questions.stem: Who is responsible for safety on site?
options: Only the COSS
Only the client
Only the sponsor
Everyone
questions.rationale: Everyone has a duty to look after themselves and others.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'toolbox talk'?
options: A short safety briefing on a specific topic
A talk about which tools to buy for the van
A meeting about the team's pay and bonuses
A training course for COSSs only
questions.rationale: Toolbox talks share lessons and reminders.

questions.stem: Why might you be asked to sign in and out at a site compound?
options: So pay can be calculated to the minute
So drivers know when to slow down
So everyone can be accounted for
So the compound can be locked early
questions.rationale: In an emergency, the list shows who is on site.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a colleague's safety boot laces undone on ballast?
options: Ignore it, it is their business
Tell them, as it is a trip hazard
Laugh about it at break time
Tie them yourself while they work
questions.rationale: Small things can cause falls near the line.

questions.stem: What does 'intervene' mean in safety culture?
options: Interrupting a briefing to ask about pay
Taking over another person's job
Stepping in to stop unsafe behaviour
Reporting a colleague anonymously only
questions.rationale: Lifesaving Rules expect people to intervene if something looks unsafe.

questions.stem: Which of these is a safe practice when using a ladder away from electrification?
options: Lean out to reach further
Keep three points of contact
Stand on the top rung
Carry heavy loads in both hands
questions.rationale: Use ladders only for short, light work and maintain contact.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid working alone at height?
options: Nobody can raise the alarm if you fall
It is lonely and boring
It takes longer
It is lonely and the work feels much slower
questions.rationale: Plan rescue arrangements for work at height.

questions.stem: Why should you not run across a road at an access point?
options: Running wears out safety boots
Drivers find it rude
It confuses the signaller
Road traffic is a serious hazard too
questions.rationale: Road risks near access points are real.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find a defect on a work vehicle before driving?
options: Report it and do not drive until it is safe
Drive carefully to the nearest garage
Ignore it if it is only a light
Ask someone else to drive it instead
questions.rationale: Vehicle defects cause accidents.

questions.stem: What is the safest action if a lifting operation looks unplanned?
options: Help so it finishes faster
Stop it and ask for a plan
Stand underneath to guide it
Film it for training later
questions.rationale: Lifting needs a plan and competent people.

questions.stem: Why are site welfare facilities important?
options: They are only for visitors
Rest and hygiene support safe work
They replace the need for breaks
They count towards overtime
questions.rationale: Tired, cold or unwell people make mistakes.

questions.stem: Which of these is a Network Rail Lifesaving Rule theme for driving?
options: Always take the motorway, even when it is longer
Never speed
Always drive yourself rather than share a vehicle
Always drive at night to avoid traffic
questions.rationale: Driving rules include never speeding.

questions.stem: Under the Lifesaving Rules, what should you do before touching electrical equipment?
options: Touch it lightly with the back of your hand first
Make sure it has been proven dead under authorised arrangements
Ask a colleague whether they think it is switched off
Touch it lightly with the back of your hand to check it is not live
questions.rationale: Never assume it is isolated; test before touch.

questions.stem: What is the main risk addressed by the 'work at height' Lifesaving Rule?
options: Falls
Being struck by trains on the line below
Electric shock from overhead wires
Dropping your mobile phone
questions.rationale: Falls from height cause serious injuries and deaths.

questions.stem: What is the main risk addressed by the 'moving equipment' Lifesaving Rule?
options: Being struck or crushed by plant or machinery
Being late because equipment arrives slowly
Losing tools when equipment is moved
Getting dirty from machinery oil
questions.rationale: Stay out of exclusion zones.

questions.stem: What does 'personal responsibility' mean in the Lifesaving Rules?
options: Only managers are responsible for safety on site
Each person can choose which rules they follow
Each person takes care of their own and others' safety
Responsibility passes to the client once on site
questions.rationale: Everyone has a role.

questions.stem: Why do the Lifesaving Rules focus on a small number of activities?
options: They cause most deaths and life-changing injuries
They are the easiest rules to remember
They are the only rules set by law
They apply only to managers and supervisors
questions.rationale: Targeting the biggest risks saves lives.

questions.stem: What is the right response if you see someone breaking a Lifesaving Rule?
options: Ignore it if they are more senior than you
Copy them if it saves time
Wait until the end of the shift to mention it
Intervene safely and report it
questions.rationale: Intervention can save a life.

questions.stem: Which is a safe practice for working near a deep excavation beside the line?
options: Jumping across the trench to save time
Barriers and safe edges to stop falls
Leaving it open and unmarked overnight
Storing heavy materials at the edge
questions.rationale: Excavations need edge protection.

questions.stem: What should you do before digging near the railway?
options: Start digging, as the railway owns the land
Dig carefully with a metal bar
Check for buried services and get permission
Ask a passer-by if they know of cables
questions.rationale: Buried cables may be live and important.

questions.stem: Why should you report damaged signalling cables you find?
options: They are expensive to replace
They can affect train safety
They look untidy on site
They might be stolen
questions.rationale: Signalling faults matter to train safety.

questions.stem: What is a 'permit to dig' or similar control for?
options: Allowing workers to keep what they dig up
Letting the public dig near the railway
Charging contractors a fee for each hole they dig
Making sure digging is planned around buried services
questions.rationale: Controls avoid striking services.

questions.stem: Which of these could be hazardous in a lineside compound?
options: Clean welfare cabins
Reversing vehicles
Marked walkways
Good lighting
questions.rationale: Use banksmen and keep to walkways.

questions.stem: What is a banksman?
options: A person who guides vehicles when reversing or manoeuvring
A person who builds and repairs railway banks and embankments
A person who builds railway banks and embankments
A person who checks Sentinel cards at the gate
questions.rationale: Banksmen help prevent vehicle strikes.

questions.stem: Why should you not walk behind a reversing vehicle?
options: The exhaust is too hot
The driver may not see you
You will slow it down
It is against dress code
questions.rationale: Blind spots kill.

questions.stem: What is the danger of storing materials too close to the line?
options: They might get wet in the rain
They might be hard to find later
They could foul the line or be blown onto it
They might be counted twice in the stock check
questions.rationale: Keep materials clear and secured.

questions.stem: What should you do if lineside stacked materials look unstable?
options: Climb on them to straighten them
Report it and keep clear
Kick the bottom one to settle them
Ignore them
questions.rationale: Falling materials can injure or foul the line.

questions.stem: Why are spill kits kept on some sites?
options: To clean up after lunch breaks
To store spare PPE
To contain fuel or chemical spills
To mark the edge of the site
questions.rationale: Spills can harm people and the environment.

questions.stem: What should you do if fuel spills near a drain beside the line?
options: Wash it into the drain with water
Use the spill kit if trained and report it
Cover it with ballast and leave it
Wash it into the drain with plenty of water
questions.rationale: Prevent pollution and fire.

questions.stem: Why are wildlife and environmental rules relevant to track work?
options: Animals may report you to the police
Trains run slower near wildlife
Some species and habitats are legally protected
They are not relevant to safety-critical work
questions.rationale: Follow environmental instructions in your briefing.

questions.stem: What should you do if you find nesting birds in vegetation you are told to clear?
options: Carry on, as railway work comes first
Remove the nest carefully yourself
Burn the vegetation
Stop and get advice
questions.rationale: Nesting birds may be protected.

questions.stem: What is a 'method statement'?
options: A statement taken from witnesses after an accident on site
A document describing how a task will be done safely
A statement from witnesses after an accident
A timetable for engineering trains
questions.rationale: Method statements set out safe working steps.

questions.stem: What is a 'risk assessment'?
options: A test of how fast you can work
A record of past accidents only
A test of how fast each person can do the work
An assessment of hazards and the controls needed
questions.rationale: Risk assessments underpin safe work.

questions.stem: Why should you read the method statement before starting a task?
options: To see how much the job pays
To understand the steps and controls
To check the weather forecast
To find out who is on site
questions.rationale: Know the plan before you start.

questions.stem: What should you do if a task cannot be done as the method statement says?
options: Improvise a different method
Stop and get it reviewed
Skip the difficult part
Ask a colleague to sign it off
questions.rationale: Changes need review.

questions.stem: What is the danger of rushing to finish a job before a possession ends?
options: It makes the job more expensive
Shortcuts lead to mistakes and injuries
It annoys the signaller
It makes the job more expensive for the client
questions.rationale: Time pressure is a known risk factor.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are asked to break a rule to finish on time?
options: Refuse and raise it
Agree, just this once
Agree if the COSS takes the blame
Agree if nobody is watching
questions.rationale: No job is worth a life.

questions.stem: Why should you report a 'near hit' with plant?
options: So the cause can be fixed before someone is hurt
So the operator can be dismissed
So the operator can be dismissed before the next shift
So the site can close early
questions.rationale: Close calls help prevent accidents.

questions.stem: What should you do before using a disc cutter near flammable vegetation?
options: Control the fire risk, for example with a fire watch
Nothing, as sparks go out quickly
Nothing, because sparks go out before they reach the ground
Cut faster to reduce sparks
questions.rationale: Sparks can start lineside fires.

questions.stem: What is a 'hot works permit' for?
options: Working in hot weather
Heating the welfare cabin
Controlling welding, cutting and other fire-risk work
Working outdoors during very hot summer weather
questions.rationale: Hot works need fire controls.

questions.stem: Why should fire extinguishers be checked on site?
options: So they look tidy
So they can be sold
So they work when needed
So they can be used as seats
questions.rationale: Check equipment is ready.

questions.stem: Which type of extinguisher should not be used on live electrical equipment?
options: Carbon dioxide
Dry powder
Water
One rated for electrical fires
questions.rationale: Water conducts electricity.

questions.stem: What is a 'permit to work' generally used for?
options: Allowing staff to start any job early
Proving you have a Sentinel card
Allowing staff to start any job before the briefing
Controlling high-risk work under specific conditions
questions.rationale: Permits ensure controls are in place.

questions.stem: What should you do if lighting on site is too poor to work safely?
options: Carry on carefully
Use phone lights
Stop and get better lighting
Work faster to finish
questions.rationale: You need to see hazards.

questions.stem: Why are designated walkways used in compounds?
options: To make the site look tidy
To save on ballast
To separate people from vehicles
To guide visitors to the café
questions.rationale: Separation prevents vehicle strikes.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to carry rail clips in quantity?
options: Loose in your pockets
Thrown into the four-foot
Loose in your pockets so your hands are free
In a suitable container with help if heavy
questions.rationale: Use proper containers.

questions.stem: Why should you keep a safe distance from someone using a sledgehammer?
options: The noise is too loud
They need room to rest
The hammer or fragments could strike you
They need room to rest between hammer blows
questions.rationale: Keep out of swing areas.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are cold and wet on a long night shift?
options: Keep working until you warm up
Light a small fire beside the line to warm up
Tell the COSS and use welfare facilities
Go home without telling anyone
questions.rationale: Cold affects concentration.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a site induction?
options: To explain site-specific hazards and rules
To introduce staff to each other socially
To hand out pay slips
To sell PPE
questions.rationale: Inductions set expectations.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see an unsecured trench left at the end of a shift?
options: Ignore it, it is not yours
Report it so it can be made safe
Fill it with rubbish
Jump over it
questions.rationale: Open trenches are fall hazards.

questions.stem: Why are drones controlled near the railway?
options: They can hit OLE, trains or distract drivers
They are too noisy
They are expensive
They are too noisy for people living nearby
questions.rationale: Drone use near railways needs permission.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes a 'safety culture'?
options: A set of posters about safety hung in the welfare cabin
Shared attitudes where safety comes first
A department that deals with accident paperwork
A training course taken once at the start of a job
questions.rationale: Culture shows in everyday behaviour.

questions.stem: What is the right attitude to reporting your own mistake?
options: Hide it so you are not blamed by the COSS
Wait to see if anyone else noticed it
Report it so lessons can be learned
Tell only your closest colleague
questions.rationale: Fair culture encourages honest reporting.

questions.stem: What is 'complacency' in safety terms?
options: Being very careful with every task you do
Becoming careless because a task feels routine
Following every rule exactly as written
Asking lots of questions in a briefing
questions.rationale: Familiarity can breed complacency.

questions.stem: How can you guard against complacency on routine jobs?
options: Treat each job as new and check the plan
Skip the briefing to save time
Do the job faster each time
Rely on memory instead of documents
questions.rationale: Conditions change; check every time.

questions.stem: What is 'situational awareness'?
options: Knowing where the café is
Knowing what is happening around you
Knowing the train timetable
Knowing the name of every worker
questions.rationale: Stay aware of trains, plant and hazards.

questions.stem: Which of these reduces situational awareness?
options: Looking around regularly
Listening for warnings
Using a phone while working
Following the briefing
questions.rationale: Distractions are dangerous near the line.

questions.stem: Why should you speak up if a briefing is unclear?
options: It makes the briefing longer
Others may also be confused
It shows you are clever
It annoys the COSS
questions.rationale: Clarity helps everyone.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a 'stop work authority'?
options: Only managers can stop work on site
Work can only be stopped by the client
Anyone can stop work that is unsafe
Work can only stop at the end of a shift
questions.rationale: Everyone has the right to stop unsafe work.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of a 'hazard'?
options: The chance that harm will happen
An accident that has already happened
Something with the potential to cause harm
A safety rule
questions.rationale: Risk is the likelihood and severity of harm from a hazard.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of 'risk'?
options: Any object found on site
A warning sign
The likelihood and severity of harm
A type of PPE worn on high-risk sites
questions.rationale: Risk assessments rate and control risk.

questions.stem: What is the hierarchy of control's first step?
options: Issue PPE
Eliminate the hazard
Write a warning sign
Train the staff
questions.rationale: Removing the hazard is most effective.

questions.stem: In track safety, what is an example of eliminating the hazard of trains?
options: Wearing brighter hi-vis
Blocking the line so no trains run
Using a louder horn
Working faster so you spend less time on the line
questions.rationale: Line blockages and possessions remove the hazard.

questions.stem: What is an example of an engineering control on site?
options: A briefing about the open line
A hi-vis jacket
A fixed barrier between workers and an open line
A warning sign telling people to keep away from the line
questions.rationale: Physical controls are better than relying on behaviour.

questions.stem: What is an example of an administrative control?
options: A physical fence
A safe system of work briefing
A line blockage
A pair of safety boots with toe caps
questions.rationale: Procedures and training are administrative controls.

questions.stem: Why should you keep emergency routes on site clear?
options: So vehicles can park there
So tools can be stored there
So people can escape quickly
So visitors can take photos
questions.rationale: Blocked routes cost time in emergencies.

questions.stem: What should you do with broken glass found on site?
options: Remove it safely with gloves or report it
Kick it into the ballast
Leave it for the cleaners
Throw it onto the line where nobody will step on it
questions.rationale: Prevent cuts.

questions.stem: Why should you avoid carrying too many tools at once?
options: Tools may get scratched
You may trip or be unable to react
It takes longer to unpack
It looks untidy to the public
questions.rationale: Keep yourself able to move quickly.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to deal with a wasp nest found in vegetation on site?
options: Knock it down with a stick
Spray it with diesel
Keep clear and report it
Ignore it
questions.rationale: Stings can cause serious reactions.

questions.stem: Why are allergies relevant to site safety?
options: They affect pay rates
Severe reactions need quick treatment
They change PPE colour
They can stop trains if a worker is taken ill
questions.rationale: Tell colleagues about severe allergies if relevant.

questions.stem: What should you do if a colleague has a severe allergic reaction?
options: Give them an energy drink
Leave them to rest
Drive them to hospital yourself without calling anyone
Call 999 and help use their auto-injector if trained
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is an emergency.

questions.stem: Why is good communication important within a work group?
options: It makes shifts more fun
Everyone needs to know the plan and changes
It reduces paperwork
It is a union rule that groups must talk regularly
questions.rationale: Miscommunication contributes to incidents.

questions.stem: What should you do if you see a near miss but nobody else did?
options: Still report it
Keep quiet
Mention it only if asked
Tell your family
questions.rationale: Every near miss is a lesson.

questions.stem: Why should you not work while angry or upset?
options: Strong emotions can distract you
It makes you work slower
It makes you work more slowly than others
It is against dress code
questions.rationale: Stay focused or speak to your supervisor.

questions.stem: What is the danger of 'normalising' risk?
options: Unsafe acts start to feel acceptable
Rules become easier to remember
Work becomes more interesting
Briefings take longer
questions.rationale: Normalised risk precedes many accidents.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good habit at the start of every shift?
options: Checking social media for news of delays
Skipping the briefing
Starting work straight away
Checking you are fit, equipped and briefed
questions.rationale: Start safe.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good habit at the end of every shift?
options: Leaving tools on site ready for the next shift
Leaving without signing out
Driving home straight away tired
Making sure everyone and everything is clear
questions.rationale: Finish safe.

questions.stem: What is the safest way to deal with an argument on site?
options: Settle it with a fight
Ignore safety until it ends
Step away and involve the COSS
Leave the site
questions.rationale: Arguments distract people.

questions.stem: Why is it important to follow local site rules as well as national rules?
options: Local rules replace national rules
Local rules are optional
National rules do not apply on site
Local rules cover specific site hazards
questions.rationale: Both apply.

questions.stem: What should you do if you do not understand a safety sign?
options: Ask the COSS
Ignore it
Guess
Take it down
questions.rationale: Signs warn of hazards.

questions.stem: Which statement about safety rules is correct?
options: They are designed to slow work down
They only apply to new starters
They were often written after someone was hurt
They change every day depending on the COSS
questions.rationale: Rules carry lessons from real incidents.
